articles.title: Avec le CrushBoss, Ninja réunit trois appareils et des fonctions intelligentes dans un seul robot
articles.text:
Avec le CrushBoss, Ninja sort l'artillerie lourde et propose un véritable robot 3-en-1 (blender, robot culinaire et blender nomade), le tout réuni sur une seule base intelligente.
Le CrushBoss n'est pas le premier robot 3-en-1 de l'écurie Ninja, puisque nous avions notamment testé le Ninja Detect avec ses trois bols (blender, robot et gourde).
Ici, la marque réunit encore une fois les trois appareils sur une base moteur d'une puissance de 1200 W. Celle-ci intègre des fonctionnalités de détection automatique pour adapter l'action des lames selon les aliments, via les modes SmoothSense (pour le blender) et PrepIQ (pour le hachage). En mode manuel, on ne compte pas moins de 10 vitesses de mixage.
Côté tarif, le CrushBoss s'affiche au même prix que le Ninja Detect, soit 250 €.
On a comme une impression de déjà-vu au déballage de l'appareil avec son grand bol blender de près de 2 l (équipé de trois paires de lames), celui du robot culinaire pour hacher les aliments, et la tasse-gourde. Si cette dernière diffère du modèle nomade fourni avec le Detect, elle reprend les traits de celle du BlendBoss, le petit blender coloré de la marque.
Ce qui frappe également lors de “l'unboxing”, c'est la multiplicité des pièces. En plus de la base moteur et des trois récipients (dont la gourde avec son capuchon et sa paille), le carton renferme des lames pour hacher et pétrir, ainsi qu'un disque à trois lames pour râper fin ou épais, tailler en julienne ou réaliser des coupes ondulées.
Une fois monté, l'ensemble s'avère assez imposant avec ses 45 cm de hauteur et 4,4 kg sur la balance, malgré une conception 100 % plastique. Ce gabarit n'incite guère à ranger le CrushBoss dans son carton après chaque utilisation. L'appareil est plutôt pensé pour rester à demeure sur le plan de travail, où il est solidement arrimé à la surface à l'aide de ventouses.
Pesant à lui seul 1,4 kg, le grand bol du blender est coiffé d'un couvercle assez facile à fermer. Il intègre une ouverture faisant office de bec verseur, très pratique pour le service des préparations liquides, avec un design d'ailleurs très similaire (voire identique ?) à celui du Ninja Detect.
Le bol du robot de cuisine bénéficie quant à lui d'un conduit d'alimentation extra-large (13 cm), ce qui permet d'y insérer des légumes entiers sans découpe préalable.
Le blender-gourde, doté de son anse, possède son propre jeu de lames et, comme évoqué plus haut, un couvercle hermétique avec paille intégrée pour se muer en tasse à emporter.
L'ensemble vient se clipser sur la base de 1200 W, capable de détecter automatiquement le bol installé et la nature des ingrédients à mixer.
Après avoir mis l'appareil sous tension et sélectionné la langue (oui, le robot communique en français), l'utilisation se révèle d'une grande simplicité. Point de modes prédéfinis ici : on glisse les ingrédients dans le récipient, on opte pour le mode automatique (idéal pour les novices ou les cuisiniers pressés), on sélectionne SmoothSense pour le blender ou PrepIQ pour le hachage, et l'on laisse la machine opérer. Les utilisateurs préférant garder la main peuvent toutefois basculer en mode manuel, qui donne accès à 10 vitesses de rotation.
Nous avons préparé la recette que nous testons avec tous nos blenders, composée d’une pomme, une banane et un yaourt. Avouons-le, la vue des trois paires de lames du CrushBoss nous a donné envie de le mettre à l'épreuve en conservant la banane et les quartiers de pomme entiers, sans les émincer. À titre de comparaison, lors de notre test du BlendBoss, nous avions coupé ces mêmes quartiers en deux ou trois, ce qui nous avait donné une préparation parfaitement lisse.
Nous avons dès lors lancé le programme automatique. Au bout de 47 s, nous avons obtenu un mélange dans lequel la banane était parfaitement mixée, contrairement à la pomme. Cette dernière s'est retrouvée broyée en de fines tranches dont on sentait la peau sur la langue, en témoignaient les morceaux projetés sur les parois du bol. Bref, un smoothie peu agréable à boire.
Autre ambiance pour le test de la glace pilée, épreuve pour laquelle nous avons confié 300 g de glaçons au CrushBoss. Toujours sur le mode de détection automatique, le blender a lancé un programme de 60 s. La moitié du temps lui a suffi pour réduire les glaçons en une neige très fine, peut-être même un peu trop pour servir un granité, par exemple.
Les lames se retirent assez aisément en tirant sur le haut du bloc, ce dernier n'étant pas fixé au bol. Il suffit alors de les laver (avec précaution, elles sont très tranchantes !) à l'eau claire ou savonneuse.
Les différents bols, eux, passent au lave-vaisselle et peuvent être nettoyés à la main assez simplement.
Il serait trompeur de dire que le Ninja CrushBoss est discret, mais il fait mieux que son grand frère, le Detect, en diffusant 75 dB à 250 W (80 dB pour le Detect) et 77 dB à puissance maximale (82 dB pour le Detect).
Ces mesures le placent dans la moyenne, voire en dessous à puissance maximale, parmi les blenders testés à ce jour par Les Numériques.
Plus qu'un simple blender, le Ninja CrushBoss est un robot de cuisine qui offre trois appareils en un, le tout pour 250 €, incluant notamment son blender nomade BlendBoss très en vogue. S'il peine parfois à réduire certains gros morceaux d'aliments en purée, nul doute qu'après une petite période d'adaptation, le CrushBoss devient un vrai compagnon en cuisine. On regretterait presque qu'il ne cuise pas !
En mode blender, nous pourrions comparer le CrushBoss au Moulinex Perfect Mix Cook, qui affiche une puissance similaire tout en étant plus abordable (190 €) et offrant une fonction chauffante supplémentaire. Toutefois, la polyvalence du CrushBoss et la multiplicité de ses accessoires en font un appareil qu'il est difficile de comparer avec la concurrence directe. L'alternative la plus évidente reste finalement un autre modèle de la marque, le Ninja Detect. Le CrushBoss s'en démarque néanmoins par une ergonomie et un design plus travaillés, à l'image du conduit XL de son robot et l'ajout d'une tasse colorée.

articles.title: 16GB Raspberry Pi 5 hiked to $385, more than triple its launch price — makers are already shifting to Pico/ESP32 for small projects, mini PCs for more ambitious tasks
articles.text:
16GB Raspberry Pi 5 hiked to $385, more than triple its launch price — makers are already shifting to Pico/ESP32 for small projects, mini PCs for more ambitious tasks
The 16GB Raspberry Pi 5 launched at a price of $120 in January 2025.
Raspberry Pi boss Eben Upton has officially announced price rises for some 16GB products. Specifically, the price of the 16GB Raspberry Pi 5 is being raised by $80 to $385, and the 16GB Raspberry Pi Compute Module 5 will go up by $40. In a glimmer of better news, the price of the Raspberry Pi 500+ all-in-one desktop, which also features a 16GB model, is being held, but it was already rather pricey.
| Model | Launch price | Current price | 
| Raspberry Pi 5 16GB | $120 | $385 | 
| Raspberry Pi CM5 16GB | $135 | $425 | 
| Raspberry Pi 500+ 16GB | $199 | $485 | 
Upton framed the decision to raise prices as being due to “the steep rises in the cost of memory over the past two years.” He explained that other computer makers have had to make similar decisions recently. That sounds fair, and he added that Raspberry Pi had been doing what they could to minimize costs passed on to customers.
The price rise of the headline 16GB Raspberry Pi 5 to $385 is effective immediately. As is the $40 increase to the CM5 16GB variant. Of course, both these 16GB devices have seen prior increases in price since being launched at $120 and $135, respectively.
Some moderately good news was that there would be no price increase today for the Raspberry Pi 500+ 16GB all-in-one keyboard wedge computer. Upton didn’t mention that this is already rather expensive at $485, though.
Indeed, there have been several waves of price increases affecting Pis since the components RAMpocalypse began. Only a month ago we saw a similar cost-of-memory post by Upton on the official blog, this time accompanied by news that there were price increases being implemented for the 2GB Raspberry Pi 4 and Raspberry Pi 5 models. Prices of both rose by $12.50, to $67.50 and $77.50, respectively. Perhaps this price gulf between the 2GB and 16GB Pi 5 helps highlight the heavy impact of RAM pricing even more clearly than today’s blog. 1GB devices haven’t seen price rises recently.
The price rises, and comparison in prices between high-and-low memory density models makes it all the more important “to make sure you’re not paying for more memory than you need,” indicates the Raspberry Pi blog about the latest price increases. Sadly for the Pi business, hobbyists and makers already seem to be moving away from the full-sized Pi and CM products for many DIY projects.
The Pi/pricing relationship
Higher pricing is affecting all sorts of computer products, but it might have a particular impact on Raspberry Pi’s business. Generations of this device were explicitly designed around a strict budget constraint, and very famously stuck to a $25–$35 target price for many years.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
Now the core Raspberry Pi business is being squeezed by simpler microcontrollers at the low end, where the use of Picos and ESP32 boards have become increasingly popular for small projects. At the other end of the market, with some Pis approaching $400 or $500, makers start to eye entry-level x86 SBCs and mini PCs. Even a cheap mini PC can be powerful with a stronger CPU, GPU, NPU, and more. Mini PCs can win on flexibility and expandability too, and there’s a wide variety to choose from capable of running the most popular and capable OSes and applications.
Follow Tom's Hardware on Google News, or add us as a preferred source, to get our latest news, analysis, & reviews in your feeds.
Mark Tyson is a news editor at Tom's Hardware. He enjoys covering the full breadth of PC tech; from business and semiconductor design to products approaching the edge of reason.
- King_V Definitely seems to be the case these days. I like the RPi, and have an RPi4 4GB, but it still wasn't quite up to the level of desktop use that I wanted, and I don't really have tasks for it (yet) that are suited to it. The super-tiny form factor is quite impressive, though.
I've got an older Pi3B that I might finally stop being lazy about and turn into a Pi-hole, though.
But, so far, anything that I've wanted for small/light work, I use a 1L mini PC for. Reply

articles.title: VC funding into Indian startups plunge 66% in October
articles.text:
VC funding into Indian startups plunges 66% in October
The steep drop in venture capital funding into Indian startups has been primarily due to near absence of large value deals in the month of October
Venture capital (VC) funding into Indian startups touched a new low in October, with a decline of 66% against October of last year.
When compared with the VC funding raised in September 2025, the drop was 49%.
The total VC funding in October came in at just $581 million as compared with $1.6 billion in October 2025, according to YourStory Research. In the month of September 2026, the funding amount was $1.1 billion.
October saw 107 VC deals. In contrast, the September month saw 100 deals but the amount was higher. The same was the case in October 2025, where the number of deals was 99.
This steep drop in VC funding in October was primarily due to the complete absence of large value deals for the entire period. The highest funded deal for the month was from Even Healthcare at $50 million.
The last such decline was seen in May when the total reached $651 million.
These developments highlight the challenges faced by the startup ecosystem while raising capital. Global investors, particularly in the US, are pouring capital into AI, while India still lacks a significant number of viable AI startups.
Few AI firms in India that have managed to pull funding include Sarvam, Emergent or Neysa. This shows India has a long way to go to establish AI startups that gain investor interest.
Through the first 10 months of 2026, Indian startups raised $10.4 billion, putting the ecosystem on pace to match or surpass the $12 billion total recorded in 2025.
This low funding momentum was also reflected in the stage wise funding category. The late-stage funding category which generally attracts the highest amount saw only $97 million raised for the month of October. The top category was from the growth stage (250 million) followed by the early stage ($221 million).
The dominant trend for the Indian startup ecosystem for the last three years has been the highest volume of activity in terms of number of deals has been in the early-stage funding category but this segment does not draw in large amounts of money.
In terms of the top three segments that raised capital in October, the top categories were D2C, healthtech and automotive. The AI segment just raised $42 million in the month.
The top three cities which received VC funding in October were the usual ones: Bengaluru, Delhi-NCR and Mumbai. By and large, these three metros have consistently garnered an overwhelming majority of funding flowing into Indian startups with an occasional occurrence some other metros like Chennai, Hyderabad or Pune making it to the top three.
Overall, it has not been a positive picture for the Indian startup ecosystem in terms of VC funding so far and the only hope is that the situation will turn out for the better next year.
Edited by Affirunisa Kankudti

articles.title: OpenAI y Anthropic abrieron sus primeras salas de crisis para vigilar los chatbots en las elecciones de Estados Unidos
articles.text:
OpenAI y Anthropic instalaron por primera vez salas de crisis dedicadas a unas elecciones de Estados Unidos. Ambas empresas vigilarán el uso de ChatGPT y Claude para frenar la desinformación y el abuso de sus herramientas durante las legislativas del 3 de noviembre, según informó Semafor el 2 de noviembre.
OpenAI anunció su centro a Politico el 28 de octubre. Se llama Centro de Operaciones Electorales, funciona desde esa semana y seguirá activo hasta que se cuenten todos los votos. Politico informó que reúne a cientos de empleados.
Su tarea principal es combatir el abuso de las propias herramientas de la empresa. El equipo sigue los hechos en tiempo real y atiende reportes de comportamientos inesperados de los modelos o de presuntas violaciones de las reglas de uso.
Josh Lawson, jefe de riesgo cívico y estratégico de OpenAI, está a cargo del centro. Dijo que este se apoya en un trabajo de años y que reúne a los equipos para “responder rápido a problemas emergentes” y aplicar las políticas “mientras la gente va a votar”.
Una sala de crisis nacida en Meta
Semafor recuerda que Meta creó la primera sala de este tipo en 2018, por la preocupación ante la desinformación electoral. Según el medio, la IA agravó esas amenazas: ahora incluyen videos falsos y resultados de búsqueda con IA que difunden datos incorrectos.
Como ejemplo, Semafor citó que la semana anterior el modo de IA de Google no respondió a una consulta sobre quién ganó la elección de 2020. Google dijo que trabajaba en corregirlo.
Un vocero de Anthropic afirmó a Semafor que, antes de la votación, hay una sala dedicada a monitorear la plataforma por usos indebidos, lista para responder a cualquier incidente. La empresa no detalló cuántas personas la integran.
Katie Harbath, exdirectora de política pública de Meta, explicó a Semafor que estas salas se crean para lo que no se puede prever: hace falta un proceso establecido para clasificar rápido los problemas que surjan.
Lo que midió Anthropic sobre el uso político de Claude
En un análisis de 250.000 conversaciones de una semana, publicado el 14 de octubre, Anthropic halló que los temas de política y asuntos públicos son el 5,75% de las conversaciones de Claude.ai en Estados Unidos. Las dedicadas específicamente a elecciones o votación son el 0,51%.
Los pedidos de recomendación de voto aparecieron en cerca del 0,01% de las conversaciones. Las que violaban sus reglas de integridad electoral, en el 0,002%. La empresa prevé que esas proporciones suban al acercarse la votación.
Dos centros de estudio independientes, el Institute for Strategic Dialogue y el McCain Institute, probaron las defensas de Claude. Según Anthropic, el sistema rechazaba un pedido dañino aislado, pero podía no detectar una campaña maliciosa repartida en muchas tareas que parecían inocentes. La compañía agregó clasificadores para esos casos.
Anthropic también informó que bloqueó las cuentas de operadores en el extranjero de un sitio de noticias falso que usó Claude para producir cobertura de las legislativas favorable a narrativas de Rusia, Irán y Corea del Norte. Otros actores buscaban lucrar con noticias fabricadas.
Vota aquí, resultados y límites de las imágenes
OpenAI informó el 20 de octubre que ChatGPT ya muestra datos de registro, plazos y lugares de votación de Democracy Works, una organización sin fines de lucro. También incorpora recuentos en vivo de The Associated Press cuando cierren las urnas. Las imágenes que muestren interferencia electoral se generan en estilo de dibujo, no fotorrealista.
Anthropic dijo que Claude empezará a mostrar información oficial de Democracy Works por estado y los resultados vigentes la noche de la elección y los días siguientes. El centro de OpenAI funcionará hasta que termine el recuento de votos.

articles.title: Enterprise architecture: Dell and Microsoft power AI at scale - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Enterprise architecture: Dell and Microsoft integrate hybrid AI
How can software and cloud giant Microsoft Corp. translate its platform vision into fully deployed enterprise architecture in the age of AI?
This central question has defined the next chapter in a decades-long partnership between Microsoft and Dell Technologies Inc. Dell provided some answers at this year’s Dell Technologies World by expanding its private cloud offering to deploy the latest Microsoft software implementations.
Since that event, Microsoft has worked to enable a disaggregated architecture, simplifying operations across Dell PowerEdge compute, Dell PowerStore storage and Azure Local. Flexibility is the key attraction for enterprise customers evaluating Dell and Microsoft’s joint solutions, according to Paul Nashawaty, principal analyst at theCUBE Research.
“Microsoft and Dell are moving beyond infrastructure partnerships to deliver a more integrated go-to-market strategy for enterprise AI, hybrid cloud and application modernization,” he said. “Since Dell Technologies World in May, the focus has been on connecting Microsoft Azure Local, SQL Server and hybrid-cloud capabilities with Dell’s automation platform and enterprise infrastructure to help customers deploy, govern and operate AI workloads wherever their data resides.”
This feature is part of SiliconANGLE Media’s exploration of the architectural shifts powering continuous, production-grade AI. Be sure to check out theCUBE’s “Dell AI Data Platform Event: From Ambition to AI at Scale,” and past coverage of this year’s Dell Technologies World. (* Disclosure below.)
Integrating enterprise architecture from hardware to workload
The market opportunity for both Dell and Microsoft centers on the need to operationalize AI applications. Meeting this goal requires integration across the full AI deployment lifecycle.
Dell Automation Platform and Dell Private Cloud provide an operational backbone for deploying Azure Local on-premises and managing the hardware lifecycle, including firmware and updates. Azure Arc provides consistent management across environments. SQL Server can be run in virtual machines or Kubernetes containers without learning separate skill sets for cloud and on-premises environments.
“The key architecture for AI capabilities is integrating with things like embedding models for vector searching or chat completion models for AI agents, but we do it all inside … the SQL Server Engine,” Bob Ward, principal architect at Microsoft, told theCUBE. “We [formed a] partnership with Dell so that we can connect to anything on premises. I can connect to Azure Local, Dell [and] Nvidia Factory. We just got a framework built in. It doesn’t matter where you’re running these AI models; we can easily integrate with it.”
A central element of Dell and Microsoft’s partnership involves integrating database, automation and hybrid cloud capabilities into a stack that can feed AI the data it needs. Data fragmentation is often cited as a top blocker to scaling AI beyond pilots, and integrating the two companies’ services addresses a pressure point that surveys have identified across enterprise information technology.
Data fragmentation remains a barrier to scaling AI beyond pilots. Dell and Microsoft’s partnership brings database, automation and hybrid cloud capabilities into a common stack.
“From an AppDev perspective, that integration matters because the challenge is no longer simply building AI applications, but operationalizing them securely, consistently and at scale,” said Nashawaty. “TheCUBE AppDev Research highlights the execution gap: Approximately 88% of AI pilots fail to reach production, while 64% of enterprise AI teams identify integration complexity as a leading barrier to adoption.”
Delivering AI for real-world outcomes
Dell’s partnership with Microsoft also extends to unstructured data storage. The two companies are bringing familiar storage capabilities into hybrid and multicloud environments.
Dell PowerScale for Microsoft Azure brings Dell’s OneFS file system software into Azure as a managed storage service. Customers can provision file storage directly from the Azure portal while retaining familiar PowerScale management capabilities.
The solution supports a wide range of production workloads across industries. These industries increasingly depend on high-throughput, low-latency file access to drive the next generation of agentic AI and advanced analytics. Media and entertainment firms can use it to handle massive video files, real-time editing and tight production timelines. Semiconductor and electronics design houses can accelerate simulation and modeling using large datasets.
“This isn’t really about running the software just in the cloud,” said Rachna Lalwani, senior consultant, director and product manager at Dell, in an interview with theCUBE. “It’s about creating a truly integrated experience that empowers businesses to do more with their data. What they really gain is the operational consistency across their entire storage landscape.”
Integrating agents with PCs
A recent IDC analysis found that 95% of enterprises already run at least one AI agent workflow in production, and it predicted 2.5 billion agents by 2030. With the rise of agentic AI, Dell and Microsoft are collaborating on solutions designed to help enterprises deploy autonomous agents while controlling costs.
Managing the cost of tokens, the fundamental units of data processed by large language models, is one of AI’s financial challenges. To help address it, Dell introduced Deskside Agentic AI in May in collaboration with Microsoft and Nvidia Corp., providing a local environment for building and testing AI agents.
“What’s resonating with customers right now is that the cost of tokens is through the roof,” explained Jon Siegal, senior vice president of Dell portfolio marketing at Dell. “We know even though the cost of a token has come down pretty dramatically, the amount of tokens that are being consumed right now is just astronomical. The cloud costs are just pretty high right now. How do customers balance that out and run the right workload in the right place? We’re trying to give customers a place to start. The PC is a great place to start.”
In early October, Dell announced an expansion of its Windows PCs and workstations for agentic AI. In partnership with Microsoft, Dell broadened its AI development portfolio to provide creators, developers and enterprises with more choice in how they build, test and scale agentic AI on Windows.
This marked a key step in the evolution of Windows, where the platform has evolved into a broader resource for agentic AI. Tools such as Windows AI Foundry give developers a structured path to build, package and scale agents inside a governed environment.
“With Windows, we’re going beyond just it being an operating system — we’re thinking about it as really a canvas for AI,” said Mary Ann Anderson, worldwide marketing director of Dell partnerships at Microsoft. “Pretty soon there’s going to be a point where individual employees are managing their own agents, maybe a small army of agents. You have to do that in a way that is governed and is very secure.”
Dell and Microsoft see a significant market opportunity in closing the gap between AI development and production deployment.
“Microsoft and Dell have an opportunity to address that gap by simplifying deployment, automating infrastructure operations and giving partners repeatable solutions they can take to market,” said theCUBE Research’s Nashawaty. “The real measure of success will be whether their combined ecosystem helps enterprises move from AI experimentation to production-ready applications with stronger governance, predictable costs and measurable business outcomes.”
(* Disclosure: TheCUBE is a paid media partner for the Dell AI Data Platform Event. Neither Dell, the sponsor of theCUBE’s event coverage, nor other sponsors have editorial control over content on theCUBE or SiliconANGLE.)

articles.title: Melhor TV com Roku OS: 6 modelos para comprar em 2026 • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Melhor TV com Roku OS: 6 modelos para comprar em 2026
Televisores com Roku TV são opções com foco em custo-benefício; conheça prós e contras de modelos da AOC, Philco, Semp, Multilaser e Britânia
TVs com Roku OS são voltadas para streaming e oferecem navegação simplificada. O sistema é uma ótima opção para quem não tem tanta familiaridade com tecnologia ou interfaces avançadas de smart TVs.
Mas não basta olhar apenas para o sistema operacional: você também deve adequar o tamanho de tela ao espaço disponível e analisar se o televisor oferece uma boa experiência de imagem, incluindo resoluções 4K e suporte a conteúdos HDR.
Para te ajudar na escolha, o Tecnoblog lista seis opções de TVs com Roku OS. Confira prós e contras de televisores da AOC, Philco, Britânia, Multi e Semp.
A AOC U7066 é uma smart TV 4K sem recursos avançados de otimização de imagem. Equipada com Roku TV, ela está disponível em versões de 50″ ou 55″ e apresenta painel VA, conhecido pelas taxas de contrastes mais altas, com taxa de atualização limitada a 60 Hz.
A taxa de atualização é de 60 Hz, o que limita seu uso para jogos. Mas há suporte ao HDR10+ para melhorias de brilho e profundidade de cor em conteúdos HDR.
A TV da AOC é compatível com Google Assistente e Alexa, tem suporte a Wi-Fi 5 e traz as seguintes conexões: 4 entradas HDMI (sendo uma compatível com eARC), 1 entrada USB 2.0 e 1 Porta Ethernet / RJ45 (rede com fio). Vale ressaltar que o aparelho não tem Bluetooth integrado para conexões sem fio.
A Philco P50VIK é ideal para quem quer uma TV 4K pagando pouco. Afinal, o televisor de 50″ combina o painel LCD com retroiluminação DLED: uma solução mais acessível, mas sem o controle de iluminação superior dos miniLEDs.
Devido ao suporte ao HDR10+, a smart TV consegue aproveitar as melhorias de contraste, brilho e precisão de cores de conteúdos HDR. Esse formato está presente em conteúdos de plataformas como Netflix, Amazon Prime Video e Disney+, que são compatíveis com o sistema Roku OS do dispositivo.
Já o sistema Dolby Audio otimiza clareza e nitidez do som para uma experiência sonora mais completa. Por falar nisso, você pode conectar soundbars e home theater somente via USB ou HDMI nativamente, já que não há Bluetooth embutido.
A Britânia BTV50VA4REGB é outra opção de smart TV 50″ com Roku OS e boa relação custo-benefício. O principal destaque do aparelho está na resolução 4K UHD, que se tornou um padrão em TVs atuais por exibir contornos e detalhes de imagem com mais nitidez.
A TV é compatível com conteúdos HDR e ainda traz uma função que eleva a qualidade de imagens SDR para níveis próximos ao padrão HDR. Contudo, não há recursos voltados para melhoria de contraste, brilho ou cor.
As opções de conectividade incluem Wi-Fi de banda dupla, três portas HDMI e duas portas USB. Não há suporte nativo para Bluetooth.
A Multi DLED TL059M é uma TV de entrada com foco em praticidade de uso, devido à leveza e intuitividade do sistema Roku OS. A tela tem 50 polegadas, sendo uma boa opção para sala de estar. E ainda traz resolução 4K para elevar a experiência de streaming.
O aparelho tem suporte ao HDR10+ para exibir conteúdos compatíveis com maior fidelidade de cor e contraste, e chega com sistema de som Dolby Audio que otimiza a nitidez dos diálogos.
Não há Bluetooth integrado, mas o televisor tem quatro entradas HDMI para conexões com consoles de videogame, home theater, soundbar, entre outros aparelhos.
A Semp S42R é uma smart TV básica voltada para streaming. Há opções de 32″, 43″ e 50″, mas todos os modelos são limitados à resolução Full HD (1920 x 1080 pixels). Na prática, as imagens vão exibir menos detalhes e contornos, já que há quatro vezes menos pixels em comparação com TVs 4K.
O sistema Dolby Audio traz equilíbro para o sistema sonoro e ajuda a deixar os áudios mais nítidos. Porém, o dispositivo não oferece suporte a conteúdos HDR e nem conta com recursos de otimização de imagem.
Ao menos, o sistema Roku OS é bem intuitivo e facilita a navegação e uso dos apps de streaming, sendo uma boa opção de smart TV para quem não tem tanta familiaridade com sistemas complexos.
A AOC S5155/78G é uma smart TV de preço acessível, com tela de 32″ ou 43″. O modelo de 32″ é limitado à resolução HD (1280 × 720 pixels) e taxa de brilho de 200 nits. Já a versão com 43″ tem resolução Full HD e nível de brilho superior, de 230 nits.
Ambos as variantes são equipadas com o sistema Roku OS e trazem sistema de som Dolby Audio para diálogos mais nítidos. Contudo, não há suporte para conteúdos HDR e os modelos não possuem Bluetooth integrado.
A escolha pela melhor TV com Roku OS deve levar em conta as especificações de tela, conectividade e recursos de otimização. Vale analisar aspectos como:
A Multi DLED TL059M é a melhor TV 4K custo-benefício com Roku OS da lista. O televisor tem tela grande de 50″ e traz suporte ao HDR10+ para aproveitar as melhorias de contraste, brilho e cor de conteúdos HDR. Fora isso, o sistema Dolby Audio otimiza a clareza dos sons.
O sistema operacional Roku OS está presente em TVs da AOC, Britânia, Multi, Philco, Semp e TCL, em modelos de 24″ a 65″.
Depende das preferências de uso. O Roku OS (ou Roku TV) é mais leve e exige menos poder de fogo do televisor. O sistema operacional também é intuitivo e atende a diferentes tipos de público, com listagem simples dos apps de streaming.
Já o Google TV (baseado no Android TV) é um sistema mais complexo e pesado que o Roku TV, com navegação baseada em rolagens horizontais e verticais. O sistema é conhecido pelas recomendações personalizadas de conteúdo e atende usuários que gostam de uma ajudinha na hora de escolher um filme ou série.

articles.title: Avant le Black Friday, le Galaxy A16 5G noté 7/10 par la rédaction est à 138€
articles.text:
Plus d’un an après l’arrivée du Galaxy A17, le Galaxy A16 5G garde l’argument qui l’avait distingué dans notre test : six ans de mises à jour majeures d’Android promises par Samsung. Il passe à 138 € chez Cdiscount avec un code promo, à condition d’accepter des performances très modestes.
Lancé à 249 €, le Samsung Galaxy A16 5G occupe le bas de la gamme Galaxy A avec un écran Super AMOLED de 6,7 pouces, 128 Go de stockage et une batterie de 5 000 mAh. Avec le code 10DES99, Cdiscount affiche ce modèle Bleu nuit à 138 € au lieu de 148 €, une remise réservée aux paniers d’au moins 99 €, que le smartphone atteint à lui seul. Il s’agit d’une version internationale.
L’offre vise ceux qui veulent un smartphone 5G simple et suivi longtemps. Les joueurs et les adeptes du multitâche ont intérêt à regarder ailleurs.
Le Samsung Galaxy A16 5G 128 Go est à 138 € au lieu de 148 € chez Cdiscount avec le code 10DES99, valable dès 99 € d’achat.
Pourquoi choisir le Samsung Galaxy A16 5G ?
- Un suivi logiciel au long cours : Samsung promet six ans de mises à jour majeures d’Android, un record à ce niveau de prix lors de notre test.
- Un écran bien calibré : La dalle Super AMOLED Full HD+ de 6,7 pouces affiche 90 Hz et avoisine 1 000 nits. Notre test a relevé une colorimétrie excellente, agréable pour les vidéos.
- Un format pratique au quotidien : Le stockage de 128 Go s’étend par carte microSD, la prise jack 3,5 mm et le NFC sont présents, et la certification IP54 protège des éclaboussures.
Messages, vidéos et photos de jour : ce qu’on peut lui demander
Le Galaxy A16 5G se prête aux usages simples : messagerie, réseaux sociaux, navigation et vidéos. Sa batterie de 5 000 mAh a tenu 11 h 29 au test d’autonomie PCMark, de quoi passer une journée sans chercher de prise. En photo, le capteur principal de 50 Mpx livre des clichés détaillés en plein jour, et la caméra selfie de 13 Mpx nous a surpris par son piqué. La recharge plafonne en revanche à 25 W, soit environ 1 h 30 pour un plein, et aucun chargeur n’est fourni.
Ce modèle convient à un premier smartphone, à un téléphone de secours ou à qui veut un Samsung sans fioritures. Comme le relève notre test du Samsung Galaxy A16 5G, l’Exynos 1330 et ses 4 Go de mémoire vive entraînent des ralentissements, et les applications se rechargent souvent quand on passe de l’une à l’autre. Genshin Impact peine, même au minimum. Sans stabilisation optique, les photos de nuit et les vidéos restent médiocres, et l’ultra grand-angle de 5 Mpx fait de la figuration.
Face au Galaxy A17 et aux autres smartphones à moins de 300 €
Son successeur, le Galaxy A17 5G lancé à 229 €, reprend le même Exynos 1330 et 4 Go de mémoire vive, mais ajoute une stabilisation optique sur le capteur principal et un verre Gorilla Glass Victus sur l’écran. Le A16 n’a pas cette protection : sa dalle n’est couverte que d’une fine couche de plastique Dans notre comparatif des meilleurs smartphones à moins de 300 €, il tient le rôle du choix durable, quand le Xiaomi Redmi Note 14 mise sur l’autonomie et le POCO X7 sur la puissance en jeu. Le A16 se distingue par la durée de son suivi, pas par sa vitesse.
✅ Les points forts
- Six ans de mises à jour majeures d’Android promises
- Écran AMOLED de 6,7 pouces lumineux et bien calibré
- Stockage extensible par microSD et prise jack conservée
- Selfies nets et photos correctes de jour au grand-angle
- Une journée d’autonomie, 11 h 29 sous PCMark
❌ Les limites
- Performances très modestes avec 4 Go de mémoire vive
- Pas de stabilisation optique : photos de nuit et vidéo décevantes
- Pas de Galaxy AI, Wi-Fi 5 seulement
- Remise de 10 € par code, chargeur non fourni
Le code 10DES99 ramène le Galaxy A16 5G Bleu nuit à 138 € chez Cdiscount : vérifiez qu’il s’applique bien au panier avant de valider.
À 138 €, le Samsung Galaxy A16 5G coûte 111 € de moins que son prix de lancement, pour un smartphone que nous avions noté 7/10. Son intérêt tient à un écran agréable, une journée d’autonomie et six ans de mises à jour promis. La remise du jour reste modeste, 10 € obtenus par code, et la mention de version internationale justifie un coup d’œil aux conditions de vente.
Si vous cherchez un téléphone pour appeler, échanger des messages et regarder des vidéos pendant plusieurs années, l’équation tient. Si vous jouez, gardez de nombreuses applications ouvertes ou tenez à la photo de soirée, la mémoire vive et l’absence de stabilisation vous rattraperont vite. Mieux vaut alors viser un modèle plus puissant, quitte à dépasser ce budget. Le Galaxy A16 5G reste un téléphone pensé pour durer, pas pour aller vite.

articles.title: Un militar australiano subió a la gran fragata española y se quedó a cuadros: era un calco del diseño de su propio destructor
articles.text:
Que un militar australiano suba a una fragata española durante unas maniobras internacionales no es noticia. Que cuando lo haga se encuentre con un diseño calcado a su propio buque de guerra, ya es otra cosa. El oficial del destructor HMAS Sydney descubrió que la estructura de la fragata Álvaro de Bazán era prácticamente idéntica a la del barco en el que servía. La explicación de aquel parecido se encontraba a miles de kilómetros.
El descubrimiento. El teniente Nicholas Newton, oficial de guerra de superficie del HMAS Sydney, embarcó en la fragata española Álvaro de Bazán durante el ejercicio multinacional Pacific Dragon, centrado en la defensa aérea y antimisiles. Su misión consistía en trabajar como oficial de operaciones dentro del equipo de mando estadounidense desplegado en el buque español.
Allí descubrió hasta qué punto conocía la arquitectura de aquella fragata: según explicó a Navy News, la publicación oficial de la Armada australiana, era exactamente el mismo barco que el Sydney, cuaderna por cuaderna. La semejanza resultaba especialmente llamativa porque Australia clasifica su buque como destructor y España denomina fragata al Álvaro de Bazán.
¿Qué demonios estaba ocurriendo?
El origen estaba en España. La explicación se encuentra en las fragatas españolas F-100, una familia de buques diseñada y construida por Navantia en Ferrol, cuya primera unidad fue precisamente la Álvaro de Bazán. Australia eligió esa arquitectura como base para desarrollar sus tres destructores de la clase Hobart: HMAS Hobart, HMAS Brisbane y HMAS Sydney.
Navantia participó en el diseño y proporcionó apoyo técnico, mientras que la construcción se realizó en Australia mediante un programa industrial en el que intervinieron ASC, Raytheon y el Gobierno australiano. El Sydney, tercera y última unidad de la serie, entró en servicio el 18 de mayo de 2020. Dicho de otra forma, la experiencia de Newton puso de manifiesto hasta qué punto la ingeniería naval española había influido en la renovación de la flota australiana.
Dos barcos casi idénticos, dos marinas diferentes. Aquí viene la segunda parte que explica el entuerto. El parentesco estructural no implica que ambas clases tengan exactamente los mismos equipos, capacidades o configuraciones, ya que Australia adaptó el diseño español a sus propios requisitos operativos. Los destructores Hobart incorporan el sistema de combate Aegis, que integra la información de los radares con sus armas para detectar y combatir amenazas aéreas, una tecnología que también utilizan las fragatas españolas F-100.
El Sydney dispone además de misiles antibuque, torpedos, sonares, artillería naval y capacidad para operar con helicópteros. Newton encontró diferencias especialmente llamativas en la organización cotidiana de la tripulación española, cuyos horarios y procedimientos eran distintos de los australianos. También destacó el ambiente a bordo, las barbacoas en la cubierta de vuelo, la música y la hospitalidad de los marineros españoles.
Siete barcos y un huracán acercándose. Curiosamente, la estancia del australiano en la fragata española terminó convirtiéndose en una prueba de coordinación internacional. Una vez completados los principales ejercicios de defensa antimisiles de Pacific Dragon, los buques participantes debían abandonar la zona ante la llegada de un huracán con vientos de hasta 121 kilómetros por hora.
Había un problema: siete barcos necesitaban repostar combustible antes de poder alejarse con seguridad. Newton participó en la coordinación de los movimientos y del abastecimiento desde la Álvaro de Bazán, mientras el buque logístico estadounidense USNS Washington Chambers suministraba combustible a las unidades. La operación permitió que los siete barcos se dirigieran hacia zonas seguras antes de la llegada de la tormenta.
El valor de un diseño que cruzó medio mundo. Si se quiere también, la experiencia de Newton refleja el alcance internacional de un programa naval desarrollado originalmente para la Armada española. Las F-100 proporcionaron a Australia una plataforma sobre la que construir sus destructores de defensa aérea, adaptando un diseño ya existente a sus necesidades militares e industriales.
Durante Pacific Dragon, ese parentesco permitió al oficial australiano reconocer inmediatamente la estructura de un barco extranjero, al tiempo que descubría al mundo las diferencias entre las dos marinas. La anécdota resume, además, una realidad poco conocida de la industria militar española: que uno de los pilares de la defensa naval australiana tiene su origen a miles de kilómetros, en los mismísimos astilleros de Ferrol.

articles.title: VCs bet $30M on Larridin's ability to help enterprises demonstrate AI's value for money - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
VCs bet $30M on Larridin’s ability to help enterprises demonstrate AI’s value for money
As enterprises jack up their spending on artificial intelligence tools, it’s only right for senior executives to want to know exactly what they’re getting in return for their costly investments. Larridin Inc., a startup focused on AI adoption measurement, has just raised $30 million in early-stage funding to try to provide them with the answers.
Today’s Series A round was led by Pelion Ventures and saw participation from existing backers Andreessen Horowitz and Gradient Ventures, as well as new investors like GFT, W23, Thayer, DG Daiwa Ventures, Cougar Capital and Alumni Ventures. The round brings the company’s total amount raised so far to $47 million.
Larridin’s funding comes at a time when enterprise leaders are facing growing pressure to demonstrate the value they’re getting for their spiralling token consumption costs and application programming interface bills. Shareholders of publicly traded companies, especially, are eager to see those investments are driving real growth, and aren’t easily swayed by vanity metrics showcasing adoption without value.
Co-founder and Chief Executive Russ Fradin says this pressure stems from the flawed way in which most organizations evaluate their AI investments. He argues that traditional adoption metrics such as seat licenses and login counts do not reflect the true operational impact of AI.
Indeed, one of Larridin’s own customers is a case in point. That organization’s own surveys showed that 92% of its engineers were active AI users, which seems like a good rate of adoption. But when it started using Larridin’s tools to dig deeper, it found that a single engineer accounted for 65% of the company’s entire AI budget.
These aren’t the only kinds of blind spots AI has created. In Larridin’s newly released Engineering AI Impact Report, based on a survey of more than 1,000 developers, it found that though AI-assisted pull requests increased from 35% in April to 62% in September, it didn’t provide much value for enterprises because it simply created bottlenecks further downstream. For instance, organization’s median code review wait times increased more than 50% over the same timeframe.
Fradin says this is why companies cannot just monitor AI output volume. What’s needed is a complete picture that also covers the cost and quality of AI outputs, and the friction it creates.
Larridin’s goal is to give companies more visibility into their AI technology with what it says is the industry’s first AI value measurement platform. It links data on AI tool adoption with employee productivity metrics and expenditure data, and also looks at the value generated by, and the cost of autonomous AI agents that do work on behalf of humans.
By tracking complete workflows, Larridin can help companies to identify where and how AI is actually driving value and where spend is being wasted. It can also highlight new processes that are ripe for agentic automation.
Such insights can be extremely compelling. In one case, Larridin identified a 66-fold cost discrepancy per shipped code change between two competing AI coding tools that were being used by different employees for similar tasks. The customer was able to cancel its subscription for the much more expensive tool without any impact on productivity.
“Companies must be able to prove tangible business value from skyrocketing AI spend,” Fradin said. “Our investors share that conviction, and our Series A reflects the belief in our technology and its ability to solve this critical challenge.”
Larridin’s customer base includes enterprises such as SurveyMonkey Inc., Vertiv Holdings Co., Kalviyo Inc. and Gainsight Inc., and it’s planning to build on this traction by expanding its go-to-market and engineering teams.
Pelion Ventures’ Jeff Kearl said he’s backing Larridin because it fills a vital gap in enterprise analytics by tying every dollar spent on AI directly to measurable business outcomes. “As AI adoption scales, Larridin empowers executive teams with the intelligence to maximize their return on investment and build a clear path to long-term value creation,” he said.

articles.title: 'America hates data centers,' new database reveals more than 90% of 10,000 public comments are negative, only 21% mention AI — 73% of meetings had no data center supporters, water is the number one concern
articles.text:
'America hates data centers,' new database reveals more than 90% of 10,000 public comments are negative, only 21% mention AI — 73% of meetings had no data center supporters, water is the number one concern
A new website seeks to distill over 10,000 public comments across more than 410 local governments, and it's bad news for data center builders.
As more and more AI data centers are being built across the United States, the backlash is starting to gather pace. Following the recent news that Amazon canceled plans to build four new facilities after a public outcry, a new website seeks to detail how sour public sentiment on the subject has turned. American Sentiment is operated by Prophecy Gov, an AI startup based in San Francisco, and it has turned 10,202 public comments at 417 local government meetings from 2026 into a scrollable collection of facts and figures that will give data center builders nightmares, revealing that more than 90% of public comments on data centers are negative.
The website notes that, while public comments don't always match the country's true sentiment, it's clear that the discussion around data center buildouts has reached a "fever pitch" of late. That's something borne out by the data, which takes in 48 states and 417 local governments, with 906 public meetings tracked. Of the 10,202 comments, 90.5% were negative, with just 7% saying positive things about the potential for a new data center being built in their backyard. The remaining 2.5% simply asked questions about the subject. A staggering 73% of meetings had no data center supporters whatsoever. Even those who did support the prospect of a data center being built found themselves outnumbered 6:1, according to the stats.
Predictably, a range of concerns were raised in opposition to data centers, with water use being the most common. In May this year, it was reported that a single AI data center project had consumed 29 million gallons of water. It used so much water, in fact, that local residents noticed a drop in water pressure as a result. A month later, Microsoft claimed its new AI data centers use as little water annually as a restaurant. Beyond water consumption, the impact on local quality of life and the lack of transparency around the project made up the top three complaints. These concerns aren't offset by the benefits of building such facilities, with many people saying that they didn't believe that the claimed benefits would ever come to fruition. Perhaps surprisingly, AI and its potential negative effects weren't mentioned in 4/5 of the comments. Just 21% made any mention of AI as a whole.
Members of the public called out some of AI's biggest players when arguing against data centers, including Google, Amazon, Meta, and Microsoft. Concerns also turned personal, with SpaceX/xAI CEO Elon Musk by far the most mentioned during meetings, followed by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman. Notably, Palantir's Peter Thiel was third, ahead of Meta's Mark Zuckerberg and Jeff Bezos when discussing Amazon.
At a time when the United States may seem more divided than ever, the lack of desire for local data centers appears to be a thoroughly bipartisan issue. Red and blue counties oppose the prospect at almost exactly the same rate, although rural counties raised different issues than urban and suburban ones. The former most commonly worried about the impact on a community's character, farmland, and property rights. Commenters in urban and suburban areas raised the issues of transparency, government distrust, air pollution, and utility bills more often. Pollution is one issue that has been raised previously — a report earlier this month warned that U.S. data centers could wipe out 15 years of progress in greenhouse gas emissions.
There was one group of people largely in favor of new data centers, however. 79% of commenters who said they were union workers were in favor of data centers. Conversely, just 3% of property owners and 3% of residents agreed. Even just 40% of data center workers were in favor of actual data centers, according to the figures.

articles.title: Work crews remove 120 defunct Flock cameras in US county after company fails to fulfil ‘contractual obligations’
articles.text:
Work crews remove 120 defunct Flock cameras in US county after company fails to fulfil ‘contractual obligations’
Flock is reportedly refusing to acknowledge canceled contracts
- Henrico County in Virginia was forced to remove Flock cameras by hand
- Officials say the company is failing to fulfil its “contractual obligation”
- A growing number of police forces are cancelling contracts with Flock
Work crews in a Virginia county have removed more than 120 Flock cameras after officials said the surveillance tech company had failed to fulfil its “contractual obligation” to remove them.
An image obtained by news outlet 12 On Your Side shows a pile of cameras and solar panels that were collected after Henrico County ended its contract with Flock in early October over privacy concerns.
Reportedly, the poles upon which the cameras were mounted still remain, as crews claimed Flock has to remove these itself.
The removal of the automatic license plate reading technology comes as public trust wanes, and concerns over privacy continue to grow.
Plymouth, Massachusetts also canceled its contract with Flock cameras after a high-profile case involving a motoring journalist made national headlines.
Joel Feder, a writer for The Drive, was ambushed by police when the license plate of the $155,000 Range Rover he was test-driving was flagged as belong to a stolen vehicle.
The car belonged to Jaguar Land Rover's media fleet. According to Feder, the police had used Flock’s camera system to track the journalist down over a number of days.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
A very similar license plate on another Jaguar Land Rover media vehicle was also falsely flagged by the Flock system in Nebraska a few days later, leading to another journalist facing lengthy questioning over the vehicle.
Plymouth Police Chief Eric Fadden told The Drive that the City Council voted to discontinue using the Flock system in September of this year.
Fadden stated that the police force “did not hear any reply from Flock Safety Corporate or Legal, other than some communication with our local representative.”
As a result of the lack of communication, he subsequently directed staff to “disconnect the power cords from the cameras,” according to The Drive.
However, the cameras remain the property of Flock, and both Henrico County and Plymouth are still waiting for a response from the company as to when they will be collected.
Analysis: controversy refuses to go away
Flock’s automated license plate recognition cameras have caused plenty of controversy in the past few months, with stories surfacing of police department misuse, hackers gaining access to millions of images, and general concern over personal privacy.
Some people have been taking matters into their own hands by disabling cameras, while a number of software companies have been mapping the location of the cameras to help drivers avoid them.
MapQuest enjoyed a resurgence in popularity after it added a new Surveillance Layer to its app, showing the location of cameras from Flock, as well as those from rival companies.
But during the TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 event last month, Flock’s CEO Garrett Langley said we shouldn’t "pause progress” in the face of privacy concerns. “If we want to live in a society where, if you commit a crime, you have a higher probability of being held accountable, we shouldn’t pause progress,” he said.
Many privacy advocate groups have raised concerns over Flock’s technology, including the recent news that it was capable of processing ambient audio in order to determine screams, gunshots and even car crashes before alerting emergency services.
Flock pulled its plans to implement that particular feature, owing to suggestions from consumer rights groups that it could be classed as "mass surveillance", but a huge amount of public mistrust remains.

articles.title: PowerUp Money raises $10M to expand AI-led wealth management
articles.text:
PowerUp Money raises $10M to expand AI-led wealth management
The Bengaluru-based company plans to use a significant portion of the capital to develop its AI-powered wealth management platform and expand its managed advisory business.
PowerUp Money, a wealthtech platform offering mutual fund advice and digital wealth management services, has raised $10 million in a funding round led by Flourish Ventures, an early-stage investment firm.
Existing investors Peak XV Partners, Accel, Blume Ventures, Kae Capital, 8i Ventures and DeVC also participated.
The Bengaluru-based company plans to use a significant portion of the capital to develop its AI-powered wealth management platform and expand its managed advisory business.
PowerUp claims more than 1.5 million users track mutual fund portfolios worth over Rs 2.5 lakh crore on its platform. Its paid subscription service, Elite, provides research-backed mutual fund advice and is said to have crossed 1,00,000 paid members in less than a year.
The company has now introduced Elite Prime, an AI-enabled digital wealth advisory service designed to provide a more comprehensive financial planning experience. It assesses investors’ financial goals, risk appetite and existing holdings to suggest asset allocation, systematic investment plans (SIPs), lump-sum investments, portfolio rebalancing and withdrawal strategies. It can also identify gaps in portfolios and suggest diversification into assets such as gold, silver and international investments.
An AI wealth coach and personal assistant are intended to help users understand recommendations and make informed decisions.
Founder and chief executive officer Prateek Jindal said, “AI makes it possible to deliver a much more comprehensive, wealth-manager-like experience digitally”, bringing personalised guidance within reach of investors who may not be able to afford traditional wealth management services.
PowerUp is also looking to expand Infinite, its managed wealth advisory offering. The service combines financial planning, portfolio construction, multi-asset allocation and ongoing portfolio management with dedicated human advisers.
According to the company, Infinite has accumulated nearly Rs 500 crore in assets under management (AUM) within around nine months of launch, despite being available to a limited customer base. Making the service accessible to more investors is another priority for the new funding.
The expansion comes amid sustained growth in India’s mutual fund market. According to the Association of Mutual Funds in India (AMFI), industry AUM stood at Rs 82.64 lakh crore at the end of September 2026, up from Rs 15.8 lakh crore a decade earlier. Monthly SIP contributions also reached Rs 32,490 crore in September, reflecting the growing adoption of regular, long-term investing.
Investor interest has encouraged further funding across the wealthtech sector. Debt investment platform Wint Wealth raised Rs 250 crore in a Series B round in January, while wealth management firm Centricity secured Rs 280 crore in August. AI-focused advisory startup Novelty Wealth also announced a $1.4 million seed round in March.
However, growth brings its own challenges. Digital advice must remain suitable, transparent and compliant as platforms expand their customer base. SEBI issued an updated Master Circular for Investment Advisers in February, reinforcing the regulatory framework governing investment advice.
The opportunity, as Flourish Ventures’ Asia head Ravi Kaushik noted, lies in helping investors manage increasingly complex financial lives.

articles.title: Voitures électriques : ce tournant historique que personne n'a vu venir en Europe
articles.text:
Le temps où les voitures électriques étaient uniquement achetées par des farfelus prêts à prendre des risques pour marquer leur différence est bel et bien révolu. Les véhicules à batterie comptent aujourd’hui de plus en plus dans le mix des ventes au niveau mondial. Le constat est encore plus édifiant en Europe, où ces modèles ont dépassé pour la toute première fois les voitures essence et diesel combinées. Est-ce un tournant appelé à se poursuivre ?
Possible, vu le contexte géopolitique toujours assez tendu et très loin d’être stabilisé. L’association Transport & Environment révèle en tout cas que 492 930 voitures essence et 162 610 voitures diesel ont été vendues en Europe au troisième trimestre. Cela représente au total 655 540 véhicules purement thermiques. En parallèle, il s’est écoulé 710 580 modèles 100 % électriques sur la même période. Un record.
Ces 10 pays européens où l’électrique a pris le pouvoir
Nul besoin de faire des calculs alambiqués : les voitures à batteries ont surpassé les essences et les diesels combinés. Et cette performance impressionnante n’est pas le fruit de quelques pays éclaireurs en la matière. 13 des 27 membres de l’Union Européenne ont en effet enregistré les plus importantes ventes de modèles électriques de leur histoire. 10 pays ont même vu les électriques passer sans peine en tête de leurs immatriculations.
La Norvège reste le leader absolu, avec 97,9 % de part de marché pour les véhicules électriques. Le Danemark et la Suède suivent cette dynamique avec respectivement 81,7 % et 42,9 % de modèles à batterie pointant en tête des ventes. La France est logiquement derrière, avec 31,4 % de voitures électriques dans les ventes, ce qui les place en seconde position après les hybrides non rechargeables comptant pour 43,3 % des immatriculations.
+244 % de ventes : l’incroyable rattrapage qui s’amorce à l’Est
La situation est similaire en Allemagne, où les électriques arrivent deuxième avec 27,2 % des ventes, juste derrière les 28,5 % d’hybrides. Les modèles à batterie parviennent aussi à dépasser les 25 % de part de marché en Belgique, au Royaume-Uni, au Portugal et en Irlande. La Croatie et la Pologne sont à l’inverse à la traîne, avec respectivement 4,2 % et 5,2 % de véhicules électriques comptant dans les ventes.
Si les électriques dévissent légèrement en Pologne, le cas croate est plus intéressant, car les modèles à batterie ont augmenté de 244,6 % depuis 2025. Si cette dynamique se poursuit, la Croatie se mettra bientôt au niveau du reste de l’Union Européenne. Ce devrait être le cas, car l’offre de véhicules électriques à bas prix est amenée à augmenter dans les prochaines années. On pense notamment à la Citroën 2CV et à la Fiat Koala qui arriveront en 2028.

articles.title: Melhor TV custo-benefício em 2026: 10 modelos para comprar • Tecnoblog

Melhor TV custo-benefício em 2026: 10 modelos para comprar
Encontre a smart TV com melhor custo-benefício para sua sala, quarto ou escritório; lista inclui modelos 4K, MiniLED e QLED com preço em torno de R$ 2.500
Escolher uma TV com bom custo-benefício em 2026 exige atenção aos detalhes que realmente importam. Tecnologias como QLED e MiniLED, taxas de atualização para jogos e sistemas operacionais completos transformam a experiência, mas nem todos os recursos justificam um investimento mais alto.
Neste guia, o Tecnoblog analisa dez modelos da Samsung, LG, TCL, Philips e AOC para ajudar você a encontrar o equilíbrio ideal entre preço e desempenho.
A TCL P7L de 50 polegadas é direcionada a quem deseja uma TV 4K com tecnologia QLED e suporte a formatos HDR usados em filmes e séries. O painel LCD com pontos quânticos amplia a gama de cores reproduzidas, enquanto a tela HVA é apresentada pela fabricante como uma solução voltada ao contraste.
O processador AiPQ realiza ajustes de imagem conforme o conteúdo, e a compatibilidade com Dolby Vision e HDR10+ permite reproduzir materiais preparados para esses formatos. A diferença prática depende tanto do conteúdo disponível quanto do brilho e do contraste que o aparelho consegue entregar.
A Google TV organiza aplicativos, recomendações e serviços de streaming em uma interface unificada, com acesso ao catálogo de aplicativos compatíveis. Nesse tamanho, a P7L pode ser considerada por quem prioriza cores e compatibilidade HDR para entretenimento.
A LG NU850 de 55 polegadas combina uma tela 4K com processamento de imagem da linha Alpha 7 AI Gen9, sendo indicada para quem quer uma TV com ferramentas de aprimoramento de imagem.
O processamento pode refinar a apresentação de texturas, contraste e definição via software, mas não substitui suas características físicas. A frequência do painel é de 60 Hz e a TV aceita HDR10 e HLG, além de oferecer o recurso de upscaling para adaptar conteúdos de resolução inferior.
O webOS 26 dá acesso a aplicativos e serviços de streaming, enquanto os recursos de inteligência artificial incluem ajustes de imagem e som e ferramentas de personalização. A conectividade traz três HDMI, uma USB, Wi-Fi e Bluetooth, com eARC na entrada HDMI 2. O áudio integrado tem 20 W em dois canais.
A LG QNED70 de 50 polegadas é uma alternativa para quem procura uma TV 4K com iluminação Mini LED e recursos de processamento de imagem de 2026. O painel combina a tecnologia LCD com uma estrutura de reprodução de cores QNED e uma retroiluminação formada por LEDs menores.
Esse conjunto pode proporcionar maior controle da luz e do contraste em relação a sistemas convencionais, mas não equivale ao funcionamento de um painel OLED, no qual cada pixel emite sua própria luz.
O processador e o recurso de upscaling trabalham na adaptação de imagens, incluindo materiais de resolução inferior à nativa. O televisor aceita HDR10 e HLG, formatos utilizados por diferentes serviços e fontes de vídeo. Sua taxa de atualização nativa é de 60 Hz.
O webOS 26 concentra os aplicativos e serviços da smart TV, com suporte a Google Cast, Apple AirPlay e controle pelo aplicativo LG ThinQ.
A Samsung Vision AI Q7F de 50 polegadas combina resolução 4K e tecnologia QLED para quem deseja ampliar a reprodução de cores sem partir necessariamente para uma TV Mini LED. O painel LCD com pontos quânticos utiliza uma camada que contribui para reproduzir uma gama de cores mais ampla.
O processamento de imagem trabalha para adaptar conteúdos com resolução inferior a 4K e a plataforma Tizen reúne aplicativos de streaming e serviços conectados, enquanto os recursos de voz e integração com o ecossistema Samsung podem facilitar o uso cotidiano.
A Philips 58PUG7019/78 tem como principal diferencial a tela de 58 polegadas com resolução 4K, uma combinação voltada a quem prefere uma área de visualização maior para filmes, séries e programação esportiva.
O painel utiliza iluminação LED convencional, e o televisor aceita HDR10 e HLG, em conjunto com o Google TV. A plataforma concentra aplicativos, recomendações e conteúdos de diferentes serviços, com acesso à loja de aplicativos compatíveis.
O Google Assistente integrado e o microfone no controle remoto permitem pesquisar conteúdos e controlar funções por voz. Para quem utiliza vários serviços de streaming, essa organização pode simplificar a navegação.
A Samsung Crystal UHD U8000H de 55 polegadas atende a quem prefere uma tela maior para assistir a filmes, séries, esportes e programas de TV em uma sala de estar. O painel LED/LCD tem resolução 4K, com processamento Crystal Processor 4K para adaptar a imagem e aprimorar conteúdos de resolução inferior.
A tecnologia Crystal UHD não utiliza pontos quânticos como a QLED Q7F nem a iluminação Mini LED da M75H, o que ajuda a diferenciar as propostas neste guia. A TV possui frequência nativa de 60 Hz e compatibilidade com HDR10+.
O Tizen reúne aplicativos de streaming e serviços como Samsung TV Plus, além de recursos de conectividade com dispositivos compatíveis. A TV tem três entradas HDMI e uma USB, com suporte a eARC para conexão de equipamentos de áudio compatíveis.
A LG UA85 de 50 polegadas é voltada a quem procura uma smart TV 4K com processamento de imagem e recursos de inteligência artificial sem partir para as linhas QNED ou OLED. O modelo utiliza o processador α7 AI Gen8 e oferece upscaling, que adapta conteúdos de resolução inferior à tela.
A linha traz recursos de ajuste de imagem e som, incluindo o AI Sound Pro, que utiliza processamento para criar uma apresentação sonora virtualizada. A utilidade dessas funções depende do conteúdo e das preferências de configuração.
O aparelho também oferece acesso aos recursos da plataforma webOS, com aplicativos de streaming e integração com dispositivos compatíveis.
A AOC 50U7066/78G é indicada para quem busca uma TV de 50 polegadas com resolução 4K e sistema Roku TV, que reúne aplicativos de streaming em uma interface simples de navegar. O painel utiliza tecnologia DLED, com iluminação por LEDs, e resolução de 4K para reproduzir conteúdo em Ultra HD.
O sistema Roku TV concentra serviços de vídeo em uma única plataforma, facilitando o acesso a filmes, séries e outros conteúdos sem a necessidade de um aparelho externo. A conectividade inclui quatro entradas HDMI, uma USB 2.0, Wi-Fi, Ethernet e saída de áudio óptica, além de conexão para fones de ouvido.
A Samsung U8600F de 50 polegadas é uma TV Crystal UHD 4K voltada a quem deseja usar aplicativos de streaming com recursos de conectividade para jogos. Seu painel LED/LCD tem frequência nativa de 60 Hz, enquanto seu chip realiza o processamento de imagem e o upscaling.
Diferentemente da Q7F, a U8600F não utiliza pontos quânticos: a proposta é oferecer resolução 4K e funções de smart TV em uma categoria convencional de LCD.
O aparelho é compatível com HDR10+ e conta com recursos como Motion Xcelerator, modo Filmmaker e aprimoramento de cores. Para jogos, há suporte a ALLM e VRR, além de acesso ao Samsung Gaming Hub. O Tizen reúne os aplicativos da TV, e a conectividade inclui três HDMI, uma USB, Wi-Fi e Bluetooth.
A Samsung M75H de 50 polegadas é voltada a quem procura uma TV 4K com iluminação mais avançada do que a retroiluminação LED convencional. A tecnologia MiniLED utiliza emissores menores para controlar a luz atrás do painel LCD, o que pode favorecer o contraste.
A resolução 4K permite exibir conteúdos em alta definição, enquanto o processamento de imagem pode adaptar imagens de resolução inferior à tela. A linha M75H também oferece suporte a HDR10+ e a frequência do painel é de 60 Hz.
O sistema Tizen concentra aplicativos de streaming e serviços da Samsung, incluindo o Samsung TV Plus. A conectividade com outros dispositivos e os recursos de comando por voz ampliam as possibilidades de uso. É uma opção para filmes, séries e programação esportiva, mas não para jogos em a 120 Hz.
Considere o seguinte antes de comprar uma TV:
A TCL QLED P7L de 50 polegadas tem bom custo-benefício para quem busca uma TV 4K com tecnologia QLED e recursos de imagem como Dolby Vision e HDR10+. Além disso, a Google TV facilita o acesso a aplicativos e conteúdos de streaming nesta faixa de preço.
A Samsung Mini LED M75H de 50 polegadas é uma das melhores TVs para PS5 e Xbox Series, por combinar resolução 4K com recursos voltados a jogos, como ALLM, VRR, HGiG e Gaming Hub, tecnologias voltadas para melhorar a experiência visual e jogabilidade.
No entanto, sua taxa de atualização nativa é de 60 Hz, o que deve ser levado em conta por quem procura frequências mais altas.
Uma TV QLED utiliza pontos quânticos para ampliar a reprodução de cores em uma tela LCD. Os modelos MiniLED usam LEDs menores na iluminação traseira, o que permite controlar a luz em zonas e melhorar o contraste, dependendo do projeto do painel. Já Crystal UHD é uma denominação comercial da Samsung para TVs LCD 4K com processamento de imagem próprio.
Todas essas categorias são diferentes: QLED se refere à tecnologia de cores, MiniLED à iluminação e Crystal UHD à linha de televisores.
Uma marca, isoladamente, não garante que um aparelho terá menos falhas. Por isso, não é possível afirmar, com base apenas nos dez modelos deste guia, qual marca de TV apresentará menos problemas.
Para comparar a confiabilidade, seria necessário analisar dados consistentes sobre defeitos, assistência técnica, garantia e satisfação dos consumidores ao longo do tempo.
Sim, especialmente para quem deseja assistir a filmes, séries e esportes em 4K. A escolha da melhor TV de 50 polegadas depende principalmente da distância entre o sofá e a tela, da disposição dos móveis e do espaço disponível no painel ou rack.
Antes de comprar, confira a largura do aparelho com e sem a base e compare as medidas com o local de instalação. Se a distância de visualização for muito curta, um modelo menor pode ser mais confortável.
