articles.title: Florida Student Aid Website Hack Puts Data of 4.9 Million People at Risk
articles.text:
The Florida Department of Education (FLDOE) says hackers breached its student financial aid website, potentially exposing the personal information of roughly 4.9 million people.
The department discovered the intrusion on October 19. It says it launched its incident response procedures after detecting the threat and has since contained the breach.
“At this time, we believe the incident was limited to the Florida Student Financial Aid website (FloridaStudentFinancialAidSG.org) and may have impacted approximately 4.9 million individuals,” the department said.
The website is the online hub for Florida’s state-funded scholarship and grant programs. FLDOE warns that anyone who has applied for financial aid in the state in the past could be among those affected.
Names, Social Security numbers, dates of birth, home addresses, phone numbers, email addresses, and gender codes are among the data types the attackers may have accessed.
“Not all individuals were necessarily affected, and the specific information involved may vary by person,” FLDOE noted.
The department has not disclosed how the attackers got in or who is responsible, and no threat group appears to have publicly claimed the attack. The Florida Digital Service and the Florida Department of Law Enforcement are assisting with the response.
The department has cautioned that some of its websites and online services may be disrupted for a time as remediation continues.
According to FLDOE, students’ existing aid is safe. The breach will not delay the disbursements and tuition payments it handles, nor will it change eligibility for its scholarships, grants, and student loans.
The breach follows a September incident at the Florida Department of Highway Safety and Motor Vehicles (FLHSMV). That agency confirmed hackers had accessed its driver database after the ShinyHunters extortion group claimed to have stolen more than 200,000 driver records.
FLHSMV traced the intrusion to compromised credentials belonging to a local police department user but did not name ShinyHunters.
Related: Revolve Data Breach Impacts at Least 180,000 People
Related: Chainalysis Discloses Data Breach Following AI-Driven Cyberattack

articles.title: Grok Bot users accuse xAI of an "indirect rug pull" after usage cuts, Musk blames unsustainable costs
articles.text:
Winners & losers: It appears that even the richest man in the world has had to acknowledge that the cost of running AI is spiraling out of control. Elon Musk just admitted that Grok Bot users are hitting their usage limits much faster than usual this week due to "unsustainably high" costs relative to the revenue it generates.
Musk made the admission in a reply to an X user who asked for a usage reset after running out 4 days early. They added that lots of people had complained about their usage running out quickly over the last week.
"The cost of serving Grok Bot was unsustainably high relative to revenue," Musk replied.
 – Elon Musk (@elonmusk) November 1, 2026
Unsurprisingly, many people aren't happy about this. Grok users who say they never normally hit their 100% limit are now doing so, even without using AI agents or having Grok Bot work on heavy tasks.
One user said they went from 56% usage to 100% in one hour, while another said the usage cap had been slashed in half.
Some Redditors are angry that their usage limits were cut without them being informed ahead of time. One person claims that based on their usage, Grok Bot is essentially 3 times more expensive now – the term "indirect rug pull" has been used a lot.
Access to Grok Bot starts at $30 for the Premium tier. The Super tier is $100 per month, and there's an Ultra tier for $200 per month. Both offer much higher usage limits.
When one person on X complained about the situation, Musk asked if upgrading to the higher usage plan would be too expensive. It's unclear if only the cheapest plan or all of them were affected by the usage cuts.
 – Elon Musk (@elonmusk) November 1, 2026
The move comes just weeks after Musk called Grok Bot the fastest-growing product he has ever seen. "As we make Grok Bot more useful, we're seeing users use it more per week, not use it less," he said. SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell said there were 800,000 paying weekly Grok Bot users in early October, double the previous month's users.
Musk has not revealed any exact figures relating to Grok Bot's costs or the revenue it generates.
High costs have become a major issue across the AI industry. A June analysis found that fully utilizing a $200 ChatGPT Pro subscription could equate to $14,000 in API charges. Meanwhile, OpenAI's cost of revenue reached $7.5 billion in 2025, reflecting the expense of serving the millions of people using its models.
Wall Street is becoming increasingly nervous about whether these investments will ever pay off. The Nasdaq 100 fell more than 5.8% in October as investors questioned Big Tech's ballooning AI spending. Citadel's Ken Griffin recently suggested that the AI boom is almost certainly a bubble, warning that businesses aren't consistently getting enough value from the technology to justify the expense.

articles.title: Google finds 'LLMjacking' attackers running up $100K a day in fraudulent cloud charges - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Google finds ‘LLMjacking’ attackers running up $100K a day in fraudulent cloud charges
A new report out today from Google LLC’s Mandiant and Google Threat Intelligence Group finds that attackers who hijack enterprise access to large language models are running up fraudulent cloud charges of more than $100,000 in a single day.
The report, “The Rise of LLMJacking: How Threat Actors Monetize Compromised Cloud and Model Resources,” covers multiple LLMjacking cases Mandiant responded to this year. At some organizations, the cumulative bill reached $1 million before access was revoked.
Cryptojacking, the older way of stealing cloud compute, tends to drain resources gradually. LLMjacking charges can spike in a matter of hours.
Victims in North America, South America and Asia-Pacific included financial services and retail companies, along with technology and transportation businesses. GTIG has tied the intrusions to several financially motivated clusters and sees a growing split between the people who break in and the operators who resell the access.
In most of the investigations, attackers got in with cloud identity credentials that had been stolen or left exposed, including service account keys and GitHub personal access tokens. Others went after LLM endpoints left open to the internet, such as exposed Ollama servers.
A group tracked as UNC6993 broke into a cloud instance through a misconfigured service account key and used that foothold to reach an LLM application programming interface. A fake portal it hosted posed as a sign-up page for a group of LLM users. Visitors were sent to the real LLM service and told to paste back a raw JSON payload containing an active access token. With that token, passwords and multifactor authentication no longer stood in the way.
Another actor scraped LLM API keys from public GitHub repositories and tested each one with a request capped at a single output token. Requests that small slipped under the volume-based alerts in the victims’ security monitoring tools.
Routing software is a target too. In one case a follow-on cluster obtained pre-validated virtual keys from the group that had established access, then exploited a user ID rebind flaw in LiteLLM’s key regeneration endpoint. The bug, CVE-2026-40217, let it turn ordinary virtual keys into master administrator credentials for the victim’s gateway.
Some of the stolen access was burned through directly. UNC6993 tried to generate more API keys and switch on extra services inside victim cloud projects, and the charges quickly passed $100,000. A different actor signed victim accounts up for pay-as-you-go agreements on premium models. To get around rate limits, the actor used what GTIG calls a “burn and rotate” strategy, continuously creating and deleting short-lived service accounts.
A third went further and planted a containerized backdoor built on the Manus agent framework, which asked an upstream model to reason through instructions and then executed the resulting commands on the compromised host.
Other access ends up for sale through what GTIG calls “LLM Mixers.” These operations run stolen credentials through open-source API gateways and custom relays so usage can be metered and the origin of each request hidden. UNC6993 used tools such as new-api and gcli2api, likely to pool stolen keys, and GTIG believes the group sells access through underground storefronts.
One mixer is Jet Night, a token routing service. An actor that made more than 500,000 LLM API calls in under eight hours was using stolen third-party keys to power it, and one victim organization was left with nearly $1 million in token costs.
Jet Night sells an unlimited plan claiming frontier model access for about $60 a month. Comparable consumer plans typically cost $100 to $250, and GTIG thinks prices that low only work on stolen keys. Outages advertised on the service’s Telegram channel are likely the result of victims finding the compromise and revoking keys.
GTIG expects attackers increasingly to favor LLMjacking over cryptojacking because the mixers pay out quickly and at high margins. Exposed API tokens and model routing middleware will draw more automated targeting as companies put higher-tier models and agentic workflows into production, the report predicts.
On the defensive side, the report notes that in several of Mandiant’s cases, the victim had never enabled LLM services. Attackers used stolen keys to turn on services such as Amazon Web Services Inc.’s Amazon Bedrock and Google’s Gemini API, and a bill could balloon within minutes from there.
Any unauthorized enablement should be treated as a critical security event, it says. Spending caps, API keys scoped to specific models and environments and log monitoring for the single-token pings used to validate stolen keys are among its other recommendations.
Threat actors want artificial intelligence to give them scale over defenders, according to John Hultquist, chief analyst at Google Threat Intelligence Group, and they are getting it with agentic tools and tokens stolen from unwitting third parties.
“Locking down these resources will not only protect organizations from runaway costs, but also protect the broader community from a deluge of cheap, autonomous attacks,” Hultquist said.

articles.title: Jevons’ Paradox and the Silicon Roadmap - EE Times
articles.text:
AI usage may expand with more efficient models and hardware, just as Jevons would predict. But the silicon roadmap adds a layer of complexity to the market prediction.
Gartner vs Jevons
A couple of weeks ago, Gartner published a forecast that raises concerns about AI infrastructure. AI providers will spend close to $1 trillion on infrastructure in 2026 and another $6 trillion between 2027 and 2030. To pay for that, cover the cost of borrowing, and still earn a 12% return, the owners of AI data centers would need about $8.5 trillion in revenue through 2030. Gartner expects the AI revenue that actually reaches those data centers to be $3.6 trillion at most. On that arithmetic, says Gartner, more than $3.5 trillion of this spending could be exposed to write-downs by 2030, and more than 80% of neoclouds will no longer exist as independent companies. That is a risk estimate under Gartner’s assumptions, not a prediction that the full amount will be written off.
On the other hand, IMHO, this math assumes that AI will continue to be deployed in a similar use and business model as today. However, we might well be only at the beginning of the AI use curve. And, according to the by-now very well-known Jevons paradox, the more a technology is available, the more people will find new use-models for that technology, and therefore, even if the technology price goes down, the revenue from the aggregated usage can go up. As an illustration, when cars become more fuel-efficient, each kilometer costs less, so people drive more, take longer trips, and may end up buying more fuel in total. Cheaper petrol works in a similar way: When its price falls, people drive more, and when it rises, some prefer public transportation.
Back to AI usage, Epoch AI estimates that the price of reaching a given benchmark score has fallen by roughly 13 times a year since 2023, measured on the benchmarks it tracks, with the usual caveats about how those benchmarks are chosen.
Therefore, according to the Jevons paradox, we may expect that easier access and lower prices will enable new applications and higher overall usage. This should be the longer-term trend, although nothing guarantees that demand grows faster than prices fall.
According to that, Gartner may be showing a pessimistic view, based on today’s use cases and current demand, that may be multiplied in the next few years. Having said all that, there is an additional catch: Contrary to what happens in the gas station—that looks the same this year compared to next year—a data center (or AI factory, if you prefer) may have different chips this year compared to next, be it because of different generations or different architectures. Since these new chips require additional investment, and potentially write-off previous investments, this makes Gartner’s prediction even more complicated.
What the chip rental market is saying
So far, it looks like “old chips” are keeping their value for longer than expected. Recently, a16z posted a chart, built on Ornn rental data as of Oct. 19, comparing what each major Nvidia generation rents for today with a projected price. The projection is simple: Take the first rent observed for each chip and assume it falls in a straight line to zero over six years, roughly the way the hyperscalers write these servers off in their accounts. Because each chip’s line starts from its own first observed rent, the series begin at different points in each chip’s life. Every generation is now renting above that projection: the A100 by 9%, the H100 by 54%, the B200 by 111%, and the H200 by 143%.
Note also that, according to a16z, most of the gap opened up after April, when token demand took off, which is consistent with the Jevons paradox at work, although the chart alone cannot prove the cause.
Two caveats are worth keeping in mind, though. For most of their lives, these chips rented below that line, and rent is not profit: A chip can rent well and still lose money for its owner once power, cooling, networking, facilities, and the cost of borrowing are paid for.
Cheap wells and expensive wells
The Economist recently described compute as the new oil, and I think this is a useful comparison in different ways. The token is the barrel, the “thing” the customer actually buys. Each GPU generation is an oil field. Some wells are easy and cheap to pump and give better-quality oil, so their cost per barrel is low. Others are harder to work and give lower-quality crude, so each barrel costs more. For GPUs, the cost of producing a token is linked largely to how much energy each generation needs to make it, and to whether it can handle the work at all.
When oil prices are high, every well pumps, even the expensive ones. When prices fall, the costliest wells are the first ones to be shut. Chips behave the same way. When demand is very high, as it has been since April, even the A100 is needed, and every generation rents above the line. That is exactly what the a16z chart shows. When a new generation arrives in volume, it is the new cheap well; prices fall, and the oldest chips are the first to be switched off. Microsoft, for instance, plans to scale its own Maia accelerators to multi-gigawatt deployments from 2027, claiming 40% more tokens per megawatt, a figure not yet independently verified.
Not all tokens are equal
The oil comparison still treats every barrel as the same, and that is where I think most of our analysis so far oversimplifies. Tokens—and the chips that generate them—are not all alike. Interactive and agentic work needs low latency and the newest, fastest memory. Bulk work, such as processing documents overnight, generating synthetic data, or running evaluations, cares mostly about cost and barely notices latency. A fully paid-off chip, whose remaining costs are mainly power, cooling, and upkeep, can be the cheapest way to produce those tokens. So, there is not one oil market but several, one for each broad type of work.
However, there is a twist here: Typically, the demand that Jevons adds is price-sensitive by nature and features uses that only become worthwhile once AI is cheap. Some of these will be high-value applications, but many will be bulk work, which is where older silicon competes best. An interesting recent example is Jev, from TypeSafe AI, a model that returns structured decisions rather than text and that its makers claim is hundreds of times cheaper than a large language model. Models like this could move a lot of agentic decision-making off expensive LLMs, and IMHO, they look well suited to older hardware, although TypeSafe does not say what it runs on.
At the other extreme, frontier models keep getting bigger, and many are increasingly sparse, activating only a small part of the model for each token, as in Mixture of Experts (MoE) models. For the largest of these, the bottleneck can be less raw compute than memory capacity and fast connections between chips, which has made the rack, rather than the chip, the unit of frontier computing. An older GPU is not too slow for these models so much as too small and too isolated. And maybe new architectures will emerge that can cope better with these models’ sparsity.
Besides these two poles, there are other types of models—from recommendation engines to image generation to scientific models—and not all of them may need the same type of hardware.
Put together, this looks to me like a barbell. The giant models pull toward the newest rack-scale systems, while small and specialized models live happily on older silicon. My hypothesis is that the squeeze falls on the middle: chips that are neither at the frontier nor already paid off, still carried on the books at a high value. If I am right, a lot of the 2024 and 2025 spending sits right there.
The heterogeneous data center
And here is another layer of complexity: In the past, data centers have always mixed different hardware, but the variety used to be modest. A cloud data center a decade ago ran different types of CPU, memory, storage, and networking, and the job was to match workloads to a fairly predictable menu. Those servers also aged gracefully. Each new CPU generation was only modestly better than the last, so an older server kept earning for years, a bit like a rental car, where last year’s model is nearly as good as this year’s.
Today, the menu is far richer. Next to the CPUs sit GPUs, TPUs, and other AI accelerators, and inference is increasingly being split into stages that run best on different chips. Nvidia announced Rubin CPX, a dedicated chip for the prefill stage, in 2025, then put it on the back burner, possibly until a later generation, in favor of decode-focused racks based on technology licensed from Groq. Add HPC, which often still needs high-precision math that many AI chips deprioritize, and the job of matching each workload to the right silicon becomes much harder, and each generation of that silicon ages much faster.
The largest operators can afford this variety. With enough scale, they can keep many kinds of hardware busy and route each job to the cheapest chip that can do it. Smaller data centers cannot, and for them the general-purpose GPU remains the safest bet, because it can step down from training to inference to batch work as it ages. Specialized parts are cheaper per task, but they are more fragile as assets, since they lose that ability to start a second and third career.
Dedicated on-premises installations are a different case again. A company running its own well-understood workloads can choose a configuration that fits them closely and does not need to chase every new generation. For such workloads, state-of-the-art silicon matters mainly for training custom models, and perhaps for a few GPU-accelerated solvers.
The silicon roadmap schedule
This brings me to what I think is the core of the matter. Many of the big operators spread the cost of these servers over about six years in their accounts, but that is a bookkeeping convention, and it says little about how long a chip actually earns more than it costs to run. That economic life is decided upstream, by the people who design the next chip. Nvidia’s annual cadence, the gains in tokens per watt each generation brings, new memory standards and number formats, and the software that keeps old chips useful together set how long any GPU stays competitive. In that sense, the silicon roadmap dictates the real investment depreciation timeline.
Seen this way, owning your own silicon gives you much more say over your own clock. Microsoft with Maia, Google with TPU, and Amazon with Trainium can shape when their own fleets become obsolete, even if demand and competitors still have a vote. A neocloud renting out Nvidia GPUs lives on a clock set by its supplier and its customers.
And Nvidia sits on both sides of the table. It sets the pace that erodes the value of its customers’ fleets, and—at the same time—has also agreed, according to a recent piece in The Economist, to cover up to $300 billion of its customers’ debt used to buy its chips, should those customers be unable to repay. A faster cadence sells more new chips and weakens the chips that secure those loans. When Jensen Huang posted in August that an A100 remains useful until 2029, he was making a technical point, but he also has a stake in this tradeoff, even as Nvidia keeps introducing new generations.
Cars and chips
Which brings us back to Gartner’s real question: Who will own the chips when the market turns? Rental car companies offer a useful comparison. They buy fleets largely with borrowed money, pledge the cars against the loans, and make or lose money on what the cars fetch when sold. In early 2024, Hertz sold off about 20,000 electric vehicles and booked a loss of about $245 million. Hertz pointed mainly to high repair and collision costs, but weak resale values played a part too, and Tesla’s price cuts on new cars had pushed down the value of used ones. A supplier’s pricing decision eroded the value of its customer’s fleet. GPUs carry the same risk in a stronger form, since each new generation is a much bigger step than a new model year; the market for used chips is far thinner and more specialized than the market for used cars, and power, unlike parking space, is scarce.
Last week’s earnings calls
Last week’s earnings calls brought new signals. Meta, which reported a week earlier, narrowed its 2026 capital spending to $135–$145 billion and cited growing infrastructure costs and payments to third parties for AI tokens.
Then, Microsoft, Alphabet, and Amazon reported. All three said that demand for AI computing still runs ahead of the capacity they can bring online, and Microsoft and Google are even renting capacity from third parties to keep up. Between them, these three plan to spend close to $600 billion in 2026, and Alphabet and Amazon both said they will spend significantly more in 2027.
A few relevant details stood out on the calls: Microsoft credited part of Azure’s growth to “continued efficiency gains across our CPU and GPU fleet,” a reminder that, as with a rental car company, getting more out of the fleet you already own is part of the business. Amazon said that short-term capacity on its previous-generation Trainium chips now rents at a premium compared with the first half of the year, which supports the a16z chart’s insight, this time on Amazon’s own silicon. It also said inference is now well over half of AWS’s AI revenue, exactly the varied, price-sensitive work where older and specialized chips can compete. And Google is now selling complete TPU systems for customers to run in their own data centers, with Amazon planning to sell Trainium outside AWS from late 2027. Owning your own silicon roadmap, it seems, is becoming something the hyperscalers can sell to others, and more of the market may end up living on their roadmaps rather than only on Nvidia’s.
Investors also got a reminder that more usage does not automatically mean more revenue. Alphabet lost about $500 billion of market value in a day after admitting that answers from AI Mode in Google search earn less than traditional search ads, according to The Economist. People are using AI more, and Google is earning less on each search, at least for now. And since advertising is what pays for much of this buildout, that matters for everyone buying chips.
More of that money now has to be borrowed. Meta, Alphabet, and Amazon all reported negative free cash flow, and even Microsoft, which is still cash-positive, announced $25 billion of new bonds the day after its earnings call.
Good old Jevons
It is worth remembering where the paradox comes from. In 1865, in The Coal Question, the economist William Stanley Jevons observed that more efficient steam engines did not reduce Britain’s coal consumption but increased it, because cheaper power found many more uses. His point held up: Britain’s coal consumption kept growing as its engines improved, even if efficiency was not the only reason. But that did not save every mine, and the owners of the least efficient pits still went under as the industry grew. I expect something similar here. AI demand will very likely keep surprising on the upside, and a good part of the money that built the first generations of this infrastructure will likely still have to be written down. Both outcomes come from the same roadmap, seen once from the buyer’s side and once from the owner’s.

articles.title: Attackers Exploit Critical Siemens IoT2050 Flaw to Plant Remote Command Backdoors
articles.text:
A maximum-severity security flaw impacting Siemens SIMATIC IoT2050 Advanced devices has come under active exploitation, VulnCheck has revealed.
The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-58115 (CVSS score: 10.0), is a case of missing authentication for a critical function that could be exploited by an unauthenticated remote attacker to run arbitrary code.
"SIMATIC IoT2050 Advanced devices running Industrial OS with Node-RED installed contain a missing authentication vulnerability in the Node-RED HTTP interface that could allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to create malicious flows and execute arbitrary code on the underlying server with maximum privileges," Siemens said in an advisory released back in August 2026.
The issue has been remediated in versions 4.3.4.1 or later. As mitigations, Siemens recommends that users uninstall Node-RED or harden the installation by following the steps below -
- Enabling HTTPS access
- Securing the editor and admin API via credential based authentication or through an OAuth/OpenID provider
- Securing the HTTP Nodes and Node-RED Dashboard using basic authentication
As of October 30, 2026, VulnCheck said it observed attackers attempting to weaponize CVE-2026-58115 against its honeypot network in an attempt to download and run a Linux bot.
"The attacker's request was a complete exploit," VulnCheck researcher Patrick Garrity said. "It deployed a Node-RED flow, triggered it automatically, and pulled a binary from an attacker-controlled server, all behind three layers of encoding."
Specifically, the malicious flow is designed to run a shell script wrapper, which uses wget to retrieve the botnet binary for AMD64 architecture from 85.215.73[.]250. Curl is used as a fallback if the wget attempt fails. In the final stage, the binary is saved as "/dev/shm/.b" and executed.
Since then, the attackers behind the campaign have switched to a two-stage process where the wget command is used to retrieve another shell script ("wget.sh") from the same server.
Another request has been found to run wget/curl against "45.194.90[.]57:38472" to fetch a payload called ".sys_update," save it on disk as "/tmp/.kworker" in an attempt to disguise it as a harmless kernel worker thread," and then execute it. The exact functionality of "wget.sh" or ".kworker" remains unknown, as they could not be retrieved.
"Several requests deployed no downloader at all. Instead, the flow exposes an HTTP in endpoint (for example /cmd, or a randomly named path) wired through a function node to an exec node with addpay enabled, so the attacker could run arbitrary commands later by passing them in a query parameter," Garrity said. "This backdoor survives even if a memory-backed implant is lost on reboot."

articles.title: VOIDJOY SkyLark S1 Pro Brings Full Gamepad Controls to Portable Play
articles.text:
Monday, November 2nd 2026
VOIDJOY SkyLark S1 Pro Brings Full Gamepad Controls to Portable Play
The VOIDJOY SkyLark S1 Pro is available at a limited-time promotional price from JSAUX GAMING. The controller is designed for players who move between handhelds, PCs and mobile devices and want a gamepad that is easy to keep in their bag. "Portability should not come at the expense of functionality," said Winnie Chen, Marketing Communications Manager at JSAUX GAMING. "We designed the SkyLark S1 Pro to be as easy to carry as a phone while still delivering the control players expect from a serious gamepad".
Measuring 133 mm × 75 mm × 24 mm and weighing approximately 113 grams, the SkyLark S1 Pro fits easily into a backpack, handheld case or jacket pocket. Players can take it along for gaming at home, on the road or during a commute. The controller works with compatible PC, Nintendo Switch, Steam Deck, Android and iOS devices. In 2.4 GHz mode, two SkyLark S1 Pro controllers can connect through one receiver, making the setup suitable for local multiplayer games such as It Takes Two and Overcooked!Do More in Less Space
The SkyLark S1 Pro uses recessed TMR thumbsticks set into the controller shell. The lowered position helps prevent accidental contact during play while preserving precise analog control for aiming, steering and movement.
Its optical linear triggers offer two travel settings. The longer setting supports gradual input in racing and simulation games, while the shorter setting reduces trigger travel for faster actuation in action and first-person shooter titles.
The controller also includes programmable rear buttons, ABXY buttons, six-axis motion controls and dual vibration motors.
Customize Controls Across Games 
The KeyLinker app lets players remap buttons, adjust stick sensitivity and dead zones, and save profiles for different games.
The SkyLark S1 Pro supports USB-C wired, 2.4 GHz wireless and Bluetooth connections. Bluetooth saves previously paired devices for quicker reconnection.
Limited-Time Offer
The VOIDJOY SkyLark S1 Pro is available for $44.99, representing 10% off its regular $49.99 price when customers use code "VOIDJOY10" during this limited-time offer.

articles.title: Why large dogs age faster than small ones, and other October research highlights
articles.text:
It’s a regrettable reality that there is never enough time to cover all the interesting scientific stories we come across. So every month, we highlight a handful of the best stories that nearly slipped through the cracks. October’s list includes an epigenetic mechanism for why large dogs age faster than smaller ones; physicists who trapped a single particle of antimatter for months; and invisible tattoo inks that only show up under UV light.
Why large dogs age faster
In many mammalian species, larger creatures tend to have longer lifespans. Mice, for instance, live an average of just two years, while some whales can last for as long as 200 years. Dogs, however, buck this pattern; larger dogs tend to age faster and die younger than smaller ones, which makes canines an ideal model for biologists to study to learn more about aging in general. Arizona State University scientists report that these lifespan differences seem to be due to so-called “jumping genes,” according to a paper published in the journal Science.
The authors used data from 864 dogs collected in the Dog Aging Project to map patterns of DNA methylation (which influences how much certain genes are turned on or off) across the entire genome. It’s part of the epigenome, whose markers can change over time in response to stress and other environmental factors. Genetic sequences, by contrast, are largely fixed. So DNA methylation is a good chemical indicator of aging and DNA regulation.
Their analysis showed that aging in dogs is linked to the decrease in the regulation provided by DNA methylation, particularly in regions where there are “jumping genes” that can move from chromosome to chromosome. These jumps can damage DNA, causing cancer and other age-related diseases, and their activity increases with the loss of regulatory markers. The authors identified a specific class of jumping genes called LINE1s that were responsible for the different rates of aging in dogs. Giant dog breeds lost roughly 35 percent more LINE1 methylation each year compared to small breeds.
“This is one of the clearest molecular signatures we’ve seen that aligns with the well-known size-lifespan trade-off in dogs,” said co-author Blaise Mariner. “It suggests that faster aging in larger dogs may be driven, at least in part, by reduced control over these jumping genes.”
One of the biggest unanswered questions in cosmology is why the early universe had a fundamental asymmetry between matter and antimatter. When matter and antimatter particles collide, they annihilate into energy, so that asymmetry resulted in matter dominating our universe, which contains much more matter than antimatter. It’s extremely difficult to create and isolate antimatter, requiring special traps. Physicists at Northwestern University have succeeded in trapping a single positron (antimatter particle) for months on end, according to a paper published in Physical Review Letters.
Co-author Gerald Gabrielse and his team built on earlier work, in which they trapped a single electron to create a one-electron quantum cyclotron. They then used the setup to make one of the most precise measurements of its magnetic moment yet. Trapping a positron was a bit trickier. They harvested the positron from sodium-22 nuclei, slowing it down enough to guide it into a near-perfect vacuum trap of electric and magnetic fields. Once inside, they chilled the positron to just 300 millikelvins (0.3° above absolute zero), thereby keeping the positron in its quantum ground state. They found they could maintain that state for months at a time.
That enabled Gabrielse et al. to manipulate and detect the particle’s individual quantum energy state using tuned microwaves—the first critical step in being able to measure the positron’s magnetic properties, hopefully with the same precision they achieved in their earlier experiments with a single electron. The Standard Model of particle physics predicts that there should be no difference between the two particle measurements. If they are not equal, “that would be the biggest discovery in physics in the last century,” said Gabrielse.
Many people sport tattoos, but there are situations where hiding them is desirable. A new line of multicolored tattoo inks could one day make that dilemma moot; they are invisible to the human eye unless one illuminates them with UV light, according to a paper published in the journal Matter & Light. “There’s a stigma, in science and in many cultures, around body art,” said co-author Carson Bruns of the University of Colorado, Boulder, who sports a green lion tattoo on one arm, among others. “I’m proud to be pushing against that.”
As previously reported, epidermal electronics attached to the skin via temporary tattoos (e-tattoos) have been around for more than a decade. So-called e-tattoos connect to skin without adhesives, are practically unnoticeable, and are typically attached via temporary tattoo, allowing electrical measurements (and other measurements, such as temperature and strain) using ultra-thin polymers with embedded circuit elements. In 2024, researchers developed special polymer-based conductive inks that can be printed onto a person’s scalp to measure brain waves, even if they have hair. This could one day enable mobile EEG monitoring outside a clinical setting, among other potential applications. And earlier this year, scientists at Pennsylvania State University developed a novel conductive ink that can be painted directly onto the skin in colorful custom designs, turning into a functional electrode for biomonitoring after drying.
Bruns et al. created their inks, known as PhotoTat, from color-changing dyes injected into tiny spheres of polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA), a material used in dermal fillers among other medical applications. Mixing the primary-colored dyes can create full-color images. The tattoos are invisible until exposed to UV light, when they turn blue, magenta, or yellow. They fade after a few hours, faster if exposed to bright LED light. It’s still a proof of concept, but Bruns did test the dyes on himself, inking a black outline of fish scales that turn red, orange, or blue, like mermaid scales, under UV light. The dyes could also help cancer patients undergoing radiation therapy, who need small tattoos so doctors can guide the beams. PhotoTat would make such tattoos invisible except when the treatment is being administered.
Over 150 years ago, archaeologists discovered a skeleton buried in a Roman sarcophagus on the grounds of Westminster Abbey, bearing an inscription to a wealthy Briton from between 300 to 400 CE named Valerius Amandinus. But there was also a Latin cross sculpted into the lid that dated to the 10th or 11th century, i.e., the late Saxon period. Were the remains actually those of someone who lived and died centuries after Valerius? According to a paper published in the Journal of the British Archaeological Association they are—specifically, these are the bones of a high-ranking medieval monk.
The authors reasoned that this was an abbot’s skeleton because it was buried within a sarcophagus, while skeletal clues suggested it was a man between 35 and 49, standing about 5 feet, 9 inches tall. The most likely conclusion is that the bones belong to a Benedictine monk named Aelfwig, who died around 1020 and was buried at Westminster Abbey, where he had served as abbot. However, the bones may also be those of Aelfwig’s successor, Wulboth, who died in 1049 and was likely buried on the grounds as well. There is also evidence that the body was originally housed in a timber coffin that decayed over the ensuing seven centuries.
In June, we reported on the research of Paolo Pozzilli of Queen Mary University of London and several co-authors into the cause of death of one of Sandro Botticelli’s models. Among his best-known works is the Birth of Venus, depicting the naked goddess, newly birthed, standing in a giant scallop shell. The model for the painting (disputed by some historians) was allegedly Simonetta Vespucci (née Cattaneo), a renowned beauty in Florentine high society whom Botticelli greatly admired. He painted her five times before her untimely death in her early 20s.
It was long believed that Simonetta had succumbed to tuberculosis, but it was argued that she may have suffered from a pituitary tumor (adenoma) that gradually increased in size due to prolactin and growth hormone secretions, citing her appearance in several portraits as evidence. This could have caused a sudden tumor-related fatal apoplexy. They examined letters between Simonetta’s father-in-law, Piero Vespucci, and Lorenzo de Medici, which described how Simonetta had collapsed during a ball a few days before her death. Her symptoms included headache, hallucinations, vomiting, and a high fever, all symptoms of a rapidly expanding pituitary tumor, per the authors.
Pozzilli et al. are back again with a paper published in the journal Medical Humanities providing further evidence for their hypothesis about Vespucci’s cause of death. They argued that the tumor could also explain the irregular eye positioning in the Birth of Venus, suggesting the model had a squint or eye misalignment. After more closely studying how Botticelli depicted the model’s eyes in Birth of Venus and several other portraits, the authors noted pronounced swelling around the left eye, likely due to fluid buildup, while some of the tissue covering the white part of the eye is loose. This and the telltale squint support the theory that Simonetta had a tumor in her pituitary gland.
Vincent van Gogh’s masterpiece, The Starry Night (1889), has long fascinated art lovers and scientists like. Some physicists have even suggested that the painting is a masterful depiction of atmospheric turbulence, and a 2024 paper found that the illusion of movement in the blue sky is also due to the scale of the paint strokes—a second kind of “hidden turbulence” at the microscale that diffuses throughout the entire canvas, although others have objected to that conclusion. Now a team of South Korean astronomers has used “forensic astronomy” to pinpoint the precise month in which van Gogh painted his masterpiece, according to a paper published in the journal Scientific Reports.
Other astronomers have previously suggested that The Starry Night is not just a symbolic representation, but shows the actual night sky at the time it was created, specifically in June 1889. This new analysis—which takes into account simulations, historical weather patterns, star positions, and van Gogh’s letters from that year—shifts that date to just before dawn on July 22, 1889. Co-author Elijah Jeong-hyun Kim told Gizmodo that his interest was piqued when he came across previous research identifying the constellation Aries. Kim thought the lights in the painting more closely resembled the Hyades star cluster in the constellation Taurus, suggesting the July date. While van Gogh said that his work exaggerated the point of view he painted, the authors note that such exaggeration “presupposes a real object to amplify.”
Kim et al. are in good company in forensic astronomy. As we reported in 2020, the so-called “celestial sleuth,” Donald Olson, applied similar tools to determine that Vermeer’s View of Delft most likely shows the city on September 3 or 4, 1659 (or earlier), at 8 am. Over the years, Olson has found evidence that the blood-red sunset that inspired Edvard Munch’s The Scream was likely an aftereffect of the 1883 eruption of Mount Krakatoa in Indonesia; that the Moon may have contributed to the sinking of the Titanic; helped identify the precise location of Julius Caesar’s landing site in Britain in 55 BC; and showed that Mary Shelley was probably telling the truth about a moonlit “waking dream” that inspired Frankenstein. And in 2015, Olson determined the precise time of day that Life magazine photographer Alfred Eisenstaedt took his most famous photograph (V-J- Day in Times Square) on August 14, 1945.
Jennifer is a senior writer at Ars Technica with a particular focus on where science meets culture, covering everything from physics and related interdisciplinary topics to her favorite films and TV series. Jennifer lives in Baltimore with her spouse, physicist Sean M. Carroll, and their two cats, Ariel and Caliban.

articles.title: Germany says lawmakers' iPhones may have been hacked with spyware | TechCrunch
articles.text:
The German government is warning politicians and public figures that they were targeted by government-backed spyware, days after Apple began sending out notifications warning victims that their iPhones may have been hacked.
Germany’s federal cybersecurity office, known as the BSI, said in a note over the weekend that it had become aware that members of the Bundestag, Germany’s parliament, and other unnamed notable individuals had received warnings from Apple that they may have been targeted by cyberattacks.
Per the Financial Times, German government spokesperson Stefan Kornelius said the government in Berlin was “taking the incident and the warning very seriously,” but he did not say who in the federal government had been targeted, including whether German chancellor Friedrich Merz was among them.
Apple periodically sends out threat notifications to people it thinks may have been targeted by spyware, which can steal messages, location data, and other sensitive information from their phones. This spyware often relies on zero-click exploits, which can hack individuals almost invisibly as they don’t require a victim to click on a link or open a file.
Apple does not attribute attacks to specific governments or say whether someone’s phone has actually been compromised. For that reason, the BSI said that anyone who receives an Apple threat notification “should therefore assume that their device may have been compromised.”
Others outside of Germany also received the recent threat alert from Apple. Radwan Mortada, a Beirut-based filmmaker, said in a post on X that he received a new threat notification warning that Apple had detected “another attack against your device,” after an earlier spyware attack targeted him in 2021.
It’s unclear who is behind this latest round of spyware attacks, or which government may have orchestrated the targeting. Per the notice received by Mortada, Apple said its latest batch of threat notifications went out to users in 99 countries.
The episode highlights again the murky business behind a growing number of attacks against members of civil society. Governments rarely build these tools themselves. Many buy them from private vendors, often called “mercenary spyware” makers, the best known being Israel’s NSO Group, which sells the controversial Pegasus spyware. Germany’s own central federal law agency, the BKA, reportedly bought access to Pegasus in 2019.

articles.title: Fóssil encontrado no Brasil pode guardar células sanguíneas de dinossauro
articles.text:
Pesquisadores identificaram estruturas semelhantes a glóbulos vermelhos em um fóssil de dinossauro com cerca de 115 milhões de anos encontrado no Brasil. A descoberta foi feita a partir da análise de ossos de uma das pernas do Aratasaurus museunacionali, espécie que viveu no território que hoje corresponde ao Nordeste brasileiro.
O estudo identificou estruturas microscópicas que lembram células sanguíneas e também detectou heme, composto orgânico associado à hemoglobina, proteína responsável pelo transporte de oxigênio no sangue. Segundo os pesquisadores, é a primeira vez que estruturas desse tipo são encontradas em um fóssil acompanhadas de evidências químicas relacionadas ao heme.
O trabalho foi liderado por cientistas da Universidade Curtin (Austrália) e publicado na revista científica Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS). A descoberta pode abrir novas possibilidades para investigar características biológicas de animais pré-históricos, incluindo metabolismo e níveis de atividade física.
Fóssil de dinossauro foi encontrado no Brasil em 2008
- Os vestígios analisados pertencem ao Aratasaurus museunacionali, dinossauro terópode que viveu há aproximadamente 115 milhões de anos, durante o período Cretáceo. O material foi encontrado em uma mina brasileira em 2008 e está sob a guarda do Museu Nacional, onde continua sendo estudado;
- Ao examinar fragmentos dos ossos da perna do animal, os pesquisadores identificaram pequenas estruturas arredondadas em canais microscópicos por onde passavam vasos sanguíneos. Imagens obtidas com microscopia eletrônica mostraram formas semelhantes a células vermelhas do sangue;
- A equipe também realizou análises químicas para investigar a origem do material. Os testes detectaram heme e produtos de sua decomposição, além de componentes associados ao colágeno, proteína importante para tecidos conjuntivos;
- A combinação entre as observações microscópicas e os resultados químicos foi importante para sustentar a interpretação dos cientistas. Afinal, encontrar uma estrutura com aparência de célula não é suficiente para demonstrar que ela realmente tem origem biológica.
Como estruturas semelhantes a células sobreviveram por milhões de anos?
A preservação de materiais biológicos por períodos tão longos é um dos aspectos mais intrigantes da descoberta. Tecidos e moléculas orgânicas normalmente se degradam durante o processo de fossilização, o que torna difícil encontrar vestígios desse tipo em fósseis tão antigos.
Uma possível explicação envolve a hausmannita, composto mineral de manganês encontrado no material analisado. De acordo com os pesquisadores, o mineral pode ter ajudado a estabilizar ou reproduzir as estruturas celulares durante a fossilização, preservando sinais químicos que normalmente desapareceriam.
A equipe também considera que as condições em que o animal foi preservado podem ter contribuído para o resultado. A hipótese apresentada no estudo envolve um soterramento rápido em ambiente com atividade microbiana e pouca disponibilidade de oxigênio.
Isso não significa, porém, que células sanguíneas tenham permanecido intactas por 115 milhões de anos. A interpretação dos pesquisadores é que estruturas e componentes químicos relacionados à biologia original do animal deixaram um registro mineralizado no fóssil.
Leia mais:
- Fóssil de 210 milhões de anos reescreve a história dos dinossauros
- Autópsia de 66 milhões de anos mostra como maior T. rex do mundo morreu
- Novo dinossauro com penas pode mudar o que sabemos sobre a origem do voo
Descoberta ainda gera debate entre cientistas
Apesar dos resultados, a identificação das possíveis células sanguíneas não é consenso entre especialistas.
Ao The Guardian, a paleontóloga Mary Schweitzer, da Universidade Estadual da Carolina do Norte (EUA), demonstrou cautela em relação à interpretação. Ela observou que os glóbulos vermelhos dos dinossauros deveriam apresentar uma saliência no núcleo, o que faria com que tivessem uma aparência abaulada nos dois lados. As estruturas encontradas no fóssil, por outro lado, são côncavas — uma característica que pode indicar outra origem.
A pesquisadora, no entanto, considerou mais convincentes os indícios químicos de heme e de componentes associados ao colágeno. O debate reforça a importância de novas análises para confirmar a natureza das estruturas encontradas.
A própria líder do estudo, Kliti Grice, defende cautela. Segundo ela, a descoberta não significa que moléculas grandes e complexas, como proteínas ou DNA, tenham permanecido preservadas em fósseis tão antigos.
O que a descoberta pode revelar sobre os dinossauros?
Se os resultados forem confirmados por novas pesquisas, a descoberta poderá ajudar cientistas a investigar aspectos da fisiologia dos dinossauros que são difíceis de estudar apenas com ossos e outros vestígios tradicionais.
A presença de informações moleculares pode contribuir para pesquisas sobre a evolução do sangue, o metabolismo dos animais pré-históricos e até seus níveis de atividade.
O trabalho também chama atenção para fósseis que já estão guardados em museus e universidades. Segundo Grice, coleções antigas podem conter informações microscópicas, químicas e minerais que passaram despercebidas em análises anteriores.
A pesquisadora ressalta, porém, que o objetivo não é encontrar DNA de dinossauro para recriar animais extintos, mas entender quanta informação molecular pode sobreviver ao longo de milhões de anos.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: AI Image Enhancement Improves Detection Of Flip-Chip Interconnect Defects (MCL, PVA TePla, ASE)
articles.text:
Home
                        TECHNICAL PAPERS
		
								November 2nd, 2026 - 
								By: Technical Paper Link
								
							
Researchers at Materials Center Leoben, PVA TePla, and Advanced Semiconductor Engineering (ASE) published “AI-Based Image Enhancement Improves Detection of Interconnect Defects in Microelectronic Packaging.”
Abstract Excerpt:
“Traditional failure-analysis (FA) methods face growing challenges due to the increasing miniaturization and complexity of modern semiconductor devices. In particular, the detection of cracks in the extreme low K layers of flip-chips, utilized in advanced packaging architectures at the back end of line (BEOL), is challenging. To improve detectability of these so-called “white bumps”, we propose an AI-based image-enhancement workflow, specifically tailored to improve scanning acoustic microscopy (SAM) images.”

articles.title: MobiKwik posts Rs 11.83 Cr profit in Q2 of FY27
articles.text:
MobiKwik posts Rs 11.83 Cr profit in Q2 of FY27
MobiKwik’s revenue grew 9.4% in Q2 FY27, driven by higher gross merchandise value (GMV) and improved margins.
MobiKwik reported a net profit in the second quarter of FY27, compared with a loss in the year-ago period, marking its fourth consecutive profitable quarter and its highest-ever quarterly profit.
The fintech company posted a net profit of Rs 11.83 crore for the July-September quarter, against a loss of Rs 28.61 crore in Q2 FY26.
Revenue rose 9.4% year-on-year (YoY) to Rs 295.70 crore. MobiKwik attributed the quarter’s performance to higher gross merchandise value (GMV) growth and improved margins.
“We believe that the operating leverage in our business model will compound as we evolve into an AI-first company. Our continued focus on cost optimisation and operating efficiency is further strengthening our operating model and will drive profitability as we scale,” said Bipin Preet Singh, MD & CEO, MobiKwik.
According to MobiKwik, its payment business recorded a 35% year-on-year (YoY) growth in gross merchandise value (GMV) to Rs 59,677 crore in Q2 FY27. Consumer payments GMV grew 27% YoY to Rs 46,375 crore, while lending disbursals rose 34% to Rs 1,082.6 crore during the quarter.
The company’s registered user base increased to 196.3 million in Q2 FY27, compared with 183.5 million in the corresponding quarter last fiscal.
MobiKwik is also accelerating the adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) across engineering, lending, customer experience, and risk management. According to the company, AI now generates 92% of its code, helping accelerate go-to-market initiatives by 55%. Its Help LLM resolves 91% of customer queries, while fraud detection is entirely AI-led.
The fintech company added that its AI-powered collections platform facilitates 55% of early collections and has improved collection rates by 33%. Voice AI has also helped achieve 30-40% higher customer connect rates.

articles.title: Zelda: Ocarina of Time : le voyage rapide a été supprimé pour préserver « l'exploration et la découverte »
articles.text:
Le retour de The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time est l’occasion pour Nintendo de revenir sur les choix de conception de l’un des épisodes les plus importants de la saga. Dans un nouvel épisode de la série Les développeurs ont la parole, publié sur son site officiel ce lundi 2 novembre, Eiji Aonuma, producteur de la série, et Hidemaro Fujibayashi, tous deux producteurs du remake, évoquent notamment les changements envisagés pendant le développement, dont certains n’ont finalement pas été conservés.
C’est le cas du voyage rapide. Dans Breath of the Wild, les nombreux points de téléportation permettent de parcourir rapidement le monde particulièrement vaste de cet épisode. Eiji Aonuma a donc souhaité reprendre cette idée dans le remake d’Ocarina of Time, afin d’éviter aux joueuses et aux joueurs de devoir traverser Hyrule à chaque déplacement, en enchaînant les roulades pour avancer plus vite bien sûr.
Le jeu de 1998 permettait déjà de se téléporter. Sheik y apprend à Link six mélodies à jouer à l’ocarina, comme le Menuet des Bois ou le Boléro du Feu, qui l’emmènent à des endroits précis, le plus souvent devant les temples. Mais ce système se limite à une poignée de lieux, alors que Breath of the Wild compte de nombreux points de téléportation.
À la demande d’Eiji Aonuma, l’équipe a donc ajouté des points de téléportation absents du jeu original, offrant plusieurs raccourcis. Mais après avoir testé cette version, les développeurs ont constaté un problème : « En essayant de jouer avec ces points de téléportation, on s’est aperçu qu’on passait à côté de certains moments de découverte, lorsqu’on qu’on s’arrêtait en chemin pour se demander : « Minute, qu’est-ce que c’est que ça ? », reconnaît Eiji Aonuma.
Bien qu’à l’origine de l’idée, il a donc tout simplement marche arrière : « Cela nous a rappelé, une fois de plus, l’importance de ces moments de découverte dans la structure même de ce titre. »
Zelda: Ocarina of Time s’articule autour de l’exploration et de la découverte
Ces moments imprévus font le sel d’un bon Zelda depuis le premier épisode, sorti en 1986. Ils étaient essentiels à Ocarina of Time en 1998, et le restent aujourd’hui. En traversant Hyrule, les joueuses et les joueurs peuvent tomber sur des personnages, des ennemis ou des éléments intrigants qui incitent à l’exploration. Des points de téléportation auraient permis de sauter ces rencontres.
« Depuis le tout premier opus de la série, le gameplay s’articule autour de deux concepts clés : l’exploration et la découverte. On remarque quelque chose au loin, on se demande ce qui peut bien nous attendre là-bas et on s’en rapproche pour en savoir plus. Ce qu’on découvre sur place apporte la solution permettant de résoudre l’énigme suivante. Cette approche a perduré jusqu’aux jeux The Legend of Zelda actuels », rappelle Hidemaro Fujibayashi.
Sans nouveaux points de téléportation, la plupart des trajets se feront toujours à pied ou à cheval. Nintendo les rend tout de même moins longs : Link peut désormais courir plus vite et sauter d’une simple pression sur un bouton, et retrouve sa monture, Epona.
En retirant ces points de téléportation, l’équipe a fait passer l’exploration au cœur d’Ocarina of Time avant le confort de jeu. Le remake sort ce jeudi 5 novembre exclusivement sur Switch 2, et on pourra toujours y faire des roulades.

articles.title: Les pirates n’ont même plus besoin de trier leurs données volées : ce malware charge Claude de repérer celles qui peuvent rapporter le plus
articles.text:
Des chercheurs viennent de mettre au jour un infostealer capable de fouiller jusque dans les reçus Uber Eats de ses victimes, avant de confier son butin à Claude pour évaluer ce que les pirates pourraient en tirer. Un procédé qui pourrait leur permettre de repérer plus rapidement les comptes les plus lucratifs à exploiter, sans avoir à examiner eux-mêmes toutes les données volées.
Une facture de livraison pour retrouver une adresse personnelle, un compte Roblox pour estimer la valeur d'objets virtuels, des identifiants professionnels pour identifier un employeur : les développeurs de VOLTA-AUTODOXER ont visiblement compris l'intérêt de recouper les traces de notre vie numérique. Dans une enquête publiée le 31 octobre dernier, les chercheurs de Cisco Talos ont révélé l'existence d'un malware poussant l'exercice jusqu'à confier l'analyse des données volées à une intelligence artificielle chargée de dresser un profil détaillé de la victime et d'identifier ce qui pourrait rapporter le plus aux cybercriminels.
Protégez votre entreprise gratuitement pendant 30 jours
Découvrez Bitdefender Ultimate Small Business Security et protégez votre activité contre les cybermenaces. Aucune coordonnée bancaire requise.
Un malware qui confie à l'IA l'analyse des données volées
Dans le détail, VOLTA appartient à la famille des infostealers, ces logiciels malveillants spécialisés dans le vol d'informations. Une fois exécuté sur un PC Windows, il siphonne les identifiants et les données de cartes bancaires enregistrés dans les navigateurs, les accès aux comptes de messagerie, les sessions Discord, Telegram ou Steam, mais aussi les mots de passe Wi-Fi et les portefeuilles de cryptomonnaies qu’il peut tenter de déverrouiller.
Le programme réutilise également les sessions dérobées pour accéder aux comptes en ligne de la victime et y recueillir davantage d'informations. Il peut, par exemple, consulter Gmail à la recherche de confirmations de commandes Amazon, PayPal ou Uber Eats, et parcourir les historiques de livraison de certains services. Ces informations lui permettent de confirmer une adresse personnelle et d'enrichir le profil de son propriétaire. Il regroupe alors ses découvertes dans un dossier comprenant, entre autres, l'identité présumée de la victime, son domicile, son employeur et ses ressources numériques.
VOLTA peut ensuite soumettre ce dossier à Claude, par l'intermédiaire d'OpenRouter, un service donnant accès à plusieurs modèles d'IA, et lui demander de se comporter comme un analyste du renseignement, chargé d'évaluer les ressources de la victime selon leur potentiel financier. Il confie aussi au modèle l'examen de ses habitudes de sécurité, dont la qualité de ses mots de passe, afin de repérer les faiblesses susceptibles de faciliter de nouvelles attaques.
Les développeurs ont anticipé les éventuels refus de Claude. Si le modèle refuse de répondre ou si la requête échoue, VOLTA peut solliciter Kimi, puis Gemini. L'analyse par IA n'est toutefois pas indispensable à son fonctionnement : le malware peut transmettre les informations volées sans passer par cette étape. Les données recueillies et, le cas échéant, l'analyse de l'IA sont envoyées à l'attaquant via Telegram. Le programme peut ensuite supprimer son propre exécutable pour limiter les traces de son passage.
Comment se protéger de VOLTA ?
Pour l'heure, Cisco Talos ne documente aucune campagne d'infection active et ne précise pas comment VOLTA pourrait arriver sur un ordinateur. Impossible, donc, de désigner un piège particulier à éviter. Pour les particuliers, la prévention repose sur les précautions habituelles contre les logiciels malveillants : vérifier la provenance des programmes téléchargés, conserver une protection antivirus active et maintenir Windows ainsi que ses applications à jour.
Les chercheurs ont néanmoins identifié un moyen de contrer l'une des techniques utilisées par VOLTA pour contourner le chiffrement des données de Chrome. En limitant les programmes autorisés à lancer le navigateur sans afficher son interface, les administrateurs peuvent bloquer cette méthode de récupération des informations protégées. La mesure concerne principalement les ordinateurs administrés en entreprise et ne bloque pas ses autres capacités de vol.
Si l'infection a déjà eu lieu, la disparition du programme ne signifie pas que les comptes sont hors de danger. Les pirates peuvent conserver des sessions de connexion dérobées, même après un changement de mot de passe. Il faut donc intervenir depuis un appareil sain, renouveler les identifiants concernés et déconnecter les sessions ouvertes depuis les paramètres de sécurité des différents services. Les clés SSH et autres secrets d'authentification potentiellement compromis doivent également être révoqués ou renouvelés.
Enfin, si la phrase de récupération d'un portefeuille de cryptomonnaies était enregistrée sans protection sur l'ordinateur, Cisco Talos recommande de considérer ce portefeuille comme compromis et de transférer les fonds vers un nouveau, créé dans un environnement sûr.

articles.title: KI-Agenten sollen Zivilisation in Minecraft aufbauen – und verlieren sich in Bürokratie
articles.text:
KI-Agenten sollen Zivilisation in Minecraft aufbauen – und verlieren sich in Bürokratie
Was passiert, wenn KI-Agenten innerhalb von nur drei Stunden eine blühende Zivilisation aufbauen sollen? Diese Frage haben Forscher:innen von Y Combinator und Olam Labs in einem Experiment mit 50 KI-Agenten in Minecraft untersucht. Schnell zeigte sich: Aus dem ambitionierten Ziel wurde nichts. Anstatt eine Hochkultur zu etablieren, verbrachten die Agenten ihre Zeit in überfüllten Unterkünften und rationierten knappe Nahrungsvorräte.
Es entstand eine Art Regierung inklusive schriftlich festgehaltener Regeln und einzuholender Genehmigungen. Eine Gruppe von KI-Agenten habe allein elf Minuten damit verbracht, einen Verwalter für Dünger zu benennen. Das geht aus dem Blogbeitrag der Forschungsgruppe hervor.
KI-Agenten zeigen überraschendes Verhalten
Eigentlich sollen KI-Agenten nützliche Werkzeuge sein, aber die Realität sieht oft noch anders aus. In den vergangenen Monaten wurden zahlreiche Fälle bekannt, in denen sie sich nicht wie beabsichtigt verhielten. Ein Beispiel dafür lieferte die Meta-Forscherin Summer Yue: Sie wollte ihr Postfach von einem Openclaw-Agenten verwalten lassen – aber dieser löschte sämtliche E-Mails. Auch auf mehrfache Befehle habe die KI nicht reagiert.
Um solche Verhaltensweisen besser zu untersuchen, setzen Forscher:innen KI-Agenten immer häufiger in virtuellen Spielwelten ein. So brachten beispielsweise Wissenschaftler:innen des MIT in einer Studie 13 KI-Agenten auf eine simulierte einsame Insel und überließen sie dort sich selbst. Um sich die Zeit zu vertreiben, dachten sich die Agenten Spiele aus, was laut der Forschungsgruppe auch Einblicke in ihr Lernverhalten gab.
Jetzt hat auch ein Team aus Forscher:innen von Y Combinator und Olam Labs das Verhalten von KI-Agenten in virtuellen Welten untersucht. Als Testumgebung diente unter anderem das beliebte Spiel Minecraft mit seinen verschiedenen Modi. Die Forschungsgruppe setzte Hunderte Agenten aus und beobachtete, wie sie in der freien Welt zusammenarbeiteten – oder konkurrierten.
Der erste Test war ein einfacher Kooperationsversuch: 50 Agenten, die auf GPT-6.1-Sol von OpenAI basierten, sollten innerhalb von drei Stunden eine blühende Zivilisation aufbauen. Das Ergebnis war überraschend: Die virtuelle Gesellschaft scheiterte. Stattdessen gaben die Agenten viele ihrer anfangs gesteckten ehrgeizigen Ziele schnell wieder auf und es zeichnete sich laut den Forscher:innen eine Tendenz zur Bürokratie ab.
Wie sich die Verhaltensweisen unterscheiden
Im nächsten Schritt ließ die Forschungsgruppe zehn GPT-6.1-Sol-Agenten gegen zehn Claude-Opus-5.5-Agenten antreten. Ziel war es, die gegnerische Basis zu erobern und gleichzeitig die eigene zu verteidigen. „Die GPT-Agenten entwickelten deutlich aggressivere und ausgefeiltere Strategien“, stellten die Forscher:innen fest. Claude verhielt sich im Test defensiver.
Interessant waren demzufolge auch die Unterschiede im Umgang mit Problemen: „Ein Tool-Fehler verhinderte das Zerbrechen von Blöcken. GPT diagnostizierte den Fehler und teilte Workarounds mit, während mehrere Claudes zu dem Schluss kamen, dass das Zerbrechen unmöglich sei.“ Auch im Spiel Mindustry, einer Art leichtem RTS-Kampfspiel mit Tower-Defense-Modus, besiegten die GPT-Agenten Claude mit sechs zu eins.
Die Studie von Y Combinator und Olam Labs ist zwar begrenzt, gibt aber einen Einblick, wie sich KI-Agenten verschiedener Anbieter in konkreten Situationen verhalten. Laut den Forscher:innen hätten die GPT-Agenten eher wie ein Bienenstock agiert. Die Claude-Agenten hätten zwar ebenfalls eine:n Anführer:in ernannt, Entscheidungen aber eher demokratisch getroffen.
Der Blogbeitrag endet mit offenen Fragen: Wie ändern sich Hierarchien je nach Modellzusammensetzung eines Teams? Und könnte ein großer Schwarm weniger fähiger Agenten einen kleinen Schwarm leistungsstärkerer Agenten schlagen? Diese Fragen könnten laut den Forscher:innen Ansatzpunkte für weitere Versuche bieten.
Das eigentlich spannende Gegenexperiment wäre für mich:
Keine Agenten mit dem Auftrag „Baut eine Zivilisation“.
Nur Umwelt, Ressourcen, Bedürfnisse, Erinnerung, Beziehungen und Konsequenzen.
Und dann schauen, ob überhaupt etwas entsteht, das wir Zivilisation nennen würden.
Genau an so einem System arbeite ich gerade.

articles.title: Google disrupts million-device XCPE Android malware botnet, bans TV box maker
articles.text:
Google and industry partners have dismantled the XCPE malware botnet consisting of more than 1.3 million Android TV streaming TV boxes that Google says its manufacturer intentionally infected with malware to generate revenue through cybercrime activities.
The company attributes the botnet with high confidence to Chinese device manufacturer Videostrong Technology Co, accusing the company of deliberately installing a persistent backdoor into devices it manufactured and selling access to criminal affiliates.
These affiliates used the backdoored devices to deploy malicious modules that were used fir ad fraud, turned infected devices into residential proxies, and installed additional malware.
As part of the disruption, Google says it took down XCPE command-and-control (C2) servers used by more than a dozen related malware families, cutting off access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices.
These additional devices were compromised through malware distributed through other means than XCPE, and include retail set-top boxes, karaoke machines, and telehealth hardware. Google says that not all of them are Android devices.
Google has also terminated its relationship with Videostrong, revoked its license to manufacture Android TV devices with preloaded Google apps and services, and banned the company and its future affiliates from producing certified Android devices or supplying software to certified vendors.
"We assess with high confidence that the backdoor and botnet were intentionally developed, deployed, and operated for financial gain by Videostrong Technology Co.," Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) said in a report published Monday.
Google says the disruption involved Japan's National Police Agency and security companies Lumen, HUMAN Security, Plume, Synthient, and TrendAI, which coordinated to analyze the malicious infrastructure and disrupt its operations.
The XCPE botnet
Unlike other botnets that commonly breach devices through vulnerabilities or by tricking users into installing malware, the XCPE botnet was embedded directly into device firmware during manufacturing.
Google says Videostrong had been developing and distributing the malware across multiple device brands and models for years, evolving its capabilities to evade detection and support different criminal affiliates.
"We found this malicious software built directly into many different device models and brands over multiple years, supported by dedicated infrastructure and constantly evolving configurations to evade detection and manage their affiliates," Google says.
The main backdoor component, tracked as x.cpe and com.oemservice, run with Android system-level privileges.
The malware uses a modular architecture that separates its backdoor functions from modules designed to generate revenue for affiliates.
After an infected device starts, XCPE contacts a command-and-control server on the anyevonline[.]com domain to obtain connection information and credentials for an MQTT message broker, which is then used for receiving commands.
Google says the malware uses different subdomains of anyevonline[.]com depending on the Android version and device type. The MQTT broker, which was hosted at mqtt.szbboys[.]com, allowed operators to send commands and deploy other malware to infected devices.
Through this connection, operators can remotely control compromised devices and perform malicious actions, such as:
- Silently downloading and installing additional Android applications.
- Disabling Google Play Protect.
- Executing shell commands and scripts with system privileges.
- Capturing screenshots and injecting keystrokes.
- Collecting account information, device details, installed application lists, and system logs.
- Conducting network reconnaissance and establishing reverse shells.
The devices were also used to generate revenue by installing malware modules belonging to other operators, turning the backdoor into a plug-in cybercrime platform for other cybercriminals.
According to Google, these modules included software associated with residential proxy services such as Linkfog, AppSalt/Honeygain, GaGaNode, NetNut, and Traffmonetizer, which was used to route third-party internet traffic through infected devices without their owners' knowledge or consent.
Other modules committed ad fraud by generating ad impressions, loading hidden webpages, and clicking advertisements. Some modules installed other backdoors, including Moyu, Spirit, and Bird, to download and execute other malware.
Google says the botnet operators continuously changed the malware's architecture to avoid detection.
In late 2024, Videostrong began using a separate loader called com.abc.nexus, which ran the malicious modules while XCPE focused on communications with the C2 infrastructure.
Since August 2026, the operators began replacing that loader with smaller, specialized droppers disguised as Android system applications.
Videostrong attribution
In a separate coordinated report, cybersecurity firm Synthient explains how it traced the XCPE backdoor and infrastructure to Videostrong after discovering the malware preinstalled on a MECOOL KM9PRO Max Android TV box purchased in late 2025.
During its investigation, Synthient found a publicly accessible directory on the malware's file.anyevonline[.]com server that hosted backdoors used by the operators. The open directory also included a PDF folder containing a PDF by Owen Cao, the R&D director of Videostrong Technology Co.
Researchers also found that Videostrong's videostrong[.]cn domain pointed to the same IP address as mqtt.anyevonline[.]com, the command-and-control server that allowed operators to list compromised devices, push out commands, and manage application installations.
In addition, Synthient discovered that numerous Videostrong company email addresses had been used to sign the backdoors.
Google says the evidence indicates the manufacturer deliberately installed the malware rather than a rogue employee or a development oversight.
"We believe this campaign wasn't an isolated rogue insider or a development oversight," Google said.
Google also says it has modified its certification review process after discovering that Videostrong used obfuscation techniques to evade security testing and load malicious code after devices first booted.
While Google says the takedown has disrupted XCPE's operations, the malware has not been removed from in infected devices and will automatically reinstalls itself from the /oem/ partition if removed.
As a result, users would need to install clean firmware to remove the infection or disconnect the affected device from the internet to prevent further malicious activity.
BleepingComputer has contacted Google with additional questions about the botnet and will update the story if we get a response.

articles.title: Apple préparerait 3 nouveaux iPad pour 2027 : voici tout ce qui va changer
articles.text:
Après avoir lancé un nouvel iPad mini avec écran OLED, la firme de Cupertino ne compte pas s’arrêter en si bon chemin. Selon le bien informé Mark Gurman de Bloomberg, la petite famille des tablettes Apple va accueillir trois nouveaux membres : un iPad Air, un iPad d’entrée de gamme et un nouvel iPad Pro, tous attendus dans la première moitié de 2027.
Un passage à l’OLED pour l’iPad Air
Le prochain iPad Air pourrait franchir un cap important en adoptant enfin un écran OLED. Ce modèle, qui n’avait pas connu de refonte majeure depuis 2020, devrait malheureusement conserver une dalle avec un taux de rafraîchissement de 60 Hz, comme le nouvel iPad mini OLED, et faire l’impasse sur Face ID au profit de Touch ID. Une manière pour Apple de mettre en avant le 120 Hz sur ses iPad Pro.
Sous le capot, ce nouvel iPad Air devrait troquer sa puce actuelle contre un processeur M5, même si cela reste à confirmer. Côté tarifs, le modèle de base de 11 pouces devrait se situer dans une fourchette proche des prix actuels, soit environ 819 euros pour la version 11 pouces et 1 019 euros pour la version 13 pouces.
Un iPad d’entrée de gamme avec Apple Intelligence
L’iPad classique va lui aussi avoir droit à sa mise à jour, la première depuis début 2025. Apple intégrerait directement une puce A19 accompagnée de 8 Go de RAM, une configuration qui rendrait enfin l’intelligence artificielle d’Apple compatible avec la tablette la moins chère du catalogue.
À lire : L’iPad 12 d’Apple repoussé à 2027, mais avec de grosses surprises sous le capot
Côté connectivité, l’appareil intégrerait une puce N1 ainsi qu’un modem C1X pour doper les performances réseau. Aucun changement majeur n’est prévu du côté du design ou de l’écran, si ce n’est l’arrivée potentielle de nouveaux coloris.
Une chambre à vapeur pour l’iPad Pro
Le prochain iPad Pro pourrait quant à lui être équipé d’une chambre à vapeur pour la gestion thermique. Il s’agit d’une solution déjà déployée l’année dernière sur l’iPhone 17 Pro. Hormis l’intégration d’une nouvelle puce M6 ou potentiellement M7, les évolutions devraient se faire discrètes.
Le prix de vente de l’iPad Pro ne bougerait pas, c’est-à-dire 1 319 euros pour le format 11 pouces et 1 669 euros pour la version 13 pouces. Cette nouvelle génération arriverait environ trois ans après la dernière grande refonte de la gamme Pro. Espérons qu’Apple réserve quelques surprises sur ce modèle d’ici sa sortie.
