articles.title: The non-technical founder's dilemma — and how a new accelerator aims to solve it - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Some of Africa’s best startup ideas never become products because the person who had them can’t write code. A nurse in Kisumu knows exactly why clinic appointments get missed. A market trader in Lagos understands the cash-flow gaps that keep small vendors stuck. A logistics manager in Johannesburg can see the inefficiencies that cost businesses millions.
None of them needs to be a software engineer to spot the opportunity, but turning that insight into a working app is where many stall.
The non-technical founder is a familiar figure in African tech. They bring market knowledge, sales instincts and lived experience of the problems they want to solve. They also face real obstacles that technical founders rarely do. Understanding both sides is the first step to building something that lasts.
The downsides of building without a technical background
First is dependence on others to build the core product. For a software startup, the product is the business. A founder who can’t build it relies on freelancers, agencies or a technical co-founder. That dependence can leave them unable to judge quality, estimate timelines or spot when a project is going wrong.
This also leads to high upfront costs. Hiring developers is expensive, and good engineers are in high demand across the continent and from remote employers abroad. Many founders burn through their savings or early capital on a first version before they have tested whether customers want it.
Many such founders then hunt for a technical co-founder. But finding a skilled engineer willing to join an unproven idea for equity is hard. Many founders spend months searching, and some settle for a mismatched partnership that later breaks down.
You also have to take into account credibility with investors. Early-stage investors often ask who is building the product. A team without in-house technical capability can be seen as a risk, especially for companies pitching themselves as tech-led.
Then there is slower iteration. Startups win by testing, learning and changing fast. When every small change needs a developer’s time and an invoice, founders iterate less often and learn more slowly. And there will be communication gaps – translating a business vision into technical requirements is a skill in itself. Vague briefs lead to products that technically work but miss the point.
Why non-technical founders often have the edge
Never fear, there is an upside, or several. Non-technical founders start with the problem, not the technology. Technical founders sometimes build impressive products nobody needs. Founders who come from the industry they are serving tend to begin with a real pain point and real customers.
In addition, domain expertise is hard to copy. A former pharmacist building a medicine-supply platform, or a farmer building an agri-tech tool, understands regulation, buyer behaviour and informal workarounds that an outsider would take years to learn.
Then there are sales and distribution skills. In many African markets the hardest part is not building the app but getting people to adopt it, often through agents, partnerships and trust built face-to-face. Founders with sales, operations or community backgrounds are often strongest exactly here.
Non-technical founders are also able to just focus on building their businesses. Freed from writing code, a non-technical founder can spend their time on customers, partnerships, fundraising and hiring, which are the jobs that decide whether a startup survives. And in addition, tools like AI coding assistants, no-code platforms and specialist build partners have lowered the barrier to getting a first version live. Disrupt Africa recently covered Exten AI, a South African startup letting founders build full-stack apps in plain language. Being non-technical is less of a barrier than it was even a few years ago, as long as founders have the right support.
How Disrupt Launchpad bridges the gap
Disrupt Africa has teamed up with Kenya-based Touch Inspiration to launch Disrupt Launchpad, an app development accelerator built for founders who have a clear idea but lack the technical skills, team or resources to build it.
The partnership combines two strengths. Touch Inspiration, founded in 2017, develops web and mobile apps, AI-powered tools and business platforms, taking products from defined requirements through to launch. Disrupt Africa, the continent’s leading tech startup news platform since 2014, brings an audience of users, customers and investors.
Here is how the programme answers the challenges above:
- No team, no problem. Founders get their app professionally built by an experienced development company, removing the dependence on finding a technical co-founder first.
- Lower cost of getting started. Development is offered at startup-friendly rates. Selected ventures may qualify for an equity-based partnership, which reduces the cash needed upfront.
- From requirements to launch. Touch Inspiration’s process starts with defining requirements, which helps close the communication gap between a founder’s vision and the finished product.
- Visibility after launch. Building an app is only half the battle. Disrupt Africa helps put new products in front of potential users, customers and investors, addressing the distribution challenge many startups underestimate.
Who should apply
Disrupt Launchpad is open to aspiring entrepreneurs and existing startups with a clear app idea. It suits founders who:
- understand their market and customer problem well, but can’t build the product themselves;
- have been quoted development costs they can’t afford upfront;
- want a professional build rather than a patchwork of freelancers;
- need help getting their product noticed once it launches;
Applications are open now at launchpad.disruptafrica.com.
Being non-technical has never stopped great founders from building great companies. What has held many back is the gap between idea and product. Programmes like Disrupt Launchpad aim to close it, so founders can spend their energy where their strengths lie – understanding customers, selling and growing the business.

articles.title: Test de l'Ultenic MX50 : l'aspirateur robot à l'excellent rapport qualité/prix mais à la navigation friable
articles.text:
Le marché des aspirateurs robots connaît une concurrence de plus en plus féroce, avec des références qui dépassent allègrement les 1 000 euros. Pour les constructeurs un peu plus en retrait, cela oblige à toujours plus d’innovation et de tentatives pour se démarquer en proposant des éléments différenciants.
Sur la tranche du bon rapport qualité/prix assez peu de constructeurs se lancent sur le secteur. Ces derniers privilégiant des flagship beaucoup plus onéreux.
Chez Ultenic, le credo se porte sur le bon rapport qualité/prix afin de proposer des aspirateurs robots accessibles. L’Ultenic MX50 est certes l’appareil le plus cher du catalogue de la marque, mais reste bien moins onéreux que nombre de ses concurrents. Une différence de tarif qui se ressent au quotidien ? Pas forcément, d’après le mois que nous avons passé avec lui.
Fiche technique
| Modèle | Ultenic MX50 | 
|---|---|
| Dimensions | 32,7 cm x 43,6 cm x 23 cm | 
| Surface couverte maximum pour un cycle de nettoyage | 200 m2 | 
| Détection des obstacles | Oui | 
| Couleur | Noir | 
| Fonction lavage | Oui | 
|  | Fiche produit | 
Design
Sur le plan du design, l’Ultenic MX50 mise sur le plastique, aussi bien pour son pare-chocs que pour son sommet. Dans sa version noire, la surface brillante de l’aspirateur robot est élégante, même si elle agglomère aisément les traces de doigts.
Pour ce qui est de la mise en place, elle est assez simple. Le robot aspirateur est livré avec quelques accessoires, un détergent et sa station. Il faut remplir le bac d’eau propre ainsi que le réservoir de détergent. Ensuite, il faudra retirer les languettes de protection entourant l’aspirateur robot.
Sur notre modèle de test, le pare-chocs s’est bloqué en cours de nettoyage, ce qui a arrêté le robot. Un petit coup de tournevis afin de libérer l’espace et le tour est joué.
La station de nettoyage reste assez compacte mais s’étale un peu en largeur. Ses deux réservoirs, l’un pour l’eau propre, l’autre pour l’eau sale, ont une capacité de 4 litres. Sur la façade, le capot cache un sac à poussière de 3 litres qu’Ultenic promet de ne changer que tous les 90 jours, une durée qui dépend en réalité de la fréquence des nettoyages. Le tapis de protection étanche situé au bas de la station n’est pas autonettoyant mais permet à l’aspirateur robot de s’y ancrer.
Le robot aspirateur lui-même reprend les codes du marché. À son centre, on trouve le dôme LiDAR dToF, qui porte sa hauteur à 9,7 cm. Pour son diamètre, l’Ultenic MX50 est plutôt compact avec 33 cm. C’est un produit globalement élégant qui ne jure pas réellement dans un domicile, même si le choix de plastiques est légèrement décevant.
Application : encore un léger retard
Pour accompagner l’usage de l’aspirateur robot, le constructeur met en avant l’application Ultenic. Celle-ci permet de centraliser l’ensemble des produits de la marque. Il suffit de scanner le QR Code du robot pour commencer la liaison. Il faudra aussi remplir les informations Wi-Fi de votre domicile.
Une fois la liaison établie, le MX50 s’attache à cartographier l’ensemble de votre domicile. Dans notre appartement de 60 m², l’aspirateur robot a répertorié l’ensemble des pièces en 10 minutes.
Lorsque tout est prêt, l’application centralise les usages quotidiens. Une fois la carte validée, il est possible de paramétrer les niveaux de nettoyage selon les pièces. Vous avez aussi la possibilité de paramétrer des zones interdites pour l’aspirateur robot.
En revanche, on peut regretter que l’Ultenic ne laisse pas la possibilité d’aller nettoyer une seule pièce comme peut le faire parfois la concurrence. À défaut, l’application propose un mode télécommande pour nettoyer une zone précise.
Autre point faible, l’aspirateur robot se déconnecte régulièrement de l’application lorsqu’il est mal placé par rapport à notre routeur Wi-Fi. Il faut ainsi réinitialiser l’Ultenic MX50 pour le reconnecter.
Toutefois, la gestion de chaque pièce est intéressante avec une personnalisation intense. Il est possible de séparer des pièces, les fusionner mais aussi personnaliser le nettoyage. Ainsi une pièce comme une cuisine peut avoir droit à deux passages.
Navigation : un aspirateur qui s’oublie
Si l’aspirateur robot est efficace dans sa cartographie, il a une navigation encore un peu à l’ancienne. Malgré un dôme LiDAR à son sommet et l’évitement d’obstacles par IA mis en avant par Ultenic, l’Ultenic MX50 navigue parfois à vue. S’il évite les obstacles évidents comme les portes et les chaises, les plus petits éléments sont embarqués.
Fils de crochet, bandes de tissu ou câbles, tout y passe. L’Ultenic a toutefois trouvé une parade : au lieu d’enrouler ces fils bien serré, il libère ses patins et s’arrête. En revanche, si un objet trop lourd vient à se retrouver dans la brosse d’aspiration, le MX50 se bloque et appelle à l’aide.
Pour le reste, les trajectoires choisies par l’Ultenic MX50 sont efficaces. Au contraire de certains modèles, l’aspirateur robot perd moins de temps à « réfléchir » face à des obstacles parfois inattendus. En bref, il reste un peu décevant sans toutefois que ces points faibles soient rédhibitoires.
Les trajectoires de nettoyage sont somme toute assez classiques, l’aspirateur robot faisant des passages réguliers traversant une pièce en zigzaguant.
Ultenic annonce aussi un franchissement des seuils jusqu’à 20 millimètres, ainsi qu’une détection des tapis par ultrasons : le robot relève alors ses serpillières et augmente sa puissance d’aspiration.
Performances : quasi irréprochable
L’Ultenic MX50 affiche une puissance d’aspiration de 20 000 Pa. Sur le papier, c’est moins que le Dreame L50s Pro Ultra (30 000 Pa), mais plus que le Tapo RV50 Pro Omni (15 000 Pa). À l’usage pourtant, le nettoyage des miettes est efficace sur chaque passage, même avec des débris un peu plus importants.
Pour ce qui est du nettoyage humide, l’Ultenic MX50 adopte deux patins rotatifs. Leur action permet de désincruster les taches au sol. Le lavage humide au sol est bon notamment avec l’apport du détergent.
On peut regretter que le réservoir d’eau au sein de l’aspirateur soit un peu léger pour un nettoyage plus intensif. En effet, à l’issue du lavage, il n’est pas rare que les serpillères soient quasi sèches. Le lavage est donc très efficace sur les trois quarts du parcours, moins sur la fin, quand les serpillères s’assèchent.
Entretien : simple et efficace
Pour l’entretien, la station fait l’essentiel du travail. Une fois le nettoyage terminé, l’aspirateur robot retourne à sa station. La station aspire alors les poussières récoltées et lave les serpillères à l’eau chaude (65 °C selon Ultenic), puis stocke l’eau sale dans le bac dédié.
Au rythme de trois nettoyages par semaine, nous avons dû laver le bac d’eau sale toutes les deux semaines. L’opération est simple : un peu de produit nettoyant et un jet d’eau suffisent à décoller le dépôt accumulé.
Il est même possible de nettoyer les serpillères en les détachant de l’Ultenic MX50. La station peut ensuite les sécher.
Autonomie
Comme pour la plupart des aspirateurs robots présents sur le marché, l’Ultenic MX50 dispose d’une autonomie suffisante. Dans mon appartement de 50 m², il nettoie tout en 1 h 30.
Pour pousser l’autonomie dans ses retranchements, nous avons lancé une session de nettoyage avec tous les réglages au maximum. L’aspirateur robot a tenu 2 h 44 et couvert toutes les pièces, avec une batterie descendue à 17 %.
Ultenic annonce jusqu’à 180 minutes d’autonomie, avec une batterie de 5 200 mAh et une reprise automatique du nettoyage après recharge. Notre mesure, réglages au maximum, est donc cohérente avec ce chiffre.
Prix et disponibilité
L’Ultenic MX50 est vendu 549,99 euros sur la boutique officielle de la marque, qui affiche un prix normal de 599,99 euros. C’est l’aspirateur robot le plus cher du catalogue mais il est régulièrement proposé en promotion en dessous des 450 euros.
Pensez aussi aux consommables. Ultenic propose un pack avec six sacs à poussière et trois filtres HEPA pour 593,99 euros, soit 44 euros de plus que le robot seul. À raison d’un sac tous les 90 jours au mieux, ces six sacs couvrent environ un an et demi d’usage.
Côté service, Ultenic assure une garantie de deux ans (accessoires exclus) et un service après-vente en France. La marque vend aussi les pièces détachées et consommables du MX50 sur sa boutique en ligne.
En termes de concurrence, il fait face au Dreame L50s Pro Ultra et au Tapo RV50 Pro Omni. Sur cette tranche de prix, l’aspirateur robot Dreame a une petite longueur d’avance sur les performances de nettoyage, mais l’Ultenic MX50 n’a pas à rougir et peut être l’une de nos recommandations surtout avec ses promotions.

articles.title: « Comment allons-nous rattraper notre retard ? » : l’IA trouve tant de bugs que PostgreSQL s’inquiète de sa capacité à innover
articles.text:
Comment innover quand il faut colmater les brèches ?
Depuis une dizaine d’années, PostgreSQL, l’un des systèmes de gestion de base de données open source les plus utilisés au monde, publie sa nouvelle version majeure entre la mi-septembre et la mi-octobre. La version 19 n’aura pas tenu ce calendrier.
Début octobre 2026, l’équipe chargée des sorties a repoussé la date de publication au 19 novembre. La raison ? Tant de bugs venaient d’être découverts et corrigés dans les versions précédentes que les développeurs ont préféré intégrer d’abord ces corrections à une dernière version de test.
Une annonce qui s’ajoute au retrait, quelques semaines plus tôt, de plusieurs nouveautés pourtant attendues dans cette version, dont la possibilité d’interroger des données sous forme de graphes.
Peter Eisentraut, membre de l’équipe dirigeante du projet, attribuait en partie ces abandons tardifs à la relecture de code assistée par l’IA, qui fait désormais remonter les anomalies à un rythme inédit : « On se retrouve avec une liste d’une quarantaine de rapports d’anomalies. Même si chacune ne nécessite en moyenne qu’une correction de trois lignes, leur traitement demande un temps incompressible, et le temps finit par manquer », écrivait l’ingénieur.
Dans un billet publié le 30 octobre et sobrement intitulé« Postgres 19 est en retard, et c’est la faute de l’IA », Robert Haas, l’un des principaux contributeurs du projet, va plus loin encore dans la désignation du bouleversement : « La réponse courte, c’est que les LLM sont arrivés. »
Beaucoup plus de bugs à corriger, mais pas plus d’humains pour le faire
L’ingénieur dresse un double constat. D’un côté, les modèles de langage détectent des failles que des décennies de relecture humaine n’avaient pas débusquées. De l’autre, ils ne lèvent pas pour autant le goulot d’étranglement. Chaque correctif proposé doit encore être compris, validé, adapté aux standards du projet et intégré par des mainteneurs humains. En d’autres termes, l’IA accélère la découverte des bugs bien plus vite que leur résolution.
Pour appuyer sa thèse, Robert Haas compare les modifications apportées au code entre le 8 avril et le 25 septembre de chaque année. Celles reportées sur la version en préparation sont passées de 724 en 2025 à 1 169 en 2026, soit une hausse de 61 %, et celles qui concernent aussi la version précédente, déjà en production, de 248 à 433, soit 75 % de plus.
L’ingénieur l’assure, cette hausse s’explique moins par une multiplication des erreurs des contributeurs que par le nombre croissant d’internautes signalant des bugs découverts à l’aide de LLM.
Selon lui, le temps consacré à ces corrections, notamment celles des failles de sécurité, n’a pas servi à travailler sur la version 19, ce qui a entraîné la décision de retirer certaines fonctions.
Ces failles sont d’ailleurs de plus en plus nombreuses : la mise à jour du 13 août en a corrigé 28, contre 11 en mai. Ni ce décompte ni les chiffres de Robert Haas ne permettent toutefois de savoir combien de ces problèmes ont été découverts grâce à l’IA.
Du bruit aux vrais bugs, un second problème pour l’open source
Si Robert Haas juge le retard de la version 19, pour l’heure, modeste, il se montre moins serein sur le long terme. « Comment allons-nous rattraper notre retard ? », s’interroge-t-il, en admettant ne pas savoir non plus comment le projet pourra continuer à innover.
Il n’est pas le premier à s’inquiéter des effets de l’IA sur l’open source, mais jusqu’ici, les plaintes visaient surtout des rapports inutiles. En janvier, le projet curl, un outil de transfert de données très répandu, a mis fin à ses primes aux bugs pour décourager les signalements de mauvaise qualité.
En mai, Linus Torvalds, le créateur de Linux, dénonçait une « agitation parfaitement inutile » face aux doublons, de nombreuses personnes trouvant les mêmes bugs avec les mêmes outils. Et le 1er octobre, Google a suspendu les nouvelles soumissions à son programme de récompenses open source, en invoquant une majorité de rapports automatisés non valides.
Le problème décrit par Robert Haas est différent, puisqu’il concerne de vrais bugs, si nombreux que les développeurs peinent à les corriger tout en préparant la nouvelle version.
Pour PostgreSQL, le prochain rendez-vous est fixé au 12 novembre, avec une mise à jour annoncée comme riche en correctifs et une dernière version de test de PostgreSQL 19. Si aucun problème n’apparaît, la sortie finale suivra le 19 novembre.

articles.title: Toujours plus loin, GTA 6 s’affiche jusqu’au Stade de France, et ce n’est qu’une partie de sa campagne marketing XXL
articles.text:
Le Stade de France, les tours Mercuriales, ou l'évidence Miami, la campagne marketing de GTA 6 prend des proportions hors norme avant la sortie du jeu, le 19 novembre. Son budget atteindrait au moins 150 millions de dollars, selon un élu américain.
La campagne marketing assez folle de GTA 6 s'est accélérée ces derniers jours après avoir gagné le Stade de France, qui s’est mis aux couleurs de Vice City. Le jeu s’affiche désormais aussi sur les tours Mercuriales de Bagnolet, aux portes de Paris, avec une jaquette géante aux armes effacées, pour un covering qui fait son effet. C’est pourtant à Miami que Rockstar dépense le plus visiblement, au point qu’un élu local évalue le budget promotionnel du jeu à au moins 150 millions de dollars, un montant absolument hallucinant.
GTA 6 prend ses quartiers en Seine-Saint-Denis
Le vendredi 30 octobre, le Stade de France a publié un message sur ses réseaux sociaux, non pas pour parler des matchs à venir sur place, mais pour souhaiter « Welcome to Vice City ». Vidéo à l'appui, la plus grande enceinte du pays, avec près de 80 000 places, a décidé de se mettre aux couleurs de la ville fictive de GTA 6, à l'occasion de sa sortie le 19 novembre. Le stade des Bleus et du XV de France, habitué aux finales et aux concerts géants, laisse donc la vedette à Jason et Lucia, ce qui en dit long sur le poids marketing du jeu.
À quelques kilomètres de là, les automobilistes du périphérique ont aussi vu les célèbres tours Mercuriales changer de visage. Le 6 octobre, des cordistes ont commencé à poser la jaquette de GTA 6 sur la façade de l'une de ces tours jumelles des années 1970, à la porte de Bagnolet. On la voit jusque depuis l'autoroute A3. D'autres visuels, consacrés séparément à Jason et à Lucia, sont venus compléter l'ensemble, si bien que les deux tours affichent désormais le jeu, avec un covering également achevé fin octobre.
L'affiche a d'ailleurs fait parler d'elle, puisque les armes ont disparu. Comme l'ont repéré plusieurs internautes, Lucia a perdu son pistolet? et un fusil d'assaut a été effacé de la jaquette. Personne n'a su expliquer ni justifier ces retouches, également repérées sur des affiches à Times Square, à New York. Plusieurs hypothèses circulent néanmoins, des règles de l'affichage publicitaire à une demande des propriétaires de la tour, sans qu'aucune ne soit confirmée.
Une campagne marketing GTA 6 qui fait dans la démesure
C'est pourtant à Miami, la ville qui inspire directement Vice City, que Rockstar dépense le plus visiblement. Le même slogan qu'à Saint-Denis, « Welcome to Vice City », s'affiche sur le toit du Kaseya Center, la salle des Miami Heat, la franchise de NBA, pour 975 000 dollars. Selon Forbes, l'enseigne doit rester en place jusqu'en avril 2027, voire plus longtemps peut-être. La ville a aussi autorisé jusqu'à six bannières, pour un montant pouvant atteindre 1,2 million de dollars. Miami Beach, de son côté, a approuvé de justesse la présence du logo « VI » sur le mobilier de ses plages jusqu'au 31 décembre, contre plusieurs millions de dollars.
Alors combien coûte l'ensemble ? Rockstar et Take-Two ne l'ont jamais dit, et l'éditeur ne publie que ses dépenses commerciales et marketing globales, tous jeux confondus. Lors d'un débat sur ces contrats, René Garcia, commissaire du comté de Miami-Dade, a toutefois avancé un budget d'au moins 150 millions de dollars, sans détailler son calcul. En mai, le patron de Take-Two, Strauss Zelnick, avait promis une campagne de très grande ampleur, en précisant que l'éditeur achèterait peu d'espaces à la télévision, contrairement à l'époque de GTA V. Le montant est colossal, mais il reste à ce stade une estimation.
Selon Netflix, le Large aperçu, la grande présentation du jeu, diffusée d'abord sur la plateforme, a cumulé 31,1 millions de vues en quatre jours. Mais la campagne n'est pas terminée. À noter que le 18 novembre, veille du lancement, les Miami Heat recevront les Milwaukee Bucks avec un uniforme et un parquet aux couleurs de Vice City, un match d'ailleurs diffusé en France sur Disney+, vers 1 h du matin. Les joueurs français pourront lancer GTA 6 une heure plus tôt. Le jeu se débloquera à minuit, heure locale, le 19 novembre, sur PS5 et Xbox Series X|S, et les versions numériques pourront être préchargées dès le 12. L'attente est déjà à un niveau record. Selon le cabinet Circana, près d'un joueur américain sur trois compte l'acheter.

articles.title: Deeptech startups gain VC attention as India’s investment landscape evolves
articles.text:
Deeptech startups gain VC attention as India’s investment landscape evolves
During a panel discussion at TechSparks 2026, an incubator, early stage venture capital firm and a late stage investor provided interesting perspectives on the evolving investment landscape in India, particularly in the areas of artificial intelligence and deeptech.
India’s deeptech startup ecosystem is witnessing growing investor interest, with themes such as technological sovereignty, import substitution, AI infrastructure and advanced manufacturing emerging as key investment opportunities. After years of limited access to early-stage capital, deeptech ventures are increasingly attracting funds willing to back them from the pre-seed stage, signalling a shift in the country’s venture capital landscape.
During a panel discussion at TechSparks 2026, an incubator, early stage venture capital firm and a late stage investor provided interesting perspectives on the evolving investment landscape in India, particularly in the areas of artificial intelligence and deeptech.
Priyanka Agarwal Chopra, Managing Partner and CEO of IIMA Ventures, said deeptech had traditionally been a challenging investment segment because of its high risks and longer gestation periods, which often did not align with conventional venture capital timelines.
“When we started, our founding vision was to address gaps in India's innovation and entrepreneurship ecosystem, particularly in markets and sectors where private sector capital was not available,” she said.
IIMA Ventures was among the early investors in India's deeptech ecosystem, supporting companies in areas that were then categorised as high technology. Chopra said two major themes currently driving deeptech innovation in India are technological sovereignty and import substitution.
She added that while investing in deeptech at the early stages was once a relatively isolated proposition, more funds are now showing interest in supporting companies even at the pre-seed stage.
The growing focus on building indigenous technology capabilities is also creating opportunities for Indian startups to address domestic requirements while developing products for global markets.
Anaina Malik, Partner at VU Venture Partners, said AI infrastructure would be an important investment opportunity as India expands its AI application ecosystem. She emphasised that infrastructure development should receive attention alongside application-led innovation.
Malik also identified agriculture and advanced manufacturing as underserved sectors with considerable potential for technological disruption. She said the firm was looking at startups addressing India's domestic requirements as well as companies building products and solutions for international markets.
According to her, the boundaries between domestic and global markets are increasingly dissolving, with international capital also showing greater interest in investment opportunities emerging from India.
Meanwhile, Sandeep Sinha, Co-founder and Co-CEO of Oister Global, said India's deeptech ecosystem had matured considerably, with several companies that began their journeys eight to 10 years ago now reaching commercial readiness.
He pointed out that many of these ventures had already addressed significant technology and research and development risks and were generating revenues from both domestic and international markets.
Sinha said deeptech companies were increasingly demonstrating the ability to create value through revenue growth, margin expansion and market expansion. The emergence of commercially viable businesses with greater revenue visibility represents an important development for investors evaluating the sector.
While acknowledging that the funding ecosystem remains somewhat fragmented, he described the current activity as 'chaos by design', adding that the increased movement of capital and investors over the past 18-24 months had brought deeptech into sharper focus.
The panellists also highlighted the importance of founder capabilities in determining investment decisions, particularly at the early stages when financial and operating data are limited.
Chopra said investors at the early stage place considerable emphasis on four parameters: founder depth, founder-problem fit, the unique insight of the entrepreneur and the market opportunity.
Sinha, meanwhile, stressed the need for founders to build predictable businesses and diversify their customer base rather than depend excessively on a single customer, irrespective of its importance.
Beyond AI
On investment sizes, Malik said VU Venture Partners' initial cheque sizes remained between $250,000 and $1 million. However, the firm had increased its follow-on investments, choosing to stay invested for longer and support founders through different stages of growth.
She added that evaluating AI startups had become more challenging because of the large number of companies identifying themselves as AI businesses. Consequently, the firm was placing greater emphasis on understanding the underlying technology through deeper due diligence.
Despite the growing investor focus on AI and deeptech, Chopra cautioned entrepreneurs against assuming that opportunities in other sectors had diminished. Consumer businesses, fintech and retail continue to offer substantial opportunities, supported by strong domestic demand.
She emphasised that India's startup ecosystem has room for multiple business models and sectors, and encouraged founders to pursue opportunities they are genuinely passionate about.

articles.title: Your Mobile Carrier Stores Your Call Logs for Years
articles.text:
In 2024, AT&T lost sensitive communication logs of 109 million customers in a massive data breach. Call logs can reveal a lot about you, like your closest relationships, where you live and work, and your daily routine.
109 million people (nearly a third of Americans) suffered a massive data breach in April 2024 that exposed their AT&T communication logs.
AT&T lost sensitive information including phone numbers, call and text counts, call durations, and location data from May to October 2022, and January 2023, meaning the data was approximately two years old at the time of the breach, impacting both current and former customers.
AT&T said the records didn’t contain call content, customer names, or Social Security numbers. That’s less reassuring than it sounds, because even on their own, call logs reveal a lot about you.
What are call logs?
Every call, text, and data session generates records inside your carrier’s network. The two kinds that matter here are:
- SIP messages. Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) manages calls and texts, both within a carrier and between networks. One message starts a session and another ends it. Carriers use them mainly to troubleshoot dropped calls and failed texts.
- Call Detail Records (CDRs). CDRs summarize each call, text, and data session: who was involved, when, for how long, and often which cell site your phone used. Carriers use them for billing and for settling charges with roaming partners.
Anyone with access to your call logs can identify your closest relationships, locate your home and workplace, and reconstruct your daily routine in more detail than you could yourself. If you called an oncologist a few years ago, there’s likely a record of it, how long you talked, and where you were. If you texted an old friend afterwards, there’s a log of that too.
Call metadata can even be correlated with publicly available information to derive identities.
Malte Spitz showed how far this goes. In 2011 he sued his telecom for the data it held on him, received roughly 35,000 records, and reconstructed a strikingly specific replay of several years of his activities.
Why call logs are easy to get
Three things make them an easy target.
They’re kept for a long time. Most carriers don’t say how long. Privacy policies typically promise to retain data for “as long as necessary to fulfill the purposes” of the policy. In 2022, responding to a request from the FCC chair, carriers disclosed that they kept geolocation data for as long as five years, far longer than phone service requires. One reason is to monetize it.
They sit in a few big targets. Carrier data is frequently breached. AT&T was one of many Snowflake customers hit by credential-based thefts, alongside Ticketmaster and Neiman Marcus. Salt Typhoon, the China-linked campaign, reportedly compromised every major US carrier, which could put call metadata for any American within reach.
They have other buyers. Retained logs are used to build detailed behavioral profiles that are sold to ad networks and data brokers and, in some cases, handed to the government.
The AT&T breach is the predictable result. The records were available to steal because they existed.

| Billing CDRs | 30 days | Years | 
| Daily totals | 60 days | Years | 
When a Cape subscriber makes a call, the signaling goes to the nearest radio tower and to Cape’s partner network operator, which passes it to Cape’s mobile core. The core forwards it to the recipient’s carrier.
Cape keeps SIP messages for 14 days to debug network issues, converts them into internal CDRs, and deletes those after one day. Daily totals (counts of calls, SMS, MMS, and data used per subscriber) are kept up to 60 days for billing and spam prevention.
CDRs sent by partner networks as billing evidence are held for 30 days, long enough to dispute a bill.
Cape’s partners and the tower operators generate logs too. For that reason Cape rotates the identifiers the towers see, which weakens their ability to tie those logs to you.
The audit
A retention claim is only worth what you can verify. Cape hired Trail of Bits to audit the feature in May and July 2026 and published the attestation.
During the audit, Trail of Bits found no evidence of violation of the two given claims:
- CDR files are being deleted within the retention policy.
- Cape does not extract or retain data from CDRs about individual consumer customers, except daily totals. Daily totals are the number of calls, number of SMS, number of MMS, and amount of data a subscriber used in a day. This data is retained for no more than 60 days and then deleted.
You can read the full audit write-up or 404 Media’s coverage.
You can’t un-breach a database, but you can shrink it
Better carrier security matters, but the more reliable control is to hold less. Records deleted days after a call can’t be stolen two years later.
For journalists, executives, security staff, and anyone who calls a doctor, lawyer, or source they’d rather not advertise, your carrier’s retention policy is part of your threat model.

articles.title: Après avoir aspiré vos données, ce virus demande à une IA d’évaluer votre valeur financière avant de s’autodétruire
articles.text:
Utiliser l’IA pour savoir si l'on est une cible assez rentable pour être piratée, voici le nouveau malware VOLTA sur Windows
Un nouveau malware Windows baptisé VOLTA-AUTODOXER pille toutes les données du PC avant de demander à l’IA Claude d’évaluer la valeur financière de sa victime et de s’autodétruire.
Repéré par les chercheurs de Cisco Talos, le logiciel malveillant VOLTA-AUTODOXER illustre une nouvelle méthode de la cybercriminalité sur Windows : “ratisser large, tout voler et laisser l’IA faire le tri.” Capable de s’effacer après l’attaque, ce voleur de données ne se contente plus de piller les fichiers. Il transmet désormais l’intégralité du butin à des modèles d’intelligence artificielle pour dresser un profil financier précis de chaque victime et hiérarchiser les comptes les plus rentables à exploiter.
VOLTA-AUTODOXER : quand l'IA évalue la rentabilité des données volées
Pour agir en toute discrétion, ce nouveau malware lance Google Chrome en arrière-plan afin de contourner ses sécurités internes et d’aspirer les mots de passe et cartes bancaires enregistrés. En parallèle, il ratisse le système pour récupérer les messageries Outlook, les comptes Discord, ainsi que tous les codes wifi de l’ordinateur.
Mais VOLTA-AUTODOXER va plus loin en exploitant directement les comptes déjà connectés. Il fouille ainsi les boîtes Gmail à la recherche de reçus d’achats Uber Eats, Amazon ou PayPal pour analyser les habitudes de dépenses et recouper l’identité complète de l’utilisateur, tout en tentant de forcer les portefeuilles de cryptomonnaies et en estimant la valeur des inventaires de jeux en ligne comme Roblox.
Toutes ces données sont ensuite regroupées sur l’ordinateur avant d’être envoyées à une IA via la propre connexion Internet de la victime. Le malware ordonne alors au modèle d’agir comme “un expert en cyber-enquête” chargé d’être “direct, précis et exact” pour classer le butin sous une rubrique intitulée “CE QU’ILS VALENT” et chercher des liens entre la vie privée de la cible et ses mots de passe.
Configuré par défaut sur Claude Opus 4.6 avec un paramètre strict limitant toute créativité pour garantir des réponses prévisibles, le virus contourne les potentiels blocages de sécurité en basculant automatiquement vers Kimi K2, puis Gemini 2.5 Flash. Vendu clé en main, VOLTA-AUTODOXER envoie directement ces fiches de cibles triées sur le canal Telegram du pirate. Comme le résume Cisco Talos, l’objectif est de “décharger l’opérateur du travail d’analyse” pour lui permettre de cibler immédiatement les victimes les plus lucratives.
En cas d’infection, bien que le fichier principal se supprime de lui-même, il laisse derrière lui un journal texte nommé volta_debug.txt, qui liste tout ce qui a été dérobé. Les chercheurs conseillent alors de se déconnecter immédiatement de tous ses comptes, changer l’intégralité de ses mots de passe et transférer ses éventuelles cryptomonnaies vers un nouveau portefeuille sécurisé.

articles.title: Los expertos en psicología coinciden: quienes eligen guardar silencio durante una discusión presentan una mejor inteligencia emocional
articles.text:
Para la psicóloga Olga Albaladejo, este tipo de silencio puede ser un recurso de regulación emocional. Es lo que ella llama silencio regulador. Es decir, el individuo decide callarse para recobrar la calma. De esta manera podrá hablar y decir algo más útil que lo primero que se le ha venido a la cabeza. También se podría ver como un indicativo de mayor inteligencia emocional.
El secreto está en cómo se maneja. Por ejemplo, en este caso, el que utiliza el silencio dice lo que quiere comunicar. Que quiere unos minutos para recuperarse. Y que va a volver a hablar.
Por cierto, tiene su cara B. Por ejemplo, si se utiliza para castigar o escapar de la situación, deja de ser regulador para convertirse en un obstáculo para el diálogo.
Por qué el cuerpo necesita una pausa
Hay un motivo fisiológico. El Instituto Gottman (que lleva décadas estudiando parejas) explica que aquellos que quedan en blanco o se cierran en banda suelen estar inundados. El cuerpo entra en modo lucha o huida. Aumenta el pulso y se liberan hormonas de estrés. Ya no es posible continuar la discusión de manera tranquila y respetuosa.
Hay unas normas para utilizarlo. Por un lado, debe ser suficientemente largo. El mínimo son 20 minutos. Es el tiempo que tarda el cuerpo en tranquilizarse. Además, es recomendable establecer un código (palabra o gesto) previamente.
Otro tema es qué hacer en esos minutos. En otro texto del mismo instituto se recomienda salir a pasear o ir a otra habitación. Además, evitar dar vueltas al conflicto. Tampoco es correcto utilizar el silencio hosco como neutralidad. Esto no es poner un límite (que sería decir dónde está el límite y mantenerlo).
El opuesto (el no avisar de que uno se va) tiene mal presagio en la literatura. Un metaanálisis (que agrupa 74 estudios con más de 14.000 participantes) liderado por Paul Schrodt (Universidad Cristiana de Texas) y publicado en Communication Monographs encontró que el patrón de exigencia y retirada (uno de los miembros exige y el otro se retira) estaba asociado a menor satisfacción en la pareja, menor intimidad y peor comunicación. (Aunque no es solo el silencio).
Cuando la discusión es en el móvil
¿Qué pasa si la discusión es en el móvil? Otro estudio de la Universidad Brigham Young analizó a 276 jóvenes americanos en pareja. Asociaron el uso de mensajes de texto para pedir perdón, arreglar diferencias o tomar decisiones con una peor calidad de la relación en las mujeres. En los hombres, ya el envío de muchos mensajes estaba asociado a menor calidad.
En el caso de chats, hay un término técnico. Se trata de silenciar la conversación. En los grupos de WhatsApp podemos hacerlo por ocho horas, una semana o siempre. De esta forma no tendremos notificaciones en nuestro móvil. Nosotros tenemos que escribir el mensaje de que volvemos en un rato.
El otro lado de la moneda lo contamos en Genbeta. El psicólogo Luis Miguel Real Kotbani escribía que “Guardar silencio no nos hace maduros, sino sumisos”. Hablaba de silencio como hábito de no molestar. Con el riesgo de acabar explotando. No es contradictorio con lo que decía Albaladejo. Se trata de dos tipos de silencio.
Uno es de unos minutos. Se avisa. Y se abre a conversación. El otro no tiene fecha de regreso.

articles.title: Windows 11 n'autorisera jamais le glisser-déposer pour repositionner la barre des tâches
articles.text:
La possibilité de repositionner la barre des tâches dans Windows 11 a longtemps été demandée par les utilisateurs. Mais durant des années, Microsoft s’était toujours refusée à offrir cette possibilité pourtant bien ancrée dans les habitudes de chacun depuis Windows 10. Pour justifier cela, la firme de Redmond avait expliqué être repartie de zéro pour développer la barre des tâches de son système d’exploitation.
Ce comportement verrouillé, vu par beaucoup comme une importante régression par rapport à Windows 10 a cristallisé les tensions chez les utilisateurs déjà remontés par les trop nombreux bugs de Windows 11. En janvier dernier, l’entreprise avait encore enfoncé le clou en déployant une mise à jour truffée de bugs, rajoutant encore un peu plus d’huile sur le feu. Face au torrent de critiques, Microsoft avait finalement mis un peu d’eau dans son vin. Promesse avait été faite d’apporter les changements et améliorations réclamés depuis des années par les utilisateurs.
Pour mettre à exécution sa promesse, Microsoft avait alors mis en place son plan secret, Windows K2, pour regagner la confiance des utilisateurs. Et la firme de Redmond a honoré sa promesse. La barre des tâches repositionnable a officiellement été déployée à grande échelle avec la mise à jour 26H2 de Windows 11, qui a par la même occasion donné un coup de boost inattendu aux PC, grâce aux optimisations réalisées par Microsoft.
Mais si la barre des tâches peut être repositionnée, elle ne bénéficie toujours pas des mêmes capacités que celle de Windows 10, notamment la possibilité de la déplacer en faisant un glisser-déposer.
Le déplacement de la barre des tâches avec un glisser-déposer n’arrivera pas
Les utilisateurs qui attendaient que Microsoft offre à la barre des tâches de Windows 11 les mêmes capacités que celle de Windows 10 risquent d’être déçus. La firme de Redmond vient en effet de confirmer que Windows 11 ne permettra jamais de déplacer la barre des tâches avec un glisser-déposer. L’entreprise justifie cette décision par le fait que ce comportement peut entraîner des déplacements accidentels. Et c’est Diego Baca, le Vice President en charge du design de Windows 11 qui le dit.
 I find headlines like these unnecessarily negative. Instead of saying “you still need” a third-party app, why not say “you can also use” one? It communicates the same information without framing everything as a shortcoming.
From our research, dragging the taskbar to reposition…
— Diego Baca (@bacadd) October 30, 2026
« D’après nos recherches, faire glisser la barre des tâches pour la repositionner peut entraîner des déplacements accidentels, ce qui est l’une des raisons pour lesquelles « Verrouiller la barre des tâches » existait dans les versions précédentes de Windows. Nous avons également constaté que changer la position de la barre des tâches n’est pas quelque chose que les gens font fréquemment.
Nous avons estimé qu’offrir un paramètre facilement accessible, à un simple clic droit, offrait une expérience plus intentionnelle et prévisible. C’est un choix de conception délibéré, et non une fonctionnalité manquante. » a-t-il ainsi expliqué dans un tweet en réponse à un article de nos confrères de Windows Central suggérant une appli tierce pour gérer plus facilement le repositionnement de la barre des tâches.
Car pour l’heure, la méthode pour repositionner celle-ci n’est pas des plus intuitives. Microsoft a en effet quelques efforts à faire de ce côté-là. Il faut en effet se rendre dans les Réglages > Personnalisation > Barre des tâches (ou faire clic droit sur la barre des tâches pour accéder au menu) pour effectuer la modification, alors que des applications tierces comme Taskbar location options permettent de repositionner la barre des tâches directement depuis un clic droit sur celle-ci.

articles.title: Moonshot 2026 showed the future of Africa's tech ecosystem
articles.text:
Atop Lagos’s newly renovated National Theatre, now the Wole Soyinka Centre for Arts & Culture, The Cavemen’s rendition of Redemption Song rose into the humid evening air. It was Tuesday, October 27, the opening mixer for Moonshot by TechCabal 2026, and one of Bob Marley’s seminal works felt like a fitting place to begin. Drawing partly on the words of Pan-Africanist Marcus Garvey, the song asks listeners to imagine freedom and their own responsibility for securing it.
How many people caught the symbolism? Here we were, gathered to discuss Africa’s technological future inside a cultural landmark that had been neglected for years before the Bankers’ Committee, led by the Central Bank, committed ₦68 billion ($58 million) and effort to restore it. The venue gave the conference’s theme, “Courage and Conviction,” a physical form.
“Our ecosystem is learning again what ambition costs,” Big Cabal Media (BCM) chief executive Tomiwa Aladekomo said in his opening remarks.
With Marley’s song in mind, it’s difficult not to think about what it takes to keep believing in something long enough to build it.
Over the next two days, that belief found expression in the crowds moving through the theatre, the companies exhibiting their products and, particularly, the young people arriving with ideas of their own.
The young want to build
The young people at Moonshot were difficult to miss. They were pitching, demonstrating products and looking for people who could help their businesses grow. In a country as youthful as Nigeria, their presence made sense. What stood out was how many were entering technology with building solutions to local problems in mind.
One of the more revealing moments came not from a stage discussion but from the corridors. After interviewing Flutterwave chief executive Olugbenga Agboola, Opeyemi Kareem, one of the youngest members of the TechCabal newsroom, walked alongside him through the busy venue.
It was an ordinary encounter at a conference designed to bring people together, but it captured something important about Moonshot: the distance between an aspiring journalist, entrepreneur or young technologist and some of the continent’s most influential technology leaders can suddenly be smaller.
Access to people who have built businesses, raised capital and navigated difficult markets is one of the less quantifiable benefits of gatherings like this.
Starting a company is an unusually demanding expression of confidence in the future. The electricity may be unreliable, customers may struggle to pay, while investors may take months to reply.
Yet people keep starting.
Africa’s young population—more than 60% of its people are under 25, according to the African Union—is frequently presented as an economic advantage. Realising that advantage requires institutions, financing, and opportunities that enable people to turn their abilities into productive work. The enthusiasm visible at Moonshot creates an obligation for those with resources to help it develop.
A founder’s determination can start a company. Whether that company survives also depends on the conditions around it.
By the next Moonshot, some of these founders would have changed direction. Some businesses would have closed. Others would have found customers, hired colleagues and earned the confidence to enter another market. Giving more of them a fair chance to reach that point would be a meaningful investment in the future on display in Lagos.
Building through the friction
For many entrepreneurs at Moonshot, an ordinary workday involves solving problems that have little to do with the product they set out to build.
When power goes out, a connection drops, or a payment takes longer than expected, someone on the team spends time resolving the issues instead of speaking with a customer.
These costs do not appear in the stories told about African ingenuity. The founder finds a workaround, and the business carries on. But every workaround consumes money, attention, and time. Eventually, the question is how much more a company could accomplish if fewer things stood in its way.
Idorenyin Obong, co-founder and chief executive of Grey, a US-based cross-border payments company, described one such obstacle while speaking to journalists on the sidelines of Moonshot.
“Most times, if you’re trading within Africa, there’s always some form of intermediary currency,” he said.
A Nigerian business paying a supplier in Kenya can find itself converting naira into dollars before the money becomes shillings. Grey says it has developed direct currency routes to reduce the number of steps.
The customer wants to know how much the payment will cost and when it will arrive. The supplier wants to release the goods. Somewhere between the two is a business opportunity for whoever can make that exchange dependable.
That is worth remembering after a conference full of ambitious ideas. There is considerable value in making an everyday task work properly.
Repeated often enough, that confidence makes room for growth.
Continental ambition requires local knowledge
Another encouraging feature of Moonshot was the determination among startups to look beyond their home markets.
For businesses gathering in Lagos, the continent offered customers, partners and possibilities still to be explored. The ambition felt expansive, and the work required to fulfil it will be painstaking.
A founder can enter a second market with a successful product and discover that almost everything around it needs to be rethought. The learning starts again.
This is where gatherings such as Moonshot are important. A conversation with an operator from another market can expose a faulty assumption before it becomes an expensive decision. A useful introduction can lead to a partner who understands what a visiting founder has yet to learn.
For younger companies, another lesson came from Flutterwave chief executive Olugbenga “GB” Agboola’s account of the company’s next phase. Speaking at Moonshot, he described plans to expand beyond payment processing into other financial services.
“If you can trust us with your payment, it’s much easier to sell to actually keep the money for you,” he said.
The sequence offers important lessons to founders across the continent. Solve a problem well enough for customers to trust the business. Pay attention to what they need next. Then establish whether the company has the people, systems, and licenses to provide it.
The same discipline should travel with a business across borders. Ambition opens the conversation, but local knowledge helps turn it into a lasting operation.
A bigger room brings greater expectations
Moonshot’s move to the National Theatre was an achievement in itself. Over 7,000 people came through a venue whose size now leaves room for the annual gathering to grow.
Moving to a bigger venue was a bet on the appetite for conversations on the future of Africa’s tech—and a commitment by BCM to give them more room. The crowds at the National Theatre showed how much that room was needed.
The programme’s breadth helped. Conversations ranged from payments and telecommunications to artificial intelligence, climate technology and the creative economy, with investment and public policy running through them.
One thread running through several discussions was that Africa’s technology story cannot be told through startups alone. Behind the applications people use every day are transport networks, payment rails, reliable connectivity, location data, financing and the infrastructure that allows businesses to operate.
The creative economy faces a similar challenge: talented filmmakers, musicians and content creators need distribution, commercial partnerships and payment systems to turn their work into sustainable businesses.
These are not necessarily the most glamorous parts of the technology conversation, but they are where the next opportunities and some of the hardest problems lie.
For founders, that offered a chance to look beyond their own sector and understand how developments elsewhere could shape the business they were building.
Innovation needs a harder test
There was another question worth carrying home: how will the industry know whether all this activity is improving anything?
Another question is who gets to participate in the growth of the technology economy. South Africa’s past discussions around digital skills and youth employment offered a useful reminder that building a technology ecosystem is not only about producing more startups or attracting investment.
It is also about creating pathways into work for the millions of young Africans who may never become founders but could become developers, technicians, digital marketers, designers and other skilled professionals.
At Moonshot, the wider conversation about Africa’s digital future was therefore also a conversation about jobs, access to skills and whether the industry can create opportunities at a scale that matches the continent’s youthful population.
Uche Amaonwu, director of the Gates Foundation’s Nigeria Country Office, brought that question to the AI discussion. He argued that success should be judged by improvements in people’s lives, with healthcare, education and agriculture among the areas where the technology could prove useful.
A health product must fit into the working day of the people expected to use it. An educational service needs evidence that students are learning. A tool for farmers must offer advice they can act on, at a cost they can afford.
Somebody must adopt the product and pay for it. And the benefit must survive contact with an ordinary day outside fancy air-conditioned boardrooms.
What happens after the gathering
After the two days of these conversations, the temptation is to carry everything home: every contact, every idea, every promise to catch up.
Then the ordinary working week resumes.
The people who get lasting value from Moonshot will have to make choices. Which conversation deserves a follow-up? Which assumption needs testing? Which potential partnership addresses a problem the business actually has?
For a founder, that might mean sending a specific question to an operator who has already entered the next market. For an investor, it could be taking a second look at a company whose progress is easier to understand through its customers than its pitch deck. For an established business, it might mean giving a young supplier its first meaningful contract, and paying on time.
These are modest actions compared with the ambitions expressed on stage. They are also how those ambitions acquire substance.
Africa’s technology future will be shaped by whether more promising companies can reach the point where customers depend on them, employees can build careers within them, and investors can see a credible return. Getting there will require reliable infrastructure, financing, and institutions that make the work easier to sustain.
The young founders at Moonshot offered reasons to believe that the future is worth committing to. Their determination was visible, and the support around them now needs to become equally tangible.
By the next gathering, there should be stories of what really followed some of these conversations. A product improved because someone asked a difficult question, a market entered through a connection made in Lagos, a business kept alive by a customer willing to take a chance.
The National Theatre supplied a fitting backdrop. Restoring it required people to commit resources and stay with the work long enough for others to gather inside.
“Won’t you help to sing these songs of freedom?” The Cavemen brought an important question into Lagos.
After two days, it was a question to take home. The founders showed what they were prepared to attempt, and around them were people who could offer capital, open a door, or become a first customer.
When Moonshot 2027 returns, the most interesting question will be what its participants made possible.

articles.title: Systemic Approach to Memory, Knowledge, and Context in Agentic AI Architectures
articles.text:
Key Takeaways
- Context engineering beats prompt engineering - the system that builds context matters more than the prompt itself.
- Separate context, memory, and knowledge - each serves a different purpose and should be managed independently.
- Balance history with real-time data - great agents combine experience with live signals.
- Hallucinations are often context failures - better context leads to more reliable reasoning.
- Optimize context, don't maximize it - small, relevant context outperforms large, noisy prompts.
| This article is part of the "Agentic AI Architecture" article series. In this series, we try to establish agentic AI architecture as a new type of software architecture that will likely dominate the industry for years to come. The articles, written by industry experts, cover various elements and aspects of agentic AI architecture. We aim to present the latest trends and developments shaping the new type of architecture as it enters the mainstream. | 
As the industry moves from chatbots to autonomous agents, the architectural bottleneck is shifting. The hard problem is no longer simply retrieving data. It is deciding what an agent should know, when it should know it, how long it should remember it, and what should be forgotten. As with humans, it is one thing to know and another to remember. Hence, memory and knowledge. Knowing when to use any of the existing "knows" by bringing it to memory depends on the task context. For example, if I want to cook an omelet, I don’t necessarily need to remember how to knead dough right now.
Let’s break it down.
Agents must reason across tools, sessions, users, and live systems, given that in an engineered system we can describe the context as a control plane. Context as a control plane is an architectural paradigm in which organizational, behavioral, and situational data (the who, what, and why) serve as the centralized governing layer for system operations, rather than being hardcoded directly into individual applications, AI models, or microservices. In our world, this will determine whether an agent acts like a reliable software system. Providing the wrong context highly increases the likelihood of the model hallucinating.
Knowledge of the system is our policies, governance, and hard truth. Knowledge acts as the system’s official textbook. It holds core business logic, strict policies, and databases. Back to our omelet example, part of the knowledge would be the need for eggs and a pan.
Memory is the critical layer that bridges historical data and real-time signals into a reasoning-ready state. What needs to be remembered for the current task? This is usually information given from knowledge, historical data, and current live events.
To summarize our three components:
- Context - the immediate, active, and temporary information the agent is utilizing at any given moment. It sits directly within the model's active context window (analogous to computer RAM).
- Memory - provides persistence. It allows the agent to retain information beyond a single interaction, enabling it to learn from past experiences and adapt to users over time.
- Knowledge - the underlying foundation of facts, concepts, and rules that the agent inherently possesses before interacting with the user. It is the domain-specific data used to train or fine-tune the system, or the reference library to which it is granted access. Highly curated data.
Our goal in agentic systems is, when given the task context, system knowledge, and memory, to turn data into the right memory state at the right moment.
Beyond that, there are limitations to this dynamic architecture paradigm; hence, we need to systematically address the economic costs of large language model (LLM) limitations and the technical, architectural roots of hallucinations. As developers and architects, learning to avoid the common "culprits" of agentic systems mismanagement is crucial. Dive in to learn how to design a sophisticated, multi-tiered architecture for the next generation of reliable agentic AI.
Shift into Context Engine
An LLM is only as good as how we use it. While the model generates, our system determines what it sees. To avoid hallucinations, we need a trustworthy system around it. Leveraging context, knowledge, and memory. To architect the system, we will separate the model from the surrounding machinery. Going forward, for the machinery around it, we will call it a context engine. The context engine is part of the context control plane. This is the orchestrator responsible for selecting, filtering, ranking, structuring, compressing, safeguarding, and delivering information before it ever hits the LLM inference endpoint. It pulls information from knowledge, categorizes it in memory, and determines what the agent's context should be at any given millisecond. This is a meaningful shift from simple prompt engineering to systems engineering.
From Prompts to State/Context Systems
Prompt engineering assumes the task is to craft a better instruction. Context engineering assumes the real task is to build a dynamic substrate that continuously assembles the right state for reasoning. The prompt is no longer about "What should I ask the model?" It is "What is the minimal, highest-value context the model needs in order to reason well right now?"
In a production-grade agentic architecture, we require dynamic systems that dictate what an agent "knows" at any given millisecond. Our system goal is to take what’s relevant and compile a new prompt encompassing the required information to improve the model's success likelihood.
Context as a Compiler
To understand how the Context Engine behaves, consider the analogy of a modern software compiler. A compiler translates high-level source code into machine-executable instructions; the context engine translates vast oceans of unstructured, disconnected raw, real-time, and historical data into a structured, reasoning-ready state. It builds a deterministic state machine that allows the probabilistic agent to execute safely. It ensures that inputs are authenticated, validated against business logic, stripped of personally identifiable information (PII), and securely sandboxed before the LLM generates a plan of action.
Thinking Through Architecture
Effective software architecture for autonomous AI agents requires reconciling several fundamentally conflicting paradigms of data management and data flow.
Historical vs. Real-Time Memory Streams
A robust agentic architecture must gracefully balance long-term "episodic" memory with immediate "sensory" input. Meaning that to build a useful context engine, our architecture must reconcile two very different categories of state: historical memory and real-time input.
Historical memory is the long-lived layer. It includes prior interactions, past decisions, user preferences, domain rules, internal documentation, and accumulated observations. This is what gives an agent continuity. It allows the system to behave as though it has experience.
Real-time input is the short-lived layer. It includes the current task, the latest events, live telemetry, fresh tool outputs, and environmental changes. This is what keeps the agent grounded in the present.
While vector databases excel at retrieving historical, semantic facts, agentic workflows frequently pivot on sub-second, real-time context. For example, if an AI DevOps agent is triaging a server outage, retrieving an architectural runbook from a vector store (episodic memory) is only half the battle. The agent also needs the live error log stream from the last five seconds (sensory memory). The architecture must fuse these batch and streaming sources asynchronously, ensuring the agent acts on a unified, up-to-date reality.
This architecture must have balance. If it over-indexes on history/episodic memory, the agent becomes stale. It will keep replaying yesterday’s assumptions into today’s reality. If it over-indexes on real-time data, the agent becomes reactive and forgetful. It may respond to the latest signal but fail to incorporate the broader context that gives that signal meaning.
Luckily for us, this tension is not new. Distributed systems have always had to reconcile durable state with transient events. Agent systems inherit the same problem, but with an additional challenge: the reasoning layer is probabilistic, expensive, and bounded by a limited context window. This adds an important layer of constraint optimization to the context architecture design - deciding which information to keep, which can be compressed, which must be revalidated, and which should be excluded entirely. The goal is not just freshness or completeness. The goal is usefulness under constraint.
Figure 1: Historical Data vs Real-Time Memory Streams (Source: created by the author with Gemini)
Knowledge vs. Raw Data (SELECT * vs. Cumulative Insight)
One of the most common architectural mistakes in AI systems is treating retrieval as if it were enough, ie, operating under the semantic equivalent of a SQL SELECT *, assuming more information must be better. Architectures that attempt to consistently retrieve large volumes of data will inevitably fail at scale. We can think of retrieval as how we get data into the system, yet it does not guarantee that the data is useful, timely, coherent, or appropriately ranked for the decision at hand. This is what standard RAG pipelines are all about. They are often built to retrieve raw, fragmented, and overlapping data chunks. In actuality, using this approach would most likely result in the system dumping 10 unedited wiki pages into a prompt, making the LLM waste compute cycles trying to sort the noise from the signal - yet failing due to relevant signals buried under less important and more noisy ones. Hence, the right information and shape of the data, which we refer to as knowledge, matter more than raw data.
True Knowledge Curation focuses on cumulative insight. Instead of injecting raw data, the architecture employs background workers/ML pipelines that distill, aggregate, and rank retrieved data by relevance, using the up-to-date system state. To achieve that, we need to build dedicated pipelines that transform raw data into structured knowledge graphs or condensed summaries. For example, taking a large database and creating a pipeline that summarizes a million data entries into one entry every 12 hours. This way, we ensure the model receives a small, synthesized body of knowledge (1 entry point in the database) rather than a chaotic stream of consciousness (the whole database, sometimes).
Custom Context: The End of "One-Size-Fits-All"
Foundational models like GPT-4 and Claude, as well as vector databases like Pinecone and Milvus, have become an accessible commodity. Everyone can access them today through their services. Yet, this is not the same for context; the architectural principles for working with context are highly domain-specific. Every company should design its own context based on the business domain and the product it serves. For example, a fintech firm might choose to curate context for an autonomous fraud-analysis agent by prioritizing transaction timestamps, geolocation anomalies, and strict compliance rules. This will look entirely different for a legal tech firm. A legal tech firm might choose to curate context based on state law for use with an agent that generates contracts. We are learning that the context itself cannot be generic; it must reflect the unique domain logic, security boundaries, and vocabulary of the specific product.
The Context Lifecycle: Managing Knowledge & Hallucination at Scale
Treating context as a continuous lifecycle allows us, as engineering teams, to manage knowledge systematically and directly address the root causes of model failure and prohibitive inference costs.
The Lifecycle Stages
Generally speaking, there are 4 stages: Selection, Injection, Compression, Expiration & Refresh. Figure 2 describes how each stage could be a dedicated module in our architecture or a standalone service.
Figure 2: Agentic AI Systemic Context Lifecycle (Source: created by the author with Gemini)
Selection (Retrieval & Filtering)
The first and most important step. This is where the system identifies which data points are likely to matter for the current task. The system's goal is to identify the absolute highest-value data points across multiple data stores. Advanced architectures have moved beyond simple cosine similarity in vector spaces, implementing hybrid search algorithms that combine dense semantic search with sparse keyword search (e.g., BM25) and knowledge graph traversal to ensure precision. In this process, we want to understand intent, task type, risk, user role, and temporal relevance. It is important to remember that the same underlying corpus may yield different contexts for a troubleshooting agent, a research agent, and a support summarization agent. This is where architecture begins to diverge from product. As part of the design requirements, we need to identify and define what is risky and what is actionable.
Injection
Once the system knows what matters, it has to place that information into the model’s working context (aka context window) in a useful form. While the end result might look like simple string concatenation, the path to getting there requires more deliberate design. That design involves semantic templating, ensuring the data is formatted to match the user's explicit intent, including necessary system instructions, few-shot examples, and output schema constraints (such as JSON definitions). To understand the importance of this step, consider how it affects the entire system. In our world, this placement of information changes how models reason. Hence, order, grouping, and structured state matter.
Compression (Summarization & Distillation)
Processing a large context is expensive. To respect token limits, historical data should be iteratively compressed. Utilizing smaller, faster LLMs (or even deterministic algorithms) to summarize conversation histories or condense long documents saves massive amounts of space and reduces latency for the primary reasoning model. Test summaries carefully to avoid distortions. There are statistical models available today to assess summary validity, such as the Perplexity (PPL) Ratio, Token-Level Kullback-Leibler (KL) Divergence, the Chi-Square Test for Categorical Outputs, and others.
Expiration and Refresh
Context that never expires eventually turns into a liability. Agents need mechanisms to retire stale assumptions, refresh live facts, and separate durable truths from temporary observations. A system preference might remain stable across months or change overnight. A product configuration might change in minutes. A support incident may be relevant for a day and misleading a week later. Without expiration and refresh, systems fall into stale data loops: they keep reusing context that was once correct but is now simply persuasive. Hence, constantly testing and validating the system through feedback loops is a must. This should be tailored to the system's end goal. For example, in a car-sharing system, the goal is to satisfy users; hence, if user satisfaction drops suddenly, it’s best to explore underlying factors that may need refreshing.
Hallucination Is Often a Context Failure
LLM hallucinations are rarely the result of a "broken" model; they are almost always the symptom of an unmanaged, impoverished context window. Because LLMs are probabilistic, when an agent lacks the explicit, factual data required to answer a prompt or execute a task, its underlying mechanism forces it to "guess" based on latent training weights.
Proactive context management acts as a strict guardrail. By saturating the model with highly relevant, high-confidence knowledge and explicitly instructing it to reason only based on the provided context, we can effectively suppress latent, inaccurate associations. In a productionized agentic system, a well-engineered context engine becomes our primary defense against hallucinated actions.
Token Economics: The Cost-to-Performance Trade-off
Processing a large context is notoriously expensive. Every token injected into the prompt window incurs both a computational latency cost and a strict financial cost. Token Economics is the engineering discipline of optimizing "attention real estate" within the LLM's limitations.
The recent expansion of context windows (e.g., models boasting 128k to 1M+ token limits) has tempted developers towards lazy architecture. They dump entire code repositories or massive troves of documents into the prompt. This drastically increases Time-to-First-Token (TTFT) latency, skyrockets API billing costs, and, ironically, degrades model performance. The model suffers from the "Lost in the Middle" phenomenon, shown in Figure 3. This problem was identified by Stanford researchers Nelson F. Liu et al. in 2023, where the model fails to retrieve facts buried in the center of massive context windows and only focuses on edge case information. The larger the bottom part of the U shape (context window), the less accurate the response will be. This research explains why we want the context sent to the model to be relatively small. This approach makes the U bottom part smaller as well - hence, improving outcomes.
Architects must weigh the marginal utility of every retrieved document against its token cost and relevancy. Just because we can send 100,000 tokens doesn't mean we should. Strict context budgeting, iterative pruning, and caching mechanisms are mandatory for scalable economics.
Figure 3: Lost in the middle problem - recall vs accuracy (Source: created by the author with Gemini - based on Lost in the Middle scientific paper by Stanford)
Designing Tiered Memory Architectures
Designing systemic approaches to memory requires establishing firm boundaries for how agents retain, update, or discard knowledge across sessions. Drawing inspiration from human cognitive architecture, systems should be multi-tiered:
- Working Memory (The Prompt Window): The immediate, ephemeral state required to execute the current step in a workflow. It is highly constrained and resets per inference call.
- Short-term Memory (Session Cache): Often managed via in-memory data stores like Redis. This tracks the current conversational state, intermediate steps of an ongoing task, and recent actions over the last few minutes or hours.
- Long-term Memory (Asynchronous Persistence): The permanent storage of synthesized insights, user preferences, and historical facts. This relies on vector databases and knowledge graphs, which are updated asynchronously, so that the agent's core "understanding" grows over time without bloating the real-time retrieval pipeline.
How to Mitigate Architectural Anti-Patterns
There are a few recurring failure patterns that show up again and again in agentic systems.
| Architectural Anti-Pattern | Description | Systemic Impact | Mitigation | 
| Context Stuffing | Injecting every plausible document, log, and tool result into the prompt under the assumption that "more is better." | Creates severe noise, dilutes model attention, increases latency, and degrades precision. | Implement strict relevance scoring thresholds. If a retrieved document's semantic similarity score falls below a certain confidence interval, drop it entirely rather than stuffing it into the prompt. | 
| Stale Data Loops | Reusing historical context (like user states or system configs) without a mechanism to validate its current accuracy. | Agents become confidently wrong, consistently acting on outdated realities. | Implement metadata filtering during retrieval that cross-references timestamps, or utilize event-driven architectures (like Kafka) to proactively invalidate stale embeddings. | 
| Generic Retrieval | Utilizing a standard, one-size-fits-all RAG pipeline regardless of the specific agentic workflow. | Fails to respect domain logic, resulting in the retrieval of irrelevant chunks and missing nuanced data. | Implement query-rewriting mechanisms in which a smaller LLM (perhaps your own managed SLM) restructures the user's raw query into domain-specific, optimized search vectors before querying the database. | 
| Implicit/Explicit Mismatch | Failing to align implicit system memory (what we know about the user) with the explicit prompt (what the user is asking right now). | The agent's output feels off-target, misaligned, or occasionally intrusive and overly familiar. | Use a rigid, structured prompt template that strictly separates system context, user context, and the immediate task instruction into distinct semantic blocks. | 
| Unbounded Memory Growth | Persisting all logs, chats, and actions without an expiration or pruning strategy. | The system degrades under its own accumulation; retention without deliberate curation becomes data hoarding. | Implement Strict TTL (Time-To-Live) Policies Not all memories are created equal. Treat agent memory like a standard caching layer by applying category-specific expiration dates. | 
Conclusion: Successful Agentic Systems Depend on Their Architecture
The next generation of AI systems' success will be determined primarily by architecture design. While the industry continues to debate model parameters and raw capabilities, the core challenge for engineering teams looks remarkably familiar: state management, signal prioritization, fault isolation, data freshness, security, and cost control.
The winning architectures will treat themselves as essential infrastructure, curate context, view memory as a strict system design problem, and elevate knowledge curation to a first-class engineering discipline. This is the real shift from chatbots to autonomous agents.
