When you start to look into the social aspect, even in large organizations, they cut basically the smallest departments, even the one that is the key ones. So that probably tells you already where the mindset of the C-suite is at the moment.
Michael Stiefel: You don't actually want to have an AI agent lay people off, at least not yet. What do you think of the idea from a governance perspective? Every time you have an agent, the agent must check into a table to make sure it's not been turned off. In other words, if you have a rogue agent, you should always be able to shut that agent off at any time. And so there has to be obviously some element of governance in here, whether the human is in the loop or not.
Luca Mezzalira: Yes, completely.
Training Junior Developers in the AI Era [38:36]
Michael Stiefel: So this is a question I've asked a lot of people and no one has a really good answer for it. So I'm not expecting any revelatory flash, but if AI is doing all these easy tasks, and these are the tasks that developers used to become apprentices on, how are we going to train the next generation of developers and how are they going to develop their intuition to understand what could work, where the abstractions break down? Because this is what bothers me.
Luca Mezzalira: I'm with you on this one. The best answer I heard so far is from Kent Beck. We were talking about pair programming for ages and mob programming for ages, and now it's more important than ever, exactly for this reason. Obviously every single team is very unlikely to be composed only by senior engineers or distinguished engineers. There is always a variety of titles and experience in the team. Therefore, considering that the code generation is becoming faster because we don't have to write every line of code, we need to, let's say, review the code that is produced by AI, that means we have some time to let people grow inside these things. So if, for instance, in the past, in every company I worked at when I was an engineer, we always have this rule that two people should review a PR.
And I think this is even more important now because if we do that, the more junior person usually provides this feedback on the code generated by AI and the more senior person as well, so you can learn asynchronously on that part. At the same time, you can use pair programming and mob programming to understand certain things. I remember vividly my times as a principal when we were organizing mob programming with the tech leaders on every single team, and we were like a dozen of people more or less inside the room. And the discussion you might think is like, "Oh yes, but it's just a waste of an hour for everyone". But the discussions were so deep and so interesting overall, moving from, I don't know, shall we integrate generators inside the system or shall we do X, Y, Z?
And analyzing all the trade-offs and all the other things, that is where you really start to learn things, having these experiences that nowadays you can call community of practices or any other, let's say, office hours. There are plenty of names or occasions to have regular cadence of this kind of discussion. And I think we need to continue to do this because at the end of the day, we are doing all of this not only for delivery shipping features, we need to deploy production, we need to understand the observability, we need to know that when at 3:00 AM we wake up following the round book, we know exactly how to solve a specific problem. So there is way more that is not just code generation that we need to think about and AI can help in all of that.
And I think we can potentially even accelerate the learnings for people because if you start to chat with AI and you provide, let's say, some decent RAG system on how we are used to working on a specific product, I think people can learn and onboard faster than it was before. But at the same time, we need to remember that architecture always thought that it's an enabler for an organization. Therefore, when you choose microservices over monolith or vice versa or distribute modular monolith, you are signaling that you want to see certain characteristics inside the socio-technical system. If I think about this, it means that even with agents, the architecture we are going to choose matters.
And it will help people to think about if it's a microservice, we provide all the bells and whistles inside the microservice with, I don't know, retries, exponential backoff and gracefully degrade the system, all these nice things that very often people don't have time to build, we will be able to fill even in production but not impacting the system. And I think these kinds of things help people to gain their battle scars in the trenches and then learn from them despite the fact that they didn't write every single line of code because in the past we were used to write a portion of the code, but we didn't write every single line of code. Because in a team, I take a task, someone else takes another task. I'm comfortable reading the other person's code because we try to keep the same style.
In general, I believe, yes, it's a challenge, but I don't believe we should be desperate straight away. I think the community will figure out the best way to handle that. And the companies, to be honest, I've seen many that are still hiring juniors and I'm extremely happy to hear that because the reality, this is, let's say, the future of our society. So we basically leave with everything that is digital. I don't remember the last time I went to a bank, probably 20 years ago. Nowadays for me, everything is an app and my bank is an app.
Michael Stiefel: Well, your safe deposit box is not quite an app yet, but I remember there was a study where developers tried to use AI to help them understand, and there was another control group that didn't use the AI to understand. The two groups essentially learned at the same pace. There's no physical difference from them, but testing afterwards their recollection, those who learned with the AI had significantly less retention.
Luca Mezzalira: Of course.
Michael Stiefel: So I think what you describe, there is evidence that this is the way you have to go. Not only should you go, but you have to go.
Luca Mezzalira: Of course, because obviously it's a more shallow way to implement a feature. You provide, let's say some specs, and if you don't check the code and how it's written, you just accept blindly what is behind that. You cannot master it. The mastering part is trying, making an error, let's say start to bang your head on the wall, try to figure out if there is a better way to do specific things. That's why at the beginning I said I love refactoring because refactoring is exactly that. Give me something chunky and complex and I will unwind it for you. And that process is extremely important. I strongly believe that AI should be an accelerator and a companion, but we need still to improve our craft no matter what. Otherwise, it's very difficult for anyone to think, "Oh, but this is just code". It's not just code. There is way more behind that.
There is the optimization on specific things that will drive the behavior inside the browser, or there is an obstruction that helps you to, let's say, integrate in new systems very quickly. There are a lot of ideas that people have that are difficult to express just with a business process because unless you are there and you say, "Okay, so I know that they need to have code portability, so let's try to figure it out what is the best way? Should I apply an adopter here? Should I use hexagonal architecture there? Should I decouple the environment from the business logic? How am I going to do that? How can I create portability? How can I update a library when there is a change on multiple systems?" So there are a lot of questions that still developers need to answer that are not merely, oh, this is the spec of implementing a feature. Therefore, I think it's still a valid concern and we need to learn how to do these things properly.
Michael Stiefel: Just to pick an example that I remember more than once in my career, paradoxically, the optimal thing to do is actually to de-optimize. And that only comes with experience and understanding exactly what's going on.
Luca Mezzalira: Completely. I remember vividly when my CTO told me, I remember everything is on fire. You just need to pick your fire. And in a large system, I was handling like 550 people in the tech department. I cannot be stretched to cover everything in different locations and so on. So you pick your battles. So you decide that certain areas of the system deserve your attention, certain areas. People are good enough for handling that situation on their own. You just need to check that everything is fine. And the worst case scenario, you create a system that either is self-healing or hides gracefully inside the trenches. Even with integration within a system, we were designing in a way that if something that we don't understand because it was a third party that we integrated failed, we just hide it and we create all this logic for enabling people to move on but not compromising the platform.
And I think these kinds of discussions are extremely important and I honestly value a lot of discussion. That's why architecture for me is very interesting because there are experiences from other people coming from other industries that can provide you with completely different angles that you didn't think about because you weren't exposed to. And that's the part that I love the most.
The Architect's Questionnaire [47:24]
Michael Stiefel: Now's the time when I like to get to the architect's questionnaire. It's always interesting to me to talk to people who have experience in the architecture area and get their take on the more, I don't want to say softer side, the more human side. What's your favorite part of being an architect?
Luca Mezzalira: So in the last five years in AWS, basically I work as a consultant if you want, where I go to customers where they have a problem, I try to figure out and understand the problem and then apply architectural wisdom in order to solve the problem and then line it up with AWS services, but that's basically what they do. I found extremely interesting this context discovery. So understanding the dichotomy of teams and the balance that they have. And I have let's say a set of questions that develop over the years that helps me a lot, especially because I go in in a meeting and I might not know what the company is building. So I start to understand how many teams there are and are involved in that specific project or feature. I try to understand the resilience standard that they have. I try to understand the SLAs and SLOs or all the other things.
And this discovery of the context is very interesting because you start showing the customer or the team the holes that they have or they didn't think thoroughly on something. And sometimes you discover that in reality they are optimizing for something that no one asks for and that creates an enormous complexity that is easily solved without adding any configuration on the product, reducing the stress towards the architecture and lowering the bar to something that is more accommodating if you want. Very often when I hear, "Oh, we need to do near real time data", it's near, it's one minute, it's 30 minutes, it's one hour. There are customers that one hour would already be a huge win. Customer that within one minute they start to say, "It's not too fast for what we need to do".
Then I apply let's say techniques like event storming, Wardley mapping and all the other things that for me, going to a customer, I have no clue what they're doing, how they operate. Running an event storming session was mind-blowing because in one day I know exactly how the things are working at a high level and I know how the system could be designed or could be broken apart and I can start to stress it out and start to layer up some of the technology that they are using.
Michael Stiefel: What is your least favorite part of being an architect?
Luca Mezzalira: So there are certain designs back in the days that I couldn't bother much with. I mean either because they were too simple or because they were too skewed towards a specific area that wasn't, let's say, super strong or whatever. I remember for instance, the authentication part, authorization part. When you have done the first time, you are excited. It's the first time you do that. The second time, "Okay, I applied what I learned. Great". But after the seventh time that you're doing that, "Again, authentication authorization. Can I delegate something?" These kinds of things become a bit tedious after a while if you have multiple systems and if you move between companies as well. So that part is becoming a bit tedious. So yes, I know that this is important, but can someone else do that?
Michael Stiefel: Is there anything creatively, spiritually, or emotionally satisfying about architecture or being an architect?
Luca Mezzalira: I think emotionally it's one of the most amazing jobs that I've done in my life because when you are capable with a decision or making let's say the right call and you discover again over years, enabling the company to grow, obviously you are just a cog in a large system, but still, you know that that decision was your decision. You say, "Okay, yes, we should go in that direction". And you see the feature that is going there or the system is going there live. It's working. The customer loves it. Everyone that did a great job and whatever. You become extremely proud of your work. I remember very vividly a couple of years ago when I already left my previous company, DAZN, for a while, the principal engineers from Amsterdam met me in a conference that was telling me, "Look, I have to tell you these things. It's been eight years that we're doing micro-frontends.
We didn't change anything about your architecture because it's still enabling us to have the right level of flexibility while maintaining a solid standing that everyone understands". That for me is the most rewarding sentence that I have for ages because having an architecture that lasts for that long, like eight years, obviously in the past it was different, but nowadays it's mind-blowing, especially because it was extremely cutting edge. No one did the scale that we operated that specific architecture. I have to create patterns, anti-patterns, the vocabulary of architecture and everything. And having someone that is experienced like this person, they have worked in multiple companies and saying, "Yes, after eight years, it's still there. Still deliver what was the idea". I still remember that moment.
Michael Stiefel: So on the flip side of that, what turns you off about being an architect?
Luca Mezzalira: So we know that communication is important, right?
Michael Stiefel: Yes.
Luca Mezzalira: There are certain people in a certain organization, I think it's more cultural sometimes, that they hide behind titles. I don't know. It's probably a me mindset. I'm not saying that other people have the same thing, maybe they do, I don't know. But I don't care about the titles. For me, we are all human beings. We have a brain and you have experience and expertise no matter what. Using that leverage for not fighting on the same table fighting is like discussing on the same table and just, let's say, using your title to shut off the discussion is not something I appreciate.
Michael Stiefel: I totally agree with you. This is one of the reasons why, for example, I have a PhD, but I never put that on my business card. I know people have PhDs and they're on their business card. I don't want it to be on my business card. I either know what I'm talking about or I don't know what I'm talking about. And the fact that I have a degree has nothing to do with that.
Luca Mezzalira: I agree. And there are splendid people that I met over my 20 years in the career, obviously. Sometimes it's very cultural because they didn't expect that I was able to develop or programming or doing pair programming. And for me it was, "Okay, but I'm one of you. I'm working in the same company. I want to achieve a specific goal that is exactly the same goal that you have". If I can and I have time, I will cut my arm in order to succeed in specific things because I have this sense of community. You have a degree, I don't. I left school when I was 16, so I learned with the community. I worked in a factory for a while, but then I studied overnight and not in my language because in Italian there weren't many tech books back in the days. So therefore I have to order from Amazon.com my books and learn English.
I didn't know anything in English. So for reading a book, it took a month or more and slowly but sadly then applied this stuff and these learnings. I learn in this way. I learned with the community where social weren't there or video courses weren't there. You just open a request on a forum hoping that someone will reply to you. And because obviously it was everything in Italian, you have a subset of the world that can reply to you. So that sticks with me till now. For me, I tried to do in the beginning when you introduced me, you have seen that I did public speaking and newsletters, podcasts, et cetera.
Because I still believe that there is somewhere someone that is waiting for that content like I was doing back in the days and try to cut through the noise and figure out if my content lands in somehow because I feel lucky that I've seen a lot of stuff in my career and I don't want to hold it honestly. I think it deserved to go out and maybe I learned something new, maybe someone else is learning something new. Either case is a win for me.
Michael Stiefel: This is why I enjoy doing this podcast. I don't need to do this. It doesn't really benefit me much personally, except psychologically and emotionally. I feel that I want this knowledge from different practitioners to be spread throughout the community because as you said, there's book learning and there's actually being in the trenches with the battle scars, and that's where the real knowledge happens.
Luca Mezzalira: Completely.
Michael Stiefel: Do you have any favorite technologies?
Luca Mezzalira: Yes, I do, obviously, as everyone, but at the same time, I tend to be balanced when I decide what to go with. But in general, a combination that I found myself working pretty well is definitely JavaScript with serverless, especially people complaining about working at scale with serverless might be a challenge. Nowadays, I would say that that problem is, I cannot say solved for everything, but for a good chunk of use cases it is solved. I remember my previous system, we started in 2015 to work on that. We moved from VMs to serverless using Lambda and AWS, and we were one of the largest companies doing that in EMEA. And that was mind-blowing, to be honest, because it was just Lambda, DynamoDB didn't have global tables, didn't have many of the things.
And slowly but suddenly I grew with this thing and the more I was using it and the more I realized that I was able to express my architectural thoughts better than just having containers, orchestrators, here and there. Because spinning up a queue was a breeze and I want a broker, I want an orchestrator. Do I need to communicate asynchronously for a chunk of my domain and another part synchronous? I can. I think this flexibility for me was mind-blowing with honestly little effort for spinning up stuff because it was infrastructure managed by someone else. Obviously with these at the beginning, especially with their limits, but when there are limits, usually creativity starts to kick in, so you start to overcome these limits in different ways.
At the end of the day, we were dealing with a platform of three, four million customers. So it wasn't like a small platform that you can find, let's say, that doesn't work. And we have huge spikes of traffic. So designing things was challenging no matter what we were using, even probably with serverless sometimes slightly more, but we used a very nice combination of serverless and let's say containers through Fargate in that case, and it was quite a nice combo.
Michael Stiefel: What about architecture do you love?
Luca Mezzalira: I think it's solving problems. That's the part that I love the most about architecture because I was an engineer at the beginning of my career, so I solve a lot of problems through code and I love working on unconventional places like embedded systems, for instance. You have some quirkiness that you didn't expect. Then moving to mobile when the iPhone and Android came out was extremely interesting. I remember when we were working in gambling, some games didn't work as expected inside certain Android browsers, especially with Android 2, Android 1, because the browsers were so fragmented that even a simple CSS implementation like unload the CSS didn't work because it wasn't implementing in the browser.
So you start to have this fragmentation, that kind of problems that I had in engineering, now I translate into architecture and it's even more challenging because now there isn't one dimension like, "Oh, the browser doesn't work". My feedback group is very fast. Here, the feedback loop is way longer and therefore experience, trial and error, learning from others, just chatting with other people, try to figure out the different ideas, see which one sticks better, maybe running a POC, document this thing, understand why a certain decision was made in a certain period of time. All these kinds of things for me are extremely fascinating. I found a lot of pride in doing this job.
Michael Stiefel: Conversely, what about architecture do you hate?
Luca Mezzalira: I would say people thinking that the architecture is a problem while it's not that the architecture is a problem, it's just signaling certain things inside the socio-technical system. Probably you have experienced something similar. You work in a company when the first problem arises inside the trenches is, "Oh, the architecture is wrong". Without even thinking about, "Okay, did we analyze if it's, I don't know, the commits that were wrong, the code was wrong? Are we structured properly for enabling this architecture?" I think let's say it's the most visible thing compared to people, engineers or product, et cetera. Are we structured correctly?
I mean, if I choose to go with Elixir, for instance, and I have let's say a bunch of people that are coming out from university, then probably I need to figure out something that is less complicated to start with. Obviously, if I work on a very complex system and Elixir is needed or I want to use, I don't know, Akka with an actor model implementation, I need to adapt this architecture for a specific context. So in my opinion, architecture is just there for facing good and bad things. Friction, I always interpret as a gift because as a feedback that architecture provides you, it's telling you something doesn't work.
And that's something, it might not be in the architecture space. It could be that maybe we designed one thing that was working in the past, but now suddenly the team grows so much or they split in a way, but the code is still needed to be co-located and therefore the friction arises because probably we over indexed on the teams, we should redesign the teams in order to have better things, not necessarily the architecture is wrong or the distributed system is wrong or the monolith is wrong. I think architecture, all of them are still useful nowadays. There are some of them maybe less than others, but I still believe that having these people that immediately put their things, "Oh, this is too complicated, I don't want to even see", it's not something that honestly turns me on.
Michael Stiefel: And sometimes some people don't appreciate that there was a trade-off that was made. Yes, we consciously made this case not to be optimal because we had to achieve something else. It's that same lack of perspective.
Luca Mezzalira: Exactly. Thinking holistically about the system is the other challenge that happens very often. I think it comes with maturity and experience. It's not, let's say that you have it for free. I probably was similar to those people at the beginning of my career because I didn't see the system holistically.
Michael Stiefel: What profession other than being an architect would you like to attempt?
Luca Mezzalira: The first one I would like to do is street food, Italian street food in London. That's definitely a plan C for me. I was always interested in what I think overlaps with the skillset of an architect to a certain extent, is this idea of advocate or let's say developer advocate or evangelist or stuff like that, because I really love taking complex ideas and trying to unwind in a way that is bulletproof. And I think it's a skill. It's not something that everyone can do. You need to really go deep into that specific problem, understand deeply and remove all the noise, cutting through the most bare minimum implementation, then you build on top of that.
This is something that I really enjoy because recently I just published my second edition of Building Micro-Frontends book, and the feedback that I have most recurrently this time is, "I cannot think of something that is more clear on how you have written this book". Everything that is there is simple and I don't get why people don't get it, but in order to be simple, it's been 10 years that I'm working on that.
Michael Stiefel: Yes, yes, yes. Sometimes it takes you 10 years to get to simplicity, because to achieve simplicity, you have to learn what really has to be there and what is not necessary. And sometimes you only see that with experience.
Luca Mezzalira: Yes. And you need to try and try and try till you are bored of hearing your voice.
Michael Stiefel: Yes, yes. Do you ever see yourself not being an architect anymore?
Luca Mezzalira: No. I would say the industry will decide. It's not up to me. I can continue till the end of my life, to be honest, because I really love what I'm doing. It's the most interesting thing that honestly I have seen. I had the opportunity after being VP to move towards a more managerial career path, VP of engineering or director or CTO, et cetera. I ditched those opportunities mainly because I think I still have something to do and to say in the architecture space. And I didn't expect AI back in the days when I took that decision, but I believe now it's even more important that what I've learned, what other people have learned there in the trenches can help new joiners in the industry as well as experienced people to rationalize better what's going on with AI and how much to trust.
I've seen these more balanced approaches of the architectural community compared to the fanboy approach than other companies or communities are doing where, "Ah, we can do everything with AI". Absolutely, you can do everything with anything, but doesn't mean that because you can, you should. And I think it's important that this message lands properly. I started to write a few articles recently on these kinds of discussions that I did at conferences or watching online content and they landed very well with few people that reach out to me saying, "Oh, finally a point of view that is not indexing too much on one side or the other one. It's a balanced approach and it highlights the trade-offs".
Michael Stiefel: When a project is done, what do you like to hear from the clients or your team?
Luca Mezzalira: First of all, when a project is done, we should share that no matter if it's perfect or not, it doesn't really matter. We achieved something, it's a milestone. Personally, I don't expect a thank you or anything. It's not because I feel that it's perfect. I've just done my job and therefore I'm more interested to wait six months, one year and see if we have done our job properly. Therefore, my gut tells me that I'm still nervous even after the release. And not because I'm not confident, it's because I know that that is one part of the game.
In previous companies, I spent, you have no idea how much of my time and during the weekend especially going to the war rooms in different companies to see how the platform behaves live because I found that experience extremely interesting. They were, let's say, watching because it was a sports company, the previous one, they were watching the matches and keeping an eye on the dashboard. I was watching the dashboard and keeping an eye on the matches.
Michael Stiefel: Even if your favorite team was playing?
Luca Mezzalira: Exactly. It doesn't matter. Just saw the New Relic or the dashboard and say, "Oh yes, there is a spike here. What does it mean is we need to check on Monday". Stuff like that.
Michael Stiefel: Nevermind the winning goal was just the cause... That caused the spike.
Luca Mezzalira: It's not a problem. Someone has to win, someone has to lose, so that's fine.
Michael Stiefel: Well, thank you very much for appearing on the podcast. I enjoyed this conversation very much. I think we touched on several important things for the future as well as the present. So I would like to thank you.
Luca Mezzalira: Thank you. Thank you for having me. I hope that this conversation was helpful for all our listeners.
Michael Stiefel: Yes. Thank you very much.
Mentioned:

- Pair Programming

articles.title: Heures creuses EDF : voici comment savoir si vos horaires vont bientôt changer
articles.text:
Si vous avez l’option Heures pleines / Heures creuses chez EDF, vos 8 heures par jour à prix réduit vont peut-être bouger. Dans son guide mis à jour le 26 octobre 2026, EDF écrit que les clients qui n’ont pas encore leurs nouveaux horaires les recevront entre ce mercredi 4 novembre et le 30 novembre 2027.
Les heures creuses du matin (7h-11h) et du soir (17h-23h) disparaissent petit à petit. Elles sont remplacées par des horaires qui changent avec les saisons, avec jusqu’à trois heures creuses l’après-midi. Vous en garderez toujours 8 par jour, dont au moins 5 d’affilée la nuit, « parfaites pour les grosses consommations comme le ballon d’eau chaude ou la recharge de la voiture électrique ».
Mais pourquoi l’après-midi ? Parce que les panneaux solaires produisent beaucoup d’électricité en milieu de journée. La Commission de régulation de l’énergie (CRE), qui surveille le secteur, a donc changé les règles en mars 2025, et c’est Enedis, le gestionnaire du réseau, qui les applique. D’après la foire aux questions de la CRE, 3,5 millions des 14,5 millions de clients en heures creuses, tous fournisseurs confondus, suivaient déjà ces règles. Il reste donc 11 millions de foyers à faire passer au nouveau système.
Comment savoir si vos heures creuses vont changer
Vous n’avez aucune démarche à faire, comme l’explique Service Public : votre fournisseur doit vous prévenir au moins un mois avant le changement. Pour savoir si vous êtes concerné, regardez vos horaires dans votre espace client EDF. Si vous avez des heures creuses entre 7h et 11h ou entre 17h et 23h, elles vont changer. Si vos nouveaux horaires vous ont été donnés entre le 1er novembre 2025 et le 31 mai 2026, ils ne changeront plus.
Pendant l’hiver, du 1er novembre au 31 mars, les heures creuses restent surtout la nuit. Celles de l’après-midi deviennent plus nombreuses à partir du 1er avril. L’option Tempo n’est pas concernée, et les règles ne s’appliquent ni en Corse ni en outre-mer.

articles.title: Black Friday Switch 2/PS5 : Les promos consoles et accessoires à ne pas louper — Frandroid
articles.text:
GTA 6 sort le 19 novembre 2026 sur PS5, et le remake de Zelda Ocarina of Time est disponible le 5 novembre sur Switch 2 exclusivement. Autant dire que le Black Friday tombe à point nommé pour équiper sa console ou compléter son setup avant de s’y plonger.
Nous avons retenu sept offres : trois consoles Nintendo (Switch 2, Switch OLED, Switch Lite), la manette Pro de la Switch 2, la caméra officielle Switch 2, un casque sans fil Sony taillé pour la PS5 et des écouteurs gaming Razer compatibles. Les remises calculées vont de 8 % sur la Switch Lite à 40 % sur la manette Nintendo Switch 2 Pro.
Les meilleures offres Switch 2 et PS5 du Black Friday 2026
- Nintendo Switch 2 à 429,99 euros au lieu de 499,99 euros
- Nintendo Switch OLED à 229 euros au lieu de 349 euros avec le code promo FRD1140
- Nintendo Switch Lite à 184,19 euros au lieu de 199,99 euros
- Manette Nintendo Switch 2 Pro à 53,96 euros au lieu de 89,99 euros avec le code promo FRD1108
- Nintendo Switch 2 Joy-Con 2 à 69,99 euros au lieu de 89,99 euros
- Nintendo Switch 2 Caméra à 39,99 euros au lieu de 59,99 euros
- Sony Inzone H9 II à 199,99 euros au lieu de 229 euros
- Razer Hammerhead V3 X HyperSpeed à 81,99 euros au lieu de 109,99 euros
Pour vous équiper comme il se doit, vous pouvez également jeter un œil à nos différents guides d’achat dans le domaine du gaming, comme notre sélection des meilleurs casques audio pour jouer à la PS5, ou notre comparatif des Nintendo Switch pour mieux choisir. Nous avons également une sélection des consoles à privilégier pour lancer GTA 6.
Nintendo Switch 2
La Nintendo Switch 2 est la console hybride de Nintendo : elle se joue sur un téléviseur via son dock, en mode console de table ou en mode portable, avec ses nouveaux Joy-Con 2 magnétiques. Par rapport à la Switch originale, elle embarque une architecture graphique Nvidia Ampere, un écran plus grand aux bordures réduites, 256 Go de stockage interne et le Wi-Fi 6.
La puissance supplémentaire élargit le catalogue possible, et la fonction GameShare permet de partager une cartouche entre plusieurs consoles. L’autonomie reste le point faible à surveiller, la recharge 60 W ne compense pas entièrement un usage intensif en mode portable. Notre test de la Nintendo Switch 2 lui attribue la note de 7/10.
Les points forts de la Nintendo Switch 2
- Joy-Con 2 à fixation magnétique
- 256 Go de stockage interne
- Wi-Fi 6 et GameShare intégrés
La Nintendo Switch 2 est disponible à 429,99 euros au lieu de 499,99 euros chez Joybuy, soit 70 euros d’économie.
Nintendo Switch OLED
Sortie en 2021, la Nintendo Switch OLED reste une option solide pour qui joue essentiellement en mode portable. Son écran OLED de 7 pouces améliore sensiblement les contrastes et la richesse des couleurs par rapport au LCD de la Switch originale, et ses bordures plus fines renforcent l’immersion. Le dock intègre désormais un port Ethernet, ce qui évite de chercher un adaptateur pour le jeu en ligne.
La console est notée 8/10 dans notre test : les réserves portent surtout sur la résolution plafonnée à 720p en portable et sur une luminosité qui reste insuffisante en plein soleil. Elle tourne sur la même puce Nvidia Tegra que la Switch 2019 et n’apporte pas de gain de performance. Pour savoir si elle vous convient mieux que ses sœurs, consultez notre sélection des meilleures consoles de jeux portables en 2026.
Le 19 novembre, Vice City vous attend. Et votre PS5 ? Avec Next Mobiles, pas besoin de payer 600 € d’un coup, louez-la sur la durée que vous souhaitez, dès 16,90 €/mois.
Les points forts de la Nintendo Switch OLED
- Écran OLED 7 pouces, contrastes nettement améliorés
- Bordures réduites pour plus d’immersion
- Port Ethernet intégré au dock
Avec le code promo FRD1140, la Nintendo Switch OLED passe à 229 euros au lieu de 349 euros sur Aliexpress, soit 120 euros de remise.
Nintendo Switch Lite
La Nintendo Switch Lite est la version 100 % portable de la Switch : pas de dock, pas de Joy-Con détachables, une seule façon de jouer. Elle compense par un format compact et léger qui la rend agréable à transporter et à tenir en main. Son autonomie est meilleure que celle du modèle d’origine, et elle intègre une vraie croix directionnelle, absente sur les Joy-Con de la Switch classique.
L’écran n’est pas assez lumineux en extérieur, et le plastique de la coque est moins agréable au toucher que celui des modèles supérieurs ; notée 8/10 dans notre test, c’est malgré tout une entrée en matière cohérente dans l’univers Nintendo.
Les points forts de la Nintendo Switch Lite
- Format compact, 275 grammes en main
- Autonomie supérieure à la Switch originale
- Vraie croix directionnelle intégrée
La Nintendo Switch Lite est affichée à 184,19 euros au lieu de 199,99 euros sur Amazon.
Manette Nintendo Switch 2 Pro
Pour jouer à la Nintendo Switch 2 sur téléviseur sans se contraindre aux Joy-Con, la manette Pro est la solution la plus aboutie. Elle reprend l’ergonomie classique d’une manette de salon (sticks déportés, gâchettes, poignées allongées) et y ajoute les fonctions propres à la Switch 2 : un bouton C pour accéder au GameChat, deux boutons arrière GL/GR programmables librement, une prise jack 3,5 mm pour casque, la vibration HD Rumble 2 et les contrôles gyroscopiques. L’autonomie annoncée est d’environ 40 heures. La manette n’est compatible qu’avec la Nintendo Switch 2 et non avec les modèles précédents.
Les points forts de la Manette Nintendo Switch 2 Pro
- Boutons GL/GR arrière entièrement programmables
- Prise jack 3,5 mm pour casque filaire
- Autonomie d’environ 40 heures
Avec le code promo FRD1108, la Manette Nintendo Switch 2 Pro tombe à 53,96 euros au lieu de 89,99 euros sur Aliexpress, soit 40 % de remise.
Par ailleurs, les Joy-Con 2 de la Switch 2 (coloris bleu et jaune) sont également en promotion. Au lieu de 89,99 euros, on les retrouve à 69,99 euros sur Amazon.
Nintendo Switch 2 Caméra
La Nintendo Switch 2 Caméra est l’accessoire officiel pour tirer parti du GameChat et de la fonction CameraPlay de la console. Elle se branche sur le port USB-C supérieur de la Switch 2 et fonctionne dans les trois modes : TV, console de table et portable. Son objectif grand angle couvre environ 110 degrés, ce qui suffit à cadrer un groupe devant un écran de salon ; un capteur haute sensibilité ajuste automatiquement la luminosité. La tête pivote verticalement, et un cache de confidentialité intégré permet de couvrir l’objectif quand la caméra n’est pas utilisée. Certains jeux compatibles CameraPlay exploitent même la détection de mouvement via cette caméra.
Les points forts de la Nintendo Switch 2 Caméra
- Objectif grand angle 110 degrés
- Compatibilité GameChat et CameraPlay
- Cache de confidentialité intégré
La Nintendo Switch 2 Caméra est disponible à 39,99 euros au lieu de 59,99 euros chez Joybuy, soit 20 euros d’économie.
Sony Inzone H9 II
Le Sony Inzone H9 II est un casque circum-aural sans fil conçu en collaboration avec l’équipe Fnatic, taillé pour le jeu compétitif et en particulier pour les FPS. Il emprunte les transducteurs de 30 mm du WH-1000XM6, auxquels Sony a appliqué une égalisation spécifique pour ce type de titres. Léger à 260 g grâce à une refonte complète de l’arceau, il embarque une triple connectivité (2,4 GHz, Bluetooth LE Audio, jack analogique), une réduction de bruit active et un microphone amovible à suppression de bruit par IA.
Noté 7/10 dans notre test, il convainc sur la construction et le confort, mais son rendu sonore trop orienté FPS et son autonomie de 30 heures en retrait de la concurrence freinent l’enthousiasme – d’autant que son prix de référence dépasse les 300 euros. Pour une présentation complète, retrouvez notre test du Sony Inzone H9 II.
Les points forts du Sony Inzone H9 II
- Construction et design soignés, 260 g seulement
- Triple connectivité : 2,4 GHz, Bluetooth LE Audio, jack
- Microphone amovible avec réduction de bruit par IA
Pendant le Black Friday, le Sony Inzone H9 II passe à 199,99 euros chez Amazon au lieu de 229 euros.
Razer Hammerhead V3 X HyperSpeed
Les Razer Hammerhead V3 X HyperSpeed sont des écouteurs intra-auriculaires sans fil conçus spécifiquement pour la PS5, avec une licence PlayStation officielle. La connexion passe par le boîtier HyperSpeed, qui fait à la fois office d’étui de charge et de récepteur 2,4 GHz : il suffit de le brancher sur la console pour profiter d’un audio sans fil à très faible latence, compatible avec le Tempest 3D Audio de la PS5.
Bluetooth 5.3 et Razer SmartSwitch permettent en outre de basculer vers un smartphone ou un PC sans manipulation. L’autonomie totale atteint 35 heures boîtier inclus, et la certification IPX4 protège l’ensemble des projections et de la transpiration.
Les points forts du Razer Hammerhead V3 X HyperSpeed
- Compatible Tempest 3D Audio sur PS5
- Boîtier HyperSpeed : récepteur 2,4 GHz et charge intégrés
- 35 heures d’autonomie totale, résistance IPX4
Disponible à 81,99 euros chez Boulanger au lieu de 109,99 euros, soit 25 % de remise.
Les offres sur les jeux vidéo
Pour finir ce guide, voici une petite sélection de jeux vidéo en promotion sur les plateformes de e-commerce, d’abord sur PS5 :
- God of War Laufey en précommande à 61,99 euros sur Cdiscount ;
- Castlevania : Belmont’s Curse – Midnight Edition à 29,96 euros sur Amazon ;
- Clair Obscur : Expedition 33 à 43,32 euros sur Cdiscount ;

Et maintenant sur Nintendo Switch 2 :

articles.title: 11.11 Day AliExpress : le Ryzen 5 9600X tombe à 122,17€ avec notre code exclusif
articles.text:
Pour qui prépare une configuration de jeu avant les fêtes, le Single Day d’AliExpress, lancé le 1er novembre, ajoute aux prix affichés des codes réservés aux lecteurs de Clubic. Le Ryzen 5 9600X passe ainsi à 122,17 € avec le code CLU24, 20,19 € sous notre précédent relais d’octobre, pour une puce que notre test avait surtout saluée pour sa sobriété.
Le Ryzen 5 9600X ouvre la gamme Ryzen 9000 d’AMD avec six cœurs Zen 5, une fréquence de 3,9 à 5,4 GHz et un TDP de 65 W sur socket AM5. Lancé à 308,90 €, il est déjà passé sur nos pages à 160,53 €, puis à 142,36 € début octobre.
Pendant le 11.11, AliExpress l’affiche à 146,17 €, et le code CLU24 retire 24 € dès 139 € d’achat pour le ramener à 122,17 €. Il est expédié depuis la France par la boutique Core Deck Store. L’offre vise ceux qui partent de zéro sur AM5, pas les possesseurs d’un Ryzen 7000.
L’AMD Ryzen 5 9600X est à 122,17 € sur AliExpress avec le code CLU24, au lieu des 146,17 € affichés pendant le Single Day.
Pourquoi choisir l’AMD Ryzen 5 9600X ?
- Une chauffe qui simplifie le montage : Dans notre test, il n’a jamais atteint 70 °C en pleine charge, pour une consommation plafonnant vers 88 W. Inutile de surdimensionner le refroidissement, à prévoir de toute façon puisqu’aucun ventirad n’est fourni.
- De la marge en jeu : Sous Total War Warhammer 3, très dépendant du processeur, il se range parmi les plus rapides de notre test. Il devance aussi le Ryzen 5 7600X sous Cyberpunk 2077 comme sous Shadow of the Tomb Raider.
- Une partie graphique de secours : Contrairement au Core i5-14400F, il intègre une puce Radeon capable d’assurer l’affichage sans carte dédiée. Pratique pour démarrer la machine en attendant une carte graphique, ou pour un poste bureautique.
Ce que ce prix change pour une tour de jeu ou de travail
À 122,17 €, le processeur pèse nettement moins dans le budget d’une configuration AM5, et la différence peut aller vers la carte graphique, qui reste l’élément principal dans les jeux récents. Notre test du Ryzen 5 9600X le confirme : sous Cyberpunk 2077, son avance sur le 7600X se limite à 2 %. Sa vraie force tient à la sobriété, avec une consommation en charge ramenée d’environ 108 W sur le 7600X à 88 W. AMD a depuis officialisé un mode à 105 W, couvert par la garantie, pour ceux qui voudraient plus de marge.
Il convient à ceux qui montent une première tour de jeu, ou un poste de télétravail qui doit rester frais en charge. Les créateurs qui enchaînent rendu 3D et encodage regarderont ailleurs : sur Cinebench 2024 et Blender, les Core Intel Raptor Lake Refresh gardent l’avantage en multi-thread. Les possesseurs d’un Ryzen 7000 n’ont pas de raison de changer, Zen 5 n’apportant pas de saut suffisant. Enfin, une carte mère AM5 et de la DDR5 sont obligatoires, ce qui alourdit la facture pour qui vient d’une plateforme plus ancienne.
Face au Core i5-14400F de notre comparatif, l’avantage change de camp
Dans notre comparatif des meilleurs processeurs, l’entrée de gamme gaming revient au Core i5-14400F, noté 6/10 et affiché entre 159,90 € et 173,99 € chez les marchands relevés le 2 novembre. À 122,17 €, le Ryzen 5 9600X, noté 8/10 dans notre test, passe donc nettement sous son prix. L’Intel garde un argument : il accepte la DDR4 comme la DDR5, ce qui peut alléger une mise à niveau. Il se passe en revanche de partie graphique et n’autorise aucun overclocking.
✅ Les points forts
- Moins de 70 °C en pleine charge dans notre test
- Environ 88 W en charge, contre 108 W pour le 7600X
- 122,17 € avec CLU24, sous le Core i5-14400F de notre comparatif
- Partie graphique Radeon pour dépanner
- Compatible avec toutes les cartes mères AM5
❌ Les limites
- Aucun ventirad fourni dans la boîte
- Consommation au repos un peu au-dessus de 20 W
- Derrière Intel en multi-thread sur Cinebench et Blender
- Carte mère AM5 et DDR5 obligatoires
Le code CLU24 se déclenche dès 139 € de panier : le Ryzen 5 9600X seul le dépasse, et revient alors à 122,17 € chez AliExpress.
À 122,17 €, le Ryzen 5 9600X coûte moins de 40 % de son prix de lancement et 20,19 € de moins qu’à notre relais d’octobre. Ses performances n’ont pas bougé depuis notre test : solides en jeu, sans écart spectaculaire face à Zen 4. À ce tarif, sa sobriété et sa chauffe contenue en font une base AM5 très cohérente pour une configuration neuve.
Gardez le budget complet en tête : ventirad, carte mère AM5 et DDR5 s’ajoutent si vous partez de zéro. Les possesseurs d’un Ryzen 7000 peuvent passer leur chemin, tout comme ceux dont le métier repose sur le rendu ou l’encodage. Pour une tour de jeu fraîche et économe, c’est le prix le plus bas que nous ayons relayé pour ce processeur.
Comment profiter des offres exclusives du Black Friday ?

articles.title: Matías Prats, sobre su padre y su patrimonio: "Mi padre vivía para trabajar y yo, para vivir; he invertido en una empresa fotovoltaica junto a unos amigos"
articles.text:
Matías Prats es uno de los presentadores de informativos más veteranos de la televisión, pero también , el veterano presentador de los informativos de Antena 3, ha hablado en alguna ocasión tanto de sus inversiones en energía solar como sobre sobre la diferencia entre su manera de vivir el trabajo y la de su padre.
Un huerto solar con amigos. Tal y como explicó en 2018, Prats entró en el negocio de las renovables por invitación de unos amigos y, en aquel momento, la inversión no le estaba compensando: “Genera electricidad, pero no genera mucho más. Hicimos una inversión hace muchos años con unos amigos, que son los que invitaron a participar. Me gustó porque todo lo que es renovable me gusta. Me animé a invertir, pero todavía no da rendimiento”.
Y es que detrás de esa frase hay una sociedad con nombre propio, Fotovoltaica Tarazona Trece S.L., que se fundó en mayo de 2008 y se dedica a la producción de energía eléctrica con renovables. Eso sí, esta sociedad ya fue vendida al fondo Q-Energy, al mismo tiempo que Prats cesaba como administrador y socio único.
¿Y por qué acabó saliendo de la sociedad? Pues no lo ha explicado, al menos públicamente, pero en 2018 reconocía que la inversión "todavía no da rendimiento", aunque las cuentas, aunque Fotovoltaica Tarazona Trece cerró 2020 con un resultado positivo de algo más de 8.000 euros.
El padre que no lo quería en TVE. Prats también ha hablado en más de una ocasión sobre su padre y las diferencias en la manera de trabajar que tiene con él: “Él vivía más para trabajar y yo para vivir. Tengo la responsabilidad de cumplir con mi cometido, pero es otra cosa”.
Al locutor Matías Prats Cañete le costó aceptar que su hijo siguiera sus pasos, y el propio presentador contó en 2017 que su padre era rígido en lo profesional y que llegó a recomendar que no lo cogieran cuando entró como becario en TVE, aunque acabó confiando en él y, en sus palabras, “fue siempre mi fiel compañero, mi profesor”.
De la radio a Estudio Estadio. Nacido en Madrid en 1950, Prats estudió Periodismo y Derecho en la Universidad CEU San Pablo y empezó en la emisora La Voz de Madrid como colaborador de ‘Domingo deportivo español’. En abril de 1975 ingresó en TVE como estudiante en prácticas, y en la cadena pública acabó presentando ‘Estudio Estadio’ (de 1981 a 1993, y de nuevo en 1995 y 1997) y los telediarios en diferentes franjas entre 1991 y 1996.
Y su faceta deportiva le llevó a estar presente en ocho Juegos Olímpicos, seis Mundiales de fútbol, torneos de tenis como Roland Garros o Wimbledon y citas de golf como el Masters de Augusta o la Ryder Cup.
Más de un cuarto de siglo en Antena 3. Prats fichó por Antena 3 el 14 de septiembre de 1998, compartió la conducción de los informativos con Susanna Griso y Olga Viza, antes de pasar a la segunda edición en 2003 y de ponerse en 2014 al frente de los informativos del fin de semana. En esa etapa vivió el directo que, según él mismo, más le ha marcado: estaba al frente de Antena 3 Noticias el 11 de septiembre de 2001, conectando con Ricardo Ortega desde Nueva York.
Y si algo le ha dado popularidad entre las generaciones más jóvenes son sus chascarrillos y juegos de palabras, que le han convertido más de una vez en trending topic y en protagonista de memes.
Anuncios y sociedades. A su trabajo como presentador se sumó la publicidad, y si te suena el “Permíteme que insista”, no es casualidad: Prats había sido la cara de Línea Directa desde 2012, con anuncios como ese, y despidió la relación con una campaña en la que su compañera de los informativos del fin de semana, Mónica Carrillo, figuraba entre los posibles sucesores.
Además de la fotovoltaica, el periodista también tuvo otra sociedad, M P Babas S.L., fundada en 1993 y dedicada a la representación de profesionales de los medios de comunicación y a la producción de programas de televisión y radio.
Más de cinco décadas después de entrar como becario en TVE, Prats sigue siendo uno de los rostros más conocidos de la televisión española.

articles.title: DarkBlinders Compromises Israeli Target and Iraqi Kurdish Government Cloud Environment
articles.text:
Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a cyber espionage campaign targeting Israel and the Kurdistan Region of Iraq by an Iran state-aligned threat actor between August and October 2026.
According to a report published by Dream Research Labs, the campaign has led to the compromise of a high-profile individual in Israel, along with additional compromises affecting a government cloud environment in the Kurdistan Region.
The activity has been attributed to a threat actor known as DarkBlinders, an Iran-nexus group assessed to be active since at least September 2024 and linked to attacks aimed at aviation infrastructure and telecommunications in the U.A.E. and Iraq. It exhibits no technical overlap with other known hacking groups.
Attacks mounted by the group are known to rely on spear-phishing as an initial access pathway to lure recipients into opening trojanized utilities or clicking on attacker-controlled websites that host similar tools as direct downloads.
Previous attack chains documented by Elastic Security Labs and Group-IB have led to the deployment of SHELBYLOADER (aka HOTAIR), which is launched via DLL sideloading to ultimately execute a backdoor called SHELBYC2 (aka AEROSTAT) that uses GitHub for command-and-control (C2), data exfiltration, and remote control. Elastic is tracking the threat cluster under the moniker REF8685.
Then early last month, Palo Alto Networks shed light on a campaign dubbed Blinder Tunnel in which the threat actor, which it calls CL-STA-1178, was observed masquerading as the Dubai Airports IT department to distribute malware-laced coding challenges to high-value targets.
The bogus recruitment scheme was first detected in late March 2026, although evidence indicates that the attackers were staging and testing attack infrastructure as far back as November 2025.
The social engineering campaign is assessed to have approached specific targets with lucrative job offers to trick them into executing a self-contained application that mimicked a career portal and instructed them to complete a questionnaire.
Submitting the questionnaire does not cause any data to be exfiltrated or initiate any response from an external domain. Instead, it's meant to serve as a harmless decoy and build credibility before delivering the next stage payload containing the malware in the form of a Microsoft Visual Studio project archive that's dressed up as a coding assessment.
The attack chain makes use of three techniques to establish persistent access: A malicious C# project ".csproj" file is used to trigger AppDomainManager injection, followed by DLL sideloading to deliver an updated version of SHELBYLOADER (aka ShelbyLoader V2), which then launches SHELBYC2. Also deployed via SHELBYC2 is a tunneling utility called Blackwood.
"The attackers behind the activity used tailored social engineering techniques to masquerade as Dubai Airports recruiters, using a trojanized Visual Studio coding challenge to target a high-value job seeker based in Iraq," Unit 42 said.
"The campaign is characterized by misuse of built-in developer tools and DLL sideloading. Attackers also used AppDomainManager hijacking to bypass security monitors like ETW [Event Tracing for Windows]."
The latest findings from Dream show that the threat actor continues to rely on social engineering, while combining both credential phishing and malware delivery. This involves the use of government, webmail, and cloud-service lookalike domains to collect credentials or present attacker-controlled file downloads. Some of the highlighted domains include -
- gcc-sg[.]cloud/owa/auth/logon.aspx
- mfakuwait[.]online/owa/auth/logon.aspx
- moelcloud[.]online/drive/file/d/1JpH3ySmJpvX6TyGnF7C-S8qYiaoxyC5O
The threat actor has also been observed setting decoy brand domains for a fake videoconferencing application called StarkMeet (stark-meet[.]com, stark-meet[.]online, and stark-meet[.]website). Installing and launching the app leads to the execution of ShelbyLoader V2 and SHELBYC2.
The development is also a sign that the threat actor is trying out different methods for malware delivery, ranging from coding assessments to counterfeit software.
Dream said the DarkBlinders activity belongs to the same operational cluster as UNC5795 and Dust Specter, citing infrastructure and malware overlaps. Dust Specter, documented by Zscaler in March 2026, refers to a suspected Iran-nexus operation targeting government officials in Iraq by impersonating the country's Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
"Historical server fingerprints, overlapping victimology, and supporting attribution research lead us to assess with medium confidence that UNC5795 and UNC5187 may represent related sub-clusters within the broader APT34 group," it added.
"Their overlapping focus on Iraqi government entities adds context to this technical connection and suggests a shared intelligence collection interest. Combined with their respective APT34 associations, these findings support a medium-confidence assessment that the two clusters are operationally related and may belong to the same broader group."
Prince of Persia Hosts C2 in the U.S. for the First Time in a Decade
The disclosure comes as Prince of Persia (aka Infy), a lesser-known threat group sponsored by the Iranian government, has been observed running one of its C2 servers ("68.65.122[.]203") from the U.S. this year. The server was likely built in July 2026.
The infrastructure is a second-stage C2 server associated with Tornado, a Tonnerre variant that's dropped via one-day software vulnerabilities and uses both HTTPS and the Telegram API for C2. The emergence of new C2 servers in late May 2026 follows three months of inactivity, which has been described as the "longest downtime in nearly two decades of activity by the threat actor."
"We have been monitoring Prince of Persia's exfiltration activity for the past six months," Tomer Bar, associate vice president of security research at Semperis, said. "The number of victims remains low, which could indicate either targeted attacks or difficulties infecting new victims."
"The Iranian threat actor decided to host its new C2 server on U.S. soil — at the same time as the beginning of the recent hostilities between Iran and the United States. This is the last place we expected to find the threat actor hiding."

articles.title: Looking for a job? Estonia's Roleo just raised €2.9 million to help you on your journey | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Roleo, an Estonian personal AI career agent, has raised €2.9 million to expand across Europe and help tech professionals discover career opportunities – without the hassle of searching and applying.
The round was led by the Baltic venture capital firm Practica Capital and included participation from Nordic VC Inventure. The company has secured €3.46 million in total funding to date.
“Most people spend years building their careers, but only actively manage them when something goes wrong or they decide it is time for a change. Meanwhile, great opportunities come and go, often without the right people ever hearing about them,” says Janer Gorohhov, co-founder and CEO of Roleo.
“We believe everyone should have a personal active career agent that understands what they want, keeps an eye on the market, and brings relevant opportunities to them. You should be able to focus on doing great work without missing out on what could come next.”
Roleo’s funding comes amid a series of European investments in AI-powered recruitment and workforce technology in 2026.
In September, London-based Jack & Jill raised €34.68 million for its AI agents connecting jobseekers and employers, while Belgium’s Spott secured €18.3 million for recruitment software.
Other rounds included €6 million for France’s HrFlow.ai, €3.4 million for the UK’s inploi and €1.8 million for Belgium’s Ringtime, alongside €18.09 million for Spain’s Orbio and €5.3 million for Iceland’s 50skills.
Together with Roleo, these eight selected rounds represent approximately €90.5 million in newly announced funding.
Roleo’s lead investor announced the closing of its €80 million Baltic-focused fund in 2024 – which has presumably helped mobilise today’s investment
“We saw potential in the Roleo founders – their proven operational experience and grounded, yet very high ambition. They came with a clear short-term plan and a long-term vision that’s easy to relate to. Leading this round was a natural fit for us, and we believe they are the team best positioned to set a new standard for how people build their careers,” adds Donatas Keras, Partner at Practica Capital.
Founded in 2025, Roleo is a personal AI career agent for technology professionals, designed to help people discover relevant opportunities and manage their careers without constantly having to search for their next job.
The company was founded by Janer Gorohhov, co-founder of identity verification unicorn Veriff, and Vahur Hansen, a former member of Wise’s early engineering team and co-founder of startup Membo.
Roleo learns about each user’s experience, ambitions, and preferences, identifies relevant opportunities across Europe, and connects professionals directly with employers when there is mutual interest – without the candidate submitting a job application.
Unlike traditional job boards, which require candidates to search and apply, Roleo builds an understanding of what each individual wants from their career. This includes not only their skills and previous roles, but also their expectations around compensation, flexibility, responsibilities, and future development. Users remain in control of their visibility, personal information, and whether they wish to pursue a particular opportunity.
Roleo’s user base already includes people from leading technology companies such as Google, Amazon, Stripe and Spotify. The service is free for professionals.
“AI is already changing how people handle everyday tasks, from managing information to organising their finances. Yet career management still requires people to do most of the work themselves,” Janer said.
“We want to build something that stays with you throughout your career, learns what matters to you, and helps you make better decisions over time. The goal isn’t to have AI make career decisions for people, but to make sure they have the right information and opportunities when those decisions matter.”
Since the beginning of 2026, Roleo’s agent has connected its users with 30,000 career opportunities they explored further.
Today’s funding will support both the company’s expansion across European markets and further product development, making Roleo increasingly responsive to individual needs and expanding the ways it can support users beyond job matching.
Markus Villig, angel investor, founder and CEO of Bolt, added: “I’ve watched Janer build Veriff and I know what Vahur did at Wise. Both know first-hand how hard it is to find and hire great people across Europe.”

articles.title: En 'GTA 6' podrás romper la relación entre Jason y Lucía: la decisión es tuya
articles.text:
Noviembre ya está aquí y solo dos semanas y media nos separan del lanzamiento de GTA 6. Los fanáticos están tachando los días para acceder a lo nuevo de Rockstar Games, que nos continúa sorprendiendo con más detalles hasta aquí desconocidos. Desde el estudio han confirmado que, por ejemplo, será decisión de los jugadores mantener a Jason y Lucía como pareja o romper su relación.
Rob Nelson, cojefe de Rockstar, confirmó en una reciente entrevista con la revista EDGE que GTA 6 no forzará un componente romántico entre Jason y Lucía. Las acciones de los jugadores van a afectar el desenlace del vínculo entre los personajes, lo cual añadirá todavía más granularidad y apertura a la experiencia.
Según Nelson, GTA 6 planteará a Jason y Lucía tratando de tener una relación, pero no será obligatorio seguir por esa línea. Si los usuarios prefieren que se mantengan como socios criminales, pueden hacerlo. O pueden iniciar un noviazgo y luego distanciarse y cortar de forma definitiva. Las posibilidades que va a brindar el juego son realmente interesantes.
Hasta aquí, tanto los tráiler de GTA 6 como el vistazo extendido al juego han mostrado a Jason y Lucía colaborando y manteniendo una relación muy cercana. Sin embargo, los eventos del juego pueden cambiar el panorama, según lo que cada jugador decida cuando se le presenten ciertas situaciones. Y no necesariamente tienen que ser cosas de vida o muerte, pues ignorar las llamadas o los mensajes del otro personaje puede condicionar el vínculo.
"Al principio, ellos desean estar juntos y darle una nueva oportunidad a su relación. Pero, a medida que avanza el juego, depende de ti mantenerla o perderla", explica Nelson sobre la dinámica entre Jason y Lucía en GTA 6.
Los jugadores de GTA 6 podrán decidir si Jason y Lucía siguen juntos o no
GTA 6 no será el primer juego de Rockstar Games en el que la decisión del protagonista va a cambiar el desenlace en su relación con otros. Algo parecido ya se vio en Red Dead Redemption 2, aunque en el caso de Grand Theft Auto VI promete ser todavía más complejo y con potenciales implicaciones sobre la jugabilidad.
Las posibilidades que traerá GTA 6 son mucho más amplias de las que nos imaginamos, y hasta que el juego no llegue a manos del público no sabremos a ciencia cierta hasta dónde llegan.
El lanzamiento de GTA 6 está pautado para el 19 de noviembre en PS5, PS5 Pro y Xbox Series X|S. La expectación por el juego es tan grande que se espera que en EE. UU. su debut provoque más de 1.000 millones de dólares en pérdidas de productividad en solo un día.

articles.title: One of Google’s Android partners turned 1.3 million set-top boxes into a botnet
articles.text:
Google says one of its Android manufacturing partners secretly built a backdoor in 1.3 million devices and turned them into a botnet. The company says it has now dismantled the backdoor and “cut ties” with the manufacturer, the Shenzhen, China-based Videostrong Technology Co., which has been banned from building or selling certified Android devices or supplying software for them.
One of Google’s Android partners turned 1.3 million set-top boxes into a botnet
Google says a manufacturer ‘intentionally’ hijacked its devices with malware.
The infected devices were used without owners’ knowledge for “malicious activity,” like ad fraud, data exfiltration, and routing unauthorized network traffic. Google claims the “backdoor and botnet were intentionally developed, deployed, and operated for financial gain,” saying:
Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates’ malware modules onto infected devices. These secondary modules were conducting ad-fraud; silently enrolling infected devices into residential proxy networks; and loading additional malware onto XCPE-compromised devices. We also took action to disrupt the command and control (C2) domains that operate these affiliate modules. Because these affiliates each have diversified distribution channels for their modules beyond XCPE, we assess that taking down their C2 domains will sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices.
It wasn’t just one device that was impacted, either — the malware was found “built directly into many different device models and brands over multiple years.” Most of those were Android TV set-top boxes, but the botnet also infected other “Android-based IoT devices, including telehealth devices, karaoke machines, and digital signage devices.”
Google says Videostrong used “obfuscation techniques” to load the malware onto users’ devices after they booted up the hardware for the first time. Google also says it made changes to its review process for device manufacturers after this incident.

articles.title: Hardware Defense Blocks Memory-Dependent Prefetcher Leakage (KU Leuven)
articles.text:
Researchers at KU Leuven and EURECOM published “SecDMP: Provably Secure Data Memory-Dependent Prefetching.”
Abstract Excerpt:
“In this work, we address this gap by designing a defense that is both secure and efficient. First, we propose a classification of DMP leakage, categorize existing and novel attacks, and analyze which leakage classes are mitigated by existing defenses. We validate this analysis empirically by implementing the first open-source DMPs on a RISC-V processor, showing that the only existing defense that aims to preserve DMP performance fails to protect against entire leakage classes. Next, we propose SecDMP, a provably secure and efficient hardware-based defense. SecDMP requires secrets to be marked in memory and ensures that DMPs never encode these secrets in the microarchitecture—without compromising performance for public data. We formally prove that SecDMP introduces no leakage beyond a baseline semantics without DMPs. Notably, when combined with speculative-execution defenses, SecDMP restores complete microarchitectural security for constant-time code. Finally, our empirical evaluation shows that SecDMP prevents all DMP leakage while incurring minimal performance overhead and hardware cost.”
Find the technical paper here. October 2026
Sprengers, Jens, Marton Bognar, Lesly-Ann Daniel, and Frank Piessens. “SecDMP: Provably Secure Data Memory-Dependent Prefetching (Extended Version).” arXiv preprint arXiv:2610.37454 (2026). License: CC BY-SA 4.0

articles.title: SA’s Naked launches pet insurance, with claims paid in minutes - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
South African insurtech startup Naked launches pet insurance for cats and dogs, with claims often paid out in minutes.
Launched in 2018 by actuaries Alex Thomson, Sumarie Greybe, and Ernest North, Naked has built an end-to-end digital platform that enables customers to manage their entire insurance experience online from an app.
Its platform offers comprehensive and instant cover for cars, homes, contents, and standalone items, using AI and automation to create a new type of insurance experience. Consumers benefit from lower costs as well as more control of their insurance experience. They can get a final insurance quote in less than 90 seconds, and switch or pause their cover, all online, without speaking to a contact centre agent.
Naked secured US$38 million in Series B2 funding in January 2025 to power its growth by deepening investment in automation and AI, product and market expansion, and enhancing advertising, and in May of this year became the first platform in the world to successfully develop and deploy a native app in ChatGPT that can provide a final, binding car insurance quote.
Its latest product, available through the Naked app, offers accident-only, accident-and-illness, and comprehensive cover that includes physiotherapy and routine care. Customers can choose an annual limit, select their own excess, and use any registered vet in South Africa. Covered treatments are not subject to separate treatment-specific sub-limits.
Naked uses AI to automatically approve eligible claims, including outside office hours, with more complex claims referred to its team for review. Early data shows a median payout time of 1.3 days, with 60 per cent of claims paid within 48 hours and the fastest paid in 12 minutes.
“When a pet needs emergency treatment, you’re already worried about what might be wrong and whether they’ll recover,” said Sumarie Greybe, co-founder of Naked. “The last thing you want to worry about is how you’ll pay the vet bill or how long you’ll have to wait to get your money back.”

articles.title: ChatGPT subit des perturbations : ce que l'on sait de la panne en cours — Frandroid
articles.text:
Les signalements ont commencé à grimper sur Downdetector vers 17 h 30 (heure de Paris) ce lundi 2 novembre. Les utilisateurs décrivent une page qui tourne dans le vide ou une réponse qui s’arrête au milieu d’une phrase. De notre côté, rien de tel, le service fonctionne chez nous.
Néanmoins, une panne de ChatGPT touche vite beaucoup de monde, même quand elle est partielle : le chatbot d’OpenAI a dépassé le milliard d’utilisateurs chaque semaine.
Cloudflare en cause ?
Le site indien PaidFreeDroid a publié une explication vers 19 heures, heure de Paris. Selon lui, le réseau de Cloudflare marcherait à moitié alors que les serveurs d’OpenAI qui font tourner les modèles fonctionneraient normalement.
En revanche, certains relais de Cloudflare perdraient des données en route, en Inde, en Amérique du Nord et en Europe, et afficheraient des pages d’erreur 520, 522 ou 524.
ChatGPT peut aussi sembler fonctionner en envoyant sa réponse mot après mot, en continu, et si la connexion lâche en cours de route, le texte se coupe net ou se répète.
Ce genre de panne est déjà arrivé. Le 18 novembre 2025, une panne de Cloudflare avait coupé ChatGPT, X ou Shopify pendant plusieurs heures. Selon CNBC, la page de statut d’OpenAI avait alors attribué ses problèmes à un « fournisseur de services tiers ».
Au moment où on écrit ces lignes, ni OpenAI ni Cloudflare n’ont confirmé quoi que ce soit, en tout cas nous n’avons rien trouvé. D’autres mesures collent mal avec une panne mondiale. La sonde d’UptimeRobot teste chatgpt.com toutes les cinq minutes, et elle n’a relevé aucune erreur à 18 h 45 depuis l’Amérique du Nord. Les codes 52x ne prouvent pas grand-chose non plus. Ils s’affichent quand Cloudflare ne reçoit pas de réponse à temps du serveur d’origine, ici celui d’OpenAI. Bref, l’incident a l’air réel mais limité à certaines zones.
