articles.title: Is Your SOC Ready for AI Agents? A Maturity Check Before You Deploy
articles.text:
Forty percent of security teams now use AI every day, and another 56% are testing it. Only 4% have no plans to adopt it, according to Prophet Security's State of AI in Security Operations 2026 survey of more than 250 CISOs, SOC leaders and practitioners. For the teams still testing, the next decision is whether their own SOC is ready.
AI SOC readiness has two parts: whether a SOC has the problems AI SOC agents are built for, and whether it has the data access, context, written standards and oversight rules that AI agents need to investigate alerts accurately in its environment. A SOC does not need to be far along a maturity model to be ready. AI agents do their first work on the bottom layer, alert handling, and the analyst hours they return give a team room to work on the layers above it.
The next section describes those problems. Technical readiness covers four areas: access and context, an investigation standard with baseline metrics, rules for what the agent may do, and a plan for the time it gives back.
Which SOCs benefit the most from AI SOC agents
The SOCs that gain the most from AI SOC agents usually recognize several of the problems below, whether an outside provider works their alerts or their own analysts do.
If an MDR or MSSP works your alerts:
- Your MDR flags threats too slowly. The provider works your alerts in a queue it shares with its other customers, so the escalation for a real intrusion can arrive hours after the activity started.
- Your MDR hands alerts back for lack of context. An escalation arrives with a short summary and questions such as is this login expected, is this a production server, or is this user traveling? The provider often does not know your users, assets and business well enough to finish the investigation, so your analysts do the rest.
- Your MDR closes alerts without showing its work. When the provider marks an alert benign, the note may not say what it checked and how it came to that conclusion, so your team either trusts the call or runs the investigation again.
- Your MDR's coverage stops at the tools it supports. Many contracts cover the EDR and a set list of log sources, so alerts from everything else, such as a SaaS application or a second cloud platform, land on your team.
If your own analysts work the queue, including whatever the provider sends back:
- "Are we impacted?" takes days to answer. When a critical vulnerability or a new campaign makes the news, leadership wants an answer the same day. Getting one means hunting across the environment by hand, usually by an analyst who is also working the queue.
- Lower-severity alerts wait or get closed in bulk. A thorough investigation means pivoting across the SIEM, EDR, identity provider, cloud console and email tools, so the team keeps up with critical and high alerts and gets to the rest when it can. In the survey, 60% of respondents said an alert they had ignored or missed later turned into a serious issue, such as a breach or downtime.
- Noisy detections get switched off. Tuning a rule that fires too often takes time the team does not have, so the rule gets disabled and the technique it watched goes uncovered.
- Hunting and detection engineering wait for spare time. Proactive work happens when someone has a free afternoon, because the alert queue comes first.
- A few senior analysts carry the hard cases. Only one or two people know how to work the most difficult investigations, so a single resignation can set the team back.
- Nights and weekends are thinly covered. Staffing the queue around the clock takes more analysts than the budget covers, so alerts that fire after hours wait until morning or go to whoever is on call.
AI SOC agents are built for this work. They are designed to start on each alert as it arrives, whichever tool raised it and at whatever hour. They can pull the context an outside provider lacks from your own systems and record the evidence behind each conclusion, so your team can check it. Some can also run a hunt the day a new threat is disclosed, which turns "are we impacted?" into a set of queries with answers. The analyst hours they return can go to the detection and hunting work that waits today.
If several of these problems sound familiar, the need is there. The next question is whether your SOC can support a deployment.
Where AI agents fit on a SOC maturity model
Prophet Security's SOC maturity model, the SOC Hierarchy of Needs, has five levels: alert management, detection coverage, threat awareness, proactive hunting and posture improvements. Each level depends on the one below it. A team buried in alerts rarely gets to hunting, and a team that hunts without threat awareness has no clear idea what to look for.
Many SOCs have not yet stabilized the first level. In the State of AI in Security Operations 2026 survey, respondents said 28% of their alerts are never investigated.
AI SOC agents usually start at that first level, investigating alerts as they arrive. Newer platforms also run hunts and propose detections, work that reaches into levels two and four. Either way, the analyst hours they return go to work above the first level, so readiness depends on what the first level needs.
An AI agent can only investigate what it can query
An AI agent investigates by running queries against your tools, so it cannot see anything it has no access to. If it can query the EDR but not the identity provider, it can describe what happened on the endpoint but not which account was behind it.
Readiness here has three parts:
- API access to the sources an investigation needs. That usually means the SIEM, EDR, identity provider, cloud platforms, email and key SaaS applications.
- Context the agent can read. An agent needs asset criticality, user roles, VIP lists, business units and known-benign activity, such as scheduled scans and admin scripts, to tell an attacker from a legitimate administrator.
- Healthy data pipelines. A silent or delayed log source can make an investigation look complete when key evidence is missing, so the health of the pipelines that feed investigations needs monitoring.
A quick test: take five recent incidents and list every query a senior analyst ran to close them. Any query the agent could not run marks a gap to close before a pilot.
Data access also raises the most common objection. In our survey, 44% of teams cited data privacy and how AI models are trained, the most frequent roadblock respondents named. Ask each vendor whether your data trains their models and where your data is processed.
Define a finished investigation and record your baseline
A pilot needs a written standard to grade the agent against. In many SOCs, only senior analysts know that standard, and it is rarely written down.
The standard covers which evidence closes a phishing case, when an impossible-travel alert needs a call to the user's manager, and what counts as enough to call an alert benign. Writing it down for your highest-volume alert types also gives new analysts an onboarding document.
Also keep a list of the detections that were switched off. In our survey, up to 40% of organizations had turned off some detections because they lacked the people to check them. When an agent investigates every alert, some of those rules can come back, and the list tells you where to start.
Then record the numbers you will compare against: the share of alerts investigated, mean time to investigate, time from alert to first look, and how often closed alerts are reopened. The survey gives a reference point. A thorough investigation takes an average of 75 minutes, and alerts often wait close to an hour before anyone opens them.
You can download our guide on detection engineering to learn more about how an agentic SOC benefits detection engineering.
Decide what the agent may do, and who approves more
Investigation and action carry different risks, and most teams treat them differently. In the survey, 57% of teams require a human to review every AI decision before an alert is closed. On response, 44% have AI recommend actions that people carry out, 30% let it handle low-risk remediation on its own, and no respondent gives it full, unsupervised autonomy.
A ready SOC has these rules written down before a pilot starts:
- Default approvals. A list of the actions that stay human-approved, such as isolating a host, disabling an account or blocking a domain.
- How permissions widen. Who can grant the agent more autonomy for a category of action, and what track record they need to see first.
- Where findings land. Agent findings should appear in the case management or ticketing tools analysts already use, so nobody has to watch another console.
- Who owns feedback. A named person reviews the agent's mistakes and turns corrections into guidance it will use next time.
Starting with read-only access for investigations, then widening permissions as confidence grows, applies the same rules a SOC uses for a new human analyst. Prophet Security's framework for building trust in an AI SOC follows the same stepwise approach.
A readiness checklist mapped to the maturity model
Answer each question yes or no. Part 1 checks the need, and Part 2 checks technical readiness. The level in parentheses shows which layer of the SOC Hierarchy of Needs each item belongs to.
Part 1: Does your SOC need AI SOC agents?
- Do escalations from your MDR or MSSP arrive hours after the activity started? (Level 1: alert management)
- Does your provider hand alerts back because it lacked the context to finish them? (Level 3: threat awareness)
- Does your provider close alerts without showing what it checked? (Level 1: alert management)
- Do alerts from tools outside your provider's coverage land on your team? (Level 1: alert management)
- Does it take more than a day to tell leadership whether you are impacted by a new vulnerability or campaign? (Level 4: proactive hunting)
- Do low- and medium-severity alerts wait, or get closed in bulk without an investigation? (Level 1: alert management)
- Have noisy detections been switched off because no one had time to tune them? (Level 2: detection coverage)
- Do hunting and detection engineering wait until someone has spare time? (Level 4: proactive hunting)
- Do only one or two senior analysts know how to work your hardest cases? (Level 1: alert management)
- Do alerts that fire at night or on weekends wait until morning? (Level 1: alert management)
Each yes is a problem an AI SOC agent can take on, and the more yes answers, the stronger the case for a deployment.
Part 2: Is your SOC ready to deploy them?
- Can a new tool query your SIEM, EDR, identity, cloud and email sources through an API? (Level 1: alert management)
- Are asset criticality, user roles and known-benign activity recorded somewhere a system can read? (Level 3: threat awareness)
- Is there a written standard for what a complete investigation includes, for the alert types that make up most of your volume? (Level 1: alert management)
- Have you decided which actions stay human-approved, and who can widen the agent's permissions? (Level 1: alert management)
- Do you monitor whether the log sources your investigations depend on are arriving? (Level 2: detection coverage)
- Do you know your current share of alerts investigated and your mean time to investigate? (Level 1: alert management)
- Do you keep a list of detections that were switched off for capacity reasons? (Level 2: detection coverage)
- Is there a plan, with named owners, for the analyst hours an agent will return, such as scheduled hunts or detection work? (Level 4: proactive hunting)
A "no" on any of the first four is worth fixing before a production pilot. The other four can be worked on during it.
What to do if the answer is not yet
Most items on the Part 2 list are configuration and documentation work: issuing API credentials, exporting asset and user context, and writing down the investigation standard. A workable order:
- Close the access gaps from the five-incident test first, since every later step depends on the agent seeing the data.
- Write the investigation standards for your highest-volume alert types.
- Run the agent in parallel with your analysts for a few weeks. Record the baseline before it starts, and treat every analyst override as data about where the agent needs more context.
- Widen the agent's permissions one category of action at a time, as its record supports it.
Some teams that are not ready consider building their own agents instead. The survey suggests caution: 72% of AI users had tried building internal AI tools, and 46% of those projects were abandoned, never reached production, or were replaced by a commercial product.
Building a functioning prototype is only a small chunk of the work. Most of the work is engineering and maintenance of integrations that take weeks to build but break when a vendor changes an API; rate limits to work around; model deprecations every six to nine months that force a full round of evals, guardrails, and prompt injection testing; and audit trails explaining why each alert was closed.
How Prophet Security Works
Prophet Security is the leading AI SOC platforms for enterprise SOCs, recognized in Rising in Cyber 2026, an honor voted on by more than 150 CISOs and security leaders. Its platform, Prophet AI, works from the stack a team already runs. First-generation AI SOC tools stopped at alert triage. Prophet AI enables an agentic SOC, with specialist agents for investigation, threat hunting and detection engineering.
Prophet AI SOC Analyst investigates every alert at every severity, around the clock, with the depth of a senior analyst. It queries SIEM, EDR, identity, cloud and email tools directly and records every question, query and piece of evidence behind a determination, so an analyst can rerun any query and check the work. It takes response actions only within permissions the customer sets, with human approval as the default.
Prophet AI Threat Hunter is built to answer "are we impacted?" It keeps a profile of each organization's industry, technology stack and the threat actors that target it. When a severe new threat emerges, hunts for it run automatically in the background. Scheduled hunts, including hunts against coverage gaps and questions the team writes in plain language, run on the cadence the team sets. Suspicious leads go to the SOC Analyst for a full investigation.
Prophet AI Detection Engineer takes on the detection engineering work that waits for spare time. It keeps a live MITRE ATT&CK coverage map built from the organization's own investigations, showing which techniques are covered, which have gone quiet and which are dark. It builds and tunes detections from what investigations, hunts and coverage gaps reveal, writes them in the rule language of the SIEM or tool they run in, and backtests each one against the organization's own history. Each change arrives as a reviewable proposal with its rationale and backtest results, and by default nothing reaches production until the team approves it.
Each product's findings feed the others. Investigations show which detections are noisy and where coverage is thin, hunts look in those gaps, and what the hunts find becomes new detections. The team teaches Prophet AI in plain language, and that guidance shapes how investigations run, how hunts are scoped and how detections are written. Customer data never trains its models, and the data plane can run inside the customer's own VPC.
The full State of AI in Security Operations 2026 report, including the survey data cited here, is available to download.

articles.title: Claude’s new rules against game cloning won’t stop the AI copying boom
articles.text:
Last week, Anthropic introduced a new system prompt designed to stop its Claude models from re-creating specific, existing video games. While that move could help shield Anthropic from some liability, it’s unlikely to slow much of the massive wave of AI-assisted game porting and copying that has emerged in recent months.
A social media user and AI decompilation enthusiast going by the name “chasm” was among the first to note the prompt change late last week, saying a new rule seemed to be added to the Claude Code prompt on or around October 27. That rule—included in a json file under the name “tengu_heron_brook”—reads as follows:
Do build original games, games in a genre, and games from the user’s own designs and assets. Don’t build a recreation of a specific existing game, even if it is renamed or called original.
XDA later independently verified that the new rule appears in version 2.1.314 of the Claude Code binary, which was released on October 30. XDA also reported that the “tengu_heron_brook” rule had been used for other purposes in earlier versions and that the Claude Opus 5.5 model specifically seemed to have its own distinct and independent instructions restricting game recreations as part of its system prompt bundle.
Following chasm’s initial report, Anthropic software engineer Addy Osmani confirmed on social media that the company had “added two sentences to Claude Code’s prompt on Opus 5.5 to steer it away from recreating someone else’s specific game because using Claude to infringe IP is against our usage policy.”
He added that the new prompt was designed to still allow “original games, genre games, and games built from your own designs and assets,” even as a handful of issue reports on Anthropic’s GitHub suggest the new prompt is getting in the way of some game development use cases.

articles.title: Hypersonica secures €100 million to boost sovereign hypersonic deep-strike systems for Europe and its allies | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Hypersonica, the British-German defence company developing sovereign hypersonic deep-strike systems for Europe and its allies, has secured €100 million in Series B funding.
The Series B funding round was co-led by Lightspeed and General Catalyst, with continued participation from existing investors including Plural and 201 Ventures.
“Hypersonica is redefining how advanced defence capability gets built. The team pairs deep technical expertise with exceptional speed of execution, and the strength of our support reflects our confidence in both the technology and their ability to deliver,” said Alexander Schmitt, Partner at Lightspeed.
Founded in 2023 with engineering teams spread across its Munich HQ and its wholly-owned subsidiary in London, Hypersonic is building what it describes as a first-of-kind, sovereign and cost-effective hypersonic strike capability, one that operates without ITAR restrictions and is developed entirely within Europe.
Led by co-founders Dr. Philipp Kerth and Dr. Marc Ewenz, the startup set out to address the fundamental challenges of hypersonic flight, where extreme aerodynamic heating renders conventional aerospace technology obsolete at speeds beyond Mach 5. The startup overcomes this challenge with state-of-the-art materials, control architectures and avionics capable of delivering stable and manoeuvrable flight.
Since its €23.3 million Series A in February 2026, Hypersonica has successfully tested its prototype HS-1, achieving speeds above Mach 6 over a range exceeding 300 kilometres, becoming the first privately funded European defence company to reach that milestone. The company says its prototype achieved speeds above Mach 6 at industry-beating cost-effectiveness, claiming its development model reduces costs by more than 80% compared to conventional approaches.
The Series B funding comes as governments across the continent move from debating the need for long-range strike capability to actively funding programmes to shore up their security. The UK’s Defence Investment Plan has announced an initial €921.5 million (£770 million) over four years for the UK-German Deep Precision Strike (DPS) programme under the Trinity House Agreement, while a NATO-led multinational initiative has announced €44.28 million (£37 billion) of investment in DPS capabilities over the coming decade.
“The debate about whether Europe needs hypersonic deep-strike capability is over. Governments have recognised the requirement and begun funding programmes. The challenge now is delivery. Europe needs credible hypersonic long-range capability, and more value for every pound and euro it spends,” said Dr Kerth and Dr Ewenz, co-founders of Hypersonica.
The fresh capital will be used to accelerate the development of its deep-strike systems, increase testing cadence, expand operations and reindustrialisation across Europe. The financing will also create hundreds of highly skilled engineering and manufacturing jobs across the UK and Germany.
Hypersonica aims to have its hypersonic deep-strike systems fully developed by 2029, while simultaneously building a broader European technology and manufacturing base with a goal of production at scale.

articles.title: Readwise takes on Amazon's Kindle and Goodreads with its new app for book lovers | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Readwise, the maker of a read-it-later app and digital reading companion that keeps track of your highlights across services, is now taking on Amazon’s e-book empire with its latest app, Readwise Books. The app is an e-book store and helps you track what you’ve read, similar to Amazon’s Goodreads.
The bootstrapped startup described the new app as “a cross between Kindle and the Goodreads apps,” as it offers a single place to buy, read, and track books. However, Readwise Books aims to offer more detailed reading stats than the dates you read a book and whether you finished it. It lets readers visualize richer reading data like words read, pace, depth, immersion, and sessions.
Meanwhile, its new store offers “millions” of e-books from the big five publishers and others, initially in the U.S., with more countries to come. Print books (fulfilled by Bookshop.org’s distributor) and some audiobooks are available as well, the company notes.
The launch comes at a time when there’s been an explosion of new reading apps and book trackers, all hoping to challenge Goodreads by introducing new features like book clubs, widgets, improved discovery features, goal-setting, better lists and organizational tools, habit-tracking, and more. However, few indie developers have gone so far as to launch an alternative to Amazon’s Kindle e-books store, which remains the industry leader, with an 83% share of the market when Kindle+ (formerly Kindle Unlimited) is included in the stats.
One of Kindle’s bigger advantages is that it offers an end-to-end solution for everything related to reading e-books, from the hardware devices to the book-tracking log. Readwise isn’t selling its own e-readers, but it is attempting to create its own community around reading, complete with tools for reading purchased and uploaded e-books, tracking them (like on Goodreads), sharing your reading progress with friends, and more.
It also offers a number of ways to track books outside its ecosystem. This includes a way to track reading sessions by using Kindle’s browser-based Cloud Reader and a feature that lets you snap photos of physical books to mark your progress. Plus, you can upload any DRM-free EPUBs (a common e-book file format without copy protection). The app can read your e-books aloud via text-to-speech.
Readwise believes its more in-depth metrics could be a big selling point, too, likening them to a “Strava for reading” — a reference to the metrics-heavy exercise app.
“The desire to read books, like exercising and eating well, is laden with guilt,” the company explained in a blog post penned by co-founders Daniel Doyon and Tristan Homsi. “Many people feel like they should be reading more, but feeling bad about it tends to change nothing. The session tracking taps into a different psychological mechanism. It makes the reading you’re doing legible and, as the adage goes, that which is measured is improved.”
The company adds that the most consistent feedback from users is that the app has led them to read more without willpower tricks like goal-setting, streaks, or scheduling.
With publishers’ permission, the app will support AI-powered features as well, like session recaps, definitions and term lookups, word and phrase translations, and a location-aware ability to ask questions about the part you’re reading. (So far, only HarperCollins has opted in, though.)
Unlike Goodreads’ locked-down ecosystem, Readwise is embracing open technology. This includes a public API and an MCP server. The latter supports AI agents that could be used to research book recommendations on your behalf, use your Readwise data to create a books page on your personal website, or even wire up your hackable e-reader to log your sessions automatically, depending on how involved your AI use cases may be.
The new Readwise Books app will remain free, with some AI features later going behind a paywall. Its prior apps for reading and tracking highlights are either $7.99 per month each or $9.99 per month for both.
The Books app is currently in beta and requires an invite, unless you’re already a Readwise subscriber.

articles.title: Can't find your NHL team's game? Telus, Rogers play blame game
articles.text:
If you’ve tried to catch a regular-season NHL game recently, you’ve probably had the same problem as many sports fans: you can’t find it anywhere. However, Telus is now telling its TV subscribers it’s not their fault.
Telus sent a message to OptikTV subscribers Friday afternoon, spotted by Rob Williams, National Sports Editor at MobileSyrup’s sister sites Daily Hive and Offside, that explains why some games are missing by blaming Rogers and the new broadcasting rights deal.
“The decision, made by Rogers, impacts broadcasting access for the 2026-2027 NHL hockey season,” says Telus. “Here’s what you need to know to cheer on your favourite sport and team: NHL Monday Night Hockey has moved from Amazon Prime Video to Sportsnet+. These games are now exclusive to Sportsnet+ and are not included in your Sportsnet channel subscription.”
Telus sent out an email to customers today, helping them find NHL hockey games that are no longer available on cable television. https://t.co/kzbpzYXgRD
— Rob Williams (@RobTheHockeyGuy) October 30, 2026
“NHL Wednesday Night Hockey has moved from your Sportsnet theme pack to Amazon Prime Video. These games are now exclusive to Amazon Prime Video and are not included in your Sportsnet Channel subscription.”
Update Nov. 2, 2026, at 4:14 p.m. ET: After publication, a Sportsnet spokesperson told MobileSyrup that cable providers can make Sportsnet+ content available to customers, noting that Rogers did something similar earlier this year:
“All cable providers have the opportunity to make the exclusive Sportsnet+ content available as part of their TV offering, the same way Rogers does at no additional cost for their customers. We’d encourage fans to contact their cable provider about this option.”
This appears to contradict what Telus told customers in its email about exclusive Sportsnet+ content not being included in channel subscriptions. MobileSyrup also reached out to Telus to learn more, and will update this story accordingly.
However, it’s worth pointing out that so far, Rogers is the only provider that has reached such an agreement with Sportsnet to make this content available to cable customers.
So why would Telus point out something everyone has known (and complained about) all season? The most likely reason is that Telus has been getting an influx of complaints about why they can’t find their favourite team’s game on a Wednesday or Monday night.
Fan frustration seems to be at a boiling point. The cost to be able to even go to games in person is insanely high, and with the amount of (very expensive) subscriptions that one fan needs to be able to go and even watch all 84 games for their team, it could push fans to sail the high seas and skip the subscriptions, if you catch my drift.
It’s especially prevalent in markets where TSN is the main regional broadcaster, where fans already have to subscribe to both TSN and Sportsnet. The Ottawa Citizen pointed out that without paying for cable and satellite and strictly using streaming services, the absolute lowest price to watch all 84 Ottawa Senators games, which includes adding and cancelling the most basic streaming plans at exactly the right time, is $519.61.
Another thing is that Rogers is now into its second consecutive 12-year media rights deal with the NHL, and Prime Video signed a sub-licensing agreement to show NHL games on Wednesday. Meanwhile, CBC recently announced the end of its Hockey Night in Canada broadcast after its simulcast agreement with Rogers ended. Each market also has its own regional broadcaster. So for now, this pretty backwards streaming method will stick around for the next dozen years, unless something changes and the league needs a new broadcaster in Canada.
Update Nov. 2, 2026, at 2:56 p.m. ET: Corrected some details about the Prime Video and CBC sub-licensing deals.
Source: Rob Williams (Twitter)

articles.title: Attackers Pose as IT Support on Microsoft Teams, Abuse AD CS to Steal Company Data
articles.text:
Attackers posing as IT support on Microsoft Teams talked employees into giving them remote control of their PCs. They then used insecure Active Directory Certificate Services (AD CS) settings to obtain login certificates for privileged accounts, including one for a domain controller.
Microsoft said in a report that it investigated two such intrusions, one of which resulted in company data being copied to an external server.
The attackers exploited no flaw in Teams itself. They relied on social engineering and on AD CS that had been set up insecurely, and Microsoft did not tie the activity to any known group.
How the Attacks Began
Both intrusions started the same way, Microsoft said. The attackers messaged and called employees on Teams while posing as the company's own IT or help desk, working from outside tenants with support-themed names so the contact looked familiar.
They talked each user into opening Quick Assist, a remote-help tool built into Windows, and reading the connection code back to them. That gave the attacker direct, hands-on control of the workstation.
From there, the attacker dropped an archive into the Downloads folder, unpacked it into a new folder named to resemble a Windows update, and ran its contents with a portable Python, Bun, or Java runtime. File names alone were a weak signal, because one copy was renamed while still carrying the real runtime's version details.
What a Certificate Buys an Attacker
AD CS is the Windows role that issues the certificates users and computers present when they log in. A certificate from a poorly configured template lets whoever holds it sign in as the account it names.
Microsoft said such a certificate continues to work even after the account's password is reset or the first machine is wiped, so neither step ends the attacker's access.
Case 1: Privileged Certificates, and a Gap in Containment
In the first intrusion, the attackers found a certificate template with a weakness known as ESC1. With that kind of template, the requester can name the account the certificate will represent, so a low-privileged user can request one that stands in for a privileged account.
The first wave of calls targeted three users and one workstation, producing certificates for three highly privileged accounts. Microsoft Defender's automatic attack disruption cut those identities off and dropped their active sessions. One privileged account, though, had been left out of the automatic response, so it stayed usable.
About 90 minutes later, a larger wave hit 16 users and a second workstation, producing certificates for 8 more privileged accounts. Microsoft said more than 1,000 later attempts to reach files over SMB or to log in were blocked.
Within seconds of obtaining a certificate, the attacker signed in to a domain controller and ran DCSync, a tool for copying password data from Active Directory. The operation had already begun when containment took hold, limiting how much could be replicated. Microsoft did not say how much credential data the attacker obtained.
The excluded account was the opening. The attacker kept using it, reached a file server, and ran a renamed copy of the file-copying tool Rclone to move data from a share to an outside SFTP server. Microsoft did not say how much data was taken.
The case shows, in Microsoft's words, that "partial identity containment can reduce attack activity while still leaving a viable privileged route."
Case 2: A Certificate for the Domain Controller
The second intrusion began the same way but took a different direction because that template weakness was not present. The attacker instead used a technique called PetitPotam to force a domain controller to authenticate to a machine the attacker controlled.
That NTLM login was relayed to the AD CS web enrollment page, an abuse known as ESC8, with no password needed. The attacker used the relayed login to request a certificate for the domain controller itself. With that certificate and Kerberos (PKINIT), the attacker obtained a ticket-granting ticket for the domain controller, turning a one-off relayed login into a lasting identity.
Here the response held. Defender raised ESC8 alerts, the customer isolated the workstation, and Microsoft said no further activity followed.
The difference between the two came down to containment. In the first, automatic disruption blocked most of the attack, but the one excluded account stayed open. In the second, isolating a single workstation stopped it.
What Defenders Can Do
There is no patch, because nothing here was a software flaw. Microsoft's advice is about configuration and response.
- Have staff confirm any unexpected support request through a known internal channel before sharing a screen or handing over remote control. Limit which outside Teams tenants can reach employees, and allow only approved remote-support tools.
- Review sign-in certificate templates for ones that let the requester name the account, or that too many users can enroll in, and remove enrollment rights that are not needed.
- Require HTTPS and turn on Extended Protection for Authentication (EPA) on web enrollment endpoints, and turn off NTLM there where you can. Microsoft's KB5005413 covers this, and its Defender for Identity posture checks flag templates and endpoints exposed to ESC1 and ESC8.
- Turn on certificate auditing. If a bad certificate was issued, revoke it, but remember that revocation does not cancel Kerberos tickets already issued; review active tickets separately.
- Treat any account left out of automatic containment as a deliberate decision and assign a manual action in its place.
What Is and Isn't Known
Microsoft did not attribute the intrusions to any named group and did not give the dates on which they happened.
The methods are not new. Researchers named the ESC1 and ESC8 certificate weaknesses in 2021, and the PetitPotam coercion trick was disclosed the same year. Microsoft itself had documented the Teams help-desk-to-remote-access entry method earlier in 2026.
What this report adds is that the two techniques meet in real intrusions, along with the lesson about the excluded account.
Newer Windows is less exposed to the ESC8 step. Microsoft turned EPA on by default for AD CS in Windows Server 2025, whereas Server 2022 and 2019 require it to be enabled manually.
Indicators and Detections
Microsoft's report lists Defender alerts across Teams, endpoints, and identity signals, and four advanced hunting queries that it calls "starting points for investigation" rather than proof on their own. It also published three file hashes tied to the initial-access scripts:
- SHA-256 85b6c424117494d3056e88689dbc94c75e9afdb187a339714043aec0da109f17 (JavaScript initial-access script)
- SHA-256 f326201269f1ee2f803ae435317507263bb6e0dbfdeb70bd1bb5446e2e46f001 (Python initial-access script)
- SHA-256 06c5c14f043aee3bcc5843b5f50909623d5c9a6239a7c1fba9cddad4111469e7 (Python initial-access script)

articles.title: Los peores finales de serie de la historia de la televisión
articles.text:
Nadie lo duda: las series se han convertido en el formato rey de la televisión actual. Y razones no faltan. Desde su capacidad para encapsular historias que se vuelven eventos de la cultura pop hasta su importancia para explorar en nuestra época. Lo cierto es que el mundo a capítulos se ha vuelto imprescindible para entender la evolución del mundo del entretenimiento hacia nuevos lugares. A la vez, su crecimiento y, al final, la herencia que deja su paso para toda una generación de espectadores.
Además, las producciones representan una de las herramientas culturales más influyentes de la cultura contemporánea. Todo, al transformar profundamente la forma en que consumimos entretenimiento y comprendemos el mundo. Por lo que sus relatos van más allá del simple ocio. También actúan como poderosos reflejos de la realidad social, explorando dilemas éticos, políticos y humanos complejos. De modo que el formato episódico genera una profunda conexión emocional y empatía entre la audiencia y los personajes. Algo que permite visibilizar temáticas urgentes como la salud mental, la diversidad y los conflictos geopolíticos.
Una combinación de elementos que transforma a las series en grandes eventos de la cultura pop. Por eso, el cierre de una producción televisiva emblemática representa uno de los desafíos más complejos para cualquier equipo de guionistas. Todo debido a que deben equilibrar las expectativas acumuladas de la audiencia con una resolución coherente. Pero a lo largo de la historia de la televisión, varias series que marcaron época arruinaron su legado en sus últimos minutos. A continuación, exploramos cuáles son los peores.
Juego de Tronos
Por supuesto, no debe sorprenderte encontrar este fiasco monumental en el primer lugar de la lista. No en vano, el desenlace de este fenómeno en 2019 se mantiene como el colapso más infame y doloroso de la cultura pop. Tras casi una década de intrigas políticas meticulosas y un desarrollo de personajes impecable, David Benioff y D.B. Weiss decidieron acelerar el ritmo de la historia. Todo, en una octava temporada de apenas seis episodios, lo que destruyó la lógica interna de la serie.
Las razones son múltiples, pero la más notoria es evidente. El penúltimo episodio transformó abruptamente a Daenerys Targaryen (Emilia Clarke) en una tirana genocida sin la justificación psicológica necesaria. Lo que destruye su arco en cuestión de minutos. El capítulo final empeoró la situación con una resolución política simplista y ridícula. A saber: Bran Stark (Isaac Hempstead-Wright), un personaje que pasó temporadas enteras al margen de la trama principal, fue coronado rey.
¿El motivo? Simplemente porque tenía la mejor historia que contar, una premisa que insultó la inteligencia de los espectadores. El guion sacrificó las profecías sembradas durante años, dejó cabos sueltos monumentales y despachó la amenaza de los Caminantes Blancos de forma apresurada. La indignación de la comunidad fue tan masiva que millones de fanáticos firmaron peticiones formales para rehacer por completo la temporada final. Para la historia de los malos finales de las series.
Lost (Perdidos)
El viaje de los supervivientes del vuelo 815 de Oceanic llegó a su fin en 2010 con un desenlace que dividió permanentemente a la comunidad televisiva. También, que definió los riesgos de estirar el misterio sin un plan maestro. Durante seis temporadas, los creadores Damon Lindelof y Carlton Cuse cautivaron al mundo construyendo una mitología densa. Y no una cualquiera. La trama de Lost estaba repleta de viajes en el tiempo, monstruos de humo, osos polares en islas tropicales y escotillas electromagnéticas.
Sin embargo, el episodio final esquivó la gran mayoría de estas incógnitas científicas y sobrenaturales para refugiarse en una resolución puramente espiritual y emocional. Eso con lo que parece una revelación seudomística sin asidero alguno. La historia concluía en un purgatorio donde los personajes se reunían después de morir para avanzar juntos hacia el más allá.
Un giro que dejó a millones de espectadores con una profunda sensación de estafa. Aunque los guionistas aclararon exhaustivamente que los protagonistas no estuvieron muertos durante los eventos de la isla, el daño conceptual ya estaba hecho. El uso de la iglesia interreligiosa como escenario de reencuentro final se sintió como una salida fácil. Además, un recurso perezoso para evadir las explicaciones lógicas de la Iniciativa Dharma o los poderes de la isla. Un final de serie desastroso que dejó huella en la cultura pop.
Dexter
El asesino en serie más querido de la televisión ostenta un dudoso honor. El de haber entregado no uno, sino dos de los peores finales de la historia en diferentes épocas. El cierre original de 2013, correspondiente a la octava temporada, es recordado como un insulto a la evolución del personaje. Tras la trágica y descuidada muerte de su hermana, Dexter Morgan (Michael C. Hall) decide arrojar su cuerpo al mar. Solo para después desconectar su vida en Miami y huir a los bosques de Oregón para convertirse en un leñador solitario con barba.
Este desenlace anuló por completo las ocho temporadas de crecimiento emocional en las que el protagonista buscaba comprender su humanidad. Intentando enmendar este desastre, la cadena estrenó en 2021 la miniserie de redención Dexter: New Blood. Aunque la temporada manejó una tensión magnífica mostrando a Dexter intentando conectar con su hijo adolescente Harrison, el final volvió a decepcionar.
Los últimos veinte minutos del episodio final repitieron los mismos errores del pasado de manera acelerada. En un giro forzado y carente de lógica, Dexter asesina al inocente sargento Logan (Alano Miller) para escapar. Lo que le hace romper su propio código ético inquebrantable y obligando a su hijo a dispararle a quemarropa. Un desenlace abrupto que enfureció nuevamente a los fanáticos. Un hito absoluto de los finales basura en la historia de las series.
Cómo conocí a vuestra madre
El desenlace en 2014 destruyó en apenas cuarenta minutos una década de lealtad y cariño por parte de su audiencia. La premisa completa de la serie giraba en torno a la larga travesía de Ted Mosby (Josh Radnor) para encontrar al amor de su vida. Un misterio que se resolvió brillantemente con la introducción de Tracy McConnell (Cristin Milioti). Este, un personaje sumamente carismático que se ganó instantáneamente el corazón del público.
Sin embargo, los creadores Carter Bays y Craig Thomas cometieron un grave error. Obsesionarse con mantener un final que habían filmado con los hijos de Ted durante la segunda temporada. Por lo que, ignorando por completo el crecimiento orgánico de la serie. En el doble episodio final, los guionistas deshicieron en minutos el matrimonio de Barney (Neil Patrick Harris) y Robin (Cobie Smulders). Un arco que había tomado temporadas enteras construir. Todo para revelar de forma insensible que la madre había muerto de una enfermedad años atrás. El giro final mostró que toda la extensa historia narrada por Ted a sus hijos era simplemente una elaborada justificación.
Y una ridícula: pedirles permiso de buscar y salir nuevamente con la tía Robin. Esta decisión redujo a la entrañable Tracy a un mero vientre de alquiler y un obstáculo temporal en la obsesión eterna de Ted. Transformando una hermosa historia sobre madurez y destino en un relato egoísta y cíclico que arruinó la serie para siempre.
Seinfeld
El cierre de la sitcom más exitosa e influyente de los años noventa decepcionó profundamente a más de 76 millones de espectadores en 1998. Lo que la convirtió en uno de los eventos televisivos más polémicos de la historia. Larry David regresó para escribir un doble episodio final que decidió confrontar directamente la esencia misántropa y egoísta de sus protagonistas. Pero lo hizo a través de un recurso narrativo sumamente perezoso y artificial.
Tras violar una nueva ley de buen samaritano al burlarse de un hombre que sufría un asalto en lugar de ayudarlo, ocurre lo impensable. Jerry, George (Jason Alexander), Elaine (Julia Louis-Dreyfus) y Kramer (Michael Richards) son llevados a un juicio público. Este escenario sirvió únicamente como una excusa para organizar un desfile de personajes secundarios de temporadas pasadas.
Cada uno de los cuales testificó sobre las malas acciones de los protagonistas, transformando el capítulo en un aburrido programa de retrospectiva disfrazado de ficción. Al final, los cuatro amigos son declarados culpables y sentenciados a prisión. Lo que cierra la serie con una toma de ellos en una celda. Además, manteniendo la misma conversación trivial sobre los botones de la camisa que tuvieron en el episodio piloto. Un final desastroso para la serie.
True Blood
La serie de vampiros y fantasía gótica sureña colapsó por completo en su séptima temporada. Por lo que culminó en 2014 con un episodio final que rozó el absurdo y la desidia creativa. Durante años, el nudo del show fue el peligroso triángulo amoroso entre Sookie (Anna Paquin), Bill (Stephen Moyer) y Eric (Alexander Skarsgård). Sin embargo, el desenlace decidió traicionar drásticamente todas las dinámicas construidas. Bill, sumido en una crisis existencial provocada por una enfermedad terminal, convence a Sookie de que lo asesine clavándole una estaca en el pecho.
Todo para liberarlo de su naturaleza trágica, una escena que se alargó innecesariamente y careció de fuerza emocional. El verdadero insulto para los fanáticos llegó en los minutos finales mediante un salto temporal que mostró el futuro de los supervivientes. Eric y Pam (Kristin Bauer van Straten) terminan convertidos en millonarios corporativos vendiendo una bebida energética. Mientras que Sookie aparece embarazada y casada en una cena de Acción de Gracias con un hombre ordinario cuyo rostro los realizadores decidieron ni siquiera mostrar en pantalla.
Al ocultar la identidad del esposo de la protagonista y reducir su destino a una fantasía doméstica genérica, el guion despojó a Sookie de su autonomía. Además, transformó una saga que solía ser salvaje, transgresora y sumamente sensual en un desenlace aburrido, plano y narrativamente perezoso. Un horror para la colección de pésimos finales de serie de esta lista.

articles.title: iPhone Duo mit gebrochenen Displays: Ist das Problem größer als gedacht?
articles.text:
iPhone Duo mit gebrochenen Displays: Ist das Problem größer als gedacht?
Schon kurz nach dem Verkaufsstart des iPhone Duos meldeten sich erste Käufer:innen mit Problemen. Der innere Bildschirm ist offenbar in einigen Fällen beim Auffalten gebrochen. Die Gründe sind nach wie vor nicht ganz klar. Die Mitarbeiter:innen von iFixit machten, nachdem sie das Gerät auseinandergenommen hatten, eine Stütze, die den Bildschirm eigentlich schützen soll, als vermeintlichen Übeltäter aus. Apple selbst spricht nur von einer „kleinen Anzahl“ betroffener Geräte. Dennoch soll das Unternehmen laut Macrumors ein Memo an Store-Mitarbeiter:innen und autorisierte Verkäufer:innen verschickt haben, das Vorgaben enthält, wie mit den Defekten umzugehen ist.
Apple-Anweisungen an Stores und Reseller
Der Verdacht liegt nahe, dass das Problem größer ist, als angenommen, wenn Apple so ein Schreiben herumschickt. Allerdings lässt sich das aus der Ferne kaum verlässlich sagen. Wie viele Geräte wirklich von dem Bildschirmproblem betroffen sind, ist nicht bekannt. Sollten Kund:innen mit einem defekten Gerät jedoch einen Store aufsuchen, empfiehlt das Unternehmen Techniker:innen laut Macrumors schlicht, das jeweilige iPhone Duo zu prüfen, und danach nach dem Standardverfahren zu reparieren oder eben auszutauschen. Ob das Schreiben nur an US-Stores und -Händler oder weltweit verschickt wurde, ist nicht bekannt.
Der Defekt trat allerdings offenbar schon kurz nach Inbetriebnahme des iPhones auf, wie Macrumors mit Verweis auf Apple schreibt. Einen Rückruf der Geräte durch Apple gibt es nicht, ein Serviceprogramm, wie es der Hersteller etwa bei Kameraproblemen mit dem iPhone 14 Plus angeboten hatte, auch nicht. Bei letzterem hatte Apple den Fehler bei betroffenen Kund:innen kostenlos repariert.
Vorerst gilt damit Apples bislang einzige Aussage zu dem Fehler: Betroffene Kund:innen sollen sich an Apple Care wenden, um ein Austauschgerät zu bekommen.

articles.title: Here’s who is falling in line for Trump’s “Super Intelligence” loyalty test
articles.text:
Here’s who is falling in line for Trump’s “Super Intelligence” loyalty test
One month into the attempted rebrand of “AI,” the term is not catching on. But it’s sure to muddy our national conversation about AI anyway.
This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here.
At the end of September, President Trump signed an executive order that contained just one directive, ordering government agencies to rebrand what they had been calling artificial intelligence as “Super Intelligence.” That term beat out other contenders, including “Extreme Intelligence” and “Supreme Intelligence,” offered by the president in a poll on X a couple of weeks earlier.
Rebrands are, of course, now a White House tradition: Trump has changed names to project US dominance of certain bodies of water (the Gulf of America and Lake America), to signal new institutional priorities (Department of War), or simply to leave his mark on storied places (see the ongoing fight over renaming the Kennedy Center).
The stated reason for this name change is that today’s AI systems “amplify human ingenuity” rather than merely “imitate” intelligence, and the government’s terminology should reflect that. But if this rebrand follows the pattern of others, its effects will extend beyond government.
It will turn a choice of words into a political loyalty test: Those who use the new term demonstrate allegiance to the administration, and those who don’t become marks for attacks (recall that the Trump administration barred the Associated Press from some White House press events after the news outlet did not adopt the term “Gulf of America”).
But most Americans go months without ever pondering what to call the major lake between New York and Canada. AI, on the other hand, is at the center of our national conversation and a technology two-thirds of Americans report interacting with multiple times a week. It might be the boldest rebrand yet.
So one month in, who’s on board?
Let’s start with the government itself. The term “Super Intelligence”—or simply “SI”—now appears more often on government solicitations, like a new request by Immigration and Customs Enforcement for companies to build “SI-powered” surveillance for ICE detention facilities. The new term has been swapped in silently on most government websites. Some, including that of the National Institutes of Health, now include a banner warning visitors they might see both the new and the old terms during the transition period.
There have been hiccups. A day after the rebrand order, the Pentagon announced an ambitious new initiative to study the future of warfare, called Project Meridian; it used the old terminology. A Federal Trade Commission press release last week used “superintelligence” instead of the two-word, capitalized version ordered by the president, and recent press releases from Health and Human Services show no sign of the new language.
The term “AI” will likely stick around given the countless AI-related offices, initiatives, and programs that have sprung up in recent years, like the Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Office at the Pentagon (the executive order says it doesn’t apply to previously issued regulations or documents).
As for government employees, it appears to be taking time for “SI” rather than “AI” to roll off the tongue. One researcher at a national lab I interviewed a few weeks ago used “AI” repeatedly before sheepishly acknowledging the slip-up. Even Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth used “AI” in an interview on October 3.
But Trump’s other rebrands suggest the goal isn’t merely to change the government’s vocabulary. It’s to change how the rest of us speak, too.
In the past couple of weeks, most of President Trump’s posts on Truth Social have been endorsements for candidates in the midterms. But on October 27 he took a break from electioneering to criticize the Wall Street Journal for not using “Super Intelligence,” “the name which virtually everyone else is using, or soon will be.” He suggested that a new rule will soon go further than the executive order to outright ban “artificial intelligence” from government documents.
But the Wall Street Journal is not alone: Even Newsmax, an outlet whose founder described it as “supportive of the President and his policies,” isn’t using the president’s preferred term.
Are Big Tech executives falling in line? It’s complicated. The same day that President Trump signed the rebranding order, he also released a nonbinding statement on AI safety, the White House Accord on Super Intelligence, signed by six of the most powerful people in tech: Sundar Pichai of Google, Dario Amodei of Anthropic, Mark Zuckerberg of Meta, Greg Brockman of OpenAI, Elon Musk of xAI, and Jensen Huang of Nvidia.
But even among this group—three members of which attended Trump’s inauguration—the term has not caught on.
In an analysis of third-quarter earnings calls, CNBC reported that only Zuckerberg and Musk used the term consistently. But Zuckerberg doesn’t quite count: Meta has been saying “superintelligence” since last year anyway. Musk’s companies seem to use the term the most—and he even pledged to rename SpaceXAI to SpaceXSI. Musk himself still mixes SI and AI when posting on X.
Executives from Amazon, Microsoft, and Alphabet used “AI” in their calls, though Microsoft’s recent letter to shareholders referred to the “Super Intelligence era.” Huang has referenced the term but still uses AI too.
One objection to this rebranding project is that it will cost time and taxpayer dollars. It is Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff’s prerogative to decide that SIForce is a better name than AIForce and direct his company to implement that change. But government employees are now spending time writing guides on how departments should navigate the rebrand. And, per the executive order, leaders of federal agencies will be required to put their heads together to draft a new legislative definition of “Super Intelligence” to be run by the president by the end of this month.
But I’m more worried about what this does to our national conversation about AI than I am about the potential waste of time and money. Surprisingly often I overhear strangers at a grocery store or coffee shop who have struck up a conversation about AI. The substance of the conversation is rarely uplifting—they most often talk about a jobs apocalypse or AI-powered warfare—but what is heartening is how often I see a widespread desire among people to have a say in how this technology transforms their lives.
People may have wildly different feelings about AI, including outright hostility, but those differences don’t yet map neatly onto the partisan divisions that make it awkward for strangers to discuss immigration or climate change.
If “Super Intelligence” turns into a loyalty test, this will cease to be the case. It’s easy to imagine that two people chatting about, say, whether chatbots are good or bad for our mental health will stop once they realize one of them is saying “super intelligence” and the other “AI.” That would be a shame for us all.
Midterm elections are tomorrow. Americans say AI is more important to them in this election than environmental and climate policy (and Democrats even rank it above abortion and gun policy). We’re only just beginning to have a national conversation about what AI will mean for our lives. Whether or not “Super Intelligence” catches on, turning the terminology itself into a loyalty test will do nothing to advance a national conversation about AI that’s only just getting started.

articles.title: The Apple Watch Ultra 4 is $100 off, matching its best price to date
articles.text:
The Apple Watch Ultra 4 is the company’s most capable smartwatch. Whether you intend to put its many tracking features to the test, or you simply want the longest battery life of any Apple Watch, it’s currently on sale for $699.99 ($100 off) in multiple colors at Amazon, matching its all-time low price.
The Apple Watch Ultra 4 is $100 off, matching its best price to date
We also found a good deal on Ugreen’s soccer ball-shaped Bluetooth tracker with seven years of battery life.
Powered by Apple’s new S11 chip (also in the Series 12), the Apple Watch Ultra 4 delivers faster performance than the last-gen version, plus a handful of new Apple Intelligence features. Of note, those include Sound Recognition, which alerts you to noises like alarms and doorbells, and the Live Rewind feature that lets you revisit the last 15 seconds of an in-person conversation. An upcoming Siri Recap feature will be able to create summaries of conversations for later reference.
This model has broader health and fitness capabilities than previous models, too. Its sensors promise more accurate EKG measurements, while the watch can track your heart rate as often as every five seconds. The new Readiness feature (not available on the Ultra 3 and earlier models) also analyzes your recent activity, sleep quality, and other health metrics to generate a score from zero to 10, helping you determine whether to push yourself or take it easy.
On the hardware front, battery life is perhaps the biggest highlight, with Apple promising up to 50 hours on a charge — twice as long as the Series 12. Like its predecessor, this model features Apple’s brightest watch display and a rugged design that’s water-resistant up to 100 meters and IP6X-rated for dust resistance. It also retains conveniences like the second-generation Ultra Wideband chip for Precision Finding, and helpful gesture controls so you can you can perform actions with a double tap or flick of your wrist.
Three more ways to save
- Ugreen’s FineTrack2 Bluetooth tracker is on sale for $13.99 at Amazon, just a few cents shy of its best price to date. The soccer ball-shaped tracker stands out with its playful design, but it also offers some useful features including a non-rechargeable battery can last up to seven years. It works with Apple’s expansive Find My network to help you locate misplaced belongings, while its lanyard makes it easy to attach to your keys, bag, or other items.
- If you’re looking to spruce up your Apple Watch Ultra or Series smartwatch, a variety of Apple’s official bands are on sale for up to 69 percent off at Woot. The silicone Sport Band is down to $14.99 ($35 off), while the soft, breathable Sport Loop is available for $19.99 ($29 off). You can also grab the rugged Trail Loop for $34.99 ($64 off).
- Hoto’s new Pulse 4-in-1 Cordless Staple Gun is on sale for $69.99 ($10 off) at Amazon. The versatile tool can help with repairing stuff, or putting together decorations. It works with four types of staples and nails, letting you switch between them depending on the task, while offering two firing modes. It also features a built-in display that shows battery life and alerts you when you can safely fire the stapler and when it’s time to reload it. The stapler comes with 1,200 fasteners.

articles.title: China publicly discloses plan for a lunar landing within three years
articles.text:
Chinese space officials confirmed this weekend that the Asian nation plans to land its astronauts on the Moon within three years.
At the Seventh Manned Spaceflight Conference in Beijing, officials, including Wang Xiang, chief designer for the lunar exploration program, laid out the country’s most publicly detailed plans yet for a series of missions leading up to a crewed lunar landing “before 2030.”
China’s lunar landings will involve a lunar-orbit rendezvous similar to what NASA did in the 1960s and early 1970s with the Apollo program. However, lacking a rocket as powerful as the Saturn V vehicle, the crew and lunar lander will launch separately to the Moon.
According to slides shared on social media, the current plan involves:
- An uncrewed test of the Long March 10A rocket (a single-stick variant, with no boosters) and the Mengzhou spacecraft to low-Earth orbit. Target: early 2027
- An uncrewed test of the larger Long March 10 rocket (a core stage with two boosters) and the Lanyue lunar lander, including descent/ascent from Moon’s surface. Target: 2028
- A concurrent launch of two Long March 10 rockets, one carrying uncrewed Mengzhou and the other the Lanyue vehicle; they will dock in lunar orbit. Target: 2029
- Dual launch of Long March 10 rockets, this time with crew on the Mengzhou spacecraft, leading to crewed landing mission. Target: “Before 2030”
The public release of this new information provides a timeline for gauging China’s technical progress in its efforts to land humans on the Moon before 2030 and beat NASA and the United States back to the lunar surface.
Notably, the plan (for now, at least) omits a mission similar to Apollo 8 or Artemis II, which involved a crew flying out to the Moon and either entering orbit or passing close by before returning to Earth. The Mengzhou vehicle should still get a workout closer to Earth with humans on board as part of missions carrying astronauts to Tiangong, China’s space station in low-Earth orbit.
China’s program has been largely opaque
NASA has set a target of landing humans on the Moon by 2028, a year or so ahead of China. The United States, which has been working on the Space Launch System rocket for 15 years and the Orion spacecraft even longer, has a more established rocket and crew vehicle.

articles.title: Co-Optimizing Access Points Improves Analog Placement (UT Austin)
articles.text:
Researchers at the University of Texas at Austin published “APPlace: Co-Optimizing Device Locations and Access Points for Routing-Aware Analog Placement.”
Abstract
“Analog layout automation remains challenging in Analog/Mixed-Signal circuit design, because parasitics and mismatches introduced during layout strongly affect circuit performance. Placement is especially critical among the layout stages, as it constrains the routing solution space and the achievable post-layout performance. Existing analytical placement methods optimize device coordinates under center-based wirelength proxies and leave access point (AP) selection to routing. In analog circuits, however, a routing pin is an extended piece of terminal metal rather than a fixed point, and the best AP on it depends on where the other connected devices are placed, so a coordinate-only placement optimizes for connection points that the router will not use. We present APPlace, a routing-aware analog placement framework that co-optimizes device locations and AP selections during global placement, followed by a legalization stage that preserves the structure established by global placement. Experimental results on four real-world analog benchmarks show that APPlace achieves better overall post-layout performance than representative baselines at comparable layout area. Ablation studies further show that removing AP co-optimization causes up to a 13 dB CMRR loss among the OTA benchmarks and a 23% increase in comparator delay.”
Find the technical paper here. October 2026
Liu, Bingyang, Xiaohan Gao, Souradip Poddar, and David Z. Pan. “APPlace: Co-Optimizing Device Locations and Access Points for Routing-Aware Analog Placement.” arXiv preprint arXiv:2610.39515 (2026). License: Attribution 4.0 International.

articles.title: Niger-based Likita Care wins 2026 Africa Prize for Engineering Innovation - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Niger-based medical monitoring startup Likita Care has won the 2026 Africa Prize for Engineering Innovation, taking home GBP50,000 (US$67,000).
Delivered by the Royal Academy of Engineering, the Africa Prize is the continent’s biggest engineering prize. Finalists were selected from a cohort of 16 entrepreneurs who completed an eight-month training and mentoring programme.
Founded by Mamane Kabirou Ousseini, the first engineer from Niger to participate in and win the prize, Likita Care builds locally manufactured monitoring devices that can be maintained and repaired in Niger, addressing the frequent breakdown of imported equipment in resource-limited hospitals.
The platform combines connected hardware, clinical software and an AI module that interprets vital signs in real time, supporting patient, cardiac and prenatal monitoring. More than 70 units have been deployed across five medical centres in Niger.
“Winning the Africa Prize is a dream come true,” said Ousseini. The startup will use the funding to commercialise in Niger and prepare for expansion into neighbouring West African markets.
Three runners-up each received GBP10,000 (US$13,500 – South Africa’s Pee-Cycling, a urine-to-fertiliser recovery system; Kenya’s MoyoECG, a portable heart monitor; and Kenya’s Renal Roads, a mobile dialysis clinic. Ghana’s Fusion Wind Turbine won the GBP5,000 (US$6,500) One-to-Watch Award.

articles.title: Synology warns of C3RB3R ransomware attacks targeting NAS devices
articles.text:
Taiwanese network-attached storage (NAS) appliance maker Synology warned customers to update their devices immediately due to a surge in C3RB3r ransomware attacks.
The company urged users to enable automatic updates and upgrade the DiskStation Manager (DSM) software running on their NAS devices to the latest version to protect their data.
"Synology has identified threat actors exploiting a vulnerability patched in December 2024 to target devices running outdated versions of DSM. These attacks aim to encrypt data and extort ransom," it said in a Thursday advisory.
"Synology strongly urges all users running vulnerable versions to update DSM immediately to protect their systems. Synology also recommends enabling automatic updates to keep DSM up to date at all times."
A Synology spokesperson was not immediately available when BleepingComputer reached out for more information on these C3RB3r ransomware attacks.
While Synology has yet to share which vulnerability is being exploited in these ongoing attacks, it linked to a November 2024 security advisory with information about patches released for vulnerabilities allowing attackers to execute arbitrary code (CVE-2024-10441), read files (CVE-2024-50629), and write files (CVE-2024-10445) on unpatched devices.
Synology users are advised to immediately block access to the management web interface from the Internet and update their DSM software to block attackers' attempts to hack and encrypt their devices.
| Product | Severity | Fixed Release Availability | 
|---|---|---|
| DSM 7.2.2 | Critical | Upgrade to 7.2.2-72806-1 or above. | 
| DSM 7.2.1 | Critical | Upgrade to 7.2.1-69057-6 or above. | 
| DSM 7.2 | Critical | Upgrade to 7.2-64570-4 or above. | 
| DSM 7.1 | Critical | Upgrade to 7.1.1-42962-7 or above. | 
| DSM 6.2 | Moderate | Upgrade to 6.2.4-25556-8 or above. | 
Synology rarely issues security advisories warning of attacks targeting its customers' devices, with the last such alert published in August 2019 following large-scale brute-force attacks that led to eCh0raix ransomware infections.
Last week's advisory follows a massive wave of reports from Synology customers whose data was encrypted and who were prompted to buy "C3rb3r Decryptor" tool from a dark web portal for thousands of dollars.
The first reports surfaced more than two weeks ago, with affected users saying the ransomware dropped a ransom note (read-me3.txt) and added a .L0CK3D extension to encrypted files.
"All your important files have been encrypted. Any attempts to restore your files with thrid-party software will be fatal for your files! The only way to decrypt your files safely is to buy the special decryption software 'C3rb3r Decryptor'," the ransom note warns.
"At this page you will receive the complete instructions how to buy the decryption software for restoring all your files. Also at this page you will be able to restore any one file for free to be sure 'C3rb3r Decryptor' will help you."
The Cerber ransomware (also known as C3RB3R and CerberImposter), now deployed in attacks targeting Synology NAS devices, borrowed its name from a notorious Ransomware-as-a-Service (RaaS) with the same name that emerged in 2016.
Before disappearing at the end of 2019, the old Cerber ransomware operation accounted for more than 80% of all ransomware attacks and a quarter of all ransomware infections on enterprise endpoints.
Starting in December 2021, when it was first spotted, C3RB3R was also deployed on Atlassian Confluence and GitLab servers as part of several attack waves exploiting remote code execution (CVE-2021-26084 and CVE-2021-22205) and authentication bypass (CVE-2023-22518) flaws.
Internet threat watchdog Shadowserver now tracks over 380,000 Internet-exposed Synology NAS devices, but doesn't provide information on how many have already been secured against these attacks or are honeypots.
