articles.title: Your AI coding agent now runs on a budget — and it can cut you off mid-task
articles.text:
Your AI coding agent now runs on a budget — and it can cut you off mid-task
The days of pointing an AI agent at a backlog and letting it burn through compute without much oversight may be coming to an end. Cognition is introducing hierarchical budgets for Devin so enterprises can manage AI coding agent spending across departments, projects, and individual engineers. Administrators can assign budgets to different teams, track how much each one spends, and approve more capacity based on engineering efficiency. There’s a catch for developers, though; if a budget runs out while Devin is working on a task, the session stops.
If a budget runs out while Devin is working on a task, the session stops.
The feature grew out of conversations with customers, according to Lukas Burger, who works across go-to-market and engineering at Cognition. “Most of what we build starts with our forward deployed engineers (FDEs), who work on-site with customers. Budgets came straight out of those conversations,” Burger tells The New Stack. Once Devin moved past pilots and into broader deployments across organizations, he explains, the blunt controls that had worked for a single team — org limits, per-user tiers, and separate Devin Desktop settings — stopped holding up.
From Pilots to the P&L
The problem Budgets sets out to solve is one of scale and sprawl rather than raw price. “That’s fine for one team. It doesn’t hold up when a bank is dividing a large ACU commitment across hundreds of groups,” Burger tells The New Stack of the older spending controls. Some of those customers had started building and maintaining their own internal tools just to parcel out capacity to the leaders of each business line, a workaround that mapped the exact gap Cognition set out to close.
Cognition built the feature with some of the world’s largest enterprises as design partners, testing the model with customers managing millions of Agent Compute Units, the consumption-based units used to measure the work Devin performs.
Burger is keeping quiet on individual customer spending figures, but he is clear about what changes as deployments widen. “Devin stops belonging to one team,” he says. “A pilot might sit with a single platform group. A broad rollout means many departments, each with its own priorities and its own budget owner.”
Budgets follow the org chart
Budgets is designed to work with the way enterprises already manage spending, meaning, an administrator starts with one overall budget, divides it among business units, and from there, those leaders can distribute funds to their own teams and projects, with budgets extending up to three levels deep. Central IT can still see where the money is going and set limits without approving every request. “The enterprise keeps guardrails and visibility across all of it,” Burger says.
Companies can also set aside budgets for specific projects rather than tying all spending to individual teams. A major legacy modernization effort, for example, could have its own budget even if engineers from several departments are working on it. Separate controls apply to Devin running in the cloud and on engineers’ desktops, so companies can track and limit spending in both environments.
When a budget runs out
The promise is that none of this should intrude on the work. “We designed Budgets so engineers can do their work without thinking about them,” Burger says, and the mechanics warn engineers before spending limits interrupt their sessions.
Engineers see alerts on their homepage when they are on track to exceed a limit, and they can request more ACUs from the budget owner without leaving the product. Each budget’s administrators decide whether to review those requests manually or clear them automatically.
Grading engineers on efficiency
That automation is where the feature turns pointed. Admins can enable efficiency-based approvals, which automatically lift an engineer’s limit when their Efficiency Score is strong, up to a ceiling the admin sets. Cognition introduced the scoring system in October to estimate productive engineering hours relative to Devin consumption, which permits administrators to allocate more capacity to engineers who appear to get more useful work from their usage. The score estimates efficiency, however, and does not directly measure code quality or business outcomes.
When a budget does empty, the session stops, which is why Burger frames the alerts and in-product requests as the first line of defense rather than the last.
“We’re also working on letting teams switch to lower-cost models after a soft limit, so important work can finish,”
“We’re also working on letting teams switch to lower-cost models after a soft limit, so important work can finish,” Burger tells The New Stack. That option is still in development, so for now, budget increases and advance warnings are the most effective ways to avoid interruptions to date.
Cognition is just as wary of the opposite failure, the controls drawn so tight they strangle the productivity they were meant to protect. “We also don’t want controls so tight that customers stop being productive with Devin,” Burger tells The New Stack, which is why the company suggests defaults with enough headroom to keep productive users from being blocked unnecessarily.
Much of the surprise in agent spending, he notes, “comes from not knowing where usage lands,” a gap that cheaper tokens alone may not close when agents run complex, multi-step tasks and a round of price cuts doesn’t necessarily translate into a smaller bill.
Proof in the Pull Requests
Consumption pricing cuts both ways, and Cognition knows it. “With consumption pricing, customers who can’t see value stop using the product, so we’ve put a lot of work into cost control and measurement,” Burger tells The New Stack.
“With consumption pricing, customers who can’t see value stop using the product, so we’ve put a lot of work into cost control and measurement,”
Each Devin session is tied to a specific budget, so companies can see exactly how much individual teams, projects or business units are spending. Instead of looking at one company-wide total, leaders can track the cost of a particular initiative. Some customers also link that spending to internal billing codes or charge it back to individual departments.
Measuring consumption is the easy half of the equation. For the harder question of whether the money is well spent, Burger says most customers fall back on the metrics they already trust, tracking merged pull requests, productive engineering hours, and DORA metrics.
Burger says the teams getting the most out of Devin look at business results, citing “how much faster the roadmap moves, how much unplanned work goes away, and how much less they spend on engineering toil.”
FinOps for AI agents
Burger doesn’t hesitate when asked whether agent budgeting is becoming a discipline of its own, much like FinOps did for cloud infrastructure. “Yes, and it’s already starting,” he tells The New Stack. Because agents are billed by consumption, finance teams are asking familiar questions about who is spending, where the money is going and whether it’s worth it. Burger says the shift is happening faster than it did with cloud computing because companies already have processes in place to manage those costs.
The FinOps Foundation’s 2026 “State of FinOps” report quantifies how far that has spread, finding that 98% of its 1,192 survey respondents now manage AI spending, up from 31% two years ago. Companies are still working out how to connect that spending with measurable returns. What makes Cognition’s approach different is that companies can manage budgets, assign spending limits and track costs directly in Devin instead of relying on separate tools.
Burger expects the responsibility to land squarely on finance teams. “I see this becoming a major new responsibility for strategic finance and FP&A teams,” he tells The New Stack. “On top of their day jobs, they’re now managing massive AI budgets and making sure that spend shows up as real impact on the P&L.”
Learning Path

articles.title: Prepare web content for Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases with Crawl4AI | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Prepare web content for Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases with Crawl4AI
When you build Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) applications, answer quality depends on the data that you ingest. Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases is the fully managed RAG capability of Amazon Bedrock. With Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base, you connect your data sources, and Amazon Bedrock manages ingestion, storage, indexing, and retrieval for you. You don’t provision or scale a vector store, and embedding and reranking use service-managed models by default.
For web content, start with the Amazon Bedrock Web Crawler data source connector for managed knowledge bases. You give it the seed URLs or sitemaps that you’re authorized to crawl, and it crawls within the scope and rate limits that you set. Scheduled syncs keep your knowledge base current as pages change, and the connector can wait for content that loads with JavaScript. There’s no crawler for you to build, host, or operate, so this connector is the starting point for most public website content.
Some sources need more control over what reaches the knowledge base. You might want to index only the main content region of each page, remove navigation and other boilerplate, or attach your own metadata attributes to every document. For that class of source material, you can extend the reach of your knowledge base with a preparation step built with Crawl4AI, an open source Python crawler. The step writes Markdown and a metadata sidecar for each page to Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), and the knowledge base ingests both through its Amazon S3 data source.
In this post, we show you how to choose the appropriate web ingestion path and implement custom preparation for content that needs additional processing. You then start ingestion into a managed knowledge base and validate retrieval quality. The companion aws-samples repository provides the complete workflow as a sample implementation.
This is batch ingestion of known web properties, not real-time web access at inference time such as Web Grounding with Amazon Nova.
Solution overview
Start with the Amazon Bedrock Web Crawler when it can reach and index the pages you need. It respects robots.txt, and after the first full crawl, each sync captures only added, updated, and deleted content.
Use the Crawl4AI preparation path when public source material needs one or more of the following before ingestion:
- Structured Markdown preparation: Use DefaultMarkdownGenerator with a pruning content filter to reduce navigation and other boilerplate while preserving headings, lists, and tables. Because pruning is heuristic, review representative output from your sites.
- Bounded, targeted extraction: Extract only the page region that an optional CSS selector matches. Constrain breadth-first traversal by seed origin, page/path/host scope, depth and page caps, and URL patterns.
- Custom metadata: Attach source URLs, crawl timestamps, content type, and your own attributes to each document, so that you can filter retrieval results on them.
Because managed and customer-managed knowledge bases both support Amazon S3 data sources, the Crawl4AI path works with either type. This post uses a managed knowledge base and notes where a customer-managed knowledge base differs.
The rest of this post follows the companion sample. Treat its architecture and defaults as a starting point, not as requirements of Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases.
By default, the sample runs the AWS Fargate task in a public subnet, where it reaches your configured websites through an internet gateway. Crawl4AI’s role ends once it has prepared the source documents and metadata sidecars. From ingestion onward, Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases handles parsing, chunking, embedding, indexing, and retrieval. The following diagram shows the Crawl4AI path from the schedule through to retrieval.
The numbered steps in the diagram map to the following workflow:
- Amazon EventBridge starts the Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) task on AWS Fargate on the configured schedule.
- The task crawls the public websites you configured and prepares Markdown with a metadata sidecar for each page.
- The task uploads the prepared files to the Amazon S3 bucket that backs the knowledge base data source.
- The task starts an Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases ingestion job.
- Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases reads the new and changed objects, parses them, and applies the chunking strategy you selected.
- It creates embeddings and indexes them in the knowledge base’s vector store, which Amazon Bedrock manages for a managed knowledge base.
- Your generative AI application queries the knowledge base for relevant chunks or for a generated response with citations.
The task reads its non-secret pipeline configuration from AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store at startup.
The workflow processes public pages only and doesn’t implement authenticated sessions. For sites that require sign-in, evaluate the Amazon Bedrock Web Crawler authentication options first, which include basic, form-based, and SAML authentication. Extending the sample with authentication requires session handling, credentials in AWS Secrets Manager, and a security review.
How the workflow works
The AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) app packages the implementation in a container image during deployment. When the schedule fires, the container runs scripts/container_entrypoint.py and executes crawl, upload, and ingestion in sequence. The following three steps explain the core logic.
Step 1: Crawl and extract content
The crawl step performs bounded crawling and writes a Markdown file with a metadata sidecar for each successfully prepared page. The following excerpt is simplified. The module src/crawl4ai_bedrock_kb/crawl.py contains the complete seed pacing, URL filtering and scoping, page limits, and redirect checks:
Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases supports several document formats for Amazon S3 data sources, including plain text, HTML, Markdown, PDF, and DOCX. The workflow writes Markdown because it preserves headings, lists, and tables without carrying all raw HTML into ingestion.
Step 2: Upload to Amazon S3
The upload step sends each prepared Markdown document and its matching metadata sidecar to the configured S3 bucket, under the workflow’s s3Prefix. For page.md, the sidecar must be named page.md.metadata.json, the complete source filename with .metadata.json appended. The workflow stores each sidecar in the same S3 location as its document. Amazon Bedrock limits each metadata sidecar to 10 KB. If a sidecar would exceed that limit, the run stops with an error before it writes either file.
Each attribute in the sidecar uses the typed format that both managed and customer-managed knowledge bases accept for Amazon S3 data sources. The following abbreviated sidecar, formatted for readability, shows three of the attributes that the workflow writes:
The pipeline uploads only the paths produced by the current crawl, so stale local files are not sent.
Step 3: Let Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases chunk, embed, and index
After content is in S3, an ingestion job hands each document to the data source’s ingestion pipeline. By default, a managed knowledge base parses each file with its managed parser, which automatically selects a parsing approach for your content. You select the chunking strategy when you connect the data source. You can’t change it afterward, so evaluate the options before you create a production data source. A managed knowledge base offers the following chunking strategies:
- Default chunking uses fixed-size chunks of 300 tokens with 20 percent overlap.
- Fixed-size chunking splits content by a maximum token count and an overlap percentage that you set.
- No chunking treats each file as a single chunk, for content that you have already split.
Chunk boundaries and retrieval results depend on the content and the selected strategy, so compare the options with representative pages and evaluation questions. To change strategies later, create a new data source. For more information, see Customize ingestion for a data source. A customer-managed knowledge base also offers semantic and hierarchical chunking and additional parsing options. For details, see How content chunking works for knowledge bases.
The workflow then starts an ingestion job so the knowledge base processes the new documents. The following simplified excerpt from src/crawl4ai_bedrock_kb/ingest.py shows the call:
The same StartIngestionJob and GetIngestionJob calls work for both knowledge base types, and you can also monitor progress on the console.
Deploy the solution
In this section, you deploy the workflow into your AWS account with AWS CDK. Only the knowledge base prerequisites differ between the two knowledge base types. When you’re finished, follow the steps in the Clean up section to remove the resources.
Prerequisites
Before you start, make sure that you have:
- An AWS account.
- One of the following knowledge bases: 
         
  - A managed knowledge base, which this post uses, in an AWS Region where managed knowledge bases are available. For instructions, see Create a managed knowledge base and the Amazon S3 connector. On the data source, leave Metadata files prefix empty, because the workflow writes each metadata sidecar alongside its document.
  - An existing customer-managed knowledge base. To add an Amazon S3 data source, see Connect to Amazon S3 for your knowledge base. The workflow writes a metadata sidecar for every document, so confirm that your vector store can store and filter those attributes, as described in Metadata and filtering. For example, an Amazon OpenSearch Serverless vector index must use the faiss engine. An Amazon Aurora vector index needs a custom metadata column or a column for each metadata attribute. With Amazon S3 Vectors, a capability of Amazon S3, you can attach up to 1 KB of custom metadata to each vector, so keep attributes that you add short.
- An Amazon S3 data source in that knowledge base whose status is AVAILABLE. It can be a new data source or one you already use. It must use the S3 bucket that you configure for this workflow. If the data source filters content by prefix or file pattern, the filters must allow the files that the workflow writes under its s3Prefix (default web-content/).
- The knowledge base, the S3 bucket, and the stack you deploy all in one Region.
- Authorization to crawl the public websites you configure.
- A deployment workstation with Git, Python 3.10 or later, Node.js, the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) version 2, the AWS CDK CLI v2, and a running Docker-compatible container engine. The deployment guide lists the minimum AWS CDK CLI version.
- AWS credentials configured on the deployment workstation with permission to bootstrap the target environment and deploy the CDK stack.
- A bootstrapped CDK environment in the target account and Region. The deployment steps include the bootstrap command.
You need the workstation only to build and deploy. After deployment, the schedule runs the task in AWS.
Deploy the scheduled workflow
Clone the companion repository and install the deployment dependencies:
Keep Docker running. Set AWS_DEFAULT_REGION to your knowledge base’s Region first, because cdk deploy uses the Region from your environment or AWS profile, not the one in the bootstrap command. Bootstrap the target account and Region once, if needed. Then deploy the stack with your knowledge base, data source, S3 bucket, and authorized seed URLs:
Replace every example value, including ACCOUNT_ID, REGION, and the four required context keys, with your own. The example values are syntactically valid, so an unedited command deploys a stack that points at a bucket you don’t own. You can also set these keys in cdk.json.
The maxDepth and maxPages values limit the first crawl to one link level and 25 pages. Raise them after you review the prepared output. To preview which pages a crawl prepares, you can also run the pipeline locally with --dry-run, as described in the README. The stack name is fixed, so another cdk deploy in the same account and Region updates this stack.
The sample builds an ARM64 container image by default. If Docker on your x86_64 workstation can’t build ARM64 images, add -c cpuArchitecture=X86_64 to the cdk deploy command.
If your account turns on VPC Block Public Access, the task can’t reach the internet from the default public subnet. To check the mode, run aws ec2 describe-vpc-block-public-access-options. In ingress-only mode, deploy with -c egressMode=nat, which adds a NAT gateway with hourly charges. Bidirectional mode also needs an exclusion, as the deployment guide describes.
The stack doesn’t create or change your knowledge base or data source.
With the default rate(24 hours) schedule, the first run starts when the deployment creates the Amazon EventBridge rule. To follow that run, use the command in the TailLogsCommand output, which cdk deploy prints when it finishes. A successful run logs job_status: COMPLETE. To start another run outside the schedule, use the command in the RunTaskCommand output after the current run finishes. To list the outputs later, run aws cloudformation describe-stacks --stack-name Crawl4aiBedrockKbCrawler --region REGION --query "Stacks[0].Outputs".
The deployment guide covers the remaining configuration, including crawl boundaries, the schedule, networking, container architecture, monitoring, and on-demand runs.
Validate retrieval quality
After ingestion, test representative questions with Retrieve before you add generation. A managed knowledge base uses hybrid search. When it uses the default managed embedding model, it also reranks results with its managed reranker. You can narrow results with the metadata from the sidecars. The sample’s default configuration adds content_category set to web to every page. The following example returns up to five chunks from those pages that were crawled in the last seven days. It requires the AWS SDK for Python (Boto3) 1.43.32 or later, which you can install with python -m pip install "boto3>=1.43.32". Replace the Region and knowledge base ID with your own values:
The example passes an integer timestamp, which both knowledge base types accept in number filters. A managed knowledge base doesn’t support the startsWith and stringContains filters. For a customer-managed knowledge base, pass the same filter in vectorSearchConfiguration instead of managedSearchConfiguration. The operators it supports depend on its vector store.
Metadata filtering can improve retrieval precision, but it is not an authorization boundary. If different users should see different pages, the Amazon S3 connector for managed knowledge bases supports document-level access control with access control list (ACL) files that you provide. The sample doesn’t create ACL files.
To generate responses from a managed knowledge base, use agentic retrieval. The AgenticRetrieveStream operation returns the retrieved results and a generated response with citations to those results. For a customer-managed knowledge base, use RetrieveAndGenerate. In both cases, each cited result includes the source_url metadata from its sidecar, which your application can present as the user-facing source.
Evaluate retrieval relevance, source-page coverage, and citation quality whenever you change content preparation, chunking, or retrieval settings. For the retrieval settings that you can tune, see Configure and customize queries for managed knowledge bases.
Running it repeatedly
Each scheduled event launches one standalone Fargate task. The stack doesn’t prevent overlapping runs, so choose an interval longer than the expected crawl and ingestion duration. A failed run isn’t announced, because the sample adds no retry policy, dead-letter queue, or alarm. An ingestion job can also report COMPLETE when some documents fail to ingest, and the task then exits with code 0. The task logs the job’s failure reasons. Add the monitoring you need, including an alarm on those failure reasons, before you rely on the schedule.
Each run incurs Fargate charges for the configured task size, which defaults to 2 vCPU and 4 GB. The task keeps running while it polls the ingestion job for up to 30 minutes, so a slow ingestion job extends billable task time. If ingestion takes longer, the task exits with a nonzero code, and the ingestion job keeps running. The stack turns on Container Insights for the cluster, and flow logs for an Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) that it creates. Both add Amazon CloudWatch charges. The stack’s AWS KMS key has a monthly charge, and the task’s public IPv4 address is billed while the task runs. With egressMode=nat or privateEndpoints=true, the NAT gateway and interface endpoints are billed hourly, even when no task is running. Knowledge base usage is billed separately. For details, see Amazon VPC pricing and Amazon Bedrock pricing.
Uploads are additive: removing a URL or missing a page during a later crawl doesn’t delete its existing S3 objects. To remove stale content, delete the obsolete document and matching sidecar under the configured prefix, then start ingestion again. If you turn on the document deletion safeguard (deletion protection) for a managed knowledge base data source, check its threshold. A sync that would delete more than that percentage of documents skips its delete phase, so those documents stay indexed. To start ingestion automatically whenever objects in the bucket change, see Build and deploy an automatic sync solution for Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases.
Responsible AI considerations
Retrieved passages become the context that a foundation model uses to generate a response. Apply the following controls before you run this workflow in production:
- Amazon Bedrock Guardrails: Attach a guardrail to your agentic retrieval or RetrieveAndGenerate requests to apply content filters, denied topics, word filters, and sensitive information filters. Agentic retrieval supports only the guardrail BLOCK action, not MASK.
- Contextual grounding checks: Turn on the Guardrails contextual grounding check to score each response for grounding against the retrieved passages and for relevance to the query. The guardrail blocks responses that score below the thresholds you set. For agentic retrieval, you can run the check on the generated answer with the ApplyGuardrail API. The check supports question answering and summarization, not conversational chatbot use cases.
- Treat crawled content as untrusted input: Prepared web pages become model context, so text on a public page can attempt prompt injection through retrieval. Don’t rely on guardrails alone to catch it. Restrict seed URLs to sites you trust, and apply the ingestion filtering patterns described in the next section before content reaches the knowledge base.
- Citations and human review: Return citations with every generated response so users can verify claims against the source page. For higher-risk use cases, keep a human reviewer in the loop.
Security and compliance considerations
Review the following considerations before you run this workflow against production content:
- Use trusted public crawl targets: Seed URLs and crawl settings are deployment configuration, and the Fargate task allows outbound access so it can reach public websites. In the sample’s default networking mode, the task runs in a public subnet with a public IP. Configure only authorized public sites. Don’t use this sample to crawl private or internal endpoints. Review network egress and destination controls before adapting the workflow for other trust models.
- Respect crawl directives: The workflow turns on Crawl4AI’s robots.txt check by default, and the CDK path pins it on with no context key to disable it. Verify you have authorization to crawl the target sites, consistent with the AWS Acceptable Use Policy.
- Rate limiting: Configure delays between requests to avoid overwhelming source websites.
- Encryption at rest: The stack creates an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) customer managed key with automatic key rotation and encrypts its CloudWatch log groups with it. Amazon S3 encrypts new objects with server-side encryption with Amazon S3 managed keys (SSE-S3) by default. If your data classification requires a customer managed key for the bucket, configure the bucket to use it. Then grant the uploader and the knowledge base service role the required AWS KMS permissions in both AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) and the key policy. The stack’s task role doesn’t include AWS KMS permissions. A managed knowledge base encrypts its data with an AWS owned key by default, or with a customer managed key that you specify when you create it. For a customer-managed knowledge base, review encryption for its vector store.
- Least privilege IAM: The CDK stack grants the Fargate task role s3:PutObject on the configured bucket prefix. It also grants bedrock:StartIngestionJob and bedrock:GetIngestionJob on the target knowledge base, plus ssm:GetParameter for its single configuration parameter. Separate roles cover Amazon EventBridge task launch and the standard container image pull and log delivery. The pipeline doesn’t read or list S3 and doesn’t call InvokeModel or Retrieve.
- Container and template checks: The container runs as a non-root user, and the CDK app runs cdk-nag AWS Solutions checks on every synthesis with resource-scoped suppressions.
- Protect deployment configuration: The CDK app stores non-secret pipeline settings in a plaintext Parameter Store String parameter. Only the parameter name is placed in the task definition. Don’t put passwords, cookies, tokens, or other secrets in CDK context or this parameter.
- Ingestion pipeline security: See Securing the RAG ingestion pipeline: Filtering mechanisms for filtering and validation patterns to apply before content reaches the knowledge base.
Clean up
To avoid ongoing charges, delete the resources created during this walkthrough:
- From the repository’s deploy/ directory, run cdk destroy in the same Region, with the same four required -c values that you passed to cdk deploy. The app checks them on every command. This removes the stack’s Amazon EventBridge rule, ECS cluster, task definition, log groups, IAM roles, Parameter Store parameter, and security groups, and the VPC if the stack created it. It also schedules the stack’s AWS KMS key for deletion after a 30-day waiting period. It doesn’t delete an imported VPC, your knowledge base, your S3 bucket, or the objects that the workflow uploaded. CDK also keeps the container image and templates in its bootstrap resources. It also leaves the cluster’s Container Insights log group, whose name starts with /aws/ecs/containerinsights/Crawl4aiBedrockKbCrawler-.
- To remove the ingested web content, delete the prepared objects under s3://<bucket>/<prefix> and sync the data source again. If the document deletion safeguard is on for a managed knowledge base data source, a sync that would delete more than its threshold percentage of documents skips its delete phase.
- Delete the managed knowledge base only if you created it solely for this walkthrough. A managed knowledge base has no separate vector store to delete.
- For a customer-managed knowledge base, delete the Amazon S3 data source only if you created it for this walkthrough. Its data deletion policy determines whether Amazon Bedrock also deletes the data source’s vector embeddings from your vector store.
Conclusion
In this post, you learned how to extend Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases to authorized public web content that needs preparation before ingestion. A scheduled Fargate task uses Crawl4AI for bounded crawling, prepares Markdown with page.md.metadata.json sidecars, uploads them to an Amazon S3 data source, and starts ingestion. The knowledge base then handles parsing, chunking, embeddings, indexing, retrieval, and grounded responses with citations.
Start with the Amazon Bedrock Web Crawler in a managed knowledge base for most public websites. Use the Crawl4AI path when you need control over which part of each page is indexed or which metadata travels with it. To get started, deploy the scheduled Fargate workflow from the companion sample-crawl4ai-bedrock-knowledge-base repository, and then validate retrieval quality and citations with representative content before scaling.

articles.title: An internet tax that would charge by the gigabyte just squeaked through France's lower house
articles.text:
WTF?! These days, moving a gigabyte of data across the internet usually costs companies well under a cent. France, however, wants them to pay several times that just in tax. Lawmakers there narrowly voted on Friday to charge content providers 5.5 cents for every gigabyte they send to French users – though the measure still has a long way to go before it becomes law.
Socialist deputy Laurent Lhardit's amendment passed the National Assembly by just 11 votes to 10. In fact, only 35 of the chamber's 577 deputies were even in the room at the time. Both the government and the budget's own rapporteur had advised against it, too.
If it survives, subscribers wouldn't be billed directly. Instead, ISPs like Orange, SFR, Bouygues Telecom and Free would tally how much data reaches their customers from each sender. Content providers would then owe €0.055 per gigabyte. That bill would be capped at 15% of French revenue or 2% of global revenue.
All told, Lhardit's group expects the tax to raise €10 billion a year. That figure leans on telecom regulator Arcep's estimate that about 200 billion gigabytes flow to French subscribers annually. Roughly half of that traffic comes from just five companies – Google, Meta, Amazon, Netflix and Akamai.
Budget minister David Amiel has his doubts, though. For one, he questioned whether the count could even work without flow sensors on networks or measurements taken on users' own devices. He also reckoned about half the bill would land on smaller content providers, many of them French. Meanwhile, VideoLAN, the French nonprofit behind VLC, warned it would be on the hook for more than €1 million a year.
For his part, Lhardit insists subscribers won't have to pay a thing. But Philippe Juvin, the budget's rapporteur, cautioned during the debate that the biggest platforms could simply pass the cost on to advertisers.
That kind of pass-through has already played out in France once. When its 3% digital services tax kicked in back in 2019, Amazon responded by raising fees for French marketplace sellers by 3%. Apple and Google later followed with higher charges for app developers and advertisers in the country.
If platforms pass the cost along again, the per-gigabyte math adds up quickly for games. Grand Theft Auto VI's reported 210 GB download alone would cost its distributor about €11.55 for every copy grabbed in France.
Before any of that matters, the tax still has to clear the Senate, where a conservative Les Républicains majority is unlikely to back it. Assembly president Yaël Braun-Pivet has also urged Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu to force the budget through without a vote under Article 49.3. If he does, the government can simply leave the amendment out.

articles.title: Marble Cognition raises $3.75M for its AI agent workers that watch and learn how people work - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Marble Cognition raises $3.75M for its AI agent workers that watch and learn how people work
Artificial intelligence agents have become two a penny in the enterprise today, but just because they’re rapidly being commoditized does not mean organizations know how best to use them.
That’s the challenge a startup called Marble Cognition is trying to solve after raising $3.75 million in pre-seed funding to coincide with its launch today. The round was led by Heartcore and Seedcamp, and saw participation from angel investors that include executives from McKinsey & Co., Mistral AI and a board member of Datadog Inc.
Munich-based Marble was co-founded by the German AI engineers Felix Rösner (pictured, left) and Christophe Schmit (right), who were among the first to realize that AI agents have already become a commodity, used by almost every enterprise in some capacity or other. Most organizations are using AI agents primarily for writing software, but Rösner believes that to see the real value of those autonomous workers, companies need to provide them with the granular operational context that tells them what they actually need to build and automate.
But building this picture is a notoriously difficult challenge because few corporate workflows run according to neat blueprints. Though a study by McKinsey & Co. suggests that it’s theoretically possible to automate 57% of all work hours in the U.S., most companies haven’t gotten anywhere near that goal.
That’s because more than 90% of business processes live within things like messy email threads, scattered spreadsheets and inside the minds of employees. To teach AI agents what needs to be built and automated, companies need to piece all of those processes into a picture they can follow.
This is exactly the challenge Marble seeks to address. Its AI agents are designed to capture those business workflows at the source. The startup has developed a dedicated desktop application that sits and monitors how employees work using different tools and processes. It takes screenshots and captures worker’s clicks and keystrokes, before transforming this data into a structured process map that AI agents can read and execute, similar to code.
“Every company we talk to wants AI to take over real work,” Rösner said. “But nobody can tell the AI how that work is actually done. So we solve that first. Our Coworkers watch how the work happens before they take it over. They do it the same way your best people do.”
In case employees or their bosses are worried about privacy, Marble reassures them that all of the data it records of their workers working day-to-day is anonymized and can be reviewed before it touches any AI models. In addition, all of its model’s processing can be done within the customer’s private cloud or on-premises environment. It learns to identify non-business-associated computer use too, so if an employee is browsing Facebook during a lunch hour, it will exclude that from the data it collects.
Once the data is gathered, Marble then deploys its Coworkers, which are designed to take over the most repetitive work processes from people and run them end-to-end an organization’s existing software stacks, with humans remaining in the loop when important decisions need to be made.
Rösner said Marble has already delivered some serious efficiency gains for early adopters like EGYM GmbH, Mutares SE & Co. KGaA and Enam GmbH. In the case of one private equity-backed U.S. financial services firm, Marble’s Coworkers were configured to create settlement offers for human review. As a result of that work, the company was able to slash its case-handling times by 90%, which meant that its human staffers could process around 50% more claims without needing to hire anyone else.
Seedcamp General Partner Reshma Sohoni, an early backer of the robotic process automation firm UiPath Inc., said the vast majority of companies in the world want to learn how to automate more of their work. “The hard part has always been mapping out how the work gets done, so you can actually automate it,” he said. “Marble fills that gap, giving companies vital context for AI transformations that could define their future.”

articles.title: Paris-based Gallium Defence emerges from stealth with €7.1 million to scale affordable drone detection | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Gallium Defence, a Paris-based startup working on drone detection at a fraction of the cost of legacy systems, has emerged from stealth with a €7.1 million Seed funding round.
The round was led by Keen Venture Partners and 360 Capital, with participation from Omnes Capital and Polytechnique Ventures. This announcement coincided with European Defence Week 2026, held from 2nd to 6th November in Paris.
“Great defence starts with superior visibility. Gallium Defence has the team, the industrial partners and the cost model to make drone detection a standard layer at every critical site – the kind of European capability our fund is proud to back,” said Alexander Ribbink, General Partner, Keen Venture Partners.
Gallium Defence was founded in April 2026 by Eric Fournier, Florian Lemoine, and Robin Mandel, three individuals with defence and industrial backgrounds. Fournier spent 17 years advising defence and aerospace leaders at Boston Consulting Group, while Lemoine has over 15 years’ experience in defence and served as a former adviser to NATO SACT. Mandel also brings over 15 years’ experience across industry and consulting through roles at Thales, BCG and Safran.
The company says more than 80% of critical infrastructure sites and military assets remain exposed to modern drone threats because of lack of affordable, field-ready radars capable of addressing the threat at scale. Gallium Defence was formed to address this gap by making high-performance radars affordable and easier to deploy, for both air security and air defence.
“As drones proliferate, traditional radars are reaching their operational and economic limits. At Gallium Defence, we started from a blank sheet with a simple question, asked by operators in the field: how do you meet 80% of the need at 20% of the price? Our answer: a radically rethought AESA radar architecture that makes extensive use of commercial off-the-shelf components and the power of embedded computing,” said Fournier, CEO and co-founder of Gallium Defence.
Gallium’s flagship product is called the GDS-10, an X-band AESA radar with a software-defined, AI-native architecture. It is designed for dual use and comes in two versions: one for critical infrastructure operators and one for armed forces.
The GDS-10 is capable of detecting Class 1 and FPV drones at a range of 10km. It provides 360° azimuth coverage and 90° elevation coverage with no blind spots, and can track multiple drones simultaneously, including within a swarm, day and night, in all weather conditions. Since GDS-10 is software-defined by design, its capabilities can evolve as new threats emerge.
“Our radars are designed to be manufactured and deployed by the hundreds, not one at a time,” said Mandel, COO and co-founder of Gallium Defence.
Just four months after closing its Seed round, the company conducted its first open-air field trials. The funding is being used to industrialise production of its first products, strengthen the team, train AI models, and run demonstrations for civil and military operators around the world.
With the Seed funding raised and monthly field demonstrations underway, Gallium Defence is pitching itself as the sovereign European answer for drone detection at scale. The company plans to open orders for the GDS-10 in the first quarter of 2027.

articles.title: Polymarket Returns $3.9 Million to Traders as DebugBear Cites DNS Hijack
articles.text:
Polymarket says it is returning $3.9 million to traders following last week’s supply chain attack. Website performance monitoring firm DebugBear, meanwhile, has disclosed that its DNS records were compromised.
On October 29, the prediction market halted trading on its international platform after users reported unauthorized withdrawals. Hudson Rock researchers linked the activity to malicious JavaScript served from a DebugBear address that Polymarket’s site loaded.
The script targeted logged-in traders. It checked their portfolios, and then either dumped positions or shifted assets to a wallet chosen by the attacker. The code read credential-related data stored in the browser, but Hudson Rock saw no evidence of it sending passwords, seed phrases or private keys back to the attacker. Instead, it piggybacked on the trading permissions of the open session.
In an October 30 update, Polymarket said 726 wallets were affected. At that point, all but 37 had been made whole, and the rest were being paid once their details were checked.
Polymarket is also covering traders hurt by the trading halt or whose positions were sold or transferred by the malicious script, paying out $1.19 million across roughly 5,500 wallets. Together with the roughly $2.7 million stolen directly, that brings the payout to $3.9 million.
“The attack came through a compromised 3rd party provider which we removed within the hour. We are in active investigation with law enforcement & will share a postmortem,” Polymarket said.
DebugBear, whose real user monitoring (RUM) script lets websites measure page load performance for visitors, initially told customers to remove the embed code and has now shared its initial findings.
“Our DNS server records were compromised through our domain registrar. We are currently unable to receive emails sent to our domain,” the company said.
According to DebugBear, the attackers appear to have gone after one customer’s website specifically, though it stressed that this is a preliminary finding. It did not name the customer, and Polymarket has not named the compromised provider.
DebugBear has not explained how the attackers obtained access at the registrar level, and its investigation is ongoing. The company said it found no indication that its internal systems were compromised.
Polymarket faced a similar incident in June, when it said a third-party vendor compromise resulted in a malicious script being injected into its frontend. The theft was reported at around $3 million.

articles.title: James Webb revela novas pistas sobre a origem do visitante interestelar 3I/ATLAS
articles.text:
Um artigo publicado recentemente no periódico científico The Astrophysical Journal Letters traz dados surpreendentes obtidos pelo Telescópio Espacial James Webb, da NASA. A pesquisa revela que o cometa interestelar 3I/ATLAS possui grãos de gelo misturados com poeira – configuração que difere da observada nos cometas nativos do Sistema Solar.
O objeto, que foi identificado entrando na nossa vizinhança em julho de 2025, é apenas o terceiro objeto visitante vindo em regiões distantes da Via Láctea a ser observado pela humanidade, logo após as passagens históricas do asteroide 1I/’Oumuamua e do cometa 2I/Borisov.
Em razão dessa raridade, a comunidade científica mundial mobilizou os instrumentos infravermelhos do Webb para acompanhar a trajetória do corpo celeste em detalhes.
Cometa 3I/ATLAS tem o dobro da idade do Sistema Solar
A equipe liderada por Silvia Protopapa, pesquisadora do Southwest Research Institute (SwRI), dos Estados Unidos, confirmou as suspeitas anteriores de que o viajante nasceu no disco protoplanetário de gás e poeira ao redor de uma estrela jovem, possivelmente há mais de 10 bilhões de anos. Esse tempo estimado de existência supera o dobro da idade do Sistema Solar.
Segundo o estudo, após formado, o corpo acabou sendo ejetado de seu sistema de origem por forças gravitacionais e passou bilhões de anos vagando solitariamente pelo espaço sideral.
Assim como acontece com os cometas tradicionais que orbitam o nosso Sol, o calor da estrela provoca a evaporação dos gases na superfície à medida que o objeto se aproxima. Esse processo lança os materiais congelados e os detritos para fora, formando uma ampla nuvem brilhante ao redor do núcleo, chamada de coma, além de desenhar a característica cauda do cometa, de onde os instrumentos científicos conseguem extrair dados de composição.
A análise da luz refletida pelos gases do corpo celeste revelou um comportamento inesperado. Nos cometas nativos do Sistema Solar, o gelo de água produz três marcas de absorção bem definidas no espectro luminoso. No entanto, as medições do 3I/ATLAS indicaram a presença de apenas uma dessas marcas, gerando um enigma sobre a verdadeira estrutura física do gelo presente na nuvem do visitante.
Para decifrar o mistério, os cientistas recorreram a simulações de computador para reproduzir os dados coletados no espaço. Os modelos virtuais demonstraram que o objeto é formado por grãos microscópicos de gelo de água extremamente empoeirados. Nos cometas que surgiram ao redor do nosso Sol, o gelo se apresenta em um estado consideravelmente mais puro e com baixíssima quantidade de contaminação por poeira.
Estudo levanta hipótese de colisão cósmica antiga
A proporção de poeira misturada aos grãos gelados funciona como um registro fóssil sobre as condições ambientais no momento de nascimento do corpo celeste. Como os cometas preservam a matéria-prima original do nascimento das estrelas, o estudo desse corpo vindo de fora oferece uma oportunidade única para compreender como outros sistemas planetários se formaram em áreas remotas da galáxia e comparar esse processo com a origem da Terra.
Apesar das diferenças em relação aos cometas locais, o corpo interestelar guarda semelhanças com outro grupo existente no Sistema Solar: os objetos transnetunianos, corpos gelados localizados na região periférica situada além da órbita de Netuno. Essas formações distantes também possuem grande abundância de dióxido de carbono congelado e compostos orgânicos ricos em carbono em suas superfícies.
De acordo com um comunicado do SwRI, outros estudos já haviam apontado que o 3I/ATLAS possui uma das concentrações mais elevadas de dióxido de carbono já registradas pela astronomia moderna. Essa composição indica que ele se formou nas regiões mais afastadas e frias do seu sistema original, em uma dinâmica muito parecida com a que deu origem aos objetos transnetunianos do nosso próprio sistema solar, revelando padrões comuns na construção de planetas.
Os pesquisadores sugerem inclusive a hipótese de que o viajante seja o fragmento resultante da colisão e destruição de um corpo gelado muito maior em seu sistema nativo. Essa descoberta confirma que os pequenos grãos de gelo empoeirados se agrupam primeiro nos discos ao redor das estrelas jovens para formar corpos maiores, mostrando que a receita fundamental para construir mundos pode ser parecida em toda a galáxia.
Flávia Correia é jornalista do Olhar Digital, cobrindo Ciência e Espaço.

articles.title: This Halloween, make sure your sensitive data Is wearing a mask
articles.text:
This Halloween, make sure your sensitive data Is wearing a mask
Protecting sensitive data as AI access expands
If you work in cybersecurity for long enough, you learn that we really love an analogy or a metaphor and come October you can barely move for talk of security nightmares, cyber monsters and threats lurking in the shadows.
I enjoy a good analogy as much as anyone, but there’s one Halloween comparison I don't hear very often. And, for data security at least, I think it might be the most useful one right now: the mask.
A mask doesn't make what's underneath disappear. It simply means you don't have to reveal its true identity to everyone who encounters it, and that’s what we’re trying to achieve with sensitive data.
VP of Data Security Products at cybersecurity company Thales.
Developers need data to test applications, analysts need it to find patterns, and AI tools and agents increasingly need access to enterprise information to do useful work. But needing to use this data isn't necessarily the same as needing to see every sensitive value it contains.
That's precisely where data masking comes in. By replacing sensitive information with realistic but unusable values, organizations can preserve the usefulness of data without unnecessarily exposing what's underneath.
With AI dramatically increasing where data can travel, who can find it and what can act upon it, that distinction is becoming much more important.
A disguise with a serious purpose
At its core, data masking replaces sensitive information with realistic but unusable values. The resulting dataset can retain characteristics necessary for development, testing, analytics and other business processes without unnecessarily exposing the sensitive information underneath. Think of it as a Halloween costume with a security purpose; the data can still show up to the party without revealing its true identity.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
That distinction matters because protecting data shouldn't simply mean preventing people from using it. Modern businesses depend upon being able to analyze, test against and increasingly train or ground AI systems in enterprise information. Instead, the question should be: does this person, application or AI system actually need the original sensitive value to perform this task?
A developer testing an application may need representative customer data, for example, but not necessarily genuine customer identities. An analytics workload may need to preserve relationships and patterns without revealing every account number or personal identifier.
If the real value isn't required, exposing it creates risk without creating corresponding business value.
Masking removes that unnecessary exposure. Depending on the use case, organizations can also use techniques including tokenization and encryption. The important principle is to match protection to how the information needs to be used rather than defaulting to exposing raw sensitive data.
You can't mask what you can't find
There is an obvious complication: before deciding what should wear a mask, businesses need to know where their sensitive information is.
That remains surprisingly difficult.
The 2026 Thales Data Threat Report found only 34% of surveyed organizations had complete knowledge of where their data was stored. Only 39% said they could classify all of it. Meanwhile, the average organization reported using seven different tools for data protection and monitoring.
Cloud infrastructure compounds the problem. Information can be copied into data lakes, SaaS platforms, development environments and backups. Unstructured documents can contain sensitive information nobody realized was there. Applications created years after the data was collected can suddenly gain access to it.
AI makes that visibility problem considerably more consequential because finding information is precisely what these systems are becoming very good at.
This is where data security posture management (DSPM) becomes important. Rather than treating data security purely as a question of defending infrastructure, DSPM starts with the data itself: discovering and classifying sensitive information and understanding where it resides, who or what can access it, how it is being used and whether its protection is appropriate.
Once an organization identifies unnecessarily exposed sensitive data, it can decide whether access should be removed, restricted or protected using controls such as masking, tokenization or encryption.
AI data: trick or treat?
This becomes particularly important as businesses progress from experimenting with generative AI towards embedding AI into everyday operations.
AI applications need data. Agents may need considerably more of it because they are designed not simply to generate content but to retrieve information, make decisions and potentially take actions across different systems.
The security implications are already becoming visible. The same research found 61% of organizations reported their AI applications were being targeted by attackers, with sensitive data the leading target. Rapid change within the AI ecosystem was also the most commonly cited AI security risk.
The important question, however, isn't simply whether AI can be secured. Organizations also need to ask a more fundamental question:
What data are we allowing AI to see in the first place?
Giving an AI application access to a database shouldn't automatically mean giving it access to every raw sensitive value contained within it. The same least-privilege principle used for human identities can be applied to data: expose what is necessary for the task and protect what isn't.
That could mean masking personal information before it reaches development and testing environments. It could mean tokenizing particularly sensitive values used by an application. It could mean encrypting information and tightly controlling which identities can decrypt it. And in some circumstances, it should mean preventing an AI system from accessing a dataset altogether.
Don't make AI security harder than it needs to be
There is a tendency to treat AI security as an entirely new discipline requiring entirely new answers.
Some risks certainly are new. But one of the most useful things organizations can do is apply established data-security principles to this new environment.
Know where sensitive data resides. Understand its context. Minimize unnecessary access. Protect the underlying value according to how it needs to be used. And continually reassess those decisions as applications and AI systems change.
AI may dramatically increase how much value organizations can extract from their data. It doesn't follow that every system extracting that value needs to see everything underneath.
Halloween only comes around once a year. For sensitive data, however, having the option to wear a convincing mask year-round is becoming a non-negotiable.

articles.title: Google Search has a fun retro easter egg for The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time
articles.text:
Google is celebrating the release of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake in a pretty neat way.
If you type Zelda or Ocarina of Time into Google Search, you’ll see a Master Sword icon appear on the bottom right. Upon clicking it, you’ll hear Link’s signature “Hya!” before the TriForce logo appears and the screen transitions to none other than a 90s-themed version of Google Search.
It should be noted, however, that these retro Google Search results for Zelda are limited to a single page, so its actual functionality is minimal. Still, it’s a fun nod to the fact that Ocarina of Time originally debuted on the N64 in 1998. As some social media users have pointed out, it’s also a throwback to a time when search engines were minimalist and, arguably, more functional, free from all of the AI garbage that’s been shoved into them.
The Google easter egg comes just a few days before The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time launches exclusively on Nintendo Switch 2 on November 5. It’s a remake that dramatically overhauls the visuals and makes some smaller gameplay tweaks but overall remains highly faithful to the 1998 classic.
In related news, EB Games and Best Buy are both holding midnight launches for Ocarina of Time this week. One of these stores, Toronto’s flagship EB Games on Yonge St., is also now home to Nintendo’s first-ever store-within-a-store in North America.
