articles.title: SpaceX reportedly wants to buy Boost Mobile to compete with AT&T, T-Mobile, and Verizon | TechCrunch
articles.text:
SpaceX is looking to buy Boost Mobile from EchoStar, according to a report from The Washington Post. If the deal goes through, it would help the Elon Musk-owned company build a hybrid cellular-satellite network that could help catapult it into fourth place among the top U.S. wireless providers.
The space-launch company has been dabbling in cellular connectivity, rolling out satellite access to T-Mobile’s subscribers in 2024. Last year, SpaceX bought $17 billion worth of wireless spectrum from EchoStar for cellular services, which could help the company’s Starlink service reach inside buildings, for example, something it currently struggles with.
“This is the last critical piece of the spectrum puzzle needed for SpaceX to provide complete phone coverage in America,” Musk said on X at the time of the spectrum acquisition. Yet, if Musk is still looking to buy access to terrestrial networks, it apparently wasn’t the last piece.
Elon Musk, SpaceX’s CEO, reportedly spoke directly with EchoStar chairman Charlie Ergen in October about acquiring Boost Mobile, the mobile virtual network operator. EchoStar has about 7.5 million customers between Boost Mobile and Gen Mobile, its other mobile service offering.
Musk has also approached AT&T, T-Mobile, and Verizon about buying capacity on their networks. All three rejected Musk, and they may still have a say in a SpaceX acquisition of Boost Mobile. Boost doesn’t operate its own towers, instead leasing capacity from AT&T and T-Mobile, which might need to approve such a deal. Sources speaking to The Post said that network leases are usually nontransferable.
The big three providers each have over 100 million subscribers, dwarfing Boost Mobile. But while the acquisition would give SpaceX an immediate bump in subscribers, the true value of the deal would be giving the company access to terrestrial cellular networks.
Gaining access to towers leased to Boost Mobile would expand coverage significantly — Boost currently covers most of the 48 contiguous states in the U.S. — allowing Starlink to cover devices when they’re outdoors and relying on cell towers to handle devices when Starlink signals can’t reach them.

articles.title: Cómo navegar por la Deep Web: aplicaciones y herramientas que debes conocer
articles.text:
La internet que vemos a diario es solo una pequeña parte de una gran red de redes. Por muchas razones, gran parte de esa red está limitada a ciertos usuarios, como pueden ser bases de datos, redes internas de empresas y organismos públicos, servidores privados… Todo lo que no aparece en los buscadores o que no está indexado se conoce como deep web o internet profunda. Así que navegar por la Deep Web es algo que cualquiera puede hacer. Y no tiene nada que ver con saltarse la ley o cometer un delito.
Sin embargo, los medios y la cultura popular suele confundir la parte con el todo. La parte ilegal de la Deep Web, que conocemos como Dark Web, es la que más fama tiene. Mala fama, claro está. Y es fácil confundir esa parte de la internet profunda con toda ella. En la Dark Web es donde se cometen delitos, se venden y compran datos robados o herramientas para robarlos, etc. Siempre que vemos noticias como la venta de documentos personales, esos contenidos ilegales están en la Dark Web.
En realidad, cada día accedes a la Deep Web sin darte cuenta. Cuando miras tu correo electrónico o tus mensajes privados (WhatsApp o Telegram), cuando entras en la web de tu banco, cuando consultas tu historial médico desde la app de la sanidad pública, cuando miras las redes sociales de tus amigos… Incluso cuando ves películas o escuchas música por streaming. Todo eso es internet profunda. Pero, claro está, la parte de la Deep Web que te interesará visitar con las siguientes aplicaciones es más esquiva. Y requiere de herramientas especiales. Veamos las más interesantes.
Consejos antes de navegar por la Deep Web
Si te interesa acceder a sitios web o plataformas de la Deep Web que por motivos varios no está a simple vista o disponible con enlaces o direcciones IP, conviene tener en cuenta algunas recomendaciones y consejos de seguridad. Más vale ser precavido.
- No abras cuentas personales.
- Evita compartir datos personales, bancarios, etc.
- No reutilices nombres de usuario, correos ni contraseñas.
- Rellena formularios con cautela para proteger tu identidad.
- Procura no navegar por la internet profunda y la internet visible al mismo tiempo.
- En resumen, separa identidades y sesiones.
- Evita descargar aplicaciones, documentos o archivos.
- Las aplicaciones P2P como BitTorrent pueden realizar conexiones directas y revelar tu IP. Así que vigila qué contenidos descargas desde la internet profunda.
- Si es inevitable, toda precaución es poca.
- Empieza por sitios conocidos y fuentes verificadas.
- No compres nada ni hagas pagos online.
- Al terminar de navegar por la Deep Web, cierra la sesión, borra el historial, la caché y cualquier dato o archivo que haya guardado tu navegador.
Tor Browser
Si hablamos de navegar por la internet profunda es inevitable mencionar el proyecto Tor y su navegador Tor Browser. Tor lleva décadas en activo. Surgido en los años 90 del siglo pasado dentro del Laboratorio de Investigación Naval de EE. UU., la tecnología de enrutamiento de cebolla sirve para añadir a internet una capa más de privacidad. Básicamente, dirige el tráfico a través de varios servidores y lo cifra en cada paso. Como curiosidad, Tor es el acrónimo de The Onion Routing, es decir, el enrutamiento de cebolla.
Hoy en día, utilizar esta tecnología es tan simple como descargar, instalar y abrir el navegador Tor. O Tor Browser. Está basado en Firefox, disponible para Windows, Mac, Linux y Android y está configurado con todo lo necesario para navegar por la Deep Web de forma segura y privada. Aunque siempre hay que recordar que, en seguridad, no hay nada 100% eficaz. Para iOS y iPadOS hay también versión, aunque no es oficial. Puedes elegir entre Onion Browser y TOR Browser.
Existen otras tecnologías y protocolos para navegar por la internet profunda y, de paso, por la internet oscura o Dark Web, como I2P, Freenet o ZeroNet. Pero la más popular, de lejos, es Tor. De ahí que existan otros navegadores que ofrecen la posibilidad de navegar por la Deep Web sin salir del navegador.
Brave
Para navegar por la internet profunda de forma ocasional, que tu navegador de cabecera sea también compatible con Tor puede serte muy útil. Por ejemplo si quieres saltarte algún bloqueo o prohibición de determinadas páginas o sitios web. Precisamente, una de las razones de ser de Tor Browser es eludir la censura.
Brave es posiblemente uno de los navegadores con Tor más populares. También existen navegadores enfocados en la privacidad, y la mayoría de ellos apuestan por integrar VPN, como ocurre con Opera, Vivaldi, Firefox o Mullvad Browser. Precisamente, este último navegador ha sido desarrollado por Tor Project. Aunque emplea VPN en vez de Tor. Las diferencias entre usar VPN y Tor, según la página oficial del proyecto Tor, son mínimas. La principal es que vía Tor puedes acceder a páginas web tipo .onion.
Tails
Para navegar por la Deep Web, un navegador Tor es suficiente. Pero es posible que busques más privacidad todavía. Nunca se sabe quién puede estar al otro lado, en especial si accedes a plataformas y servicios de dudosa procedencia por motivos lícitos. Y para ello, desde el proyecto Tor tienes una opción más segura, Tails.
Tails es un sistema operativo portátil basado en Tor. Gratuito, basado en Linux y de código abierto. Diseñado para activistas, periodistas, investigadores, expertos en ciberseguridad y, básicamente, todo aquel que quiera protegerse de la vigilancia o la censura en internet, este sistema operativo se dio a conocer entre el gran público gracias a figuras como Edward Snowden.
¿Qué lo hace tan especial? Para empezar, puedes instalarlo en una memoria USB y ejecutarlo en un ordenador en lugar de Windows, macOS o Linux. También puedes instalarlo en una máquina virtual. El instalador tan solo ocupa 1,8 GB, tarda media hora en instalarse y con un USB de 8 GB tendrás suficiente. Y funciona en cualquier ordenador con, al menos, 3 GB de RAM.
Lo que convierte Tails en más seguro que otros sistemas operativos es que no escribe nada en el disco duro. Cuando lo inicias, todo empieza desde cero. Aunque de manera opcional puedes guardar archivos y configuraciones en un apartado especial del USB. Por lo demás, cuenta con todas las herramientas que puedas necesitar. Algunas son de uso común como LibreOffice, GIMP, Inkscape o Rhythmbox. Y, otras, específicas para tu seguridad y privacidad como el navegador Tor Browser, OnionShare para compartir archivos, su propio gestor de contraseñas, una app para eliminar metadatos de documentos e imágenes y su propio monedero de Bitcoin.
Qubes OS
Qubes OS, o simplemente Qubes, es un sistema operativo gratuito y de código abierto, también basado en Linux. Y también recomendado por Edward Snowden. Sus creadores lo definen como un “sistema operativo orientado a la seguridad para ordenadores de sobremesa de un solo usuario”. Y en su documentación te explica por qué es tan seguro. Y puedes elegir entre instalarlo en un disco SSD o en un USB.
A diferencia de otros sistemas operativos, Qubes opera con máquinas virtuales, llamadas qubes, empleando el software Xen. Estas máquinas virtuales, que pueden funcionar de manera simultánea, te permite realizar tareas de manera separada y aislada entre sí. De manera que no haya cruce de datos e información. También la conexión a internet está aislada, y los periféricos que conectes por USB. Y en la parte que nos ocupa, integra Tor para que puedas navegar por la internet profunda de forma anónima y segura.
Whonix
Otra potente herramienta que sirve tanto para navegar por la Deep Web como para acceder a internet con una capa adicional de seguridad. Whonix es un sistema operativo, gratuito y de código abierto, muy particular. En la práctica, funciona como una aplicación más en tu ordenador, así que no tendrás que prescindir de Windows, macOS o Linux. Es más. Puedes instalar Whonix en esos sistemas operativos. E incluso en máquinas virtuales con VirtualBox, KVM o Qubes.
Lo que hace Whonix es combinar Linux y Tor para ofrecerte privacidad en todo lo que hagas con tu máquina. Para ello se compone de dos máquinas virtuales basadas en Debian Linux. Una ejecuta Tor y funciona a modo de filtro, puerta de enlace y cortafuegos. La segunda máquina virtual es la que tú utilizada para las tareas que quieras mantener en secreto: navegar por la internet profunda, mirar el correo, enviar y recibir mensajes… La conexión de esa segunda máquina pasa a través de la primera. De ahí que la recomienden activistas y expertos en seguridad.
Buscadores para navegar por la Deep Web
Al igual que buscadores como Google son la puerta de entrada a internet para muchos, si quieres navegar por la internet profunda puede que necesites un punto de partida. Y para ello existen buscadores especializados en contenidos de la internet profunda, que como hemos visto, no hay que confundir con la internet oscura o Dark Web. Aquí van algunos buscadores recomendados para buscar lo que quieras:
- Ahmia: en versión web y en versión Onion
- DuckDuckGo: en versión Onion
- Onion Search: en versión web
- Onion Search Engine: en versión web y en versión Onion
- Torch: en versión web
Con estos buscadores, más las aplicaciones y herramientas que hemos mencionado y los consejos y recomendaciones que te hemos dado, deberías poder empezar con pie a moverte y navegar por la internet profunda. El grado de precaución que debas tomar dependerá de qué contenido o servicio quieres visitar.

articles.title: Weihnachtsgeschäft: Warum Shops Zahlungsarten nicht erst im Checkout zeigen sollten
articles.text:
Weihnachtsgeschäft: Warum der Checkout schon auf der Produktseite beginnt
Die Kaufentscheidung fällt nicht erst an der Kasse
Der Warenkorb ist gefüllt, das Produkt ausgewählt, der Kauf fast abgeschlossen. Doch erst jetzt erfährt die Kundschaft, welche Zahlungsmethoden verfügbar sind. Was lange zum Standard im E-Commerce gehörte, passt möglicherweise nicht mehr zu den Erwartungen vieler Verbraucher:innen.
Denn die Customer Journey beginnt deutlich früher. Kund:innen vergleichen Produkte, planen Ausgaben und entscheiden, bei welchem Anbieter sie einkaufen möchten, häufig lange bevor sie den Checkout erreichen.
Eine im Auftrag von PayPal durchgeführte repräsentative Morning-Consult-Befragung von 2.079 Erwachsenen in Deutschland zeigt, wie ausgeprägt diese frühzeitige Planung gerade im Weihnachtsgeschäft ist.
Fast Jede zweite Person (49 Prozent) gibt an, bei Weihnachtseinkäufen ab 100 Euro bereits vor Beginn der Rabattaktionen entweder eine Kaufentscheidung vorzubereiten und auf einen Rabatt zu warten oder Produkte zu recherchieren und erst während der Angebote final zu entscheiden. Nur 16 Prozent beginnen ihre Suche erst, wenn die Aktionen bereits laufen. Für Onlineshops bedeutet das: Der Wettbewerb um Kaufinteresse beginnt nicht erst am Black Friday.
Payment wird Teil der Kaufentscheidung
            
            
        
    
            PayPal
    
      PayPal Business ermöglicht Unternehmen jeder Größe Zahlungen zu erhalten und Wachstum zu fördern.
Interessant ist dabei nicht nur, wann Verbraucher:innen recherchieren, sondern welche Informationen sie währenddessen erwarten.
41 Prozent der Befragten würden es spätestens auf der Produktseite hilfreich finden zu wissen, ob Buy Now, Pay Later (BNPL), also PayPal „Später Bezahlen“, verfügbar ist. Rund drei von zehn sagen, dass sie einen Artikel eher in den Warenkorb legen würden, wenn diese Information bereits auf der Produktseite erscheint.
Auch die Händler:innen-Wahl kann davon beeinflusst werden: 28 Prozent würden bei vergleichbaren Produkten und Preisen eher einen Shop wählen, der BNPL („Später Bezahlen“) bereits auf der Produktseite anzeigt. Lediglich 12 Prozent bevorzugen einen Anbieter, der diese Information erst im Checkout bereitstellt.
Dies sind Angaben zur Kaufabsicht, keine tatsächlich gemessenen Conversion-Steigerungen. Dennoch liefern sie einen wichtigen Hinweis: Zahlungsinformationen können bereits in der Consideration-Phase relevant sein.
PayPal „Später Bezahlen“
Wenn die Wahl der Zahlungsmethode zur Conversion-Frage wird
Wie wichtig die bevorzugte Zahlungsmethode sein kann, zeigt ein weiteres Ergebnis der Studie. 67 Prozent der deutschen Befragten haben nach eigenen Angaben bereits einen Online-Kauf abgebrochen, weil ihre bevorzugte Zahlungsoption im Checkout nicht verfügbar war.
Von diesen Personen kauften 43 Prozent anschließend denselben oder einen ähnlichen Artikel bei einem anderen Anbieter. Nur jede siebte Person (15 Prozent) kehrte zurück und verwendete eine andere Zahlungsmethode.
Diese Ergebnisse beziehen sich auf Zahlungsoptionen allgemein, nicht ausschließlich auf BNPL („Später Bezahlen“). Für Händler:innen ist die Konsequenz dennoch relevant. Eine gute Produktauswahl, überzeugende Preise und eine funktionierende Shop-Oberfläche allein reichen möglicherweise nicht aus, wenn die angebotenen Zahlungsmethoden nicht zu den Erwartungen der Kund:innen passen.
Bekannte Zahlungsmethoden schaffen Vertrauen
Wenn Verbraucher:innen bereits während der Recherche wissen möchten, welche Bezahlmöglichkeiten zur Verfügung stehen, sollten diese Informationen dort erscheinen, wo Kaufentscheidungen vorbereitet werden: auf der Produktseite, in der Produktübersicht oder spätestens im Warenkorb. So können Kund:innen Zahlungsoptionen frühzeitig in ihre Budget- und Kaufplanung einbeziehen.
Davon profitieren auch kleinere oder weniger bekannte Onlineshops. Laut der PayPal-Studie sagen 44 Prozent der deutschen Verbraucher:innen, dass ein bekannter Zahlungsanbieter ihr Vertrauen in einen ihnen bislang unbekannten Händler stärken würde. Payment wird damit nicht nur zum Mittel für den eigentlichen Bezahlvorgang, sondern zu einem Vertrauenssignal innerhalb der Customer Journey. Für Händler:innen kann die Sichtbarkeit vertrauter Zahlungsoptionen dazu beitragen, Kaufbarrieren frühzeitig abzubauen und sich im Wettbewerb, um Aufmerksamkeit und Conversion besser zu positionieren.
Win before checkout
Für Händler:innen ergibt sich daraus ein Perspektivwechsel. Payment ist nicht nur ein technischer Schritt am Ende der Customer Journey. Informationen zu Zahlungsmethoden können bereits vorher bei der Produktauswahl, der Budgetplanung und der Entscheidung für einen Shop helfen.
PayPal bietet mit „Später Bezahlen“ unter anderem die Optionen „Bezahlung nach 30 Tagen“** und „PayPal Ratenzahlung“*** an. Beide Angebote unterliegen einer Kreditwürdigkeitsprüfung und den jeweiligen Produktbedingungen.
Bei unterstützten Shopsystemen können Händler:innen die bereits vorhandenen dynamischen PayPal-Später-Bezahlen-Banner je nach Integration direkt im Backend ihres Shopsystem-Anbieters oder im PayPal-Geschäftskonto aktivieren. Eine zusätzliche technische Integration ist dafür nicht erforderlich. Wer die verfügbaren Zahlungsmethoden frühzeitig, verständlich und regelkonform kommuniziert, kann Kund:innen schon während der Kaufentscheidung Orientierung geben. Denn der Checkout beginnt aus Kund:innensicht häufig lange vor dem letzten Klick.
Es ist ganz einfach, die „Später Bezahlen“-Banner zu aktivieren. Hier klicken, um mehr zu erfahren:
*Studie: Morning Consult im Auftrag von PayPal, repräsentative Online-Befragung von 2.079 Konsument:innen in Deutschland, 4.–10. September 2026.
Hinweis: PayPal „Später Bezahlen“ unterliegt einer Kreditwürdigkeitsprüfung sowie produktabhängigen Betragsgrenzen, Konditionen und Verfügbarkeiten. Alle Informationen zu Wachstum unterstützen mit „Später Bezahlen” findest du hier.
**Bezahlung nach 30 Tagen: Vorbehaltlich Kreditwürdigkeitsprüfung. Für Einkäufe zwischen 1 Euro und 3.000 Euro. Alle Informationen findest du hier.
***PayPal Ratenzahlung: Vorbehaltlich Kreditwürdigkeitsprüfung. Laufzeiten von 3, 6, 12 oder 24 Monaten. Ab 99 Euro und bis zu 10.000 Euro Bestellwert. Alle Informationen findest du hier.

articles.title: Raising the quality of insights in agentic analytics
articles.text:
Sponsored
Raising the quality of insights in agentic analytics
The top reason analytics agents produce substandard insights is a lack of business context, prompting investment in semantic layers and governance, rather than bigger models.
In partnership withSnowflake
In just a few years, generative AI has changed the face of enterprise analytics, notably by making analytics accessible to users across the organization. Agentic AI promises to do even more, by automating entire workflows and taking actions based on agent insights. But there is a problem: The quality of insights that agents currently generate leaves much to be desired.
Fewer than half of agent-generated insights at the organizations surveyed for this report lead to business improvement. And while most respondents praise the quality of their agents’ descriptive insights, reviews of their prescriptive insights—those on which actions are based—are decidedly mixed.
Failure to produce insights that improve the business deprives organizations of their desired return on investment in agentic analytics. Worse, flawed insights that trigger incorrect actions can cause reputational or financial damage. This report gauges how companies view the quality of the outputs produced by their analytics agents and explores how organizations are seeking to boost insight quality and get their agents working harder for the business.
Some key findings from the report include the following:
Agentic analytics is only just starting to deliver. On average, 48% of insights generated by analytics agents at the surveyed companies lead to actions that improve the business. That is a marked advance from the 37% average the respondents say generated such actions one year ago. But it means that more than half of the insights generated by analytics agents today are still failing to help businesses.
Better quality of insights leads to clear business advantage. At a small cohort of organizations, which we term “insight leaders,” AI agents perform much better than the average. In this group, more than 70% of agent insights lead to actions that improve the business. The insight leaders also give the quality of their agents’ insights higher marks than do the total respondents overall. The quality gap is particularly wide when it comes to prescriptive insights.
Insufficient context reduces insight quality. When analytics agents deliver insights of substandard quality, the main reason is a lack of business context, as cited by 55% of surveyed executives. Fragmented or inaccessible data is the other major factor, according to 45%. Fewer insight leaders say their agents struggle with access to context.
Insight overload further inhibits agent effectiveness. At a majority (52%) of surveyed organizations, analytics agents generate too many insights to be properly evaluated and therefore acted upon. Less than one-quarter (24%) are able to evaluate all agent insights; most do so on a case-by-case basis, and that process is currently human-intensive.
Governance and semantics are areas of focus for improving insights. The surveyed companies are prioritizing initiatives that enable better agent insights by strengthening AI and data governance (cited by 60%). They are also adding a semantic layer to their data architecture (45%). The experts we interviewed agree that the semantic layer is crucial to ensure high-performing agents.
This content was produced by Insights, MIT Technology Review’s custom content arm, not its editorial staff. It was researched and written by humans, with any AI tools that may have been used limited to production processes under human oversight.

articles.title: Ford promises not to sell your driving habits to data brokers
articles.text:
Ford vowed to never sell customer driving data to third-party data brokers as part of a new privacy promise aimed at setting the automaker apart from competitors that have faced legal and regulatory blowback for sharing telematics with data brokers without authorization.
Ford promises not to sell your driving habits to data brokers
Following GM’s $220 million settlement, Ford promises to never sell customer driving data to data brokers, attempting to set itself apart in an industry rife with tracking.
As part of its new promise, Ford says it will strive to protect customer data by using aggregating and anonymizing techniques. It will also “provide clear and easy-to-understand information about how we use your personal information.” And while Ford says it will still use data to improve safety, it will allow customers to adjust how much or how little data they would prefer to share.
In making an explicit pledge not to sell customer data to outside firms, Ford is trying to position itself as one of the better actors in an industry rife with shady practices. “We know that trust is earned,” Kristin Jones, chief privacy officer at Ford, writes in a blog post. “Protecting your personal information is one way we intend to earn it every day.”
“We know that trust is earned.”
— Kristin Jones, Ford’s chief privacy officer
The promise comes in the wake of General Motors agreeing to pay $220 million to settle claims that it illegally sold driver and location information to data brokers. The agreement requires GM to limit the driving data it collects and obtain “express consent” from drivers before collecting their information.
Other automakers have been caught with their hands in the customer data cookie jar. A recent examination of 21 vehicle brands found that every single one transmitted data to at least one third-party domain over Wi-Fi. Over half contacted domains that specialize in advertising, tracking, or analytics (ATA), like Adobe, LexisNexis, and Amplitude, which gather details about your vehicle or driving behavior to sell to insurance companies or target you with ads.
In a recent report, Mozilla crowned modern connected cars “the worst category of products for privacy” ever reviewed. The global nonprofit found that 92 percent of the reviewed automakers provide drivers with little (if any) control over their personal data, with 84 percent sharing user data with outside parties.
Ford said it surveyed over 1,000 US customers, both Ford and non-Ford owners, who agreed that privacy is a top concern while over half of the respondents said they understand that some data sharing is okay. Forty-one percent said they were extremely or very concerned about data privacy in the auto industry, which was less than other groups like social media companies, the government, and financial institutions.
To be sure, Ford’s promise isn’t just words on a screen. In the US, the Federal Trade Commission stops companies from misleading the public through deceptive claims. If Ford publicly promises something like, “We never sell your driving data to brokers” but breaks that promise, the FTC and state attorneys general can step in. They can sue Ford, force the company to sign legally binding agreements to correct the issue, and impose substantial financial fines.
It should be noted that a company’s blog post or public promise is not a legal contract. The actual rules that apply to you are found in Ford’s official privacy policy and connected vehicle terms. Those legal agreements contain standard exceptions that allow Ford to share your data, such as complying with police requests or working with outside service providers. Also, opting out of data sharing does come with tradeoffs. While Ford states that data collection depends on the features you want to use, turning off vehicle tracking or location sharing often disables key features like built-in navigation, remote start, and wireless software updates.

articles.title: Government Linux Servers Targeted With SysGoRAT and Suspected AI-Generated Scripts
articles.text:
Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a cyber espionage campaign specifically targeting Linux infrastructure associated with government entities and state-affiliated infrastructure.
The activity, observed by Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 between October 2025 and April 2026, has been tracked under the moniker CL-UNK-1211, where "CL" refers to cluster and "UNK" stands for unknown motivation.
A notable aspect of the campaign concerns the use of large language models (LLMs) and/or automated artificial intelligence (AI) agents to generate payloads and execute malicious code.
"The attackers behind this cluster of activity focused on Linux environments to conduct extensive reconnaissance and maintain persistent network access to support intelligence-gathering," researchers Roey Porat and Tom Fakterman said. "The attackers attempted to dump sensitive databases and exfiltrate government mailboxes to access social media accounts."
The campaign employs a "versatile operational playbook," leveraging a combination of open-source tools, custom cross-platform backdoors, and web shells to maintain access. Another hallmark involves attempts to disable endpoint protections, wipe system logs, and plant deceptive red-team markers so as to disguise the activity as a legitimate security assessment.
The threat actor has also been observed using malicious PHP and shell scripts, likely generated using AI, to maintain persistence, perform reconnaissance, and exfiltrate data.
"Rather than standard developer documentation, multiple scripts contained conversational, step-by-step reasoning notes. These notes explained the code's logic to the operator who provided the initial instructions," the cybersecurity company said. "Their presence suggests that the code was either copied directly from an AI prompt output or deployed by an automated AI agent."
A mix of open-source and bespoke PHP web shells is used as a way to maintain a persistent backdoor into the host networks. The access is then abused to gather credentials from the targeted environment using three different methods -
- Replacing the .bashrc file with a malicious version containing a command to steal passwords.
- Injecting code into PHP login pages to harvest admin credentials.
- Scanning for cleartext email, SMTP, and database passwords within configuration files and command history files.
Also deployed as part of the attacks is a custom, multi-platform remote access trojan written in Go that supports various persistence methods to maintain long-term access on Windows and Linux systems. Called SysGoRAT, it establishes a command-and-control (C2) connection over WebSocket to a hard-coded IP address ("104.194.158[.]65:443") and fetches seven types of commands -
- command, to execute arbitrary commands via /bin/sh -c (Linux) or cmd /C (Windows)
- control, to spawn via sub-commands an interactive shell (shell_start), screenshots (screenshot), exfiltrate files to the C2 server (download), and install persistence (persist)
- list_dir, to list directory content
- shell_input, to create an interactive shell session
- proxy_connect, to establish a TCP connection to an arbitrary target
- proxy_data, to relay data bidirectionally to an established proxy connection
- proxy_close, to terminate and remove a proxy session
Furthermore, the attacks make use of in-memory reverse shells to avoid leaving forensic artifacts on disk, as well as enumerate "/var/qmail/mailnames/" directories to count the number of emails stored in specific folders.
"Next, the attackers searched for social media-related emails," Unit 42 explained. "They deployed a PHP script, named search_social.php, that searched for specific keywords in email headers and displayed the results in a user-friendly format."
"The script then parsed the response and displayed the exact file path, social media account email sender, recipient and subject."
The attackers have also been found attempting to generate a bash script named "zip_mails.sh" in a bid to compress emails of interest into ZIP archives and exfiltrate the information. However, syntax errors present in the script meant that the program failed upon execution.
"This campaign demonstrates how attackers are combining traditional post-exploitation techniques with AI-accelerated workflows to target governmental Linux server infrastructure," Unit 42 said. "By leveraging AI to rapidly generate, adapt and deploy operational scripts, the attackers behind CL-UNK-1211 maintained a fast pace of operation while minimizing manual developer overhead."
The development comes as Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant, along with Microsoft, documented threat actors' abuse of open-source agentic penetration testing frameworks like ARTEX, PentAGI, Hexstrike, and CAIRN to carry out a "broad range of actions" across various stages of the attack life cycle at an unprecedented speed and scale.
Although ARTEX was taken down by its author after reports of widespread misuse emerged, it has spawned multiple versions, including a commercial offering dubbed ARTEX PRO and a localized variation called ScopeWeaver.
Some of the cases are listed below -
- Use of ARTEX by Storm-0940 (aka UNC7228) to orchestrate data theft campaigns targeting entities in the U.S. and Europe across the enterprise software, industrial automation, semiconductor manufacturing and design, and telecommunications industry verticals.
- Use of ARTEX by financially motivated threat actors to facilitate data theft extortion, including the targeting of the financial sector in Asia.
- Use of ARTEX by North Korean state-sponsored hacking groups like Onyx Sleet (aka Andariel) and Pearl Sleet (aka Lawrencium) in operations.
- Use of PentAGI for WHOIS asset mapping and systematic reconnaissance and vulnerability scanning against organizations in Asia.
"The emergence of ARTEX and similar agentic offensive intrusion frameworks underscores a broader shift toward threat actor adoption of open source multi-agent offensive frameworks, as well as potentially custom agentic harnesses," GTIG and Mandiant said.
"Frameworks such as ARTEX compress attack timelines to machine speed; however, they currently trade stealth for velocity. Unrestricted autonomous execution generates forensic traffic, relies on recognizable identifiers, and leaves behind distinct code-level traces, increasing the likelihood of detection and mitigation."

articles.title: F1 in Mexico City: Yet another Ferrari fiasco, but that’s not all
articles.text:
Formula 1 has a new World Drivers’ Champion. Just a few months after turning 20, Kimi Antonelli sealed his first title this weekend at Mexico City, becoming the sport’s youngest-ever champion. Elsewhere, there was drama aplenty, perhaps a consequence of the thin air affecting decision-making in some cases. The race was Ferrari’s to win, but yet again, the team handed victory to a rival this season, in this case Red Bull. Further down the grid, we saw a last-minute driver change in the Haas team, synchronized retirements from both Aston Martins, and the wheels literally coming off Cadillac Racing. And there was I, expecting a dull weekend.
It might not be as high as Pikes Peak, but at an elevation of 7,350 feet (2,240 m) above sea level, the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez provides a unique challenge on the F1 calendar. Wings that would create huge amounts of downforce at circuits like Monaco just generate Monza-like levels in Mexico, and there’s little slipstream effect when following another car.
Cooling tends to be a problem, too, with insufficient airflow across radiators, and obviously engine power is reduced with less oxygen to burn. The track is very flat, with a rather low-grip surface and mostly medium- and slow-speed corners, including a processional route through a stadium that was built in the 1990s, plus a very long run from the start into turn 1.
Friday’s first practice saw 10 rookie drivers substitute in for series regulars—each team must run a young or test driver in each of their two cars at least twice in a season. Make that six times in the case of Cadillac?
1+30+7+4=40?
Colton Herta’s road to F1 has been a journey.
Credit:
Chris Graythen/Getty Images
Colton Herta’s road to F1 has been a journey.
Credit:
Chris Graythen/Getty Images
The American startup team wants IndyCar star Colton Herta to race in F1, but Herta needs a total of 40 points over three years to get the requisite F1 super license. Sadly, his IndyCar record was too inconsistent—10th place in 2023, 2nd in 2024, but then 7th again in 2025—so he entered F2 this year, both to learn the circuits and to finish well enough in that championship to earn the remaining points.
That hasn’t happened, but you also earn a point for completing 100 km in an FP1 session, and Herta stepped into the Cadillac in Barcelona, Italy, Hungary, and in Texas. His run in Italy was cut short by unreliability, so Cadillac put him in the car again this weekend, hoping it would be the final run.
But it turns out they hadn’t added the numbers properly. Rather than pulling Herta’s IndyCar results from the official scoring, the team apparently relied on IndyCar’s erroneous website. Instead of starting the year with 36 super license points, Herta only had 35, and with four successful FP1 runs under his belt, he still needs one more point if the team wants to replace an underperforming Valteri Bottas next year, something that should happen with another run next time out in Brazil.
Friday’s second practice session also had more action than normal. Max Verstappen and Liam Lawson both sat out FP1 so rookies could drive their cars, which may have contributed to both being too eager to set a fast time in FP2. As Lawson’s Racing Bull got held up by Carlos Sainz’ slow Williams in front, Verstappen wanted past in the Red Bull, but both drivers were intransigent, and neither was prepared to yield. Paint was traded and cars were damaged, and both drivers were handed a one-place grid penalty for failing to behave themselves.
FP2 also probably marked the end of Esteban Ocon’s F1 career, at least for now. The French driver was upset with his team about their choice of tires for his long run, which evidently escalated once he was out of the car. On Saturday, Ocon had been benched and replaced with Ryo Hirakawa, Haas’ reserve driver and two-time World Endurance Champion with Toyota. Haas had already announced that Ocon was not rejoining the team in 2027, opting instead for F1 driver Rafael Camara, who will probably race for the team in Brazil, as Hirakawa will be racing his Toyota that weekend.
At 32, Ryo Hirakawa is quite old to be making his F1 debut.
Rudy Carezzevoli/Getty Images)
At 32, Ryo Hirakawa is quite old to be making his F1 debut.
Rudy Carezzevoli/Getty Images)
Max Verstappen (L) and Liam Lawson (R) getting a bit too robust during Friday practice.
Bradley Collyer/PA Images via Getty Images
Max Verstappen (L) and Liam Lawson (R) getting a bit too robust during Friday practice.
Bradley Collyer/PA Images via Getty Images
At 32, Ryo Hirakawa is quite old to be making his F1 debut.
Rudy Carezzevoli/Getty Images)
Max Verstappen (L) and Liam Lawson (R) getting a bit too robust during Friday practice.
Bradley Collyer/PA Images via Getty Images
Ferrari screwup
For most of this year, Ferrari has had a particular form. The team often tops the practice times on Friday but then fails to follow up on Saturday, often in the final qualifying session. That didn’t happen in Mexico, and Lewis Hamilton was able to claim his first pole position for Ferrari and his 105th in the sport. George Russell’s Mercedes qualified second, followed by Charles Leclerc’s Ferrari. Verstappen should have been fourth, but that Friday clash saw Antonelli moved into that spot. As it happens, the grid demotion put Verstappen on the clean side of the track, which he used to his advantage.
Both Ferraris got off the line well, as did Verstappen and Antonelli. Russell’s hybrid system derated halfway down the straight, ruining his race well before the first corner. With Hamilton in the lead and Leclerc in second place, the plan should have been obvious: settle into a 1-2 and win the race. Unfortunately, the idea of supporting his teammate is utterly alien to Leclerc, who showed us why he has 27 pole positions but only nine wins in eight years. Once more this year, the Ferraris raced each other as if a championship were at stake, and once more they snatched defeat from the jaws of victory.
Going into turn 4, both drivers went off track and rejoined. The race stewards had been extremely clear that leaving the track and gaining a permanent advantage at turns 1 or 4 on the first lap would result in a penalty unless the driver gave the place back. Hamilton did not gain a lasting advantage, but Leclerc did, staying in clean air up front and building enough of a lead that the paltry five-second penalty that was eventually handed down kept him ahead of Hamilton after their stops.
But it didn’t keep him ahead of Verstappen, who stopped at the same time as Leclerc but emerged in the lead, a lead he would keep until the end.
Charles Leclerc (L) and Lewis Hamilton (R) both missed turn 4. Perhaps they shouldn’t have been racing each other so hard.
Credit:
YURI CORTEZ / AFP
Charles Leclerc (L) and Lewis Hamilton (R) both missed turn 4. Perhaps they shouldn’t have been racing each other so hard.
Credit:
YURI CORTEZ / AFP
These cars sure break down a lot
It wasn’t an easy drive to the checkered flag, however. We’re accustomed to Lance Stroll’s Aston Martin breaking down on track and triggering a safety car or a virtual safety car, and this race was no exception. It happened early, on lap 7, while the other Aston Martin, driven by Fernando Alonso, retired to its garage.
Cadillac has also had plenty of reliability problems this year, usually with its front brakes overheating. It was even more serious in Mexico: On lap 44, Bottas’ front left suspension failed as he approached turn 1. The heavy crash forced a red flag to repair the barrier, bringing the race to a halt and necessitating a second standing start.
Verstappen kept the lead, demonstrating the superior power output of the Red Bull power unit, even at altitude, over Ferrari’s. A furious Hamilton passed Leclerc, who compounded his original error by badly locking his front tires, wearing a flat spot down to the cord. The safety car came out again on lap 59, when Arvid Lindblad’s Racing Bull was taken out by McLaren’s Oscar Piastri.
Up front, Hamilton followed Verstappen by a few tenths of a second but without ever having the speed to try an overtake. The Ferrari might not have had the legs to get past the Red Bull, but its tolerance for riding the curbs, plus the small turbo’s punch out of low-speed corners, was sufficient to give it the edge over 2025 champion Lando Norris’ McLaren, which finished in fifth behind Leclerc.
After the race, Ferrari team principal Fred Vasseur said, “I always expect everyone to show respect for the brand, the team, our partners and, above all, the 2,000 people working for us back home. They put an incredible amount of effort into what we do, working day and night at the factory to improve the car and bring upgrades to the track. That’s why missing out on a win in this way is difficult to accept.”
The three best drivers in F1? Max Verstappen (L) and Lewis Hamilton (R) hold Kimi Antonelli (M) aloft on the podium at Mexico City.
Credit:
Clive Rose/Getty Images)
The three best drivers in F1? Max Verstappen (L) and Lewis Hamilton (R) hold Kimi Antonelli (M) aloft on the podium at Mexico City.
Credit:
Clive Rose/Getty Images)
“The core thing to remember, which maybe comes with age, is that every decision you make in the car impacts all the people that work in the background for the whole team,” said a frustrated Hamilton after the race. “A part of our contract is we have to work as a team, which we could have easily done today. So it’s a shame to see us lose as we did. And that will continue unless action is taken, and a real deep, serious conversation is had, so it shouldn’t happen moving forward.”
Hamilton pointed to Leclerc’s “do-or-die, either I win or none of us do” attitude as a problem, ruing the loss of what could have been the team’s best result all year. “It was just unnecessary,” he said. “I think we could have easily had that 1-2, which would have been huge for the team and for everyone back at the factory who’s worked so hard to bring us these upgrades.”
Other teams have laid down clear rules to determine the way teammates race each other—at Mercedes, Toto Wolff began making Hamilton and Nico Rosberg pay for any damage they caused to the cars if they came together on track, and McLaren had its famous Papaya rules. At Ferrari, both drivers are free to race each other, and both are jockeying to be seen as team leader for next year. Now Vasseur has to try to get both Hamilton and Leclerc under control, because if Ferrari keeps giving away race wins like this, his position has to be increasingly untenable.
Jonathan is the Automotive Editor at Ars Technica. He has a BSc and PhD in Pharmacology. In 2014 he decided to indulge his lifelong passion for the car by leaving the National Human Genome Research Institute and launching Ars Technica's automotive coverage. He lives in Washington, DC.

articles.title: Making Kubernetes AI-Ready for NVIDIA Vera Rubin on Day One | NVIDIA Technical Blog
articles.text:
Configuring and optimizing Kubernetes for new GPU hardware such as NVIDIA Vera Rubin is complex and error-prone. Drivers, kernels, runtimes, networking, operators, and schedulers must work together, with settings tuned to the hardware and workload. Small mismatches can prevent workloads from running or limit performance.
The NVIDIA AI Cluster Runtime (AICR)—part of the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform—simplifies this work by capturing tuned configurations in reusable recipes, generating bundles for existing deployment tools, and validating the running cluster. It will help Kubernetes environments be ready for NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 compute trays on Day 1.
Overall, the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform brings together technologies to help the ecosystem design, build, and operate more efficient AI factories, including open source, modular software components purpose-built to support multi-tenant operations and scaling.
Configuring new hardware architecture in a cloud-native stack requires plumbing updates from the lowest-level bindings all the way up to the orchestration layer. It is still early days for Vera Rubin.
This post covers what changes if you run NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 today, what has been validated on early hardware access using NVIDIA GPU Operator and the Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) driver with Vera Rubin support. It also shows how AICR brings these components together in a configuration that platform teams can reproduce and verify.
What changes from GB200 NVL72: planning your upgrade
If you run GB200 NVL72 today, NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 is an evolution of the same NVIDIA MGX rack-scale architecture, now in its third generation. But several user-visible pieces change. Knowing about them now lets you plan cluster software and configuration changes alongside upcoming releases:
- GPU driver: Vera Rubin NVL72 requires a new driver branch. It has been validated with R615.23, the host-installed R615.23 open GPU driver. Early support is targeted for R610, with official platform support in R620. AICR’s GB200 baseline is R580.173.02. R615.23 is the current tested version, not a confirmed minimum for official Vera Rubin support.
- DOCA and NIC drivers: Vera Rubin NVL72 replaces the GB200 NVL72 reference design’s NVIDIA ConnectX-7 NICs and NVIDIA BlueField-3 data processing units (DPUs) with NVIDIA ConnectX-9 SuperNICs and NVIDIA BlueField-4 DPUs. DOCA 3.3.0 is the first GA release supporting ConnectX-9. The Vera Rubin system image validated on ships DOCA-OFED 3.3.0. This is the testbed version, not a requirement or a recommendation. AICR uses host-installed NIC drivers and DRANET for pod allocation here. Network Operator compatibility remains a separate qualification step (See the DOCA 3.3.0 release notes).
- Device topology: The NIC/GPU/Direct Memory Access (DMA) topology of the Vera Rubin NVL72 compute tray differs from GB200, so GPU-to-NIC affinity and NUMA placement must be checked for I/O-intensive workloads such as Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA) networking and GPUDirect Storage. Both reference trays contain two CPUs and four GPUs, but the Vera Rubin NVL72 trays expose eight ConnectX-9 PCI device groups with 32 functions, compared with four ConnectX-7 adapters on the NVIDIA DGX GB200 NVL72 compute tray. In both GB200 NVL72 and Vera Rubin NVL72 trays, GPUs 0 to 1 have CPU NUMA affinity 0; GPUs 2 to 3 have affinity 1. GPU-to-NIC connectivity is NODE within a socket and SYS across sockets. PCI function counts do not represent physical port counts (See the GB200 reference architecture).
- IMEX: As on GB200 NVL72, multi-node NVIDIA NVLink workloads use IMEX. With DRA-managed IMEX, stop, disable, and mask the host’s static nvidia-imex service to prevent ownership conflicts. DRA v0.5.0 adds an alpha host-managed option with domain isolation only; our cluster uses driverManaged mode. (See the release notes)
- NVIDIA Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) profiles: Rubin GPUs introduce new MIG profiles. R615.23 advertises these profiles on node. The AICR Vera Rubin recipes use whole-GPU allocation and do not configure MIG. MIG on Vera Rubin is not covered by this validation.
- AICR recipes: All of these deltas are encoded in the new Vera Rubin recipe family, so aicr recipe and aicr validate reflect the validated combination rather than leaving you to rediscover each change (details are in the following sections).
Validation on Vera Rubin NVL72
To validate Vera Rubin NVL72 support end to end, we deployed the AICR runtime bundle on Vera Rubin clusters using the official GPU Operator v26.7.0 release and the official DRA driver v0.5.0 release, with a host-installed R615 driver.
Both the training and inference recipe variants now validate end to end for deployment and conformance. For training, an initial performance gate: a cross-node NCCL all-reduce over the NVIDIA NVLink fabric, running through an IMEX ComputeDomain and gated on a bus-bandwidth floor. GPU pods run cleanly, and IMEX channels are injected into claiming pods across multiple nodes, shown with real cluster output below.
A note on early-silicon realities: Bringing up new silicon is a process. The first validation rounds were temporarily blocked by a hardware/fabric issue in one of the early Vera Rubin clusters—unrelated to the GPU Operator or the DRA driver—that kept one compute tray out of the NVLink fabric. After the hardware was reseated, all GPUs on both nodes joined a single clean fabric clique.
From bring-up to reproducible recipes
Validating the components is only half the story. Standing up a working Vera Rubin cluster means choosing driver mode, container-runtime wiring, component versions, and a handful of platform-specific settings. AICR captures those choices as a versioned recipe, so the configuration on real Vera Rubin hardware is explicit, reproducible, and verifiable across clusters.
The new Vera Rubin recipe family (service: rke2; accelerator: Vera Rubin NVL72 (vr200); operating system: Ubuntu; with training, inference, and NVIDIA Dynamo inference variants) ships as Preview. It’s an early-adopter path that does not yet carry the production support and lifecycle qualification of a Supported recipe while the platform itself is pre-release. It encodes the decisions made during this bring-up:
- Host-managed driver: The Vera Rubin system image pre-installs the arm64 open-kernel-module driver, so the recipe runs the GPU Operator with driver.enabled: false, while the container toolkit stays operator-managed. The recipe moves to the operator-managed driver when the official builds ship.
- DRA driver with ComputeDomains: IMEX-backed ComputeDomains are enabled for the NVL72 fabric, with whole-GPU allocation remaining on the device plugin.
- Platform floors and quirks: They’re encoded once so users don’t rediscover them. Kubernetes >= 1.34.1 — 1.34 for the GA resource.k8s.io/v1 DRA API that ComputeDomains/IMEX use, and the .1 patch because the RKE2 CDI/NRI toolkit path needs containerd 2.1 (v1.34.1+rke2r1). Ubuntu 26.04 with the Vera-optimized arm64 64k-page kernel. And smaller sharp edges, such as raising the NFD topology updater’s default 60Mi memory limit, which out of memory (OOM) kills on multi-terabyte NVL72 workers.
The first deployment of this bundle targeted a platform combination none of these components had ever been validated on together—arm64, Ubuntu 26.04, a 64k-page kernel, RKE2, and Vera Rubin—and went from cluster handoff to a healthy runtime in hours. A second Vera Rubin cluster reproduced the result the following day, and that repeatability is the point and benefit of the recipe.
The workflow on a live Vera Rubin cluster
To make this concrete, here is the actual AICR workflow, executed on a live Vera Rubin NVL72 reference cluster with the AICR v1.0.0 toolchain.
1. Generate the recipe
Recipe generation is offline: It resolves criteria against the recipe catalog and takes seconds.
$ aicr recipe \
    --service rke2 \
    --accelerator vr200 \
    --os ubuntu \
    --intent training \
    -o recipe.yaml
[cli] building recipe from criteria: criteria=criteria(service=rke2,
accelerator=vr200, intent=training, os=ubuntu)
[cli] recipe generation completed: output=recipe.yaml components=14
componentNames=cert-manager, dra-node-labeler, dranet, gpu-operator,
k8s-ephemeral-storage-metrics, kai-scheduler, kube-prometheus-stack, nfd,
nodewright-customizations, nodewright-operator, nvidia-dra-driver-gpu,
nvsentinel, prometheus-adapter, prometheus-operator-crds
overlays=5
The resolved recipe layers five overlays into 14 components. Alongside the GPU Operator (host-managed driver mode) and the DRA driver (ComputeDomains enabled), it brings up the two pieces that are most specific to this platform: DraNet, the DRA network driver that allocates ConnectX-9 devices to pods (RDMA data-path performance over ConnectX-9 is not part of this validation), and exclusive RDMA netns mode, applied through NodeWright tuning. Each pod sees only its own Host Channel Adapter (HCA).
AICR also brings together components of the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform: NodeWright applies node tuning through its native vr200/rke2 profile, KAI Scheduler provides workload scheduling, and NVSentinel monitors runtime health. Node Feature Discovery (NFD) and the Prometheus stack complete the recipe, with component versions pinned to the configuration validated on Vera Rubin hardware.
2. Render the deployment bundle
The bundle is a set of ordered, per-component Helm charts with a single deploy script:
$ aicr bundle -r recipe.yaml -o ./bundle
Files generated: 61
$ ls bundle
001-cert-manager               008-gpu-operator                 checksums.txt
002-dranet                     009-k8s-ephemeral-storage-...    deploy.sh
003-nfd                        010-kai-scheduler                README.md
004-nodewright-operator        011-nvidia-dra-driver-gpu        recipe.yaml
005-nodewright-customizations  012-nvsentinel
006-prometheus-operator-crds   013-prometheus-adapter
007-kube-prometheus-stack      
3. Snapshot and validate
AICR captures the cluster’s actual state, checks the recipe’s readiness constraints against it, and then runs its validation checks as in-cluster jobs:
$ aicr snapshot --output snapshot.yaml
$ aicr validate -r recipe.yaml -s snapshot.yaml --phase deployment
[cli] readiness constraint passed: name=OS.release.VERSION_ID
expected=26.04 actual=26.04
[cli] readiness constraint passed: name=OS.sysctl./proc/sys/kernel/osrelease
expected=>= 7.0 actual=7.0.0-2008-nvidia-bos-64k
[cli] phase completed: phase=deployment status=passed validators=4 passed=4
$ aicr validate -r recipe.yaml -s snapshot.yaml --phase conformance
[cli] phase completed: phase=conformance status=passed validators=8 passed=8
$ aicr validate -r recipe.yaml -s snapshot.yaml --phase performance
[cli] phase completed: phase=performance status=passed validators=1 passed=1
The performance phase runs the NVIDIA Collective Communications Library (NCCL) all-reduce gate as an in-cluster job: a cross-node all-reduce over the NVLink fabric through an IMEX ComputeDomain, checked against the recipe’s bus-bandwidth floor. The rke2/vr200 combination is registered in the validator’s applicability matrix and its runtime ships as an embedded template, so the validator provisions the ComputeDomain and the IMEX ResourceClaimTemplate itself—no operator prerequisites and no recipe-supplied runtime. It runs from a stock v1.0.0 release.
The full matrix now passes.
| Phase | Check | Result | Disposition | 
|---|---|---|---|
| deployment | operator-health | pass | All components are healthy. | 
| deployment | gpu-operator-version | pass | Version gate met. | 
| deployment | expected-resources | pass | All expected Kubernetes resources are present and healthy. | 
| deployment | check-nvidia-smi | pass | nvidia-smi healthy on all nodes | 
| conformance | platform-health | pass | All platform checks passing. | 
| conformance | gpu-operator-health | pass | All operator components are healthy. | 
| conformance | accelerator-metrics | pass | DCGM metrics path verified end to end, all GPUs reporting. | 
| conformance | ai-service-metrics | pass | Custom-metrics API serving. | 
| conformance | dra-support | pass | DRA/ComputeDomain support. | 
| conformance | gang-scheduling | pass | KAI gang scheduling. | 
| conformance | pod-autoscaling | pass | External-metrics API plus HPA scale-up (1->3) and scale-down (3->1). | 
| conformance | secure-accelerator-access | pass | Device-plugin mode (no gpu.nvidia.com DeviceClass) | 
| performance | nccl-all-reduce-bw-nvls | pass | First cross-node NCCL all-reduce across both compute trays over multi-node NVLink (IMEX ComputeDomain): 744.71 GB/s busbw at 16 GiB. | 
The inference variant (Dynamo platform, inference gateway, gang scheduling, DCGM metrics) passes the same deployment and conformance matrix on the identical cluster.
Two artifacts from that run are worth showing. First, the nvidia-smi banner on the pre-release driver is the exact change that tripped the validator on first contact. It’s a good example of the small surprises early silicon brings. The fix (NVIDIA/aicr#1748) is merged and verified against NVIDIA Vera Rubin hardware.
$ nvidia-smi | head -3
+--------------------------------------------------------------------+
| NVIDIA-SMI 615.23    KMD Version: 615.23   CUDA UMD Version: 13.4  |
+--------------------------------------------------------------------+
Second, live GPU telemetry flows through the standard DCGM exporter path. Note the placeholder product name, which resolves once PCI IDs are allocated near general availability:
DCGM_FI_DEV_SM_CLOCK{gpu="0",modelName="NVIDIA Graphics Device",
    DCGM_FI_DRIVER_VERSION="615.23"} 120
4. The cross-node ComputeDomain test
Finally, the DRA/IMEX path end to end: a two-node ComputeDomain whose IMEX channels are claimed by pods on each compute tray. There’s one prerequisite on images with host-managed IMEX: The host’s static nvidia-imex service must be disabled and masked, since host-managed IMEX and DRA-managed ComputeDomains are mutually exclusive (DRA driver v0.5.0 adds a host-managed option).
Note for GPU Operator v26.7.0+: The chart ships its own stricter copy of the resource.nvidia.com_computedomains.yaml Custom Resource Definition (CRD), which requires numNodes with no default (the DRA driver chart’s copy does not). This only matters on a fresh cluster install—Helm won’t overwrite an already-installed CRD, so existing clusters upgrading gpu-operator are unaffected. If you’re bringing up a new cluster, set numNodes explicitly in your ComputeDomain manifest, e.g. spec: {numNodes: 2, …}.
$ kubectl apply -f cd-2node-test.yaml
computedomain.resource.nvidia.com/cd-2node-test created
pod/cd-test-c01 created
pod/cd-test-c02 created
$ kubectl get computedomain,resourceclaims,pods -n cd-test
NAME            STATUS   NODES
cd-2node-test   Ready    vr-...-c01,vr-...-c02
NAME                             STATE                AGE
cd-test-c01-imex-channel-k9j2d   allocated,reserved   32s
cd-test-c02-imex-channel-l6tl2   allocated,reserved   30s
NAME          READY   STATUS    NODE
cd-test-c01   1/1     Running   vr-...-c01
cd-test-c02   1/1     Running   vr-...-c02
$ kubectl logs cd-test-c01 -n cd-test   # identical output on c02
crw-rw-rw- 1 root root 505, 0 channel0  # /dev/nvidia-caps-imex-channels
Going from apply to two running pods—one per compute tray, each with its IMEX channel injected and the IMEX daemons joined into a single domain—takes about 12 seconds. The same ComputeDomain path is what the training recipe’s NCCL performance gate now drives under real workload traffic: Channel injection is proven above, while the fabric bandwidth is proven in the performance phase.
The entire sequence (recipe, bundle, snapshot, and the deployment and conformance validation phases) completes in about five minutes against a live cluster. The performance phase adds the runtime of the NCCL job itself.
Validation evidence and feedback loops
These results are anchored by AICR’s deployment, conformance, and performance validation across the NVL72 reference environments, paired with the successful end-to-end ComputeDomain test. Individual check details are cataloged in the validation matrix above.
Equally important is where the validated boundary sits today. The training recipe now carries a cross-node NCCL performance gate: the first performance validation on Vera Rubin silicon, exercising the same IMEX ComputeDomain path shown above under real all-reduce traffic.
Inference serving performance remains deferred for now. vLLM merged Rubin (sm_107a) support in v0.27.0, but the SM107 kernel path is gated at build time on NVIDIA CUDA >= 13.4—and vLLM’s own published images, through v0.28.0, still build against CUDA 13.0.3. So even the newest vLLM release image carries the dispatch code without the compiled kernel. ai-dynamo’s latest release (v1.4.2) pins vllm-openai v0.26.0, which predates the code entirely; its unreleased main branch pins v0.28.0, which is not built against 13.4. A VR200 inference-perf floor needs a published, CUDA >= 13.4-built runtime image verified on real hardware—past the JIT-compile crash, not just past a version check.
The signed validation evidence for the Vera Rubin recipes is public: training (three phases, including the NCCL performance gate) and inference (deployment and conformance). Because the recipes are Preview and still moving, treat the published evidence as the historical record for the coordinate it was captured against rather than as an attestation of the current recipe content. A digest check against today’s recipe will report a mismatch.
The bring-up also worked in both directions. Running AICR validation on Vera Rubin surfaced an unmapped Rubin architecture value in the go-nvlib packages that crash-looped the DRA driver’s kubelet plugin. Because architecture support lands first in go-nvml; flows into go-nvlib; and from there into the GPU Operator, the Kubernetes Device Plugin, the MIG Manager, and the DRA plugins, the fix propagated consistently across the stack. It went from the first crash report to a validated build on Vera Rubin hardware in about three days. That fix (go-nvlib 0.11.0 → 0.12.0) shipped in the official DRA driver v0.5.0 release, so the Vera Rubin recipes pin the stock tag—no staging build is required.
Validation also surfaced that a host-managed IMEX daemon and DRA-managed ComputeDomains cannot share a node today, feedback that shaped the host-managed IMEX option shipped in DRA driver v0.5.0.
The Vera Rubin recipes are published in the open-source NVIDIA/aicr repository in v1.0.0, which registers the rke2 service and vr200 accelerator in the public catalog.
Get started
Get started with AICR on Vera Rubin using the Preview recipes in the AICR public catalog.
Generating the validated configuration is one command:
aicr recipe --service rke2 --accelerator vr200 --os ubuntu --intent training
For the Dynamo inference variant described above, the following command generates the recipe:
aicr recipe --service rke2 --accelerator vr200 --os ubuntu --intent inference --platform dynamo
