articles.title: Build efficient agents with knowledge distillation on Amazon SageMaker AI | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Build efficient agents with knowledge distillation on Amazon SageMaker AI
You built a shopping assistant on a frontier model, and it works. A shopper asks for “a black waist bag under twenty dollars from a shop with at least 4.5 stars,” and the agent searches the catalog, inspects candidates, checks the constraints, and commits to a recommendation. But what does that interaction actually cost? An agentic assistant is not one model call, it is a loop: search, read results, refine, verify, decide. A single completed task can be multiple calls to that frontier model, and you pay for every one, on every shopper. At production scale, that per-task cost compounds, erodes the project’s ROI, and stops the project from shipping.
One way to make an agentic application more efficient is to use a smaller model, which is faster to respond and more cost-effective to host. The catch is quality: a smaller model usually falls short on the task, which is why the larger one was chosen in the first place. Knowledge distillation closes that gap by transferring the behavior of the larger “teacher” model into a smaller “student”, training the student to reproduce the teacher’s outputs, so it keeps much of the quality at the smaller model’s speed and cost.
In this post you will learn how to use knowledge distillation, and specifically sequence-level knowledge distillation (SeqKD), to fine-tune a shopping agent on Amazon SageMaker AI. We cover how to generate high-quality multi-step trajectories with a frontier teacher and keep the ones that solve the task, how to encode them for supervised fine-tuning, how to run the training on serverless infrastructure, and how to evaluate the student against a held-out benchmark.
What is sequence-level knowledge distillation (SeqKD)?
The simplest applicable form of distillation is sequence-level knowledge distillation (SeqKD). It uses a teacher model to generate high-quality responses, then trains a student model on those responses with supervised fine-tuning (SFT). SeqKD needs only the teacher’s text, with no access to teacher logits and no reinforcement-learning infrastructure, so it works even with a closed or API-only teacher. Compared to other approaches such as logit-based or on-policy, it sits at the most cost-effective and portable end of the distillation spectrum. The teacher writes the answers, and the student is fine-tuned on them. Because those answers persist as a dataset, you can reuse them to train or test different students without regenerating the data.
In principle, you would want the student to match the teacher’s full distribution over possible outputs. The caveat here is that you can’t. The space of possible sequences is astronomically large, so matching it exactly isn’t feasible. SeqKD sidesteps that by approximating it with samples the teacher actually produces.
For an agent, the sequence the teacher produces is not a block of prose but a trajectory, an ordered run of reasoning, tool calls, and the observations they return, where each step is conditioned on everything before it. Training the student on that whole sequence teaches it the reasoning that leads to each action and the multi-step course of action itself, not a single paragraph of answer text. That makes an agentic task one of the cleanest illustrations of sequence-level KD, because the sequence being copied is the behavior itself.
When SeqKD is the right choice
SeqKD fits a specific set of situations:
You have the inputs but no high-quality target outputs
This is the core case for SeqKD, which is fundamentally data generation. You supply the inputs, and the teacher writes the targets, so you can fine-tune on a task or domain that has no existing high-quality labels. The targets can be as simple as single answers or as involved as multi-turn tool-use trajectories. This post takes the demanding end of that spectrum, agentic trajectories, which are especially hard to source. A single task branches into many partially correct runs, and telling a solved run from a failed one takes a reliable grader. A benchmark with a programmatic scorer supplies exactly that, so you can let the teacher generate trajectories and keep only the ones that solve the task.
Your teacher is a frontier model you can only reach through an API
This is the normal case for frontier models. You can’t access the weights to host it yourself, you can’t read its logits, and you can’t fine-tune it. That rules out logit-based distillation and on-policy methods, which all need that internal access. SeqKD needs only the teacher’s text responses, so it is the one approach that still works, and it frees you from paying frontier prices on every request after the student takes over.
You want a strong, cost-effective first step
Some of the strongest small reasoning models were built in significant part with SeqKD (supervised fine-tuning on teacher reasoning traces), so it is an effective starting point for reasoning transfer when the setup is right. The DeepSeek-R1 distilled models are a well-known example: the reasoning of a large teacher was distilled into smaller Qwen and Llama students by fine-tuning them on the teacher’s generated reasoning traces.
Prerequisites
To run this example, you need:
- An AWS account with an AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role for SageMaker AI that has read and write access to an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket and permission to invoke your teacher model.
- A frontier teacher model to generate the trajectories (this walkthrough uses one on Amazon Bedrock).
- Access to SageMaker AI model customization in a supported AWS Region.
- Amazon SageMaker Studio (or a local IDE with the AWS CLI configured), running a Python 3.12 or higher kernel, with the SageMaker Python SDK v3 and boto3 (pin your versions). Use an ml.m5.4xlarge instance at minimum for the notebook environment, since the data preparation and local scoring steps run on its CPU.
- Working knowledge of Python, supervised fine-tuning, and tool-using agents.
- The accompanying code repository and a task with a programmatic scorer (this walkthrough uses the ShoppingBench test set. Substitute your own task and grader).
Solution overview
This section walks the pipeline from end to end. A frontier teacher, GLM-5.3 on Amazon Bedrock, acts as the ShoppingBench agent to generate trajectories. The benchmark’s own scorer keeps only the ones that solve the task, and those solved trajectories fine-tune a Qwen3.5-4B student with serverless supervised fine-tuning on SageMaker AI model customization. The distilled student is then evaluated on a held-out ShoppingBench split and served behind a SageMaker AI Inference real-time endpoint that runs the tool loop.
Preparing the dataset
Sourcing trajectories worth imitating is the hard part, and the ShoppingBench scorer is what separates the successful runs from the failed ones. ShoppingBench publishes 750 synthesized shopping problems, 250 each for the product, shop, and voucher intents, each with a hidden gold answer and the constraints that define success. We split them once into 426 training problems and 324 held-out evaluation problems (product 103, shop 105, voucher 116), as fixed indices so the two sets don’t overlap.
For each training problem, a frontier teacher, GLM-5.3 on Amazon Bedrock with reasoning on and temperature 1.0, acts as the ShoppingBench agent. It searches the catalog of about 2.7 million products, inspects candidates, and recommends the ones that meet the constraints. We sample the teacher twice per problem, which gives 850 trajectories, then let ShoppingBench’s own scorer keep only the ones that solve the task. Temperature 1.0 is deliberate. Sampling rather than greedy decoding makes the two attempts explore different queries and reasoning paths, which gives more problems at least one solved trajectory and a more diverse set to learn from. This rejection-sampling step turns a capable-but-imperfect teacher into a clean training set, since the teacher only has to be right often enough that the solved runs are worth imitating.
Each solved trajectory is a complete episode: the shopper request, the teacher’s reasoning and tool calls at each step (search, inspect, recommend, terminate), and the observation the environment returned. We keep the reasoning alongside the actions, which the Results show is what carries the student most of the way to its teacher.
Encoding trajectories for training
Sequence-level distillation is supervised learning over trajectories that already exist, so nothing calls a tool during training, and the application only ever sees text. Because these trajectories are multi-step tool-use conversations, we encode each as a messages list of chat turns and let the student’s own chat template render it, so the tokens the trainer sees match the tokens the agent produces at inference.
Each trajectory becomes one training row per step. The user turn carries the system prompt and the conversation so far. The assistant turn carries that step’s reasoning and the tool call it leads to, a … block followed by a [{…}] in the harness’s native form. Loss falls on the assistant turn only, so the model learns to produce the next reasoning-and-action, not to predict the observations the environment returned. A trajectory with several steps expands into several rows. Here the solved trajectories expand to about 2,600 training and 130 validation rows after filtering.
A single row pairs the conversation so far (user) with the one next step to learn (assistant):
Each later step becomes its own row, with the new observation appended to the user content and the next reasoning-and-tool-call as the assistant target, through to the final recommend_product and terminate calls. Render every row with your model’s exact chat template.
Split the data by problem, not by row. The teacher is sampled twice per problem, and each trajectory expands into several steps, so many rows share one problem, and a row-level split would leak near-identical context across training and validation. Holding out whole problems (about five percent) keeps the validation set honest.
The cost of per-step encoding is repeated context, because each row restates the growing conversation, and serverless fine-tuning truncates anything past dataset_max_len, so a row that crosses the limit loses part of what it needs. Rather than let the limit decide what gets cut, keep rows within budget. The most effective fix is to compress tool observations, which dominate the token count. For product search results, keep only the fields the next decision depends on (id, price, rating, and the constraints being checked), drop the raw listing text, and cap how many results you retain per search. If trajectories are still over budget, cap the steps per trajectory. Here dataset_max_len is 16,384 tokens, which fits most trajectories after observations are trimmed.
After the JSONL for each split is in S3, register each as a customization dataset asset with DataSet.create from the SageMaker Python SDK v3, which returns the train_dataset and val_dataset the training job consumes.
Fine-tuning the student
Training uses SageMaker AI model customization with serverless SFT. You select a base model from the model hub, point the job at the encoded datasets, and the managed service provisions the compute, runs the job, and returns the customized model, with metrics tracked in Amazon SageMaker with MLflow. Because the data is already in a supported format, there is no training script, container image, or instance to manage.
The job writes its output into a model package group that versions every model it produces, so create the group first with ModelPackageGroup.create (reusing it if the name already exists) and pass it to the trainer. Then configure the customization job. Choose the base model and training type, point it at the train and validation datasets plus the model package group, then name an MLflow experiment so metrics stream to MLflow while the job runs.
The trainer starts from a documented set of default hyperparameters that you can inspect with sft_trainer.hyperparameters.to_dict() and override before launching. For this run we raise the sequence length to fit the multi-step trajectories, use a Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) rank of 64, and train for three epochs over the small dataset:
Validate the configuration with a dry run, then launch the managed job and read the registered Model Package ARN when it finishes. That ARN is the deploy-ready artifact the evaluation and serving steps consume:
Evaluating the student
Evaluate in two stages, lowest cost first. The full end-to-end evaluation is both time and resource intensive. It stands up a search server over millions of products, deploys the endpoint, and runs a multi-step agent loop on every held-out problem. Before running the full evaluation, run a low-cost managed pre-check using SageMaker AI model evaluation, which scores one generated step at a time against the teacher’s ground-truth action.
The pre-check needs a scoring function. Model evaluation supports a Custom Scorer reward function you supply that runs once per sample, comparing the student’s generated action against the teacher’s. For tool-call distillation, grade tool selection (did the model call the right tools, in order, ignoring argument formatting), because that is the behavior distillation most needs to transfer. To keep the focus on selection rather than syntax, the reward function reads the tool names out of both the student’s action and the teacher’s reference without requiring an exact format match.
Register that function as a versioned Evaluator with Evaluator.create(), then call evaluate() to run one Custom Scorer job per task, scoring the base model alongside the student so every result has a comparison.
The decision rule is straightforward. The student must beat the base model on this low-cost pre-check. If it does, the distillation took and it is worth running the more comprehensive end-to-end evaluation. If it does not, fix training first.
Serving the distilled agent
The distilled model doesn’t run tools on its own. Fine-tuning teaches it to emit the right tool call at the right moment as text, but something still has to execute that call and feed back the result. At inference you wrap the model in a small deterministic harness that prompts the model, parses the tool call it emits, runs the tool, appends the observation, and prompts again, looping until the model produces a final answer. This is ordinary application code, or an off-the-shelf serving framework, not reinforcement learning and not an on-policy training loop.
The student is a Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) adapter over an open-weight base, which shapes how you deploy it. Rather than merge the adapter and serve a second full copy of the weights, serve the base model once and attach the student as an adapter on top, as two inference components on one real-time endpoint. Naming the inference component at invoke time selects which one answers, so the same endpoint serves both the base and the distilled student for a side-by-side comparison.
We serve the open-weight model with the Deep Java Library Large Model Inference (DJL LMI) container, which bundles the vLLM engine for high-throughput generation, pinned to a specific version rather than latest, so redeploys are reproducible. The accompanying notebook wraps the inference-component calls in a small kd_serve helper, so deploying the base component with LoRA serving enabled and then attaching the student adapter reduces to:
The instance_types list is an ordered preference. SageMaker AI Inference deploys on the first type with available capacity and falls back down the list, so the student serves on an ml.g5.2xlarge, ml.g6.2xlarge, or ml.g6e.2xlarge depending on availability. The base weights load once, and both inference components share them, so adding the adapter costs adapter-sized memory instead of a second copy of the model.
Results
We evaluate the distilled student on the held-out ShoppingBench test split, against a set of reference points that bracket what good looks like:
- Base Qwen3.5-4B: the off-the-shelf student with no fine-tuning. This is the floor.
- Distilled student (SeqKD): the same 4B model fine-tuned on the teacher trajectories, the approach this post describes. This is the result that matters.
- GLM-5.3 teacher: the frontier model that generated the training data, on Bedrock. We report it both sampled (temperature 1.0, the setting that produced the data) and greedy (temperature 0).
- Medium-sized frontier model: a strong proprietary model run as an agent, included as a practical ceiling.
Every model runs the same unmodified ShoppingBench agent loop over the three shopper intents (product, shop, and voucher). We report Absolute Success Rate (ASR), the share of held-out problems the agent solves, averaged over the three intents, with missing trajectories counted as failures. A problem counts as solved when the recommended product or products meet every stated constraint. The following numbers come from a single run with a LoRA student, so expect a few points of run-to-run variation.
Task success
The headline result is the Absolute Success Rate on the 324 held-out problems, broken down by intent and averaged across the three:
| Model | product | shop | voucher | Average | 
| Base Qwen3.5-4B (no fine-tuning) | 0.456 | 0.314 | 0.121 | 0.297 | 
| Distilled student (SeqKD) | 0.563 | 0.638 | 0.422 | 0.541 | 
| GLM-5.3 teacher (sampled, temperature 1.0) | 0.553 | 0.619 | 0.362 | 0.511 | 
| GLM-5.3 teacher (greedy, temperature 0) | 0.544 | 0.638 | 0.439 | 0.540 | 
| Medium-sized frontier model | 0.583 | 0.667 | 0.388 | 0.546 | 
In summary, a 4B model recovered essentially all of its frontier teacher’s task quality, matching it within run-to-run noise. We report the teacher two ways because they answer different questions. Greedy decoding returns the single most likely trajectory, the stronger choice when each model gets one attempt per problem (as in this evaluation) which is why the greedy teacher scores 0.540 against the sampled teacher’s 0.511. We generated the training data the other way, sampling at temperature 1.0 so repeated attempts explored different paths, and the scorer could keep the ones that solved the task. That filtering is also why the student can edge out the sampled teacher it learned from, since rejection sampling trains it only on the teacher’s solved runs, not its average output, so it imitates a best-of slice rather than the full spread of attempts.
Reasoning in the targets matters
The student learns from the teacher’s reasoning as well as its tool calls, and that choice is responsible for a large part of the result. Training the same student on the same trajectories with the reasoning stripped, leaving only the bare tool calls, drops average ASR from 0.541 to 0.415:
Both students clear the base model, so even the tool-calls-only version is a real improvement, but keeping the reasoning is what carries the student the rest of the way to its teacher. The reasoning between the actions isn’t narration to discard, it is part of the behavior that solves the task.
Keeping general ability
ASR measures the skill we distilled for. The counterweight is whether the student kept its general instruction-following ability or overfit to the shopping task. We check with IFEval, a general instruction-following benchmark that scores verifiable format instructions such as “answer in exactly three bullet points.” Treat it as a regression check, not a leaderboard. The student’s prompt-strict score falls from 0.819 for the base model to 0.741, and its instruction-strict score from 0.872 to 0.813, a drop of roughly 6 to 8 points (Figure 6). That is the expected cost of specialization. The student traded some general instruction-following for a large gain on the shopping task. A much larger drop would be the warning sign that distillation narrowed the model too far.
Benefits and tradeoffs
A success rate on its own doesn’t justify the switch. The reason to distill is that you get most of the stronger model’s quality at the small model’s cost and speed. The clearest evidence here is that the 4B student reaches the task quality of its frontier teacher and a medium-sized frontier model, while being small enough to serve on a single G family instance (NVIDIA A10G/L40/L40S in this example).
The cost difference is as much about shape as size. A frontier model reached through an API is billed per token, on every step of every task, so the cost grows with usage and doesn’t stop, and the agentic loop from the introduction pays that toll every time. The distilled student runs on an endpoint you host, which bills for the instance by the hour whether it serves one task or thousands, so added traffic costs nothing more until you scale out. You’re trading a variable per-request charge for a fixed hourly one, and the smaller the model you can get away with, the smaller that fixed cost is.
We don’t publish a per-task cost or latency number here because it depends on your traffic: the throughput a G family instance sustains, and therefore the cost amortized per task, is a function of your request pattern, sequence lengths, and concurrency. Measure it on your own workload against the current SageMaker AI pricing and your frontier provider’s token pricing, rather than relying on a single headline figure.
Limitations and best practices
Will the task fit the student (the capacity wall)
Distillation transfers a distribution the student can already represent, not raw capability it lacks. Across too large a gap, the student copies the teacher’s format without learning to solve. A small model trained on a large teacher’s chains of thought produces long, well-structured reasoning whose answers stay wrong, and an agent trained the same way emits well-formed tool calls that make no progress, re-searches with reworded queries, and runs to its step limit without meeting the constraints. The symptom is the same in both, traces lengthen while accuracy stays flat. When you see it, stop adding data and either grow the student or lower task difficulty.
The gap that decides this is between the task and the student, not between the student and the teacher. A small student can recover a much larger teacher’s quality as long as the task itself is within its reach. That is why the shopping agent here works. The teacher is a mixture-of-experts model with roughly 40 billion active parameters, about ten times the student’s 4 billion, but the shopping task is well within a 4B model’s capacity, so the student recovers the teacher’s quality instead of only lengthening its trajectories.
Where SeqKD stops helping
SeqKD lifts easy and mid-difficulty problems but plateaus on the hardest ones, where the student must recover from its own mistakes. This is sharper for an agent than a single-step task. In a multi-step loop an early error compounds, because the student doesn’t see the states its own mistakes lead to. Closing that gap is what on-policy methods target, which is why SeqKD is usually the first stage rather than the finish line. SeqKD also asks the least of your infrastructure, since it uses only the teacher’s text, whereas logit distillation needs the teacher’s per-token distribution and on-policy methods score the student’s own rollouts. A text-only SeqKD warm start followed by an on-policy stage is a common recipe, so this post covers the first stage and pushing past the plateau is the natural next step.
Two choices that carry the result
First, match the training targets to the behavior you want. Here that meant keeping the teacher’s reasoning with each tool call rather than compressing to final answers, since the reasoning is part of what solves the task (the Results quantify the gap), and rendering every target with the chat template the agent uses at serving time. Second, evaluate honestly. Measure on data the models have not seen, since leaked benchmarks inflate scores, and compare against more than the untrained base model the student is bound to beat, setting it beside the teacher and an independent frontier model so the number shows how close the student came to what it was distilled from.
Cleaning up
A real-time inference endpoint bills for as long as it runs, so tear down the endpoint that you stood up for serving after you have your results. Because the student is served as an adapter inference component on top of a base inference component, the pieces must come down in dependency order: the adapter component first, then the base component, then the endpoint and its configuration. The accompanying kd_serve helper does this for you, finding the adapter structurally so it cleans up regardless of the exact component names:
The training job itself needs no cleanup. Serverless training provisions compute, runs, and releases it automatically, so a completed job isn’t an ongoing charge. The registered model package and its group carry no compute cost either, so you can keep them for lineage and redeploy later. The one thing that does keep costing you is your data in S3 (the encoded trajectories and output artifacts), which incurs storage cost for as long as you keep it, so delete what you no longer need or move it to a lower-cost storage class.
Conclusion
In this post, we showed how to distill an agentic shopping assistant into a smaller, lower-cost student with sequence-level knowledge distillation (SeqKD). We generated high-quality single-turn, multi-step trajectories with a frontier teacher on Bedrock and kept only the ones that solved the task using ShoppingBench’s own scorer, encoded each step as chat-formatted messages that preserve the teacher’s reasoning alongside its tool calls, fine-tuned the student on serverless infrastructure with SageMaker AI model customization, tracked training with MLflow, ran a quality gate check with SageMaker AI model evaluation, and served the result behind an inference endpoint that runs the tool loop. The payoff was a 4B student that recovers essentially all of its frontier teacher’s task quality. Because SeqKD needs only the teacher’s text outputs, it works even when the teacher is a closed frontier model you reach through an API, and you can stop paying frontier prices on every step after the student takes over.
SeqKD is a strong first step with real limits. Match the student size to the task, evaluate on a held-out suite against strong reference points rather than only the untrained base model, and when the hardest tail of problems resists imitation, follow SeqKD with on-policy methods not covered here that let the student learn from its own rollouts.
To try this yourself, see the accompanying code repository and the SageMaker AI documentation.

articles.title: Upcoming federal budget will be all “about entrepreneurs,” finance minister hints | BetaKit
articles.text:
Canada’s finance minister is teasing that this week’s budget will address pain points for the country’s small businesses.
“I think you will see in this budget a journey to … simplify the life of small and medium-sized businesses.”
Ahead of tabling the 2026 federal budget this Thursday, François-Philippe Champagne said in a conversation with CBC’s Peter Armstrong at the Canadian Club of Toronto that the government is aiming to simplify things for entrepreneurs and small business owners while continuing its campaign to bring more investment to Canada.
“This is a budget about entrepreneurs,” Champagne said on stage. “This is about a budget [for] innovators. This is about the budget for creators, and they will see themselves.”
“I think you will see in this budget a journey to fixing a number of things to…simplify the life of small and medium-sized businesses,” Champagne said. “I think that on Thursday, those who represent small businesses will see themselves in that budget.”
It’s unclear what specific measures Champagne is referring to, but recent calls from business groups could offer some clues. In its pre-budget submission, the Canadian Federation of Independent Businesses (which represents small and medium-sized businesses) recommended that the government reduce the small business tax rate from nine percent to six percent. It also suggested that the feds extend the threshold for a preferred tax rate for small businesses to their first $700,000 of income, rather than $500,000.
Several investor and business-sector groups, such as the Canadian Venture Capital & Private Equity Association and the Council of Canadian Innovators, have called for tax changes they say will incentivize investment in Canadian companies and entrepreneurship in general. These include a capital-gains deferral and a QSBS-style tax incentive that’s similar to the US system.
Canadian investment leaders have told BetaKit that the feds appear to be more amenable to pro-business changes than in the past. A pre-budget report from Scotiabank economist Rebekah Young also noted that potential capital gains incentives for startups and lower tax rates at higher incomes were possible.
RELATED: Canadian tech and investor groups call for tax incentives, capital gains rollover
Champagne also hinted that the budget could contain further changes to the popular Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) tax credit. In last year’s budget, SR&ED rules were reformed to expand eligibility and raise expenditure limits, as well as an intent to streamline the review process with AI.
“When I met people at the time, they were asking us not only to expand, but to make that more simple,” Champagne said. “And we’re going to go beyond.”
The finance minister’s remarks come after the feds announced a Productivity Mega Deduction in September, a new measure that allows businesses to immediately deduct the full cost of most new capital investments. It’s part of a broad effort to make Canada a more attractive place to invest.
“People may think it’s for big businesses,” Champagne said. “It’s for local businesses which are purchasing new kitchen equipment, a small business purchasing new tools or office technology.”
Feature image courtesy François-Philippe Champagne via LinkedIn.

articles.title: The world has a new plan to save nature, but it still needs the money
articles.text:
The world is set to miss its 2030 conservation goals as finance and action have fallen short, leaders recognized at a UN biodiversity summit in Armenia’s capital, where they agreed to step up efforts after a final overnight session.
Representatives from almost 200 countries gathered in Yerevan over the past two weeks to review progress on a landmark agreement set four years ago to protect about a third of the world’s land and seas by 2030.
The COP17 talks on biodiversity concluded on Saturday with a recognition that conservation efforts were so far too slow to realistically achieve the goals of the 2022 Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework.
A plan was agreed to accelerate progress ahead of the next summit in Ecuador in two years, dubbed the Yerevan Pathway. It would mean redoubling efforts to tackle subsidies and incentives that are harmful to nature, increasing financial, scientific, and technical support for developing countries, and strengthening monitoring and reporting mechanisms.
Steven Guilbeault, former Canadian minister of environment and climate change, said that finance remained one of the biggest obstacles to achieving global biodiversity goals.
The fact that a fund agreed at the last meeting—for companies profiting from genetic materials to voluntarily contribute to—stood largely empty was “especially disappointing.”
“We need to mobilize substantially more public and private finance, reform subsidies that harm nature, and ensure that funding reaches the countries and communities on the front lines of the nature crisis,” he said.

articles.title: New VOLTA Infostealer Uses Claude, Gemini, and Kimi AI to Rank Victims by Financial Value
articles.text:
Cybersecurity researchers have discovered a new Windows infostealer malware called VOLTA-AUTODOXER (aka VOLTA) that makes use of a large language model (LLM) to rank a victim's stolen data by their monetization value.
Like other typical stealer families, VOLTA is equipped to harvest passwords and cookies from Chromium-based web browsers; data from Outlook profiles and Slack workspaces; payment cards; cryptocurrency wallet seed phrases; Discord, Telegram, Steam, and Roblox sessions; Microsoft OAuth tokens; SSH and cloud-provider keys; Wi-Fi profiles; and screenshots.
"VOLTA builds a structured evidence bundle about the person behind the machine," Cisco Talos researcher Ryan Fetterman said. "This bundle contains geolocation and home address, employer and employer domain, inferred birth year, card last-4 digits, Slack workspaces, document authorship metadata, iPhone backup indicators, and a live Roblox account valuation."
To make this information more valuable, the malware uses stolen session access to search the victim's Gmail account for receipts to corroborate the home address by extracting emails related to Amazon, DoorDash, Uber Eats, Grubhub, Walmart, and PayPal.
Once the necessary information is collected, the bundle is serialized and fed into an artificial intelligence (AI) system for analysis using OpenRouter, a unified LLM API gateway and routing service, along with a system prompt. The requests are defaulted to Anthropic's Claude Opus 4.6, failing which it falls back to Moonshot AI's Kimi K2 and Google's Gemini 2.5 Flash.
"VOLTA uses a multi-model architecture to fall back resiliently if it hits a model's refusal, checking each response for phrases like 'I can't' or 'I'm not able,' before passing on to a chain of up to three models," Talos said.
VOLTA features a 240-word system prompt that instructs the model to assume the role of a "forensic intelligence analyst" responsible for drafting a target assessment based on data from a structured evidence bundle. "The bundle is the ONLY permissible source of facts; your training knowledge must never supply a fact about the subject," reads a line from the prompt.
"The required output includes a section titled 'WHAT THEY'RE WORTH' with valuables ranked by monetization with a low/medium/high tier, and a section on 'THEIR OPSEC' containing an assessment of the victim's security posture and password hygiene," Talos explained.
"The model is the operator's triage analyst; it turns a raw credential log into a prioritized and citation-backed dossier of the victim and their monetizable assets."
Data exfiltration happens over Telegram at three different stages -
- Right after the stealer runs, containing details about browser passwords, cookies, payment cards, cryptocurrency wallets; Discord, Steam, and Roblox tokens; Wi-Fi passwords, and screenshots
- After the AI call, which includes the captured data and the results of the LLM analysis
- After the live enrichment step, which includes Gmail receipts and order histories
What's more, VOLTA makes use of a template containing six slots that are filled in at build time. This includes the Telegram channel used for data exfiltration, API keys, and other settings.
This approach suggests that the malware author is likely either advertising a builder kit to prospective customers or operating it as a bespoke tool under their control to compile a custom binary for each order.
"If VOLTA is indeed a commoditized malware, then the AI dossier capability isn't something the author invented for their own operations," Talos said. "It is a feature which enables a customer of any level of sophistication to point it at victims and start receiving ranked target assessments in their Telegram inbox."
"VOLTA is a mature stealer with a late-stage AI layer added for one purpose: relieving the operator of analytical work. The axis of AI improvement here is not speed or scale but effort displacement."
The disclosure comes as adversarial adoption of generative AI (aka GenAI) is quickly becoming the new normal, as threat actors incorporate the technology into their workflows to develop custom tools or find valuable data, thereby increasing the likelihood of success of their attacks.
"GenAI technologies are also well suited to examine massive amounts of data for the purposes of classification or content searching," Zscaler ThreatLabz said. "Once an attacker has access to the victim’s system, GenAI can therefore be used to search all materials to which a victim's system has access, seeking the most valuable or sensitive data for theft or encryption during the next phase of the attack."
A ransomware actor can leverage this method to identify and acquire the most sensitive data from a compromised network, maximizing the chances that the victim will pay up.
Last week, Talos also detailed an AI-enabled framework called NIK C2 that gives attackers remote access, credential theft, keylogging, defense evasion, surveillance, and ransomware capabilities, while integrating an OpenAI client to send stolen data for AI analysis within the compromised session.
A Go-based, Windows remote access tool, NIK C2 grants persistent control over compromised hosts and supports over 52 commands sent by a command-and-control (C2) server to collect a wide range of data.
The OpenAI integration is notable for the fact that the threat actor can abuse a victim's own OpenAI API key to execute the AI-driven analysis. Specifically, the plant checks if the actor has supplied an API key. In the absence of one, it scans the victim's environment variables for the string "OPENAI_API_KEY" and uses it.
This is a form of LLMjacking, where bad actors steal access to another party's AI model to run their own operations – in this case, against the victim itself – while the legitimate owner pays for the computing power. In addition, it allows the attacker to evade detection by obscuring who made the requests.
"This fallback is not a backup mechanism for API key resolution. It is a deliberate design with significant operational implications," Talos said. "If the victim has configured an OpenAI account on their machine, that account's API key will be used to fund the actor's AI inference."
"NIK C2 reshapes adversary tradecraft by collapsing collection and exploitation into a single continuous session, effectively erasing the offline processing delays that historically granted defenders critical detection windows," Talos said.

articles.title: 42AI comes out of stealth with $62.5M and a world model that can 'predict human behavior' | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Here’s a question straight out of sci-fi: What if AI could predict what you were going to do before you decided to, even in a completely new situation?
Israeli startup 42AI says it is developing a “behavioral world model” that can do just that, and it has just come out of stealth with $62.5 million in seed funding. The company is initially running its predictive system at a handful of financial brokerages, where it says the model can help predict how individual traders will respond to volatile conditions.
“Behavior is not deterministic; it’s constantly probabilistic,” 42AI’s CEO and co-founder Amit Gal-Or told TechCrunch when I asked him to justify his company’s tall claim. He argues that people have underlying psychological tendencies that influence their decisions even when their circumstances change, and that’s what the startup is trying to measure and convert into data that the model can understand.
“A week from now, you might be a different person, but your tendencies will always play out in certain areas to a probability or distribution,” his co-founder and CTO Ehud Ezra added. And that, the company argues, is what the model does: show the probability of a person making a certain decision.
42AI says the model tries to figure out people’s internal motivations instead of extrapolating patterns based on their previous actions. To do that, 42AI examines how people react to seemingly unrelated events. For an investor or trader, for example, such events might include completing KYC processes, onboarding, support calls, money transfers, or trading stocks.
“When the person is talking to support or sales in the initial process […] we’re looking at the sentiment, we’re looking at the voice, we’re looking at a lot of interactions that they’re doing, how many times do they call, and so forth,” added Ezra. “And all of those data points are going into the model. Later on, you have the interactions: how you buy and sell, and when, and we’re looking at the market at that stage.”
“So we’re trying to look at how they’re looking at the world. In a world model, every individual is the world,” he added.
The company then converts those observations into mathematical representations of traits, which are then fed into a transformer-based world model that lays out probabilities for possible decisions under different circumstances. (The company uses a separate language model to generate explanations for its predictions.)
Ezra said the model is trained to preserve a person’s underlying tendencies during simulations. So if someone is usually risk-averse, but the model suddenly treats them as a risk-taker, “the target is off,” he said, explaining how the model’s training rewards are structured.
42AI spent three years developing this approach, combining psychological research with neuroscience and genetics, as well as advice from experts in psychology and PTSD, and Dan Shechtman, who was awarded the 2011 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
Gal-Or said the team first studied thousands of people via psych assessments and behavioral scenarios, before adding government and biobank datasets covering more than 2 million people. Its customer datasets have since expanded to cover almost 30 million people, he said.
In live deployments, the model analyzes customers’ existing records, including transactions and support calls. Gal-Or pointed out the system doesn’t need personally identifiable information, arguing that “the model never knows who the person is.” However, it seems the company still creates individual behavioral profiles from linked customer activity.
In predicting market trades, 42AI claims its model achieves 98% accuracy, but Gal-Or clarified that this is more a measure of whether trading flows fall within a predicted range, not if each trade was predicted correctly.
He also said the model consistently achieves an F1 score of 0.8 to 0.85 for predicting trading direction and volume. (F1 score is a metric in machine learning that measures how well a classification model can balance correct predictions against false alarms and missed events.)
And it’s not like the model can work everywhere, given it’s still a machine in a box. “There’s a natural ceiling because you really don’t have access to everything that a person experiences,” Gal-Or said. Ezra explained that the system’s accuracy also suffers when it misses important situational context, like if someone chooses to change their trading choices based on advice from a friend or a colleague.
Gal-Or said 42AI is working with 10 large brokerages, who are using it to manage liquidity, margin requirements, and hedging exposure. The company is onboarding more customers, he said, and is generating more than “seven figures” in revenue, though he wouldn’t specify a number.
Customers pay the startup a flat fee, or a percentage of the value the platform helps them gain. He claimed one brokerage generated approximately $30 million in additional value through dynamic hedging.
The $62.5 million seed funding came from the founders and Infinity Group over three years, and wasn’t entirely raised from external investors, Gal-Or said. Infinity was founded by his father, Amir Gal-Or, who is also 42AI’s chairman and a co-founder. 42AI now plans to raise more money.
Beyond finance, 42AI is now exploring applications for its model in gaming, fraud prevention, and cybersecurity, and one day wants to use it to help robots and AI agents understand people. But that may be a ways off yet: Ezra acknowledged that the model needs to be trained on rules and context for each new domain.
And like with all AI tools, there’s a potentially troubling side to 42AI’s technology: If a brokerage can anticipate what its customers may do, what’s to stop someone from using that knowledge to their own benefit? Ezra admitted that this was “a valid concern” when I raised it, and the founders pointed to regulations, monitoring, and an internal ethics committee, though they didn’t explain what, if anything, would stop their customers from using the technology to gain an advantage over the very people it’s profiling.
Amit Gal-Or, however, was confident that the technology could help address such risks. “We are very proud that actually we are part of the solution; we are the solution to this problem,” he said.

articles.title: Stop counting tokens, start counting what ships
articles.text:
Sponsored
Stop counting tokens, start counting what ships
Why rationing agentic coding backfires, and what to measure instead.
Provided byHPE
When a developer gives an AI agent a coding task, the agent does more than answer once. It plans, generates code, runs tests, and repeats the process to correct errors. A single task can use 10 to 50 times more tokens than a basic chat prompt. The more useful the agent becomes, the more calls it makes. With per-token pricing, the workflows creating the most value can also become the most expensive.
The financial pressure is already visible. Uber reportedly exhausted its entire 2026 AI budget by April after expanding its use of Claude Code. GitHub Copilot moved from flat-rate pricing to metered credits. Gartner predicts that AI coding token costs will surpass average developer salaries by 2028.
The natural response is rationing usage caps, seat limits, and approvals before developers launch agents. But blanket limits can restrict the workflows delivering value. They also optimize the wrong number. Cost per token measures consumption, not results. Some spending reflects waste, including retries and runaway loops. Some represents the work of shipping software. A meter cannot distinguish them, and neither can a spending cap.
Measure the software that ships
A better measure is cost per merged pull request: total AI-assisted development cost divided by the number of changes that pass review and are merged. Track rework and defects alongside it so cheaper changes do not conceal lower quality.
If that cost falls as AI usage rises, without compromising quality, developers are converting more consumption into useful software. The question is not how many tokens they use, but how much finished work the investment produces.
Improving that equation requires two changes: reserve expensive inference for tasks that need it, and lower the cost of routine work.
Match the model to the task
Agentic coding does not require the most powerful model at every step. Use a frontier model, or an on-premises flagship when policy requires it, for difficult planning and novel reasoning. Route suitable work, including code generation, test creation, and repeated refactoring, to open-weight models you operate yourself.
A gateway can route requests according to task complexity, data sensitivity, cost, and latency. This reserves premium inference for the moments that justify it rather than applying premium pricing to an entire workflow. Meter the exception, not the workload.
Open-weight models make this division increasingly practical. Software-engineering benchmarks show that leading open-weight models can approach frontier performance on some tasks. That does not establish equivalence across every repository or workflow. Evaluate candidates against your own code, tests, and acceptance criteria before assigning production work.
Change the economics of repeated use
Next, decide who owns the capacity. With rented inference, every call adds to the bill. With owned capacity, most of the cost is committed upfront, so each additional call gets cheaper as usage grows.
The economics are simple: per-token pricing makes heavy use more expensive, while owned capacity becomes more efficient as teams use it more. Ownership is not free, though. Power, operations, maintenance, and depreciation all must be considered. The number that matters is the fully loaded cost per merged pull request.
Owned capacity also delivers a type of value that never appears on an invoice: control over sensitive code. When code generation and testing run on-premises, proprietary code stays inside the enterprise. Only approved planning prompts and governed exceptions go to external models, through a gateway the organization controls. That opens the sensitive repositories where security usually stalls adoption, and where the biggest gains are waiting.
Test the operating model
At HPE, a hybrid AI platform routes routine workloads from more than 150 internal applications to open-weight models running on premises, including on HPE Private Cloud AI. The result: token costs down 30 to 50%.
That is the point of hybrid. With HPE Private Cloud AI, owning your inference does not mean giving up frontier models. Run the volume on capacity you own and let a gateway send the hardest work.
Data also shows that usage, not licensed headcount, drives spend. The top 5% of users generated most of the consumption, and the heaviest used roughly 450 times more than the lightest on the same license. If power users grow from a small minority to half the workforce, monthly spend can rise about 4.4 times with flat headcount. Your mix will differ, which is exactly why you need to measure it.
HPE tracks two metrics and recommends customers do the same. First, it tracks cost per active developer, because averaging across all licenses hides the power users driving spend. Second, it tracks cost per merged pull request, because it connects AI spending to software that ships.
Baseline both costs before changing infrastructure. Then run a complete development cycle on owned capacity. If both metrics do not improve as usage grows, your current model may still be the better choice.
Build for adoption, not rationing
Owned capacity is not for everyone. Low or unpredictable usage favors APIs, with no capital tied up in idle infrastructure. Ownership pays off when sustained demand keeps it busy. Most enterprises will run hybrid: frontier APIs for demanding or intermittent work, owned capacity for repeatable volume. A governed gateway decides what leaves the building, so you get frontier models without giving up sovereignty over your code.
As developers lean harder on coding agents, usage will keep rising. The real choice is whether that growth shows up as a bigger variable-cost bill or as more software shipped on capacity you own. The companies that lead AI-assisted development will not ration adoption to control costs. They will build an operating model where more AI use improves the economics instead of undermining them.

articles.title: Anthropic clamps down on Claude’s AI video game clones
articles.text:
Anthropic has updated Claude Code’s system prompt to prevent the AI tool from being used to re-create existing video games, as reported by Tom’s Hardware. Retro gaming is currently being overrun with AI-made decompilations, recompilations, and ports, but while Anthropic will still let people use Claude Code to make games, it doesn’t want people to use it for direct clones.
Anthropic clamps down on Claude’s AI video game clones
Anthropic is steering Claude away from re-creating specific titles, but users can still use it to make their own games.
Last week, a user on X posted a screenshot allegedly showing two new sentences added to Claude Code’s system prompt: “Do build original games, games in a genre, and games from the user’s own designs and assets. Don’t build a recreation of a specific existing game, even if it is named or called original.”
Anthropic’s Addy Osmani, in a reply, didn’t confirm that specific language but did say that the company had updated the prompt in Claude Code on Opus 5.5:
We added two sentences to Claude Code’s prompt on Opus 5.5 to steer it away from recreating someone else’s specific game because using Claude to infringe IP is against our usage policy.
Original games, genre games, and games built from your own designs and assets are meant to keep working.
We’ll continue to iterate to ensure we’re striking the right balance. In the meantime, if Claude turns down something that’s yours, send it my way.
We’ve asked Anthropic if it has or will be updating other Claude system prompts as well.

articles.title: Build World Models for Interactive Simulation with NVIDIA Cosmos | NVIDIA Technical Blog
articles.text:
Physical AI developers working with world models face two distinct challenges: adapting models to their sensors, tasks, and data, and getting those models into applications reliably.
NVIDIA Cosmos addresses each. Cosmos is a platform of world foundation models and development tools for physical AI. Cosmos Framework provides agent skills and recipes for world model training, multimodal data processing, optimization and inference. Cosmos NIM microservices supports GPU-accelerated serving through application APIs.
This post walks through both. The simulation section shows how to use Cosmos Framework’s inference recipes and agent skills to generate synchronized camera video and LiDAR observations for AV, robot, and surgical scenarios, starting from released checkpoints you can run today. The deployment section shows how to choose a NIM configuration for your GPU, launch the container, verify readiness, and send your first inference request.
When to use Cosmos Framework for world model development
Cosmos Framework is an open and fully modular framework for world model training, model optimization, and inference to support a full model development lifecycle using new agent skills. It is expanding beyond Cosmos 3 to support NVIDIA Alpamayo, GR00T, Qwen, pi0.5, and other compatible Hugging Face models.
Training
- Train models on text, images, video, audio, and actions faster using new skills.
- Use LoRA for parameter-efficient adaptation, or full supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to update all model parameters.
- Load data through JSONL, WebDataset, LeRobot, or custom adapters and train across GPUs and save checkpoints to resume runs.
- Point your agent to post-training skill to accelerate and automate.
Apply Reinforcement Learning
- The platform now covers online and offline RL paths. Newly supported pipelines include:
  - DPO: offline preference optimization.
  - GRPO: online RL with a rule or model reward and vLLM rollouts.
  - PPO: actor-critic RL with frozen reference and critic, including RL for embodied policies in simulation.
  - OPD: on-policy distillation from a frozen teacher.
  - DiffusionNFT: online RL for diffusion world models.
- Run rollout, reward, and training roles on shared GPUs or separate pools.
- Connect supported simulators to collect experience.
Optimize models and inference
- Distill models to reduce model size or generation steps; quantize models to reduce memory use.
- Run compatible checkpoints with Hugging Face Diffusers, PyTorch, SGLang, vLLM-Omni, vLLM, TRT-LLM and TRT-Edge-LLM or NVIDIA NIM.
- Evaluate for quality, accuracy and GPU usage and maximize compute utilization.
Use agents with Cosmos Framework
Load the setup, inference, post-training, and troubleshooting skills under .agents/skills. Give the agent a bounded task:
Prompt: Post-train <checkpoint> on <dataset> using <recipe>. Pin all revisions, validate the dataset, and keep training and evaluation episodes separate. Run the smoke test, save the configuration, and stop at <N> GPU-hours. Export and compare against the base model on held-out data using three seeds. Repeat evaluation at a supported lower precision; record quality, peak memory, and latency.
Which Cosmos simulation workflow should you use?
Cosmos Framework provides post-training and inference recipes for robot simulation, realistic scene generation, multi-camera driving simulation, and surgical policy evaluation. New Cosmos 3 Nano simulation recipes and example checkpoints enable developers to use agent runnable skills to evaluate our example checkpoints and adapt Cosmos 3 Nano to custom sensors, action space, and data domains.
These checkpoints support PyTorch and vLLM-Omni, tested on NVIDIA Hopper and Blackwell GPUs. Use the recipe to select GPU count, memory configuration, and inference settings.
Autonomous vehicle simulation:
Both AV checkpoints take a prompt and World Scenario Map (WSM) controls representing lanes, objects, road markings, traffic signs, and road boundaries. Joint RGB–LiDAR generation additionally uses HD-map rangemap controls and supports optional initial LiDAR observations. Prompts describe weather, lighting, time of day, road conditions with prefixes providing camera-rig and field-of-view context. An optional initial camera images provide visual context to guide the generated scene’s appearance.
Cosmos3-Nano-Transfer-Auto uses bidirectional generation to denoise an entire multi-view clip at once for offline synthetic data generation. It supports 30 fps input and output video, with up to 400 frames at 480p or 720p; longer sequences can be generated through autoregressive chunking. Change the prompt to turn a daytime drive into a rainy night while keeping the same road layout and vehicle trajectories. Use these variations to train and evaluate perception and driving models across weather and lighting conditions.
After Framework setup, run the four-GPU examples below from the repository root. For Transfer-Auto, use the published sample configuration with seven synchronized WSM videos, per-camera captions, first-frame RGB conditioning, and HD-map LiDAR controls. See the Transfer-Auto inference guide for setup, input preparation, and output details.
export COSMOS_TRAINING=0 COSMOS_INTERNAL=0
hf download nvidia/Cosmos3-Nano-Transfer-Auto \
  --local-dir checkpoints/Cosmos3-Nano-Transfer-Auto
AUTO_SAMPLE_ROOT="$PWD/checkpoints/Cosmos3-Nano-Transfer-Auto/assets/sample_data"
AUTO_NEGATIVE_PROMPT="$(cat .agents/skills/cosmos3-nano-transfer-auto/inference/assets/negative-prompt.txt)"
torchrun --standalone --nproc-per-node=4 \
  -m cosmos_framework.scripts.inference \
  -i "$AUTO_SAMPLE_ROOT/input-transfer-auto.jsonl" \
  -o outputs/transfer_auto \
  --checkpoint-path checkpoints/Cosmos3-Nano-Transfer-Auto \
  --resolution 720 --num-steps 35 \
  --per-view-negative-prompt "$AUTO_NEGATIVE_PROMPT" \
  --cp-size 4 --cfgp-size 1 \
  --no-use-torch-compile --no-diffusion-cache
The reference run produces seven 720p videos (297 frames at 30 FPS) and 99 LiDAR sweeps. Check sample_outputs.json for success and lidar.safetensors for finite range and intensity values, then verify WSM alignment and consistency across camera views and LiDAR.
For custom scenarios and rig adaptation, see the WSM renderer and Transfer-Auto post-training guides. For point-cloud conversion and visualization, see the LiDAR visualization utilities
Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Auto is the causal, few-step-distilled variant of Cosmos3-Nano-Transfer-Auto, enabling autoregressive streaming generation. It generates observations incrementally as an AV policy or human driving input updates the scenario through a WSM renderer. Generated camera and LiDAR observations return to the policy, enabling closed-loop evaluation
For Sim-Auto, reproduce the reference rollout using the published Sim-Auto sample checkpoint and pre-rendered WSM controls to generate synchronized camera videos and LiDAR observations autoregressively. See the Sim-Auto inference guide for setup, input configuration, and output details.
export COSMOS_TRAINING=0 COSMOS_INTERNAL=0
hf download nvidia/Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Auto \
  --local-dir checkpoints/Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Auto
hf download nvidia/Cosmos3-Nano-Transfer-Auto \
  --include 'assets/sample_data/*' \
  --local-dir checkpoints/Cosmos3-Nano-Transfer-Auto
AUTO_SAMPLE_ROOT="$PWD/checkpoints/Cosmos3-Nano-Transfer-Auto/assets/sample_data"
torchrun --standalone --nproc-per-node=4 \
  -m cosmos_framework.scripts.inference \
  -i "$AUTO_SAMPLE_ROOT/input-sim-auto.jsonl" \
  -o outputs/sim_auto \
  --checkpoint-path checkpoints/Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Auto \
  --cp-size 4 --cfgp-size 1 \
  --no-use-torch-compile --no-diffusion-cache
For human-controlled rollouts, see Sim-Auto Interactive Drive.
The Sim-Auto reference run writes to outputs/sim_auto/daytime_scene/. Apply the same output checks described above for Transfer-Auto. 
Robotics Simulation:
Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Transfer converts depth video and a prompt into RGB video with varied lighting, textures, and backgrounds while preserving geometry and motion. For robot demonstrations, it changes the third-person view while retaining actions, states, and wrist-camera recordings.
Video 3. Turn depth, segmentation, edges, or blurred video into detailed RGB observations, using language prompts while the simulator maintains physical state
Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Bimanual generates the next visual observation from the scene and robot actions. It supports interactive two-arm simulation for YAM and AgiBot embodiments, controlled by a policy or human-operated joysticks.
Here, Sim-Transfer generates visuals from a physics simulator’s updated state; Sim-Bimanual generates the next observation directly from the scene and robot actions.
Surgical Simulation:
Surgical environments are among the most challenging for classical simulators due to their complex multi-physics nature. Generative simulation offers a complementary approach: rather than explicitly modeling scene geometry, tissue deformation, and physical interactions, world foundation models learn visual dynamics directly from synchronized surgical video and robot kinematics.
Cosmos3-H-Embodied-Nano, built on Cosmos3 and post-trained on Open-H-Embodiment, generates surgical video from robot actions, predicts actions from video, or generates both together. It takes an initial RGB frame, a task prompt, the last 16 executed actions, and subsequent robot actions. Developers can use it to generate synthetic data and evaluate policies offline without building a physics model of the surgical scene.
Cosmos3-H-Dreams lets developers test how a surgical policy responds as a procedure unfolds, with each action shaping what happens next. Distilled from Cosmos3-H-Embodied-Nano, this causal, few-step model generates frames from live robot kinematics for real-time, closed-loop simulation controlled by a human or learned policy. This gives developers an interactive environment to explore surgical maneuvers and evaluate policies before testing on physical hardware.
When to use Cosmos NIM for accelerated inference
Alongside the open inference tools, the new Cosmos NIM package supported models in optimized containers for accelerated inference, making Cosmos models easy to deploy.
- Faster inference, less memory: Accelerate inference through quantization, speculative decoding, caching, token pruning, and KV-cache-aware routing. Speculative decoding delivers measured mean speedups of roughly 2–3× on H200.
- Custom models and live video understanding: Serve fine-tuned Cosmos checkpoints and process live streams with streaming VLM inference, enabling sub-second alerts with 10x lower latency for faster event response.
- Simpler production deployment: Automatic configuration selection, validated performance and quality across supported GPUs, licensing support, and quarterly feature, optimization, and security updates.
GPU memory requirements
| Capability | Model | Required GPU VRAM [GiB] |  |  | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
|  |  | BF16 | FP8 | FP8 + offloading | 
| Reasoning | Cosmos3-Edge | 16 | 14.5 | – | 
|  | Cosmos3-Nano | 23.1 | 23.1 | – | 
|  | Cosmos3-Super | 135 | 67 | – | 
| Generation | Cosmos3-Edge-DROID | 14 | – | – | 
|  | Cosmos3-Nano | 58 | 44 | 31 | 
|  | Cosmos3-Super | 150 | 93 | 38 | 
How to Launch Cosmos NIM
Choose a GPU and model configuration using the tables above, and follow the deployment guide to install the required NVIDIA driver, Docker, and NVIDIA Container Toolkit on Linux. Sign in to NGC API Keys, select Generate Personal Key, and enable NGC Catalog access. Set the key in your terminal as NGC_API_KEY:
export NGC_API_KEY='paste-your-key-here'
The following commands launch Nano Generator on GPU 0. Ensure curl and python3 are installed and sufficient disk space is available for the image and model cache. The cache permissions shown are for local development.
: "${NGC_API_KEY:?Export your NGC API key first}"
printf '%s' "$NGC_API_KEY" | docker login nvcr.io \
 --username '$oauthtoken' --password-stdin
export NIM_IMAGE='nvcr.io/nim/nvidia/cosmos3:2.0.0'
export LOCAL_NIM_CACHE="$HOME/.cache/nim/cosmos3"
mkdir -p "$LOCAL_NIM_CACHE"
chmod a+rwX "$LOCAL_NIM_CACHE"
docker run -d --name cosmos3-generator \
 --gpus '"device=0"' \
 --shm-size 16g \
 --ulimit memlock=-1 \
 --ulimit stack=67108864 \
 --ulimit nofile=65536:65536 \
 -p 8000:8000 \
 -e NGC_API_KEY \
 -e NIM_MODEL_TYPE=generator \
 -e NIM_MODEL_VARIANT=nano \
 -e NIM_PERF_PROFILE=latency \
 -v "$LOCAL_NIM_CACHE:/opt/nim/.cache" \
 "$NIM_IMAGE"
Wait for readiness (~few minutes) , then inspect the selected model and profile:
curl -fsS http://localhost:8000/v1/health/ready
curl -fsS http://localhost:8000/v1/metadata | python3 -m json.tool
To inspect startup progress, run docker logs -f cosmos3-generator in another terminal. Now you are ready to generate.
Choose latency or throughput:
- latency (default): Prioritizes finishing one request sooner. Choose it for interactive experimentation; supported multi-GPU configurations use GPUs together on a request.
- throughput: Prioritizes completing more requests over time. Choose it for dataset generation or concurrent users; independent replicas process requests in parallel.
Set NIM_PERF_PROFILE at container launch. These settings apply to Generator; throughput benefits require concurrent requests. Latency supports 1, 2, 4, or 8 GPUs, while throughput requires 2, 4, or 8 compatible GPUs. Changing only NIM_PERF_PROFILE to throughput in the single-GPU example will fail profile selection.
Get started
Explore Cosmos Framework and use its agent skills and reference recipes to train, customize, and optimize models for your application. Start with a simulation checkpoint that matches your task, reproduce the reference workflow, and adapt it to your sensors, actions, and data.
Read the full technical report.
Join us on Thursday, Nov. 5, for a livestream on how to use Cosmos Framework.
Deploy Cosmos models for reasoning and generation using New Certified Cosmos NIM for best performance on 20+ NVIDIA GPUs.

articles.title: Shift Left Is Becoming A System-Level Problem
articles.text:
Rise in complexity is pushing engineers to validate hardware, software, and physical constraints earlier in the design flow, but fragmented workflows make that difficult.
Key Takeaways:
Experts at the Table: Semiconductor Engineering sat down to discuss why shift left is pushing beyond verification to system-level validation, and where AI can and cannot help, with Frank Schirrmeister, executive director of strategy programs and system solutions at Synopsys; Ronen Laviv, vice president of business development and strategic partnerships at Hiveware; Jack Berg, vice president of business development at Silvaco; Ashish Darbari, founder and CEO of Axiomise. What follows are excerpts of that conversation. To view part one of this discussion, click here.
L-R: Silvaco’s Berg; Synopsys’ Schirrmeister; Axiomise’s Darbari; Hiveware’s Laviv.
SE: The focus of shift left in design has largely been about verification. But increasingly it’s also about validation, right?
Darbari: Yes, and it’s influencing huge decisions that could make small companies go bankrupt if they get it wrong. We’ve seen meetings with architects, designers, UVM leads, emulation leads, FPGA and software leads, and VPs, where they’re all looking at bug escapes and asking, ‘Why did this happen?’ The architect is saying, ‘It’s supposed to be this.’ The designer is saying, ‘We didn’t know that.’ The software team says, ‘It’s supposed to be this.’ And we’re sitting there as formal verification people thinking about communication and the model not being accurate, and I don’t know how well we’ll be able to solve this unless we bring the software into the development cycle.
Schirrmeister: It’s not only software. It’s all the other aspects, like multi-physics. EM, thermal, and mechanical, which all have to be integrated. To look at this differently, there are hurdles that I cannot fix in this project. But perhaps I can fix it in the next one. It’s a labyrinth. We have models that are digital twins that are irrefutable, because we’ve measured them against the real thing. We can’t overcome those. We are dependent on the application. It may be more vertical, it may be more horizontally stacked to fit into a certain form factor, like a phone or a data center. But it’s like a video game where you have these things popping up. I want to package it this way, but the packaging guy says we can’t do that, at least not today. Maybe a year from now. All of this needs to be taken into consideration as part of your model.
Dabari: Absolutely correct.
Laviv: Shrinking times for packaging or power estimation or simulation, or even emulation — isn’t that something we could look at? We’re shifting left using AI in order to do stuff earlier.
Berg: Verification traditionally has been the longest and most expensive part of doing a design, and it would be nice to say we can take everything and shift it all left. There are chunks that are being shifted left and verified, and that’s good. But how to shift everything left is something we’re still learning.
Darbari: If we pick up historical data from packaging and thermal, why can’t we start building models to say, ‘This happened last time. This time it could be done better.’
Berg: You can do that based on inference.
Darbari: But we don’t have a tool that ties everything together in one frame. ‘This is the model of functional safety, security, power, packaging, thermals. Go build it.’
Berg: We have different aspects of that, and we, as an industry, are working slowly but surely to integrate all of those. But we don’t have a single workflow that does that. And it really is a workflow, not just a single tool.
Laviv: Nowadays, with AI knowing everything with its skills and touching everything, there is kind of a common database for verification and emulation and all the physical stuff. It might benefit customers if they have access to everything is there to be used, potentially even cross-companies.
Schirrmeister: There are certain things you can shift left, and others you have to wait for. Certain things are irrefutable. Yes, you can make them faster, but you can’t bypass them. You can be smarter about how you use them. You can figure out which things should be done in emulation, which should be done in simulation, and which should be done with FPGA-based prototyping. We have customers telling us that if they find something in simulation that should have been found in formal, or simulation beforehand, they’ll review why that happened.
Laviv: Why not look at bottlenecks in formal, in verification, in emulation, and see if you can handle those bottlenecks in a way that would open the flow for faster AI?
Schirrmeister: There are two views here on this whole AI stack. I’m a firm believer that the underlying portions of the stack will still be required. They will be used in different ways by the AI objects, but you don’t take away the characterization, the simulation, the emulation. You get smarter about how to use them. But at the end of the day, you need to build the emulator. That takes some time. You need to get the design into it. And there is a certain number of things which you cannot overcome. You can make the tool flow more productive, but the underlying engines still need to execute, and there are limits to how fast they can become.
Darbari: We need to put all of these things in a singular context because if the manufacturing, or the physics, the heat, or the functional, are all sitting in separate context windows, and the software is sitting somewhere else, then you don’t have a complete picture of what this whole device will look like. I was coding for one project and I remember asking a designer, ‘What would happen to this processor if there was more than one outstanding transaction? Could you discard the later ones?’ And he said, ‘We’ll just discard them.’ Everything was exhaustively proved, and while I was taping, the software teams were running their own stuff. But a bug got missed. The software team had a completely different understanding of how they were going to drive the SoC. So they found a trace, and they said, ‘We are losing transactions.’ There was a complete misalignment between what the architect and the designer thought they were building, so they had to patch it at the end of the day. That’s what worries me now, because things are getting so much more complex. We’re putting all of this in the hands of an agent, but who is the master at the top level? Is there a master agent?
Schirrmeister: But there’s also a counter-example. It’s true that there might be a communication mismatch, but there also may be complexity issues that are hard to observe by one person, and then your context applies. I have an example from a previous life, when there were software developers and hardware developers, and you had an emulator. The software developers were writing their software, and everything was correct. They talked to each other for days, but then they started pointing fingers. Suddenly, the emulator vendor was at fault. There must be something wrong in the tool. Then we figured out that in the global setting, the code was powered down at that particular state in the system context, and the software developer didn’t see the register programming as being correct. The hardware developer saw it as correct, but didn’t know that it switched off because the clock was gated and that area was shut down. From a context standpoint, all that information needs to be communicated. That’s one issue. But then it also needs to be available in the context of the agentic AI.
Darbari: Unless we stitch the agents in ways so that we can handle all of these challenges, there will still be bugs creeping through the seams. People will be investing in agents and doing all the stuff you’re talking about, but there is still no single context where you could look at all of this together. AI could be used for this, and it’s really what AI should be used for, because it’s humanly not feasible to know and derive all of this information that should go into a single arrangement.
Laviv: With chips like [Intel’s] Broadwell, with 200 billion transistors, we’ll need much more verification. Today, the tools have challenges running such designs without emulation. We need to see if some things can get shifted left and prepare the simulation environment to pull in the emulation earlier. But if you have such a huge chip, it’s a challenge. With AI, we’ve heard how you can interact with the simulation or the API. So if you let AI have some internal insights to formal, to simulation, now you don’t have to wait two days for a test to end. In the AI era, for each of the tools, we can find hooks that AI can use in order to make better judgments and clean stuff faster.
Darbari: We’ve been looking at the power/performance/area estimate, and there are some very interesting insights we’ve received. We can look at the entire chip, analyze it to figure out if the unused area is burning power. What surprised us most, because we knew we were looking at results where synthesis isn’t going to remove it, is that we didn’t have that data. But some of this stuff would be sitting in the die, not getting used. Synthesis isn’t removing it. Lint isn’t telling you it’s bad. Coverage is not telling you it’s bad. In order for us to be efficient with the end goal, we need to start thinking about the artifacts very early on. So, for example, picking up redundant logic should not be a synthesis problem. This should be a designer’s problem or an architect’s problem. If I want to remove a register or retime it, I want to make sure the design is built correctly up front. But whether it is built for the right reason is a separate problem. Maybe that’s a validation problem. But bringing what used to be a verification or layout problem in as a design or architecture problem is what needs to happen.
