articles.title: Egypt’s Nclude fund hits US$112m final close under DPI Venture Capital - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Egyptian fintech-focused venture capital (VC) fund Nclude has reached a final close of more than US$112 million, as it prepares for its next phase of investment across Africa and the Middle East.
Nclude was launched in Egypt in 2022, and came under the management of Development Partners International (DPI) in 2025 after a restructuring, with DPI acting as investment adviser to the fund alongside the launch of DPI Venture Capital, its dedicated VC platform.
Disrupt Africa reported in April 2025 on the launch of DPI Venture Capital, which came about through the fund-restructuring transaction that saw DPI begin advising Nclude. Since then, the firm has brought additional strategically aligned investors on board to widen the fund’s LP base.
The fund backs fintech, fintech-enabled businesses and financial inclusion plays, as well as startups working where fintech meets AI and other emerging technologies. It invests at stages ranging from seed to Series C, writing cheques of between US$500,000 and US$10 million,
Egypt remains Nclude’s core market, which it sees as a springboard for startups looking to scale regionally, though up to 30 per cent of its mandate can be deployed outside the country. It has so far backed 15 companies.
“When we became adviser to Nclude, we took stewardship of an existing fund with a strong investment thesis, rooted in improving financial inclusion across Africa and the Middle East. We have grown a portfolio aligned with that central thesis and have built on those foundations by activating more of the fund’s mandate across the region. This has included expansion into themes such as affordable insurance and healthcare access, unlocking credit access for SMEs, and helping individuals save and invest for the future. At the same time, we have selectively broadened the fund’s investor base with additional strategically aligned LPs,” said Ashley Lewis, managing partner and head of DPI Venture Capital.
“At over US$112 million, we believe Nclude is appropriately sized for today’s market, giving us the firepower to invest with discipline and support ambitious founders as they grow from strong local businesses into regional technology leaders.”

articles.title: Hisense XR10 review - a 4K triple laser projector for all seasons and all viewers - Tech Guide
articles.text:
- Design
The Hisense XR10 is an all-in-one home theatre system that provides stunning 4K resolution, amazing brightness, and impressive sound. All you need to do is aim it at a wall and get the popcorn ready.
There is a lot to like about the Hisense XR10 Triple Laser projector that delivers a true big-screen cinematic experience in your home.
The XR10 has 6,000 ANSI lumens of brightness and has an optical zoom so it can create a bigger screen in a space where other projectors can’t.
Regular projectors require a longer throw distance to create a larger image but the Hisense XR10 can go bigger without losing quality thanks to the onboard optical zoom.
For our review we set up the Hisense XR10 in our home theatre where we have a 150-inch fixed screen.
But the XR10 can project an image up to 300 inches.
This is a projector aimed at the user who wants to set up a dedicated viewing space.
It certainly offers the sort of quality a serious user would be looking for to enjoy the big screen experience.
Yet, at about the size of a four-slice toaster, the XR10 is still small enough to be moved from room to room.
The projector can be packed away inside a vintage carry case which is ideal for those who only want to pull the projector out for special occasions or to move it around the home.
But priced at $9,999, the Hisense XR10 has all the features of a premium home theatre projector that, in an ideal setting, would be permanently mounted.
Yet it has the size and easy setup of a portable projector that is thousands of dollars cheaper.
Hisense is trying to deliver the best of both worlds to suit all kinds of users.
For us we view this projector as home theatre-worthy and it would be fixed to a ceiling mount.
We’re not sure if those customers looking for an easy portable projector to enjoy 4K quality in any room in the house would be willing to spend nearly $10,000 for that convenience.
That convenience is helped along by the fact the XR10 has built-in Devialet speakers.
But again which customer are we aiming this at?
Yes, the portable projector customer wants an all-in-one setup but how many of them have a lazy $9,999 to spare?
And the high-end user, like us, would prefer to have multiple speakers set up around the room rather than being limited to the projector’s onboard speakers.
And those speakers sound amazing but they lack the immersive qualities that a multiple-speaker system would offer.
Setup is simple and automated, with the projector squaring the picture up and focusing automatically.
In our setup we had to tweak the settings a little bit.
The projector wasn’t playing ball and automatically finding the edges of our screen so we had to help it along a little bit.
The good news is setup is remarkably easy and you’ll be watching your content within minutes.
The Hisense XR10 has the same interface as its TVs so you can access streaming services and catch-up apps as well as Hisense internet channels.
But you can also connect your sources through the HDMI ports on the rear of the projector if you wanted to add a gaming console, set-top box or 4K disc player.
We got the picture set up to our 150-inch screen within minutes and it achieved that with a shorter throw length than our current projector thanks to the XR10’s digital zoom, which created a bigger image without compromising picture quality
This is another great feature when setting it up in tight spaces.
On top of the optical zoom there’s also lens shift, which allows you to make even finer adjustments to your picture.
And the minute it was set up the quality was plain to see through the triple laser 4K projector system
We connected our Netflix and Apple TV accounts to showcase the XR10.
The first thing that struck us was the brightness. The 6,000 ANSI lumens brightness was unmistakable.
For our darkened theatre room it certainly was super bright but the advantage is that it could easily be viewed in high quality even during the day.
Now when it came to the colour, especially the reds, they were super bright and our first action was to dive into the settings to see what mode the projector was in.
There are several to choose from including Standard, Filmmaker, Cinema Day, and Cinema Night along with Dynamic.
Flicking between these modes really altered the character of the projector which means it will suit many tastes.
Viewers who prefer subtlety rather than glaring resolution and brightness may opt for Standard.
Others who prefer the more saturated brighter image may choose to go Dynamic.
Cinema Night for us proved to be a reasonable middle ground but we still tinkered with the brightness slightly to make it a little bit more conservative.
But there was no denying the crispness of the image and any content in 4K resolution really leapt off the screen.
The pure triple-colour laser really did the heavy lifting and was able to provide 118 per cent of the colour gamut and remarkable accuracy.
Contrast was also impressive at 6000:1 and up to 60,000:1 dynamic contrast really added to the depth of every scene.
It also achieved impressive deep blacks as well.
The XR10 also includes Dolby Vision and is compatible with HDR10, HDR10+, HLG, and HDR Vivid so you’re covered no matter where you’re watching your content.
There’s also AI at play here, with the XR10 automatically fine-tuning the colour, brightness, and sharpness in real time so you’re getting a more consistent image.
True movie lovers who want to watch the film as the director intended would probably opt out of the AI upscaling because it turns it into more of a digital medium than a film medium.
Purists, ourselves included, really enjoy the 4K resolution but we don’t think every object in the scene needs to be razor sharp to the point where it may look abnormal.
That was our only issue with the XR10 – it looked too perfect and too sharp at times.
We prefer a more natural approach to the content.
But that’s the beauty of this product: it can deliver these different outcomes to suit your taste. What I consider to be good picture quality, you might think is rubbish and vice versa.
The XR10 has a mode and settings that will suit everyone.
On the audio side the speakers tuned by Devialet delivered great quality but despite it having Dolby Atmos, it still felt quite localised because all the sound was coming from the projector.
Our home theatre has speakers everywhere, including under the screen, so that we could hear the actors’ voices coming from the screen while hearing the directional sound.
Anyone who has set up a serious home theatre may have even prioritised the audio quality and set up speakers all around the room.
The Hisense XR10 can be integrated into a system with multiple speakers, which means the Devialet-tuned speakers will go to waste.
In fact, home theatre owners like us, usually opt for standalone projectors without speakers because the audio can be handled by the multiple speakers already positioned in the room.
But these projectors are also purely monitors, which means they also need to be paired with a receiver and other outputs to be able to access content like streaming services.
That’s the Hisense XR10’s biggest advantage: it is an all-in-one solution that can be set up to provide high-quality results and performance in any room of your home.
So with that in mind it would probably suit the user who is probably not focused on having a dedicated space but on wanting to turn any space into a high-performance viewing area.
The Hisense XR10 is priced at $9999 and is available now.
VERDICT
The Hisense XR10 is an all-in-one home theatre system that provides stunning 4K resolution, amazing brightness, and impressive sound. All you need to do is aim it at a wall and get the popcorn ready.

articles.title: Ivanti patches two more Connect Secure zero-days chained in attacks
articles.text:
Ivanti released security updates to patch two more Connect Secure (ICS) remote access gateway flaws that have been chained in zero-day attacks since at least October 1.
Threat actors exploited these two flaws (tracked as CVE-2026-111357 and CVE-2026-118527) alongside an authentication bypass vulnerability (CVE-2026-104935), which Ivanti patched last month to remove the main attack surface.
CVE-2026-111357 is a high-severity privilege escalation flaw, and CVE-2026-118527 lets authenticated attackers upload files on an unpatched device.
When it released patches for CVE-2026-104935 in October, Ivanti urged admins to upgrade as soon as possible since it was aware of "limited exploitation in the wild."
"At the time of discovery of exploitation, Ivanti had a fix developed for CVE-2026-104935 which was already in QA for supported versions, and we made the decision to not delay getting a fix to customers that resolved the primary exploitation path when the LPE was discovered," Ivanti added in an advisory updated on Thursday.
"Because of this, our focus was initially centered on the disclosure of CVE-2026-104935 and providing protection for our customers as quickly as possible."
Cybersecurity firm Volexity, which found the flaw, reported at the time that a threat actor (UTA0576) was chaining the CVE-2026-104935 vulnerability since at least October 3 with two other flaws to gain unauthenticated root-level code execution on fully patched ICS devices.
"Notably, UTA0576 deployed no malware or web shell. Instead, the threat actor re-exploited the device for every command it ran and tampered with logs to cover its tracks, evading Ivanti's Integrity Checker Tool," Volexity said.
Threat intelligence firm Defused also confirmed Volexity's report, saying that it spotted the first signs of active CVE-2026-104935 exploitation starting October 1.
On Tuesday, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added CVE-2026-104935 to its catalog of actively exploited vulnerabilities and ordered federal agencies to patch their systems by Friday,
Internet threat watchdog Shadowserver now tracks over 5,000 Internet-exposed ICS instances, but there is no information on how many have already been secured against ongoing attacks.
Threat actors frequently target Ivanti vulnerabilities, often in zero-day attacks, because they provide a quick way into enterprise networks to steal sensitive corporate and customer data.
Over the past several years, Ivanti has patched several other Connect Secure zero-days exploited in the wild, some of them chained in widespread attacks to deploy malware.
It addressed a command injection (CVE-2024-21887) and an authentication bypass (CVE-2023-46805) in early January 2024, and a server-side request forgery (CVE-2024-21893) two weeks later.
More recently, Ivanti has fixed a remote code execution (RCE) bug (CVE-2025-0282) in January 2025 and a second RCE flaw (CVE-2025-22457) exploited by China-linked state hackers since at least mid-March 2025.
Ivanti has over 3,000 employees, a network of more than 7,000 partners, and over 40,000 customers using its IT asset management solutions worldwide.
Since November 2021, CISA has flagged 38 Ivanti vulnerabilities as actively exploited in the wild, including 12 that have also been abused in ransomware attacks.

articles.title: Ces 319 extensions Chrome ont espionné des millions d'internautes pendant 10 ans
articles.text:
Des chercheurs de l’entreprise de cybersécurité Socket ont identifié un réseau de 319 extensions Chrome qui détournent les recherches des internautes. Ce système serait actif depuis dix ans et aurait potentiellement touché 13,4 millions d’utilisateurs.
Des extensions Chrome destinées à enregistrer vos requêtes
De prime abord, ces extensions Chrome, destinées à détourner les recherches des internautes, semblent inoffensives en se présentant comme des convertisseurs de DFD, des outils de recherche de manuels, des moteurs de recherche sécurisés ou encore des assistants IA de recherche. Mais en réalité, elles ont un double objectif. D’une part, les requêtes saisies dans Chrome transitent sur des serveurs proxy contrôlés par les opérateurs des extensions. D’autre part, ces extensions redirigent l’internaute vers Yahoo ou Bing afin que les pirates bénéficient de commissions de parrainage, étant donné que du trafic est généré sur ces deux moteurs de recherche concurrents de Google.
Pour être plus précis, les pirates exploitent un paramètre de Chrome qui permet à une extension de remplacer le moteur de recherche par défaut. Par ailleurs, il faut noter que certaines de ces extensions ne demandent aucune autorisation particulière de la part de l’internaute.
Comment éviter tout risque ?
Ces extensions malveillantes représentent un problème principalement à deux niveaux. Le premier, le moins grave : les pirates se font de l’argent sur le dos des internautes en les redirigeant vers Yahoo ou Bing. Le deuxième, plus préoccupant : ils sont en mesure de consulter les requêtes qui transitent par leurs serveurs, et donc de détenir des informations confidentielles vous concernant (questions relatives à la santé, aux finances, à la vie intime, etc.). Les dangers sont donc notables.
Les chercheurs de l’entreprise de cybersécurité Socket conseillent donc vivement de supprimer toutes les extensions inconnues sur votre ordinateur. Pour rappel, certaines extensions peuvent se télécharger sans que l’utilisateur donne explicitement son accord. Rappelons au passage qu’il est primordial de faire très attention aux extensions que l’on télécharge, même si elles semblent à première vue inoffensives. À titre d’exemple, la plupart des extensions qui font l’objet de cet article n’étaient pas référencées dans le Chrome Web Store. Enfin, vérifiez que votre moteur de recherche par défaut est bien celui que vous avez choisi.

articles.title: Startup news and updates: daily roundup (November 02, 2026)
articles.text:
Startup news and updates: daily roundup (November 02, 2026)
YourStory presents the daily news roundup from the Indian startup ecosystem and beyond. Here's the roundup for Monday, November 02, 2026.
From AI-powered, full-stack clean energy deployment platform, Two Point O Capital (TW.O), raising $10 million in a funding round led by Transition Venture Capital, to Competition watchdog CCI approving Dutch investment group Prosus' proposal to acquire a stake in Sachin Bansal-led fintech firm Navi, here are the latest developments across sectors.
Featured Stories
Two Point O raises $10M led by Transition Venture Capital
Two Point O Capital (TW.O), an AI-powered, full-stack clean energy deployment platform for commercial and industrial (C&I) businesses, has raised $10 million in a funding round led by Transition Venture Capital. Existing investor Omnivore and angel investors Chiranjeev Singh Saluja and Sudhir M Reddy also participated in the round.
TW.O said it will use the funds to expand into new asset classes, including battery energy storage systems (BESS), and deepen its presence in existing segments such as solar, energy efficiency and wastewater treatment.
Latest News
Prosus investment in Sachin Bansal's Navi gets CCI nod
Competition watchdog CCI has approved Dutch investment group Prosus' proposal to acquire a stake in Sachin Bansal-led fintech firm Navi Ltd, paving the way for the investment group to deepen its presence in India's digital financial services sector.
"The proposed combination involves the acquisition of certain shareholding in Navi Ltd (target) by MIH Payments Holdings BV (acquirer)," the regulator said in a release. The Competition Commission of India (CCI) said it has approved the proposed deal.
Funding News
ValueQuest Tristar Fund raises over Rs 2,100 Cr for advanced manufacturing
ValueQuest Tristar Fund, a private equity fund that backs India’s advanced manufacturing sector, has received more than Rs 2,100 crore in commitments from investors. It reached this within 15 months of its first close, beating both its original target and the full greenshoe (the extra amount a fund is allowed to raise above its target).
The fund invests in aerospace, defence, precision engineering and manufacturing linked to the energy transition.
Other News
Razorpay Wins Final IFSCA Licence to Run Cross-Border Money Movement from GIFT City
Razorpay has received its final Payment Service Provider licence from the IFSCA, following in-principle approval in April 2026. The licence lets it move money in and out of India from GIFT City under a single regulatory framework.
Its infrastructure supports global investing, international collections, settlements and multi-currency accounts, with banking integrations live with RBL Bank and ICICI Bank. Investment platforms can integrate once, cutting timelines from months to two to three weeks. The move responds to rising demand, as Indian residents put $2.65 billion into overseas stocks and debt in FY26, up 56 per cent year on year.
Arrowhead AI launches Fletch, a voice model built for India and Southeast Asia's multilingual conversations
Arrowhead AI, a Bengaluru-based voice AI company, has launched Fletch, an in-house text-to-speech model for multilingual customer calls. It supports 14 languages, switches between them mid-sentence and offers 12 emotion styles. Fletch reports 80 milliseconds of latency and starts speaking in under 100 milliseconds.
Already powering over one million calls a day for clients such as Axis Bank and RBL Bank, it claims roughly 30% better pronunciation accuracy on selected names and terms, a figure the company stresses is not an overall call-resolution gain. Arrowhead is adding Malay and Indonesian support ahead of Singapore FinTech Festival 2026.
BikeWo Green Tech signs MoU with Eden Green Energy to explore electric mobility opportunities
BikeWo Green Tech Limited has signed a strategic Memorandum of Understanding with Eden Green Energy Private Limited to explore collaboration in electric mobility and sustainable transportation. The companies will look at opportunities in EV fleet solutions, vehicle leasing, charging infrastructure, and workforce, rider and operational management.
BikeWo brings expertise in leasing, infrastructure and business development, while Eden contributes workforce and operational strengths. Eden's Managing Director said the partnership aligns with plans to expand dedicated electric fleets and charging networks in Tamil Nadu, including Chennai and Tiruchirappalli. Both firms aim to build scalable, zero-emission mobility solutions.
Fibe launches UPI payments on its App after NPCI third-party provider approval
Digital lending platform Fibe has launched its UPI offering following NPCI approval to operate as a Third-Party Application Provider. The service is open to consumers across India, including those who are not existing Fibe customers. Users can pay through bank accounts, RuPay Credit Cards and eligible credit lines, all within a single UPI experience.
The launch adds an everyday payments layer to Fibe's range of products, which includes the Fibe Axis Bank Credit Card, third-party FDs and Loan Against Mutual Funds. Group CEO Akshay Mehrotra said the aim is to give users greater choice, control and value in every transaction.
DHL Express appoints Sandeep Juneja to lead South Asia and India business
DHL Express has appointed Sandeep Juneja as Senior Vice President for South Asia and Managing Director for India, effective 1 November 2026. He succeeds R. S. Subramanian, who moves to Blue Dart as Managing Director. Juneja joined DHL Express in 2004, has sat on the India Management Board since 2007 and has led the commercial function since 2013.
He will focus on customer partnerships, people and sustainable growth, and will also oversee Nepal, Bhutan, the Maldives, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh. Asia Pacific CEO Ken Lee said Juneja brings the market knowledge and customer relationships needed for the next phase of growth.
Nagaland University-led study proposes framework to evaluate AI tools for preserving India's cultural heritage
A research team led by Nagaland University, with scholars from institutions in Tamil Nadu, Delhi, Uttar Pradesh, Telangana and Karnataka, has proposed a framework to evaluate how AI can help preserve manuscripts, endangered languages, oral traditions and historical records. It assesses tools across nine areas, including text recognition, translation, cultural context and ethics, combining technical checks with expert and community review.
The researchers stress that AI should support, not replace, archivists, linguists and cultural custodians, since technical accuracy does not guarantee cultural accuracy. They recommend piloting the framework across different collections, scripts and dialects. The findings appear in Acta Innovations.
Thyrocare launches India's first pregnancy kit with bundled lab confirmation test; Yami Gautam named brand ambassador
Thyrocare Technologies has entered the pregnancy testing segment with the Thyrocare Pregnancy Kit, which it says is India's first to include a quantitative laboratory confirmation. Priced at Rs 60, the kit contains a rapid at-home test and a voucher for a Beta hCG blood test at Rs 399, half the regular Rs 800, with home sample collection included.
Users book the test by scanning a QR code, and the voucher is valid for six months. Actor Yami Gautam is the brand ambassador. Thyrocare's MD and CEO Rahul Guha said the kit pairs a quick home answer with clinical confirmation.
ICICI Lombard's Startup Shield forum helps Bengaluru startups build resilience against emerging business risks
ICICI Lombard General Insurance hosted "Startup Shield – The Risk Readiness Forum" in Bengaluru on 27 October 2026 to help startups prepare for emerging risks. Karnataka has 24,026 DPIIT-recognised startups, and the discussions covered AI-driven threats, cyber and data security, employee wellness, professional indemnity, directors and officers liability, asset protection and business interruption.
Founders, investors, CXOs and risk professionals attended, and ICICI Lombard experts shared real-world case studies. Anand Singhi, the company's Chief for Corporate, International, Banca and Government Business, said risk preparedness is increasingly a marker of business maturity that influences how investors and enterprise partners assess a company.
Avendus appoints Sumit Agarwal as Managing Director and Head of Equity Corporate Finance
Avendus has appointed Sumit Agarwal as Managing Director and Head of Equity Corporate Finance, Investment Banking, reporting to Karan Sharma, Head of Investment Banking at Avendus Capital. He will lead the firm's equity capital markets execution, strengthening its ability to deliver end-to-end IPO mandates and follow-on offerings.
Agarwal has over 18 years of experience and has led more than 100 transactions, including IPOs, FPOs, QIPs, InvITs and rights issues. He joins from Kotak Mahindra Capital and previously worked at ICICI Securities. Sharma said Agarwal brings deep execution expertise and strong institutional relationships that will broaden the firm's ECM capabilities.
Xflow launches SaaS subscription management tool for businesses to pay global vendors like AWS and OpenAI
Cross-border payments company Xflow has launched SaaS Subscription Management, letting businesses pay and track global subscriptions such as AWS, OpenAI, Figma and Slack in one place. Companies pay Xflow via SWIFT in USD or through NEFT/RTGS in INR, and use a USD virtual card for all subscription payments.
The tool addresses failed recurring payments on domestic cards and scattered renewals across teams and currencies. CEO Ashwin Bhatnagar cited industry estimates that over 30 per cent of card-based recurring payments fail in India, and said Xflow is already processing millions in volume since launch. Blume Ventures' Amit Gajaria praised the service.
(The copy will be updated with the latest news through the day)

articles.title: Agentic engineering intelligence with Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Agentic engineering intelligence with Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
When a qualified aerospace component goes obsolete or hits a long lead time, an engineer spends days cross-referencing specifications across vendor datasheets, interface control documents (ICDs), and qualification records before documenting a substitution justification for review. An incorrect substitution on a flight-critical component can cause mission failure, yet the evidence trail behind each decision is often spread across email and undocumented institutional knowledge, so there is no formal, repeatable package for a reviewer to check.
A previous post, Manufacturing intelligence with Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings, showed how the model retrieves answers locked inside engineering diagrams, thermal plots, and datasheet charts that text-only pipelines miss. This post picks up where that retrieval work left off, putting those capabilities inside a multi-agent system that assembles substitution evidence, from retrieval to a drafted assessment.
In this post, we show how to build a multi-agent engineering assistant that cuts the manual cross-referencing behind part substitution evaluation using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings, and the open source Strands Agents SDK. A planner routes work across three specialist agents that search a multimodal knowledge base, score candidates against deterministic tolerance rules, compare part photos, and ground lifecycle claims in live web data. The engineer remains the decision-maker throughout, because the system assembles evidence and drafts documents without ever approving a substitution on its own.
Solution overview
The assistant is built around one design rule, which is that the engineer makes every decision and the system assembles the evidence for it. That rule determines where we use large language models (LLMs) and where we use deterministic code instead.
Three pillars define the architecture:
- Deterministic spec-fit evaluation – Tolerance-rule code written in Python scores each candidate part against the reference part and the engineer’s stated requirements. Because the same inputs consistently produce the same pass/flag verdicts, the results can go into a formal engineering review.
- Multi-agent orchestration – A lightweight planner routes each query to one or more of three specialist agents (Catalog, Evaluation, Knowledge), and a supervisor synthesizes their findings only when more than one specialist contributed. Complex questions such as “Check if this wheel is going end-of-life, find alternatives, and score them” chain all three specialists in sequence.
- Human-in-the-loop decision – The system drafts justification memos and Integration Impact Assessments for engineering review, but it doesn’t recommend or approve a substitution. Every evaluation also writes an audit trail entry aligned with AS9100 sections 8.4 and 8.5.6.
The following diagram shows the architecture.
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. In this solution, chat requests from the engineer’s application flow into a multi-agent graph hosted on AgentCore runtime: a planner (Claude Haiku 5.5) produces a routing plan, specialists (Claude Sonnet 5.5) execute their tools, and a supervisor (Claude Opus 5.5) synthesizes their results when more than one specialist ran. The specialists retrieve from a managed knowledge base that we created with Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Bases using Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings, routed through an AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, alongside the Web Search connector for live web data. For image-as-query (uploading a chart to identify a part), the agent calls a native Amazon S3 Vectors index directly, because the managed knowledge base retrieval API doesn’t accept image input. Amazon S3 Vectors is a capability of Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3). A separate fixed chain (Knowledge, then Evaluation, then Supervisor) produces the formal Integration Impact Assessment (IIA) document.
Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings appears in two distinct roles:
- Multimodal retrieval – Datasheets, ICDs, and performance charts are embedded with Nova Multimodal Embeddings so text and visual content share one semantic space. An engineer can enter “torque curve for the 0.06 Nms wheel” or upload a chart image, and retrieval returns the matching diagram with source attribution.
- Visual similarity scoring – When two candidate parts are compared, Nova Multimodal Embeddings produces a quantitative cosine similarity between their photos, and Claude analyzes the specific physical differences (mounting pattern, connector placement, housing geometry). The score adds supporting evidence to the deterministic spec comparison, which is what the fit verdict is based on.
Prerequisites
To follow along, you need:
- An AWS account with access to Amazon Bedrock in the US East (N. Virginia) AWS Region.
- Model access to Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings, Claude Haiku 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5, and Claude Opus 5.5 in Amazon Bedrock. For model availability by Region, see Model support by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock.
- A managed knowledge base created with Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Bases, using Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings over your parts corpus (datasheets, ICDs, descriptions) for text and document retrieval.
- An Amazon S3 Vectors index over your part photos and datasheet chart crops, for the image-as-query path.
- An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway with the Web Search connector and a managed knowledge base target.
- Python 3.10 or later and Jupyter for running the notebooks.
- Docker, if you adapt the deployment recipe in notebook 03 to host the agent on AgentCore runtime.
- The sample code from the GitHub repository.
Solution walkthrough
The following sections describe each part of the system in the order a query uses it. We start with the parts corpus and the specialist agents, then cover routing, deterministic scoring, the two ways the assistant uses Nova Multimodal Embeddings, the fixed chain that produces formal documents, and deployment to AgentCore runtime.
The complete code sample is a set of five Jupyter notebooks in the GitHub repository, and each notebook runs on its own. The notebooks import from mei_core, a self-contained copy of the agent and tool modules in the same folder, and they include their own parts data, chart crops, and evaluation query set. You can run every snippet in this post from the notebooks without other application code.
Structure the parts corpus
The sample dataset is seven reaction wheels from a fictional manufacturer (AnyCompany) spanning 0.003–5.0 Nms of momentum storage. Each part is a folder that pairs structured data with the source documents an engineer actually reads, and this mix is what makes the corpus multimodal. The specs.json file holds the machine-readable fields that drive deterministic scoring, while the ICD, product photo, and rendered datasheet page carry the visual and narrative detail that structured fields leave out.
The specs.json file captures both the engineering specifications and a lifecycle profile, which is what lets the assistant flag obsolescence and lead-time risk alongside spec fit.
The vendor field is stated explicitly for every part. Because catalog folder IDs and file names are reused across datasets, every specialist prompt treats the structured vendor value returned by get_part_specs as authoritative and is forbidden from guessing a manufacturer from an ID, a file name, a photo, or a web search result. Taking the manufacturer from structured data keeps the assistant from attributing a part to the wrong supplier because the model thinks it recognizes the hardware.
Each part folder also carries two assets that text-only indexing cannot use. The product photo feeds visual similarity scoring, and the rendered datasheet page carries torque-box and torque-curve plots that answer performance questions no OCR text layer captures. Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings embeds both into the same vector space as the text, so a query can match a spec value, a paragraph, or a plot.
The following sample shows four datasheet pages from the corpus, spanning three orders of magnitude of momentum storage.
The template repeats across the family, but the product photo and the pair of performance plots change with every part. These Regions show the housing geometry, mounting pattern, torque envelope, and power draw, which the spec fields don’t state directly, so we embed them alongside the text.
Define specialists with scoped tools
Each specialist is a Strands agent with a narrow prompt and only the tools it needs. Scoping tools per specialist keeps behavior predictable, because the Knowledge specialist has no access to the catalog discovery tools and the Catalog specialist has no access to the evaluation tools. The following code creates the Evaluation specialist.
The following diagram shows how the planner routes a query to the specialists and when the supervisor synthesizes their results. The list after it describes what each specialist does.
- Catalog – Discovers parts through knowledge base search and exhaustive spec filtering (kb_search, filter_parts_by_spec, get_part_specs, get_substitution_requirements).
- Evaluation – Scores candidates deterministically and compares parts visually (score_substitution_fit, compare_parts, visual_similarity_score, check_qualification_status, generate_substitution_memo).
- Knowledge – Answers questions from datasheets and ICDs, checks live end-of-life status, and retrieves visual content (get_part_specs, web_search_eol, retrieve_visual_content).
Use a small model for routing and a large model for synthesis
Routing is a classification task with no tool calls, so it doesn’t need a large reasoning model. A Haiku-based planner returns a numbered routing plan in a couple of seconds. The Opus supervisor runs only when two or more specialists contributed, because synthesizing a single specialist’s already-complete answer adds about 8 seconds of latency with no quality gain.
Splitting the work across three model tiers matches cost and latency to each stage. Haiku classifies the query, Sonnet runs the tools, and Opus writes the combined answer, which is the step where response quality matters most.
Keep the scoring deterministic
The spec-fit evaluation runs as ordinary Python code against a hand-written requirements schema. The schema defines the critical specs and tolerance rules for each component category, and score_substitution_fit compares each spec, counts passes and flags, and surfaces lifecycle risk. Because the verdict must be reproducible for an engineering review package, no LLM is involved in this step.
The tool returns a structured verdict with an explicit disclaimer:
The specialist presents this table and explains the flags, but it can’t change a verdict. The audit trail follows the same division of work. After every evaluation, the orchestration layer reads the specialist’s tool-call history and writes the audit entry itself, so logging doesn’t depend on the model remembering to do it.
Score visual similarity with Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings
Form factor matters when a substitute must fit an existing bracket. The visual_similarity_score tool embeds both part photos with Nova Multimodal Embeddings and computes cosine similarity, then asks Claude to describe the specific observable differences.
The embedding similarity is deterministic and reproducible, returning around 0.84 for two wheels of the same product family and 0.40 for wheels of different classes. Claude’s vision analysis then explains what drives the difference, for example noting that one housing is roughly twice the diameter of the other and has a six-hole mounting pattern where the other has four.
Retrieve charts and diagrams with two retrieval paths
Text and document queries go through the managed knowledge base backed by Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings, routed through the AgentCore Gateway. Image-as-query (uploading a chart or photo to find matching content) uses a native Amazon S3 Vectors index called directly from the agent, because the managed knowledge base retrieval API doesn’t accept image input.
The Knowledge specialist’s retrieve_visual_content tool provides one interface for both paths. An engineer can paste a performance curve from a requirements document into the chat and ask which part matches it, or describe the chart in a text query instead.
On the image path, the upload is embedded with Nova Multimodal Embeddings at 1,024 dimensions using the IMAGE_RETRIEVAL purpose, then matched against the S3 Vectors index:
Because one part contributes several vectors (its photo, the whole datasheet page, and each cropped chart region), results are deduped to the best-scoring vector per part before they reach the model.
We learned three practical lessons while building the retrieval paths:
- Crop the charts before indexing them – Whole datasheet pages make poor index entries, because roughly 90 percent of a page (header, spec table, footer) is boilerplate that every part shares, and that shared content dominates the embedding. Indexing cropped chart regions alongside the full page solved this. In our testing, chart-upload matching went from 3 of 7 parts correct with whole-page indexing to 7 of 7 with chart-band crops. We define the crop Regions as fractions of the page, which keeps them correct across datasheet resolutions.
- Filter results when the engineer names a part – Cross-modal text-to-image similarity alone doesn’t reliably return the right part’s chart, because a torque curve image contains no visible part name. When the engineer names a specific part, the tool keeps only results from that part’s indexed content, which it identifies by parsing the part folder out of each result’s S3 URI. Because the filter runs in the tool, it works without custom metadata in the index.
- Log every fallback on the image path – The image path returns None on errors and falls through to text retrieval. That fallback is reasonable, but it means a missing s3vectors:QueryVectors permission on the AgentCore runtime execution role doesn’t raise an error. Image-as-query stops working without warning, and the model then names a wrong part with high apparent confidence. The problem is easy to miss during development, because local developer credentials usually have broader permissions than the runtime role. The tool now logs an explicit S3 Vectors image query FAILED warning with the bucket, index, and Region whenever that path falls back. Instrument every silent fallback in a retrieval path, because a hard failure is much easier to diagnose than a quiet one.
Produce formal documents with a fixed specialist chain
Chat uses dynamic routing because the right specialists for a freeform question can’t be known in advance. The Integration Impact Assessment works differently. When an engineer requests an impact assessment for a reference and candidate pair, the required sequence is already known, so the service composes the same specialist factory functions in a fixed order with a purpose-built synthesis prompt.
The resulting document covers interface changes, mechanical integration, electrical integration, thermal integration, qualification delta, and supply chain impact. The narrative sections need LLM synthesis, because the pinout and protocol details must be extracted from ICD prose. The summary statistics (matches, differences, total fields) are computed directly from compare_parts output, so the numbers shown alongside the narrative are exact.
Ground lifecycle claims in live web data through AgentCore Gateway
Catalog data goes out of date, so the Knowledge specialist’s web_search_eol tool checks current end-of-life notices, vendor announcements, and lead times through an AgentCore Gateway with the Web Search connector. The Gateway exposes the connector as a governed Model Context Protocol (MCP) endpoint. Because the Gateway also handles managed knowledge base retrieval, you can attach policy and observability to both external and internal data access in one place.
Deploy to AgentCore runtime
For production, you package the agent as an ARM64 container, push it to Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR), and AgentCore runtime hosts it serverlessly with session isolation and auto scaling. Notebook 03 in the GitHub repository walks through this deployment as a reference recipe, covering the Dockerfile, the build and push commands, the execution-role permissions, and the Cedar policy. The notebook shows these steps without running them. Its Dockerfile packages application code that goes beyond the sample, so adapt it to your own application layout before you build. The following diagram shows the deployment path from agent code to a hosted AgentCore runtime endpoint.
Give each image an immutable tag. A runtime that has already resolved the digest behind a moving :latest tag keeps serving the old image after you push a new one. Prompt, router, and tool changes all require a new image and a new runtime version to take effect.
The runtime role needs bedrock:InvokeModel, bedrock:Retrieve, bedrock-agentcore:InvokeGateway, and s3vectors:QueryVectors for the image-as-query path. The Cedar policy shown in notebook 03 encodes the human-in-the-loop rules, requiring a prior evaluation before memos and an audit log entry on every substitution decision. The application enforces these rules in its own logic today, and attaching the policy to a Cedar authorization engine is the next step.
Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings is now available in AWS GovCloud (US), which matters for aerospace and defense programs subject to data residency, ITAR, and FedRAMP requirements that govern where a workload can run. The multimodal retrieval and visual similarity capabilities this post depends on are reachable inside an AWS GovCloud (US) boundary. Availability of Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore features varies by AWS Region, so check AWS Services by Region before you plan a deployment.
Evaluating the assistant
We measure quality in two ways, with continuous online scoring through AgentCore Evaluations, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and offline validation against curated query sets.
AgentCore online evaluation
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations, generally available since March 2026, scores agent traces using LLM-as-a-judge techniques. It reads the OpenTelemetry traces that Strands agents already emit, so an instrumented agent needs no application changes to be evaluated. The service offers two modes. Online evaluation continuously samples live production sessions, and on-demand evaluation runs programmatic tests that fit into a continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipeline.
We use online evaluation, with results published to Amazon CloudWatch for dashboards and alarms. Notebook 05 in the GitHub repository creates an online evaluation configuration and sends test queries to the deployed runtime to generate sessions for scoring.
Thirteen built-in evaluators ship with the service, alongside support for custom evaluators defined by a prompt or hosted as an AWS Lambda function. We enable seven, spanning all three scoring levels:
| Level | Evaluator | What it scores | 
| Session | Goal Success Rate | Did the conversation achieve the user’s goal end to end? | 
| Trace | Correctness | Is the information factually accurate? | 
| Trace | Helpfulness | Is the response useful and valuable? | 
| Trace | Faithfulness | Is the response faithful to the retrieved context? | 
| Trace | Response Relevance | Does the response address the user’s actual query? | 
| Tool call | Tool Selection Accuracy | Did the agent pick the right tool? | 
| Tool call | Tool Parameter Accuracy | Did the agent extract parameters correctly? | 
The curated query set holds 36 queries across six categories: catalog discovery (8), Knowledge and ICD retrieval (8), multi-specialist chains (6), deterministic evaluation (5), text-to-visual retrieval (5), and human-in-the-loop safety refusals (4) that assert the agent refuses to recommend or approve. Each query carries its expected catalog part IDs, except the safety queries, where the expected outcome is a refusal.
Results
AgentCore samples live sessions on an ongoing basis, so each evaluator’s score is a moving aggregate that shifts as traffic accumulates and as the agent changes. The following numbers are a snapshot from the synthetic dataset run. Use them as a baseline for setting CloudWatch alarm thresholds, and expect the numbers from your own runs to differ.
| Level | Evaluator | Score (30-day avg) | 
| Session | Goal Success Rate | 0.892 | 
| Trace | Correctness | 0.968 | 
| Trace | Helpfulness | 0.956 | 
| Trace | Faithfulness | 0.981 | 
| Trace | Response Relevance | 0.968 | 
| Tool call | Tool Selection Accuracy | 0.861 | 
| Tool call | Tool Parameter Accuracy | 0.980 | 
All trace-level quality metrics scored at or above 0.95, and tool parameter extraction was near-perfect at 0.980. The most notable improvement between evaluation runs was Tool Selection Accuracy, which rose from 0.809 to 0.861. Three changes drove the gain: consolidating to a single managed knowledge base, fixing a missing permission on the image-as-query path that had caused silent fallback to text search, and tightening the planner’s routing to avoid chaining unnecessary specialists.
Goal Success Rate is lower, at 0.892, because of how the query set is designed. The query set includes safety-category prompts that ask the agent to recommend or approve a substitution. The agent correctly refuses, but the evaluator scores a correct refusal as an unmet goal. We expect this result, because in a human-in-the-loop system the agent must not approve a substitution on its own.
Adapt the pattern to your own catalog
The code is a reusable pattern that works for other part categories, beyond reaction wheels. Swapping domains requires three changes: replace the parts data (a specs.json, description, ICD, datasheet page, and photo per part), edit the requirements schema to define your category’s critical specs and tolerance rules, and point the knowledge base at your S3 corpus. The agents, tools, and scoring engine carry over unchanged. Because the deterministic tools in mei_core are plain Python functions, a PLM or ERP integration can call score_substitution_fit directly, with no agent in the loop.
Clean up
To avoid ongoing charges, delete the resources you created:
- Delete the AgentCore runtime agent and its Amazon ECR repository.
- Delete the AgentCore Gateway and its Web Search and knowledge base targets.
- Delete the online evaluation configuration and the CloudWatch alarms you created.
- Delete the managed knowledge base and the S3 Vectors index.
- Delete the S3 bucket holding the parts corpus.
Conclusion
In this post, we showed how to build a multi-agent engineering assistant that replaces manual part substitution research with automated evidence assembly. The architecture pairs Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings, which handles visual similarity scoring and chart retrieval that text-only systems miss, with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, which provides the production scaffolding of runtime hosting, Gateway-governed retrieval and web search, and quality evaluations. Three design choices matter most. Deterministic code produces every pass/fail verdict, each task runs on the smallest of the three model tiers that handles it well, and only the engineer can approve a substitution.
To get started, clone the GitHub repository, run the notebooks with your own AWS account, and swap in your parts catalog and requirements schema. To go deeper on the retrieval foundations, read Manufacturing intelligence with Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings and A practical guide to Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings. For production agent patterns, see the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore documentation and the Strands Agents SDK.

articles.title: Le télescope Swift va se désintégrer dans quelques jours, et la Nasa n'est même pas inquiète
articles.text:
Dernier vol pour Swift. Désormais, le télescope spatial mis en orbite 22 ans auparavant est en train de vivre ses derniers moments dans l’espace avant de finir désintégré dans l’atmosphère. Après une perte d’altitude due aux bombardements solaires, puis une mission de sauvetage d’urgence qui a échoué, tous les instruments de Swift ont été coupés et sa chute devrait intervenir prochainement.
Pour l’instant, le télescope se trouve sous les radars de la Nasa et de l’US Space Force et le but est de savoir où et quand aura lieu la chute. D’après un article du site Space.com, les simulations indiquent que Swift devrait retomber dans l’atmosphère le vendredi 7 novembre 2026. Les équipes de la Pennsylvania State University ont fait en sorte que tout soit coupé et que le télescope puisse redescendre « naturellement » sous l’effet de la densité atmosphérique.
Tout se jouera en quelques minutes pour le télescope Swift
Pour commencer, une bonne nouvelle : Swift était déjà la semaine dernière sous la barre des 275 kilomètres d’altitude, ce qui signifie qu’il a évité la plupart des constellations de satellites situées plus haut et avec qui il aurait pu entrer en collision, même si les chances sont minces. Il est également plus bas que la Station spatiale internationale (ISS) et pourra donc continuer sa chute sans aucun risque.
Pas d’inquiétude à avoir non plus au sol. Le télescope a beau être plus gros qu’un satellite Starlink qui tombe sur Terre quotidiennement, il y a de fortes probabilités pour qu’il soit entièrement désintégré en arrivant dans l’atmosphère. Cela se passera en quelques minutes lorsqu’il arrivera à une altitude de 120 kilomètres. Le frottement de l’air va chauffer la carcasse du télescope, les panneaux solaires et les antennes vont se désintégrer, puis le reste une fois à 78 kilomètres dans les airs.
Un risque insignifiant, qui n’inquiète pas la Nasa
Il n’est pas complètement exclu que certaines parties du télescope retombent au sol, mais les chances sont extrêmement maigres. Et puis si c’est tout de même le cas, tout porte à croire que ce serait dans l’océan. Pour l’instant, les simulations orbitales indiquent que la chute aurait lieu sur une latitude de 21 degrés en dessous de l’équateur.
Swift pourrait donc tomber quelque part du côté de Sao Paulo du nord du Chili, ou encore vers l’Afrique du sud ou le Botswana, voire l’Australie. Mais dans la plupart des cas, cette bande traverse essentiellement les océans. Il est donc extrêmement peu probable qu’il y ait un quelconque accident. D’ailleurs, la Nasa n’a même pas publié de déclaration de risque, ce qui signifie que le danger est bien trop faible pour faire l’objet d’une communication publique.
Le lieu de la chute ne sera connu avec précision que lorsque le télescope sera presque déjà désintégré, ce qui signifie qu’il n’y aura que quelques minutes de délai. Ce n’est qu’après que, selon la localisation, la Nasa pourra chercher quelques fragments du télescope, sachant que tous les instruments scientifiques ne sont pas les morceaux les plus solides, et que rien d’identifiable ne pourra être détecté.

articles.title: „Wir Vibe-Coder sind gefundenes Fressen für Hacker“
articles.text:
„Wir Vibe-Coder sind gefundenes Fressen für Hacker“
Obwohl er nicht programmieren kann, baut Ben Sufiani, Gründer der Plattform Pirate Skills, Websites, Apps und KI-Agenten. Vibe-Coding bringt ihm zwar Chancen, jedoch auch Abhängigkeiten und mehr Verantwortung. Wie er damit umgeht, teilt er im Podcast t3n Arbeit in Progress. Das Interview ist gekürzt, die vollständige Fassung gibt es in der verlinkten Podcast-Folge.
t3n: Was ist Vibe-Coding und was Vibe-Design?
Ben Sufiani: Ich entwickle Software allein mit meiner natürlichen Sprache. Das war vorher Entwicklern vorbehalten. Es ist eine Art Hogwarts-Moment: Wir Muggel, die Nichtprogrammierer, lernen auf diese Art und Weise zaubern. Beim Vibe-Design spreche ich und das Design entsteht vor meinen Augen, während ich spreche. Man kann iterieren, wie man es früher mit einer Designagentur gemacht hat.
t3n: Welche Tricks nutzt du, wo dir Wissen fehlt?
Früher hätte man von einem T-shaped Skillset geträumt: Du weißt von allem etwas und hast ein oder zwei tiefe Skills. Meine tiefen Skills waren früher immer Analytics und Performance-Marketing. Schwächen habe ich in Design und Softwareentwicklung. Für diese Schwächen schaue ich nach etablierten Lösungen und vor allen Dingen Skills, die eine Vorlage für Agents sind, für Softwareentwicklung. Dafür suche ich auf der Plattform skills.sh. Ich mache viel mit next.js. Damit konnte ich selbst eine Website entwickeln und weg von WordPress gehen. Von Vercel gibt es verschiedene Skills, das ist wie ein Auffangbecken für meine mangelnden Skills und bewahrt mich vor den schlimmsten Fehlern. Mit dem Design ist es schwieriger, weil es auch Geschmackssache ist – vor meinem eigenen schlechten Geschmack kann ich mich schlecht schützen. Aber ich kann mir vom ein Buffet von Designrichtungen bieten lassen und selbst der Kurator sein.
Wie prüfst du den Code deines KI-Agenten CaptainAI?
Ich nutze einen stabilen Tech-Stack, den die KI gut kennt. Ich nutze als Web-Framework, also mein WordPress-Ersatz, Next.js. Das kennt die KI hervorragend in- und auswendig. Der Hoster Vercel protokolliert für mich alle Fehler bei Nutzern. Mein Agent liest sie regelmäßig aus. Ist der Fall klar, behebt er sie direkt. Im Zweifelsfall werden sie mit mir besprochen. Das heißt, man baut sich einen Apparat um ein Produkt herum, das konstant die Lage beobachtet. In voller Ausbaustufe heißt das Software Factory.
Du musst dich permanent auf Künstliche Intelligenz verlassen, etwa bei der Einschätzung von Fehlern. Wie gehst du damit um? Hast du noch jemanden im Hintergrund, der für dich etwas überprüft?
Nein, ich habe niemanden im Hintergrund, außer die Agents. In meiner Beobachtung ist es manchmal sogar vorteilhaft, nicht alles zu verstehen. Dann hat man keine Befangenheit. Außerdem kann ich mich beraten lassen. Für lange Konversationen nutze ich Whisperflow. Mit dem Tool kann ich einfach reden. Ich gebe so viel Kontext und teile meine Bedenken. Über die Zeit entwickelt man so eine gewisse Kompetenz und sieht, wann es nochmal bessere Antworten braucht. Ich hatte jetzt noch keine größeren Incidents. Wir sollten uns nur nicht vormachen, dass wir Vibe-Coder nicht gefundenes Fressen für Hacker sind. Es gehört sehr viel Verantwortung dazu, Vibe-Coding vernünftig zu nutzen. Und wer da draußen suggeriert „Du kannst mit diesem Framework von Github in einem Satz die ganze Adobe Suite klauen“ erzählt Schwachsinn.
Was macht professionelles, sicheres Vibe-Coding aus?
Vibe-Coding hebt den Boden für Leute, die vorher gar nicht programmieren konnten. Das komplementäre Stück dazu nennt sich Agentic Engineering. Wenn wir über diese Software-Factories reden, dann reden wir deutlich mehr über Agentic Engineering als nur Vibe Coding, das immer den Beigeschmack von diesem One-Shot-Prompt hat. Vibe-Coder müssen sechs Kernbereiche beherrschen: Produktmanagement, Tools, User Experience, skalierbare Systeme, Security und Compliance sowie Shipping.
Podcast t3n Arbeit in Progress anhören
Ihr könnt den Podcast t3n Arbeit in Progress bequem in der Podcast-App eurer Wahl abonnieren. In der Regel findet ihr den Podcast einfach über die Eingabe „t3n Arbeit in Progress“ in der Suche. Ansonsten könnt ihr auch den RSS-Feed manuell in der App eingeben.

articles.title: Black Friday AliExpress : coureurs et cyclistes sur route, ce casque Shokz à oreilles libres tombe à 92,09€
articles.text:
Depuis le 1er novembre, le Single Day d’AliExpress s’accompagne de codes de réduction réservés aux lecteurs de Clubic, déclenchés selon le montant du panier. Le Shokz OpenRun Pro 2 y descend à 92,09 € avec le code CLU13, soit 33,31 € de moins qu’à notre précédent relais fin octobre, pour un casque pensé d’abord pour la route.
Shokz a bâti sa gamme sur une idée simple : écouter de la musique en courant sans boucher ses oreilles. Lancé à 199,99 € en septembre 2024, l’OpenRun Pro 2 en est la déclinaison la plus aboutie, avec un haut-parleur réservé aux basses en plus de la conduction osseuse.
Pour le 11.11, la fiche AliExpress l’affiche à 105,09 €, et le code CLU13 retire 13 € dès 79 € d’achat pour atteindre 92,09 €. Le casque est expédié depuis la France par la boutique Core Tech Store. L’offre parle surtout aux coureurs et cyclistes qui s’entraînent sur route, bien moins à ceux qui veulent s’isoler du bruit.
Le Shokz OpenRun Pro 2 passe à 92,09 € sur AliExpress avec le code CLU13, contre 105,09 € affichés sur sa fiche pendant le Single Day.
Pourquoi choisir le Shokz OpenRun Pro 2 ?
- Deux transducteurs par côté : Shokz partage le travail entre la conduction osseuse, chargée des médiums et des aigus, et un haut-parleur à conduction aérienne dédié aux basses. C’est sa réponse au rendu creux que l’on reproche d’ordinaire à ce format, sans rien glisser dans le conduit auditif.
- Une recharge qui rattrape un oubli : Shokz annonce 12 heures d’écoute, et cinq minutes branché suffisent à récupérer environ 2 h 30. Le port USB-C, protégé par un cache étanche, se contente d’un câble ordinaire.
- Un arceau à la bonne taille : Le modèle standard S820 pèse environ 30 g, et une version mini S821 raccourcit l’arceau de 21 mm pour les têtes plus étroites. L’offre porte sur le S820 : contrôlez la référence sélectionnée avant de valider.
Courir de nuit sur route : ce que changent les oreilles libres
Avec les jours qui raccourcissent, beaucoup de sorties se font à la nuit tombée, sur des routes où entendre une voiture arriver compte autant que le rythme de la playlist. C’est le terrain de l’OpenRun Pro 2 : ses transducteurs se posent devant l’oreille et laissent passer les bruits ambiants. Sa certification IP55 le protège de la sueur et de la pluie, et le site allemand Netzwelt l’a même passé sous l’eau courante sans dommage. Ses mesures donnent plutôt une dizaine d’heures d’autonomie réelle, soit environ trois semaines entre deux charges pour trois sorties d’une heure par semaine.
Le profil type : le coureur urbain, le cycliste sur route ouverte, le marcheur qui écoute des podcasts en gardant une oreille sur la circulation. La connexion multipoint permet de rester associé au téléphone et à l’ordinateur à la fois. Il convient nettement moins aux trajets en transports, où le son s’échappe vers vos voisins à volume élevé, et près d’un axe très fréquenté, le volume maximal peut sembler juste. Les nageurs regarderont ailleurs, l’IP55 n’autorisant pas l’immersion.
Face à l’OpenRun classique et aux écouteurs ouverts, ce que vaut ce prix
Chez Shokz, l’OpenRun classique reste vendu 139 € sur la boutique de la marque, avec une étanchéité IP67 mais 8 heures d’autonomie et sans haut-parleur de basses. Pendant l’opération, le modèle Pro 2 coûte donc moins cher que le prix public de son petit frère. L’autre voie passe par les écouteurs ouverts à crochet, comme les Shokz OpenFit 2 et OpenFit Pro retenus dans notre comparatif des meilleurs écouteurs pour le sport, qui se passent d’arceau derrière la nuque. L’OpenRun Pro 2 se limite en revanche au codec SBC, suffisant pour un podcast, moins pour une écoute attentive.
✅ Les points forts
- DualPitch : des basses plus présentes qu’en conduction osseuse seule
- 92,09 € avec CLU13, sous le prix public de l’OpenRun classique
- IP55 et port USB-C protégé, adaptés à la pluie et à la sueur
- Environ 2 h 30 d’écoute récupérées en cinq minutes de charge
- Deux tailles d’arceau et connexion multipoint
❌ Les limites
- Autonomie réelle plus proche de 10 heures que des 12 annoncées
- Volume maximal un peu juste près d’une route très passante
- Fuite sonore à fort volume, gênante dans les transports
- Codec SBC uniquement, micros sensibles au vent en course
Le code CLU13 ne s’active qu’à partir de 79 € de panier : le casque seul suffit à le déclencher, pour un total de 92,09 € chez AliExpress.
À 92,09 €, l’OpenRun Pro 2 coûte 33,31 € de moins qu’à notre relais du 22 octobre, et moins de la moitié de son prix de lancement. C’est le tarif le plus bas parmi ceux que nous avons relayés pour ce modèle, expédié depuis la France. Pour un coureur ou un cycliste qui veut garder l’oreille sur la circulation pendant ses sorties d’hiver, l’offre mérite clairement l’examen.
Ceux qui cherchent avant tout un son riche, une isolation dans le métro ou un compagnon de piscine seront mieux servis ailleurs : ce n’est pas le métier de ce casque. Des écouteurs intra-auriculaires classiques répondront mieux à ces besoins. Vérifiez aussi la taille de l’arceau, la version mini visant les têtes plus étroites.

articles.title: Liquid-Cooled NVIDIA Servers at the ASRock Rack OCP 2026 Booth
articles.text:
At OCP Global Summit 2026 in San Jose, we stopped by the ASRock Rack booth and saw a broad set of NVIDIA systems. That included a full NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 rack. Next to it were HGX Rubin NVL8 servers in both 2U and 5U, two NVIDIA MGX RTX PRO servers, and a dual NVIDIA Vera CPU server. We also spotted the liquid-cooled NVIDIA Spectrum-X SN6600-LD switch and the passively cooled NVIDIA RTX PRO 4500 Blackwell Server Edition GPU.
A big theme was liquid cooling. ASRock Rack used direct-to-chip liquid cooling on its rack-scale system and HGX servers, including an 8x RTX PRO 6000 PCIe server.
ASRock Rack XGMRACK-VR/NVL72 NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72
The XGMRACK-VR/NVL72 is ASRock Rack’s version of the NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72. It is a 48RU NVIDIA MGX rack with a 5000A busbar and a liquid manifold. Inside are 18 Vera Rubin compute trays and nine NVLink 6 switch trays, for a total of 36 NVIDIA Vera CPUs and 72 NVIDIA Rubin GPUs.
NVIDIA lists the full rack at 3,600 PFLOPS of NVFP4 inference (sparse) and 2,520 PFLOPS of NVFP4 training (dense). It has 20.7TB of HBM4, and each Rubin GPU gets 288GB. Power comes from four 3RU 19″ power shelves. Each shelf is rated at 110kW and uses six 18.3kW PSUs plus bulk capacitors. ASRock Rack offers in-rack, in-row, RDHx, or liquid-to-air sidecar CDU options.
Each compute tray is a 1U NVIDIA MGX design with two Vera Rubin Superchips. Each Superchip connects two Rubin GPUs to one Vera CPU over NVLink-C2C. Networking is eight 800Gbps OSFP ports from NVIDIA ConnectX-9 SuperNICs, plus two 400Gbps QSFP112 ports from an NVIDIA BlueField-4 DPU. There are even management switches up top for the lower-speed networking.
The trays are fully liquid-cooled, which helps lower the total power consumption in the rack, and is something that NVIDIA has been advancing along with its partners for a few generations now.
For those who want a more traditional HGX 8-GPU form factor, there were options for that as well, but with a twist.
ASRock Rack 2U16X-GNR2/DLC RUBIN with NVIDIA HGX Rubin NVL8
The 2U16X-GNR2/DLC RUBIN was one of the most impressive systems at the booth. It puts an NVIDIA HGX Rubin NVL8 board, with eight Rubin GPUs, into a 2U chassis. It is fully liquid-cooled, covering the E1.S drives, CPUs, and GPUs, with no fans. Networking includes NVIDIA ConnectX-9 SuperNICs and BlueField-4 DPUs. Power comes in over a 54V DC busbar.
The host is a dual-socket Intel Xeon 6 platform. It supports the Xeon 6700P, 6500P, and 6700E series in LGA 4710 sockets, with 16+16 DIMM slots at 2DPC. While it supports other series, given the cost of the rest of the system, we would imagine the vast majority of folks buying these will opt for the Xeon 6700P series.
There are eight 800Gbps OSFP ports via NVIDIA ConnectX-9, along with 8x hot-swap E1.S NVMe bays. NVIDIA quotes 400 PFLOPS of NVFP4 compute (sparse) for HGX Rubin NVL8.
The HGX 8-GPU platform underwent major changes in this generation, including a change in GPU orientation in the tray. This change enables it to work in high-density, liquid-cooled racks.
There was more in the booth, including hybrid-cooled servers, so let us get to those next.

articles.title: Vigilancia con drones y multas de hasta 45.000 euros: así controla la policía de Vilanova de Arousa (Pontevedra) a los vecinos que tiran mal la basura
articles.text:
En Vilanova de Arousa (Pontevedra), la Policía Local también usa drones para controlar los vertidos ilegales. Los agentes persiguen a los ciudadanos que dejan muebles o escombros en la vía pública. Se les advierte de sanciones que pueden llegar a ser de 45.000 euros. Pero esa cifra no es una multa acreditada por un error de contenedor.
Se trata de una búsqueda de posibles orígenes. Cuando encuentran algún residuo, buscan con el dron si hay alguna obra cercana. Según explica uno de los agentes, “el infractor suele estar más cerca de lo que parece”. Algunas de las conductas que han detectado son, por ejemplo, dejar somieres en la acera o tirar pintura en zonas verdes. Para advertir de la vigilancia también han puesto carteles.
Este tipo de vigilancia aérea ya está registrada desde agosto de 2025. En ese momento se hablaba de un protocolo policial para combatir los vertidos que incluía este tipo de vigilancia junto a registros de grabación y alerta ciudadana para detectar responsables.
Las sanciones dependen de la infracción
Los agentes hablan de sanciones de 200 o 500 euros, hasta 45.000 en función de la peligrosidad. Es importante destacar que en este caso estamos ante situaciones diferentes a la de error de contenedor (por ejemplo, en el caso de dejar residuos de reforma o bien de sustancias peligrosas).
Además, tampoco es cierto que sea el límite máximo de la legislación. El artículo 84 de la ley gallega especifica que las infracciones graves tienen unas sanciones de 901 a 45.000 euros. Para los residuos peligrosos es otro escalado.
Por otro lado, la ley estatal sobre residuos establece que las infracciones graves tienen unos límites de 2.001 a 100.000 euros. Si son residuos peligrosos o bien suelos contaminados, estos límites aumentan. También se tipifica como leve el hecho de depositar residuos domésticos y comerciales (no peligrosos) fuera de lo establecido en las ordenanzas locales.
En cualquier caso, es necesario conocer cuál es la infracción que se le imputa al ciudadano y qué normativa se aplica. Además, se debe resolver de manera motivada tras abrir el correspondiente expediente.
Ya hemos contado cómo se usaban los drones para controlar piscinas. En Vilanova explican que hacen una búsqueda de indicios y posibles responsables cerca de los residuos.
Qué ocurre con los datos personales
En la guía sobre drones de la AEPD se diferencian los casos en los que no se tratan datos personales de aquellos en los que se obtienen de manera accidental o bien se pretende tratarlos (como ocurre en videovigilancia). El hecho de que aparezcan personas identificables en la imagen de la cámara tiene implicaciones diferentes a que solo haya un montón de escombros.
Desde la Agencia Española de Protección de Datos se recomienda que se capture lo estrictamente necesario. Se debe evitar guardar información que no sea relevante para el fin del vuelo. Por ejemplo, se pueden poner restricciones de resolución o activar/desactivar las capturas durante el vuelo.
Hay un precedente concreto en la resolución sobre Fuenlabrada de 2021. En ella se analiza el uso de drones por parte de la Policía Local para el control de tráfico. Se señala que se cumple con el deber de información (hay carteles, redes sociales y web municipal). También se concluye que es necesario llevar a cabo una evaluación de impacto previa.
Tras analizar toda la documentación facilitada (incluida la evaluación de impacto), se ha decidido archivar el expediente. Esto es en el contexto de ese sistema de tráfico. No podemos generalizar a otros sistemas (como el de residuos de Vilanova) ni sacar conclusiones automáticas.
