articles.title: INEC’s AI photo problem is deeper than registration officers
articles.text:
AI-generated photographs in Nigeria’s preliminary voter register raise a question that goes beyond the technology used to create them: how did suspicious entries get into a database meant to establish who can vote? Ahead of the 2027 general election, the controversy puts the Independent National Electoral Commission’s (INEC) verification procedures, access controls, and accountability under scrutiny—not simply its ability to detect synthetic images.
The preliminary register lists more than 103 million voters, up from approximately 93 million in 2023. While INEC attributes this surge to new registrations, persistent questions surrounding anomalous records have intensified demands for a clearer accounting of how raw records are checked—and who bears responsibility when systemic irregularities slip through.
Speaking on ARISE News, Clement Nwankwo, director of the Policy and Legal Advocacy Centre (PLAC), challenged the register’s credibility, pointing to alleged AI-generated photographs and unexplained statistical surges in registered voters. His concerns underscore a broader institutional test for INEC: removing dubious entries is only a starting point; the commission must demonstrate that its entire pipeline for collecting, verifying, and auditing electoral data is robust and trustworthy.
Responding to these criticisms on 30 October, Lawrence Bayode, INEC’s director of information and communication technology (ICT), stated that the commission was working to address irregularities ahead of releasing the final register on 15 December 2026.
However, Bayode’s explanation exposed a deeper operational vulnerability: some suspicious entries were inserted directly by registration officers holding authorised access to INEC’s core database.
Bayode acknowledged that registration officers across multiple states introduced irregularities into the system, encompassing both AI-generated imagery and flawed registration conduct.
“They have access to register people,” Bayode said, noting that the commission flagged these discrepancies during automated biometric identification system (ABIS) checks.
This admission complicates the narrative that generative technology is the primary culprit behind vulnerabilities in voter lists. While generative AI simplifies the creation of synthetic visuals, the core issue identified by INEC stems from insider privileges—the individuals authorised to operate registration terminals and the governance controls surrounding their access.
This breakdown raises critical questions regarding internal oversight: how are registration officers monitored in real time, what validation rules are run before data is committed to the master database, and why were suspicious records not quarantined before reaching the public preliminary register?
The incident also highlights the boundaries of automated safeguards. While biometric algorithms can detect duplicate prints or abnormal features, their efficacy depends on the integrity of the submitted data, effective workflow design, and rigorous follow-through on flagged anomalies.
INEC has yet to specify how many AI-generated photos or invalid entries were detected, how many officers were implicated, or what disciplinary or legal actions have been initiated. Without these details, public stakeholders cannot accurately gauge the scale of the compromise or evaluate whether existing safeguards are sufficient to restore trust.
A bigger register and a transparency problem
INEC reported registering over 11 million individuals during its Continuous Voter Registration (CVR) drive for the 2027 polls. Automated biometric checks subsequently purged roughly 1.2 million invalid entries, thereby adding over 9 million voters to the 93 million recorded in 2023.
According to Bayode, the automated filtering yielded the preliminary total of more than 103 million voters.
Yet the significant expansion has fueled public concern, particularly because observers and electors continue to identify glaring errors within the published rolls.
The issue extends beyond numerical growth to whether citizens can independently scrutinise data updates and verify INEC’s methodologies. Public transparency is paramount given statutory publishing mandates and the discrepancies already uncovered.
Under Section 19(1) of the Electoral Act, INEC is required to publish and display the preliminary voter register on its website and at every registration ward and local government office at least 90 days prior to an election. With Presidential and National Assembly elections set for 16 January 2027, the statutory deadline fell on 18 October 2026. Section 20 further obligates the commission to publish the final register at least 30 days before polling, following the claims, objections, and de-duplication process—establishing a mid-December 2026 deadline.
INEC missed the 18 October digital publishing deadline, making the preliminary register available online on 26 October—just 81 days before the election. While the commission argued that physical displays at ward centres from 9 to 15 October satisfied its obligations, physical displays alone fail to fulfil Section 19(1), which explicitly mandates both physical and online availability. This delay compressed the window for public audit and raised valid questions regarding statutory compliance.
The public review phase has further highlighted system discrepancies. Bayode acknowledged receiving complaints concerning missing voter records, clerical errors, and unreflected address transfers. While INEC assured the public that these issues are under review prior to the final publication, resolving individual claims solves only part of the problem. Voters also require transparency around investigation workflows, verification standards, and audit trails.
This scenario illustrates a fundamental principle of digital election management: external crowdsourcing can surface defects, but it cannot replace institutional internal controls. Nor can public scrutiny restore faith without clear visibility into how errors are rectified and prevented.
INEC’s AI ambitions face a governance test
These developments unfold as INEC expands its technological footprint and formulates policies to govern artificial intelligence across its operations.
Bayode stated that the commission currently limits AI deployment to low-risk functions, such as public-query chatbots and logistics planning for election materials, emphasising that these tools do not affect core electoral results.
INEC is also finalising a formal AI governance framework ahead of the 2027 polls to establish operational boundaries for automated tools and ensure human oversight over sensitive decisions.
Additionally, the commission established a specialised AI division within its ICT department and engaged with regional initiatives focused on the responsible deployment of AI in elections.
While these steps indicate awareness of technical risks, the voter register controversy highlights why governance cannot focus exclusively on software tools. Governance must address how human operators interact with systems, how user privileges are audited, and how accountability is enforced when internal controls fail.
Bayode pledged to release the AI policy guidelines publicly. Publishing these rules would enable political parties, civil society organisations, and voters to independently evaluate INEC’s operational safeguards.
Trust will depend on what INEC fixes
INEC’s commitment to purge synthetic imagery and resolve data discrepancies before 15 December represents a critical test of its operational responsiveness ahead of 2027.
Yet cleansing the register addresses only the symptom. To rebuild lasting trust, the commission must disclose how rogue data bypassed system checks, identify the institutional vulnerabilities, and detail the technical mechanisms implemented to prevent recurring compromises.
The ongoing dispute reinforces a key reality of digital governance: digitising processes does not inherently guarantee credibility. While technology can streamline administration and flag anomalies, weak access governance and inadequate oversight risk replicating—and amplifying—the very flaws digital tools were deployed to solve.
For INEC, the imperative ahead of 2027 is not merely deploying sophisticated software but proving that the human and technical systems safeguarding Nigeria’s elections are secure, transparent, and fully accountable.
Ultimately, electoral integrity rests not just on the volume of corrupt entries removed, but on whether citizens can trust the pipeline through which their data is collected, verified, and secured.

articles.title: Nuevo sorteo exclusivo para suscriptores de Xataka Xtra: así puedes conseguir un calefactor inteligente Dreo 714S
articles.text:
Noviembre ya no perdona. Las mañanas se han puesto serias, la ducha a primera hora cuesta el doble y el frío empieza a hacer de las suyas. Por suerte, tenemos un sorteo para ponerle remedio: un Dreo Whole-Room Heater 714S, un calefactor inteligente que empieza a soltar calor prácticamente desde que lo enciendes.
El calefactor está valorado en 109,99 euros y su sorteo está reservado a los miembros de Xataka Xtra. Si ya formas parte de la Comunidad, ya sabes de qué va esto. Si todavía no, por solo 30 euros al año puedes acceder a sorteos exclusivos como este, a un catálogo creciente de descuentos en servicios digitales, a un servidor privado de Discord y a línea directa con los editores de Xataka a través de El Consultorio. Tienes toda la información aquí.
Cómo participar en el sorteo de un Dreo 714S
Participar en el sorteo de este calefactor es tan sencillo como formar parte de Xataka Xtra, acceder a tu área de socio y marcar la casilla que aparece señalada en rojo en la imagen inferior. Cuando lo hayas hecho participarás en este sorteo y en todos los que están por venir.
Si ya formas parte de Xataka Xtra y has participado en sorteos anteriores, no tienes que hacer nada. Participarás automáticamente en este y en los futuros. En lo que respecta al sorteo de hoy, estas son las coordenadas:
- Requisitos: ser suscriptor de Xataka Xtra y residente en España.
- Comienzo del sorteo: lunes, 2 de noviembre de 2026.
- Fin del sorteo: viernes, 13 de noviembre, a las 9:00.
- Selección del ganador y resolución: viernes, 13 de noviembre.
¿Cómo se elegirá el ganador? Desde Xataka elegiremos un suscriptor al azar y dos suplentes. Si el ganador no responde en el plazo estipulado en las bases legales de cada sorteo, se pasará al primer suplente y, si este tampoco, al segundo. Ganar un sorteo no impide que puedas ganar en los siguientes. Puedes encontrar las bases legales en este enlace.
En lo que respecta al premio, el Dreo 714S es un calefactor compacto con resistencia cerámica PTC, un tipo de resistencia que se autorregula para no pasarse de temperatura y que empieza a calentar casi al instante, según Dreo. Su cabezal oscila hasta 90 grados en horizontal y 60 en vertical para repartir el calor por la habitación, con una potencia máxima de 2.000 W.
¿E inteligente por qué?. Se controla desde el propio panel, con el mando incluido, desde la app de Dreo o con la voz a través de Alexa y Google Assistant. La app permite programar rutinas (que se encienda cada mañana antes de la ducha, por ejemplo), avisa si detecta una ventana abierta y tiene un modo Eco que apaga el calefactor al llegar a la temperatura fijada y lo vuelve a encender cuando baja un grado.
En nuestro análisis, el dispositivo brilló especialmente en espacios pequeños, como un baño o un despacho de unos 10 metros cuadrados. Para esos rincones a los que la calefacción no termina de llegar, cumple de sobra. Y cuando vuelva el calor, hace de ventilador. ¡Mucha suerte a todos!

articles.title: C'est le moment idéal pour basculer de Windows 10 à Windows 11 avec le support de la version 26H2
articles.text:
Windows 10 : Microsoft propose de passer directement à Windows 11 26H2 sur les PC compatibles
Windows 11 26H2 peut désormais être directement installé depuis les PC Windows 10 compatibles. Il peut s'agir d'un bon moment pour basculer, grâce notamment aux efforts effectués par Microsoft pour rendre l'OS plus performant.
Microsoft Windows 11 Famille
Depuis fin septembre dernier, la mise à jour majeure 26H2 de Windows 11 est disponible. Très légère et permettant surtout d'activer des fonctionnalités dormantes ajoutées au fil de l'eau à l'OS de Microsoft, celle-ci promet surtout de sérieusement améliorer les performances du système d'exploitation grâce à des optimisations variées. C'est surtout vrai sur les PC modestes, où Microsoft annonce de sérieux gains en réactivité.
Avec ce constat en ligne de mire, les réfractaires à Windows 11 utilisant toujours Windows 10, généralement sur un ordinateur vieillissant, ont là un argument solide pour mettre à jour. D'autant que Windows 11 en version 26H2 est directement proposé dans Windows Update sur les PC compatibles, permettant de ne pas avoir à tout réinstaller ou à se compliquer la vie.
Windows 11 se rend désirable et accessible sur Windows 10
Si quelques bugs peuvent éventuellement subsister, Microsoft semble confiant dans son déploiement de la version 26H2, aujourd'hui pleinement disponible pour tous les PC sous Windows 11 24H2 et 25H2. La firme indique : "Windows 11, version 26H2, est désormais disponible pour tous les appareils éligibles. Cette nouvelle version intègre toutes les fonctionnalités récemment annoncées dans les versions 25H2 et 24H2 de Windows 11, et sera déployée via la technologie de mise à jour, offrant ainsi une installation rapide."
Si la mise à jour vers Windows 11 26H2 n'est pas proposée dans Windows Update, plusieurs méthodes permettent de faire la transition malgré tout. Un assistant dédié est notamment de la partie.
Pour les personnes qui préfèrent toujours attendre ou qui ne sont pas éligibles à Windows 11, rappelons que les PC Windows 10 utilisant le support étendu (prolongé jusqu’au 12 octobre 2027) ont encore un peu de temps devant eux. Il reste également toujours la solution de passer sur Linux, dont le regain de popularité ne semble pas vouloir faiblir.

articles.title: OpenAI's plan to make data centers less hated: Rename them "compute campuses"
articles.text:
WTF?! With all the negativity associated with the facilities, it's fair to say that the term data center has become a dirty word. OpenAI is well aware of this, which is why the company wants to call them something else: compute campuses.
An OpenAI spokesperson told Business Insider about the rebrand. "Compute campuses better describes the scale and role of the infrastructure we're building for AI," the spokesperson said. "These are long-term investments in computing, energy infrastructure and skilled work."
It seems that the ChatGPT maker is trying to appeal to those living near data centers by convincing them that they are part of this beautiful AI revolution.
"We want the communities hosting that infrastructure to help shape it and share in the opportunities it creates," the OpenAI spokesperson added.
Whether the locals angry about the noise, pollution, falling house prices, increased water consumption, and higher electricity bills will care about this shaping and sharing remains to be seen.
Several companies have tried offering incentives to local residents to appease them (or convince them not to sue), but even handing over thousands of dollars isn't enough to tempt many people. A survey from earlier this year found more Americans would rather live next to a nuclear power plant than a data center.
Data centers have become one of the most contentious topics in US politics. President Trump, who has long supported the building of the facilities, recently said that the companies behind them should make financial deals with local communities to win over residents. But similar incentives, including the promise of a $10,000 "grant" from a data center developer in Pennsylvania, have failed to convince people in the past.
Some data center supporters have accused those who oppose them of being influenced by Chinese social media campaigns designed to slow America's AI advantage – even though these campaigns use facts that are actually true. Fox News even compared the pushback to protesting against tank and plane factories during World War II.
OpenAI appears to be taking the lead in this name change, but it wouldn't be the first time that a technology has started being called something else recently.
In September, Trump signed an executive order renaming artificial intelligence to "superintelligence," turning AI into SI. The Department of Justice was an early adopter of this term, using it in a statement about a fraud case. Meanwhile, Elon Musk was so committed that he renamed SpaceXAI to SpaceXSI.

articles.title: FBI Flags Over 600 Addresses Tied to North Korea’s Binance Heist
articles.text:
The FBI has formally blamed North Korean state-sponsored hackers for the record-breaking Binance cryptocurrency heist and is asking the crypto industry to help stop the stolen funds from being laundered.
The attack was conducted on October 29. Hackers emptied Binance hot wallets on multiple blockchains, moving most of the funds out within roughly 20 minutes. Binance estimates the impact at roughly $6.3 billion, the largest crypto theft on record.
Within hours, blockchain intelligence firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis linked the attack to the North Korean group TraderTraitor. Binance initially said the intrusion may have started with a DevOps engineer’s compromised laptop, and pledged to cover all losses.
The FBI released its attribution on October 31, two days after the theft.
“The FBI, together with partners at the USSS and IRS-CI, has observed TraderTraitor actors converting stolen assets primarily into Ethereum (ETH). It is expected these assets will then be further laundered by converting them using DeFi and instant swap services as they prepare them for further laundering stages,” the agency said.
The alert names 608 Ethereum addresses, 19 Bitcoin addresses and one Solana address that currently hold, or previously held, proceeds of the theft.
Together with the Secret Service and IRS-CI, the FBI called on THORChain node operators, RPC node operators, instant exchanges, DeFi services and blockchain analytics firms to refuse transactions linked to these addresses.
The FBI previously blamed the same group for the $1.5 billion Bybit hack in February 2025.
Binance says the attack went beyond one laptop
Binance has since expanded on its early findings. “Our initial investigation suggested that the security incident may have involved a compromised laptop, however our subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach,” Binance co-CEO Richard Teng said in a statement.
Teng described the incident as a complex attack that “was not carried out by one person.” He said the attacker also deployed a self-destruct mechanism that wiped its tooling and evidence, complicating the investigation.
He said the attacker’s use of Ethereum’s EIP-7702 delegation feature “did not pass through our normal approval controls.” Binance has not yet detailed the additional breach points, and has promised a technical post-mortem once the facts are verified.
Binance began a phased resumption of withdrawals on November 1, starting with the Bitcoin network. By mid-morning on Sunday, it said it had processed about $4.6 billion in withdrawals and $1 billion in deposits.
According to the exchange, about 95% of the stolen amount has now been replaced using company funds, and Binance is buying the remaining less liquid tokens on the market and through over-the-counter deals.
“Our commitment remains clear: Binance will absorb the financial impact of the stolen funds, not our users,” Teng said.
Laundering appears to be automated
Blockchain analytics firm Elliptic puts the theft at $6.43 billion across 11 blockchains. Of that, it has confirmed $2.85 billion as frozen or seized on-chain.
According to Elliptic’s latest figures, the attacker controls about $3.25 billion in assets that no issuer can freeze, spread across more than 800 addresses. These include roughly 584,000 ETH, 18,327 BTC and 233 million XRP.
“In the Bybit hack, the laundering followed human working patterns. The Binance funds are being moved by something that does not sleep,” Elliptic said.
The main wallet distributing funds on Tron kept paying out hourly for more than a day, around the clock. When a cross-chain bridge refused deposits, the system rerouted the money to the same destination through freshly created wallets.
By late October 31, about $196 million had flowed from that wallet to roughly 200 other wallets. THORChain was the largest exit route, at about $31 million.
Elliptic said on-chain data cannot show whether the automation relies on AI agents or conventional scripts. It expects the laundering to take months, as it did after the Bybit heist.
Chainalysis also reported laundering patterns indicating automation, including thousands of transactions in a short period and many new addresses whose first transfer was exactly 1 TRX.
Related: $2 Million+ Drained From Polymarket Traders in New Supply Chain Attack
Related: Hackers Return $263 Million Stolen From Liquid Network

articles.title: Munich’s Marble Cognition raises €3.35 million to build AI coworkers that learn business processes before automating them | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Marble Cognition (Marble), a Munich-based startup building AI coworkers that understand how work is executed to optimise and automate business operations, has raised €3.35 million ($3.75 million) in a pre-Seed round.
The round was co-led by Heartcore and Seedcamp, with participation from angels including a board member of Datadog, a founder of Personio, and executives from McKinsey, Mistral AI and Lovable. The funding will scale inference, grow the engineering team in Munich, and support a US launch.
Reshma Sohoni, General Partner at Seedcamp, said, “Seedcamp has a long tradition of backing founders who change how we work, from UiPath and Synthesia to Marble today. Most companies want to automate more, but the hard part has always been mapping out how the work gets done. Marble fills that gap, giving companies vital context for AI transformations that could define their future. We’re proud to back them from the start.”
Marble Cognition was founded in late 2025 by Felix Rösner and Christophe Schmit, who met at Munich’s CDTM programme. The company states that it learns how work actually gets done inside a company, turns it into systems AI can read, and then deploys Marble Coworkers: AI agents that take over manual white-collar work.
The company highlighted that, in an era when software is becoming a commodity, and so is building AI agents, the real value lies in knowing exactly what to automate. However, it notes that this is difficult, because every company runs on processes nobody has written down. 
“McKinsey estimates that today’s technology could, in theory, automate about 57% of US work hours. Yet in almost every company Marble works with, around 90% of core processes live only in inboxes, spreadsheets and the heads of the people doing them. That, not the technology, is the biggest blocker to AI transformation. What is missing is an exact picture of how the work is done,” the German startup mentioned in the press release. 
Marble claims to build that picture. It observes how teams work, turning every process into a structured map that AI can read like code. It then builds Marble Coworkers that run the process end to end in the tools teams already use, with humans in the loop where judgement matters.
It argues that traditional automation bends a standard product to fit a company’s processes. Marble states that it productises the understanding of the process itself.
Explaining its privacy and security measures, Marble says it anonymises everything it captures before any person or AI model sees it, even in the customer’s own cloud. Marble’s desktop app records screen activity, clicks, and keystrokes in the business apps people use at work, never private apps, private tabs, or anything outside working hours. It further notes that employees can pause it at any time, and data is only analysed in aggregate, not based on individuals.
“Every company we talk to wants AI to take over real work. But nobody can tell the AI how that work is actually done. So we solve that first. Our Coworkers watch how the work happens before they take it over. They do it the way your best people do,” said Rösner.
Notable customers include EGYM, Mutares and Enam, alongside other tech unicorns, PE-backed organisations and AI roll-ups backed by top-tier funds.
The company reported that at a PE-owned US financial services company, a Marble coworker slashed handling time per case by 90%. In the first month, the team handled 50% more cases without hiring anyone new. The coworker prepares every settlement offer for a specialist to approve. Marble learned the process by watching the team, not from documentation.

articles.title: Terra pode sofrer danos irreversíveis mesmo se aquecimento global diminuir
articles.text:
Ultrapassar temporariamente o limite de 1,5 °C de aquecimento global pode provocar perdas irreversíveis de gelo e acelerar a elevação do nível dos oceanos, mesmo que as temperaturas voltem a cair posteriormente. O alerta está em novo relatório elaborado pela International Cryosphere Climate Initiative (ICCI), em coordenação com o Programa das Nações Unidas para o Meio Ambiente (Pnuma), divulgado nesta segunda-feira (2).
Intitulado Overshoot and the Cryosphere: Averting Global Meltdown (Ultrapassagem e criosfera: evitando o colapso global, em tradução livre), o documento reúne contribuições de mais de 80 cientistas especializados nas regiões polares e montanhosas.
O estudo analisa os riscos do chamado overshoot, termo utilizado para descrever cenário em que a temperatura média global ultrapassa o limite de 1,5 °C estabelecido pelo Acordo de Paris e, posteriormente, retorna a níveis inferiores.
Segundo os pesquisadores, a duração e a intensidade desse período são determinantes para o tamanho dos danos. Mesmo que o planeta consiga voltar a temperaturas mais baixas, algumas consequências sobre geleiras, mantos de gelo, solos congelados e oceanos polares podem persistir por séculos ou até milênios.
Derretimento do gelo pode elevar o nível dos oceanos por séculos
- Um dos principais riscos identificados pelos cientistas envolve as grandes camadas de gelo da Groenlândia e da Antártida. As duas regiões já apresentam perdas aceleradas, com taxa de derretimento aproximadamente seis vezes maior do que a registrada na década de 1990;
- O fenômeno tem consequências diretas sobre o nível dos oceanos. À medida que grandes volumes de gelo continental derretem e chegam ao mar, o nível das águas aumenta, ampliando os riscos para comunidades e cidades costeiras;
- O relatório alerta que parte dessa elevação já está comprometida em razão da instabilidade e do recuo prolongado das camadas polares. Ao longo dos próximos séculos, o processo pode resultar em vários metros de aumento no nível do mar;
- A velocidade desse avanço também preocupa. Em determinados cenários, a elevação pode alcançar vários centímetros por ano, dificultando a adaptação de regiões costeiras e aumentando a frequência de inundações;
- Os pesquisadores ressaltam que retornar a temperaturas inferiores a 1,5 °C ajudaria a desacelerar o processo, mas não seria suficiente para recuperar automaticamente todo o gelo perdido.
Leia mais:
- Como as mudanças climáticas favorecem doenças infecciosas no Brasil
- Relatório da ONU revela novo recorde de gases de efeito estufa
- Um quarto dos data centers do mundo está em áreas com escassez de água
Meta de 1,5 °C pode não ser suficiente para proteger o gelo
Outro ponto destacado pelo estudo é que o limite de 1,5 °C não representa necessariamente uma condição segura para todas as regiões congeladas do planeta. Segundo os cientistas, um nível de aquecimento mais próximo de 1 °C, ou até inferior, seria mais adequado para preservar as grandes camadas de gelo ao longo dos próximos séculos.
A diferença é importante porque alguns processos de derretimento apresentam respostas muito lentas às mudanças de temperatura. Mesmo depois de uma redução do aquecimento global, geleiras e mantos de gelo podem continuar perdendo massa devido às alterações acumuladas anteriormente.
O problema não se restringe às regiões cobertas por gelo. O aquecimento e a acidificação dos oceanos polares também podem provocar mudanças duradouras nos ecossistemas marinhos e nas grandes correntes oceânicas que ajudam a regular o clima mundial.
Além disso, o descongelamento do permafrost — camada de solo que permanece congelada por longos períodos — pode liberar gases de efeito estufa armazenados no terreno, intensificando o próprio aquecimento global.
Brasil também pode sentir os efeitos da elevação do nível do mar
Embora as maiores perdas de gelo estejam concentradas nas regiões polares, os efeitos podem alcançar países distantes, incluindo o Brasil. A elevação do nível dos oceanos aumenta a exposição de cidades costeiras a inundações, erosão de praias e danos à infraestrutura. Também favorece a entrada de água salgada em aquíferos e áreas agrícolas próximas ao litoral.
O Plano Nacional de Adaptação à Mudança do Clima, apresentado pelo governo brasileiro à Convenção-Quadro das Nações Unidas sobre Mudança do Clima, já identifica a elevação do nível do mar como fator de risco para a zona costeira brasileira.
Nesse cenário, comunidades que vivem em áreas baixas podem enfrentar dificuldades crescentes para proteger moradias, atividades econômicas e fontes de abastecimento de água.
Cientistas defendem cortes rápidos nas emissões
Diante dos riscos, os autores defendem redução acelerada das emissões de gases de efeito estufa para limitar tanto a intensidade quanto a duração de qualquer ultrapassagem de 1,5°C.
A recomendação é reduzir as emissões em pelo menos 5% ao ano, a partir de agora, e alcançar emissões líquidas zero até meados do século.
O relatório também destaca a necessidade de abandonar progressivamente os combustíveis fósseis e ampliar o uso de fontes renováveis de energia.
Embora algumas perdas já sejam inevitáveis, os cientistas afirmam que ainda é possível evitar os piores cenários. Uma redução mais rápida do aquecimento poderia desacelerar o derretimento das geleiras, limitar o descongelamento do permafrost e, em determinadas condições, permitir a recuperação parcial de áreas de gelo e neve.
A mensagem central do documento é que cada fração de grau adicional importa. Mesmo que a humanidade consiga reduzir as temperaturas depois de ultrapassar o limite estabelecido pelo Acordo de Paris, nem todos os danos provocados durante esse período poderão ser desfeitos.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: Cohere pledges to invest $4 billion into R&D, create 1,500 jobs
articles.text:
At the end of last week, the Government of Canada announced a $1.6 billion investment in Toronto-based AI company Cohere. Following that announcement, Cohere has provided some updates on its larger plans for Canada.
Most notably, Cohere says it’s investing over $4 billion in R&D and AI infrastructure through 2031. The company says this will create over 1,500 jobs, 1,000 of which will focus on “AI research, engineering, product development and other advanced technical disciplines.”
The feds’ investment in Cohere comes as part of the company’s wider $7 billion fundraising round. Altogether, this will put Cohere’s valuation at about $36 billion, which the government says makes it the largest AI company outside of the U.S. and China. In a statement last week, Prime Minister Mark Carney said these Cohere investments will help produce “affordable, secure, sovereign AI, built in Canada for the benefit of Canadians.”
However, there’s naturally been a lot of scrutiny into all of this news. For one, the Cohere investment is believed to be the largest-ever federal equity investment in a single private tech company. And yet, there’s still many questions surrounding the terms of the deal, including what degree of control the feds have over Cohere.
And on a wider level, there’s a lot of apprehension regarding AI companies in general. Not only is there a huge lack of regulation across the board, including in Canada, but data centres also carry significant energy, water, and land costs.
Digital sovereignty is certainly important, especially as our once-close U.S. allies have betrayed us with a senseless trade war and threats to our sovereignty. Still, many questions must be answered about Cohere and Canada’s larger AI push.
Image credit: Cohere
Source: Cohere

articles.title: Elon Musk throttles Grok Bot limits due to 'unsustainably high' costs | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Over Halloween weekend, some Grok Bot users awoke to something especially spooky: Their weekly usage limits were unexpectedly maxed out, even if they hadn’t been using SpaceX’s agentic AI overnight. Some users reported on X that their usage jumped from as low as 50% to 100%.
SpaceX CEO Elon Musk confirmed in an X post on Sunday that this was not a glitch.
“The cost of serving Grok Bot was unsustainably high relative to revenue,” he wrote in a reply to a question from a user. He has not addressed the issue on his main feed but has continued boasting that Grok Bot can help you buy gifts for your family.
Grok Bot has been positioned as a success story for the newly public SpaceX, which said in a filing last month that AI now makes up 52% of company income. Its renamed “Super Intelligence” division actually turned a profit of $431 million, which is a rarity in the AI industry. Its profit would’ve been higher if not for $1.2 billion of one-time costs related to its acquisition of Cursor. Musk recently referred to Grok Bot as having “the fastest growth of a product that I’ve ever seen in my life.”
Musk has not yet shared how subscribers’ usage limits will be impacted moving forward.

articles.title: The Download: the agentic web arrives and the drive for safer roads
articles.text:
The Download: the agentic web arrives and the drive for safer roads
Plus: A $1 trillion tech selloff has deepened fears of an AI bubble.
This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.
The agentic web is here
In 2001, a decade after inventing the World Wide Web, Tim Berners-Lee articulated a new vision: an internet navigated by autonomous software agents that address our every need, without requiring us to muck about with browsers and search engines ourselves.
At the time, the idea seemed far-fetched. But a quarter-century on, AI agents are beginning to make it a reality. They can triage your inbox, do your grocery shopping, and even access your bank accounts.
This new era is being called the agentic web. It will inevitably transform the internet—and whether the human web survives this transition is anyone’s guess.
Find out how AI agents are transforming the internet, and what we stand to lose in the process.
—Grace Huckins
Are we there yet? Eliminating traffic deaths
Every year, traffic crashes kill more than 1 million people worldwide. They’re also the leading cause of death for children and young adults. Cheap, proven ways to make roads safer exist, including tightening intersections with planters and lowering speed limits. But government logjams and red tape can make it difficult to roll out these changes.
Still, some cities are making impressive progress by investing in public transit, extending curbs, and using cameras to spot danger zones in need of a redesign.
Here’s how close we are to eradicating traffic deaths.
—Sara Kiley Watson
This story is the final part of “Are we there yet?”, our series that takes stock of six technologies that have long promised to change the world—and scores them on a progress meter. Subscribe to read the other five instalments in our new Impossible issue.
The must-reads
I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.

3 Binance users withdrew $3.6 billion after the largest ever crypto hack
The funds moved when the exchange reopened on Sunday. (Guardian)

4 An AI agent injected drugs into a live mouse’s brain
It chose the gene therapy and controlled the needle itself. (Wired $)

They also criticized security flaws and Egypt’s government.(Gizmodo)
10 A new 3D map reveals instability in interstellar space
The discovery could help explain why stars form so inefficiently. (Quanta)
Quote of the day
“It would be great if all this was just a house of cards.”
—Kevin Roose, a technology columnist at the New York Times, tells NPR that an AI investment crash would be preferable to the technology permanently upending work and society.
One more thing
Useful quantum computing is inevitable—and increasingly imminent
Last year, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang jolted the stock market by saying that practical quantum computing is still 15 to 30 years away. He also suggested that those computers would need Nvidia GPUs to function. But Huang’s predictions miss the mark—both on the timeline and the role his company’s technology will play.
Quantum computing is rapidly converging on utility. And that’s good news, because the hope is that they will be able to perform calculations that no amount of AI or classical computation could ever achieve. Read the full story.
—Peter Barrett

articles.title: Xbox’s former COO has ‘serious concerns’ about her abrupt departure
articles.text:
Xbox’s former chief operating officer, Helen Chiang, suddenly left Microsoft less than two weeks ago after being promoted into the role in July. I wrote in my Notepad newsletter last week that it seemed very weird for Chiang to suddenly depart Microsoft after 21 years with a surprisingly short memo from Xbox CEO Asha Sharma. Now, Chiang says she has “serious concerns” about how she was treated.
Xbox’s former COO has ‘serious concerns’ about her abrupt departure
Helen Chiang is setting the record straight on her sudden exit from Microsoft.
In a lengthy LinkedIn post — entitled “Clarity is Kindness,” a reference to Sharma’s WSJ profile — Chiang doesn’t dispute that she was fired, but she doesn’t say why she was let go. Eurogamer reported last month that Chiang had been “terminated for policy violations,” but she says this is “not accurate.”
Chiang denies unfounded rumors that speculated she was leaking confidential information, or that she left to join a competitor. It’s clear the decision to leave Xbox was out of her hands. “You don’t spend two decades somewhere without developing a deep loyalty to the people, teams, and businesses you’ve helped build,” says Chiang. “Xbox was never just another stop in my career. My end game was always to keep building here.”
She also denies engaging in “discrimination, bullying, harassment, insider trading, embezzlement, or other fraudulent activity.” Like I wrote in Notepad last week, Chiang has been described to me by multiple Xbox employees as highly respected, with high integrity. “I stand by my record: both the results I delivered and the way I have treated people throughout my career,” says Chiang.
The most significant part of Chiang’s post is a paragraph on fairness and accountability, hinting that she wasn’t treated fairly:
I believe in fairness, accountability, and holding ourselves to the standards we expect of others. Those standards only mean something when they’re applied consistently. I have serious concerns about how they were applied in my case, and I believe those concerns deserve to be taken seriously.
Chiang also says “This is not how I ever imagined my story here would end. And it is not the whole story.”
We’ve reached out to Chiang to ask if she’s pursuing legal action against Microsoft. We’ve also asked Microsoft to comment on Chiang’s post, but the company didn’t respond in time for publication.

articles.title: Hey Cleo wins $100,000 investment at DMZ’s Black Innovation Summit | BetaKit
articles.text:
A trio of Black-led businesses walked away from the sixth-annual DMZ Black Innovation Summit with combined winnings of $170,000.
The news: Last week, 10 Black-led startups from across Canada pitched their businesses in front of more than 300 guests. DMZ, the startup incubator housed inside Toronto Metropolitan University, hosted the event.
The top prize went to edtech platform Hey Cleo, which received $100,000 in investment from DMZ Ventures and $10,000 in grant funding from the Black Founders Network for its conversational assessment platform.
Healthtech platform Cuvris, which automates transitional care follow-ups, received $50,000 in investment from DMZ Ventures, while Carbon Saver, which automates building carbon assessments and regulatory compliance for architects, received $10,000 in grant funding from Pitch Better.
From the source: The event intended to drive home that “investing in Black founders is a strategic imperative that drives economic growth and powers the startup economy,” DMZ said in a news release.
The context: The Black Startup Funding Report, released by BKR Capital and Rep Matters earlier this year, found that only 0.15 percent of all venture capital deployed in Canada in 2025 went to Black founders. That figure is 97 percent below where it would be if VC dollars invested were proportional to the total Black population in Canada.
The Black Innovation Summit is the marquee event for DMZ’s Black Innovation Programs, which were created to increase the number of Black-led startups in the tech ecosystem and break the “cycle of inequity.” To date, DMZ claims it has supported over 2,500 Black-identifying founders and distributed over $3.2 million in grants and services.
Final thought: This year’s Black Innovation Summit pitch competition wasn’t as lucrative as its predecessor, which saw a record-breaking $400,000 handed out to three winners. However, the $170,000 prize pool is still a step up from prior years, in which the winners typically split $60,000 or less.
Feature image courtesy DMZ.

articles.title: Une suite de Portal annulée par Valve redevient jouable 20 ans plus tard
articles.text:
Les projets annulés de Valve continuent de faire rêver les joueuses et les joueurs. Parmi eux, F-Stop occupe une place particulière. Ce jeu devait servir de préquelle à Portal, mais son concept était bien différent de celui des deux épisodes sortis respectivement en 2007 et 2011. Longtemps resté à l’état de projet abandonné, il vient de refaire surface grâce à plusieurs fuites. Contre toute attente, des fans en ont tiré une version jouable, montrée sur la chaîne YouTube de ToothpasteVixen le 1er novembre 2026.
Pour remettre le jeu dans son contexte, nous sommes en 2007, et Valve lance une série d’expérimentations baptisée Directed Design Experiments. Pendant trois mois, cinq équipes sont chargées d’imaginer chacune un concept de jeu. L’une d’elles donne naissance à F-Stop, pensé comme une préquelle à Portal, mais sans Portal Gun et ses portails permettant de traverser les murs.
Le gameplay repose sur un appareil photo expérimental d’Aperture Science qui permet de photographier des objets pour ensuite les déplacer dans l’environnement à l’aide des clichés obtenus, et ainsi, jouer avec la perspective et la disposition des éléments pour résoudre les énigmes
Si F-Stop avait séduit Gabe Newell, le patron de Valve, les retours des testeurs étaient moins enthousiastes. Le projet avait finalement été abandonné, mais certains éléments, comme des mécaniques, des personnages ou des dialogues, avaient été retravaillés pour être intégrés à Portal 2.
Le gameplay de F-Stop avait déjà été montré dans Exposure, une série documentaire du studio indépendant LunchHouse Software. On y voyait par exemple un ventilateur de plafond photographié puis reposé au sol, qui servait à se propulser vers un étage supérieur. Jusqu’ici, on ne pouvait que regarder le jeu, pas y jouer.
Trois fuites ont servi à reconstituer F-Stop
Si F-Stop est aujourd’hui jouable, c’est grâce à la combinaison de plusieurs fuites distinctes. La première remonte au 29 août, quand environ 12 à 13 téraoctets de fichiers stockés sur les anciens serveurs de Steam entre 2003 et 2013 ont été mis en ligne. Cette archive, surnommée Steam2, contenait la majorité des ressources graphiques et sonores de F-Stop.
Pour reconstituer F-Stop, il manquait toutefois deux éléments essentiels : le code source du jeu et les données permettant de reconstruire ses cartes. Ces fichiers ont fini par fuiter ce 1er novembre sur le serveur Discord de Valve Cut Content, une communauté de fans qui exhume le contenu coupé des jeux Valve. Selon les modérateurs du serveur, cités par Kotaku, la personne à l’origine de la fuite des cartes aurait d’abord demandé 1 000 dollars (environ 880 euros) avant de les partager gratuitement.
L’équipe de Valve Cut Content a vérifié l’authenticité des cartes, puis la communauté a assemblé les différents fichiers en une version jouable. Ceux qui l’ont essayée la disent complète à environ 99 %. Quelques textures et lignes de dialogue manquent encore, mais l’essentiel du jeu est bien présent.
Le jeu est court : les vidéos de la campagne complète durent moins d’une heure, ce qui colle à un prototype conçu en trois mois. Se le procurer est une autre histoire, car le serveur Discord de Valve Cut Content est passé sur invitation après l’afflux de curieux, selon TechPowerUp ce 2 novembre.
Ces vidéos permettent déjà de découvrir ce qu’aurait pu devenir Portal si Valve avait conservé cette mécanique photographique. Si cette version reconstituée donne un aperçu des expérimentations menées par Valve à l’époque, pour les fans de Portal, c’est surtout l’occasion de découvrir un pan oublié de l’histoire d’Aperture Science.

articles.title: This $48 e-paper display can be whatever you want it to be
articles.text:
One of the most useful gadgets in my kitchen is now a screen that never asks me for anything.
I recently bought a $48 DIY display kit from Seeed Studio (yes, that’s three E’s), developed in collaboration with TRMNL, that lets me display whatever I want, using whichever software ecosystem I prefer.
I previously built something similar by modding a Lenovo ThinkSmart View, which was selling for around $30 on eBay during a liquidation. The Lenovo device was only ever intended for business-to-business video, but it does a decent job of running a fork of LineageOS. Unfortunately, its limited RAM makes it sluggish. So when I came across the TRMNL kit and its e-paper display, I was sold.
I’d have an always-on display that shows me the information I want, with no subscription required. And since the screen populates automatically, I would never have to wrestle with a slow interface.
I think they can live in harmony.
Credit:
Nick Indge
I think they can live in harmony.
Credit:
Nick Indge
The Seeed Studio kit and TRMNL ecosystem aren’t trying to compete with products like the recently announced Apple HomeView, a $299 home hub designed to get the whole family interacting with it. If anything, the TRMNL kit is the HomeView’s antithesis. It’s designed to be entirely passive: The e-paper display stays on, cycling through potentially useful information on your desk or in your kitchen, from calendars and weather to news and all sorts of ideas thought up by its community members.
Here’s how it works.
Choosing a path
TRMNL, the platform company, was founded by indie hardware enthusiast Ryan Kulp in 2023. Its first e-paper device launched via crowdfunding in 2024.
Seeed Studio provides the hardware. The established Shenzhen open hardware company is best known for its XIAO microcontroller boards.
In March 2025, Seeed teased an XIAO e-paper panel on social media, prompting a community member to ask whether it could run TRMNL firmware. The question brought the two teams together, and in July 2025, they announced an official partnership to develop a DIY e-paper kit combining Seeed’s hardware designs with TRMNL’s firmware packages.
Seeed Studios monochrome display.
Credit:
Nick Indge
Seeed Studios monochrome display.
Credit:
Nick Indge
Seeed designs and manufactures the hardware, while TRMNL maintains the firmware, plugins, and hosted service. But you’ll still need to make some decisions about how to set up the kit. There are three ways to get it running, depending on your budget and how comfortable you are with managing software yourself.
The stock TRMNL setup connects you with the company’s “BYOD ecosystem” (bring your own device), letting you use trmnl.com as your information server with a 14-day free trial. After that, you’ll need to pay a one-time $50 license fee to keep your device connected to TRMNL servers.
If you’d rather go your own way, Seeed offers software options, including Home Assistant compatibility, that don’t require a TRMNL connection or license. You can also access the SenseCraft Seeedash platform, which includes a plugin repository and design workspace. It’s worth checking out the options before committing to a $50 TRMNL license. The browser-based platform also includes a firmware-flashing tool Seeed describes as simple enough for anyone to use.
If you already have a server up and running, you can point the device right at it. Terminus is TRMNL’s open source container for this setup. The Terminus GitHub page describes the BYOS as providing “privacy first functionality by empowering you to run your own private server, network, and devices. You own the stack and the data.”
The e-paper display and control board simply ping an API to retrieve the information to display. You can even write plugins in HTML, which the screen renders as a bitmap. The trade-off is that your server needs to stay online, and maintaining it may bring some system-admin headaches some users may want to avoid. But hey, that’s why there are options.
An example of a weather app on the Seeed firmware.
An example of a weather app on the Seeed firmware.
The display refreshing feeds while loading.
The display refreshing feeds while loading.
You can edit the list from your phone.
You can edit the list from your phone.
The display refreshing feeds while loading.
You can edit the list from your phone.
What’s in the box?
XIAO ePaper Display Dev Board with XIAO ESP32-S3 Plus onboard
Two official case designs are available for 3D printing: a triangular prism and an L-shaped case. I went for the latter, and although I’d hoped assembly would be as simple as plugging everything in and slotting the pieces into place, it proved to be a bit more involved.
The kit came with all the hardware I needed, with one slight hiccup: I’d forgotten to order a case or display stand. Fortunately, TRMNL is a proper DIY project, and there are print files available for recommended stand setups. A quick print at my local library’s Bambu printer and $8 solved the problem. I probably should have chosen something other than “dealer’s choice” for the PLA color, as I ended up with a bright canary yellow device case. At least it stands out on my kitchen countertop.
The hardware is included, not the stand.
Credit:
Nick Indge
The hardware is included, not the stand.
Credit:
Nick Indge
I’d recommend trying the prism shell design over the L-style case I chose because the latter required me to cut a channel for the ribbon cable extension. It wasn’t a huge deal for a project like this, but you may need to do some extra work and fiddle with the fit. You’ll also need needle-nose pliers to remove the print’s support trees from the narrow space.
Be prepared to clear out tiny rows of support trees.
Credit:
Nick Indge
Be prepared to clear out tiny rows of support trees.
Credit:
Nick Indge
Assembly
Before trying to fit everything into the printed case, I wanted to make sure the hardware worked, so I connected the parts on my workbench. The case-less assembly couldn’t be simpler: Connect the battery or a USB-C power source, plug the display directly into the board, and you’re good to go. From there, connect your phone or tablet to the device’s Wi-Fi and enter your local Wi-Fi credentials.
It lives!
It lives!
If you attempt this build, be aware that it involves some delicate parts. The FPC is extremely fragile and can break if you force it to bend in a direction it doesn’t want to go (say, around the sharp angle of an L-shaped case). Getting the cable to conform to the design was challenging; I tried using tweezers to coax the cable around the bend but got nowhere fast.
Connecting and routing the ribbon cable extension was the most stressful part of the assembly. The case design just doesn’t accommodate the path the ribbon cable naturally wants to take. Following a helpful tip from a commenter on MakerWorld, I managed to snake the cable through the narrow passage by attaching a bit of paper tape to the end of the ribbon connector.
Don’t do what I did. Try the prism stand design. This was a pain.
Credit:
Nick Indge
Don’t do what I did. Try the prism stand design. This was a pain.
Credit:
Nick Indge
After powering on the kit for the first time, you’ll see the TRMNL logo and a QR code on the e-paper display. Scanning the code redirects you to a “How to set up a new device” guide written by Kulp, the TRMNL creator. The guide had been updated just 15 minutes before I clicked the link—a promising sign of a living document that is constantly evolving.
OK, now what?
OK, now what?
TRMNL.com
I wasn’t planning to use the trmnl.com service, but I wanted to get a sense of what it offered for its $50 access fee. The 14-day “free” trial is a misnomer, though. Before you can register your device, you’ll need to enter your credit card information and pay $1 for access. After plopping down a buck, the next screen welcomed me to my trial.
After registering your kit’s MAC address with trmnl.com, you’ll receive what the service calls a “friendly code,” a much shorter identifier that’s easier to remember than an entire MAC address. From there, you can install plugins to display content on a schedule throughout the day.
The options are vast. The marketplace contains standard fare like Google Calendar, weather, and stock quotes, alongside more niche offerings like rotating factoids about the Ferengi Rules of Acquisition in Star Trek.
The TRMNL cloud plugin marketplace.
The TRMNL cloud plugin marketplace.
If you’re looking for a hassle-free solution that “just works,” it’s hard to fault the package trmnl.com has put together. I’m a fan of any service that offers a one-time license fee over yet another forever subscription, and I think $50 is a fair price for the people behind the platform to be compensated for their work. After all, it handles all the rendering; the device simply displays information pulled from the APIs.
We need an Ars plugin!
We need an Ars plugin!
SenseCraft
On the Seeed side, there’s SenseCraft, a similar marketplace to trmnl.com’s but without the license fee. The website offers a browser-based flashing tool that promises to “flash official firmware from the browser. No coding. No terminal. Just clicks.”
The process was as simple as promised—once I figured out that I needed a USB-C to USB-C cable. I connected the board to my PC via the onboard USB-C port, opened the website in a Chromium-based browser (sorry, Firefox), selected my device from a drop-down menu, and clicked “Flash.” Once the device rebooted, setup followed essentially the same process as it did with TRMNL, minus the credit card. The tradeoff for free access is that Seeed is based in China and operates under its own privacy policy. Your call, but it’s certainly nice to have options.
Flashing the new firmware package.
Credit:
Nick Indge
Flashing the new firmware package.
Credit:
Nick Indge
After registering a Seeed account, I entered a code displayed on the device, just as I had with TRMNL. SenseCraft’s marketplace is similarly packed with community contributions, but I had trouble determining which plugins were intended for my device and which might not be compatible. I tried publishing several different feeds to the display, but I couldn’t get them to render.
Initial screen on the Seeed firmware package. Guest starring Desk Pickle.
Credit:
Nick Indge
Initial screen on the Seeed firmware package. Guest starring Desk Pickle.
Credit:
Nick Indge
SenseCraft leans heavily into AI-powered custom designs. While the platform offers a bit of everything, much of its content is geared toward the Chinese market, with English-language apps sprinkled throughout. I can see why US users reached out to ask about TRMNL compatibility.
You can import images directly to the screen in the Seeed FW. Check out this desk inception thing I’ve got going on.
Credit:
Nick Indge
You can import images directly to the screen in the Seeed FW. Check out this desk inception thing I’ve got going on.
Credit:
Nick Indge
Bring your own server
As TRMNL puts it, “the goal isn’t for BYOS to match parity with our hosted solution but to provide enough of a pleasant solution for your own customized experience.” Even a modest homelab server should have no trouble running the Terminus package, which acts as an API point that takes in information, renders the designs, and sends them to your e-paper display. The process shouldn’t put meaningful strain on most systems.
It’s great that there’s an “easy” version for a fee, but homelabbing is one of my favorite hobbies, and I love self-hosting projects wherever possible. When I first saw the DIY TRMNL/Seeed package, I was hoping I’d be able to control the feed myself.
We’re in.
We’re in.
For now, getting Terminus running on your server isn’t as simple as heading to your OS’s Docker app store and downloading a host service. TRMNL has a great guide to walk you through the setup, but if you’re not comfortable working with docker compose files, you may want to pay the one-time license fee and leave the hosting to TRMNL.
I won’t lie: I spent some late nights banging my head against the desk trying to get everything running. I’d initially tried hosting it on my main Unraid machine, but I kept running into bridge networking issues. The Terminus package is a multi-container compose stack with pieces like Sidekiq worker, Postgres, Valkey, and a certificate initializer. If those containers can’t communicate with each other, nothing works.
Thankfully, I’m a weird nerd who also runs a CasaOS deployment on another machine. After I executed the bin/setup script there, everything worked as it should. The next issue was flashing back to the latest TRMNL firmware package. My unit arrived with FW 1.5.12, well behind the current 1.8.18 release.
Flashing proved to be an annoyance again because I struggled to keep the unit in flashing mode and get the web flasher to communicate with the serial port on my Fedora PC. After about 30 minutes of troubleshooting without making progress, I switched to my MacBook Pro, where the process worked on the first try. Go figure.
The Terminus Dashboard running on my CasaOS server.
Credit:
Nick Indge
The Terminus Dashboard running on my CasaOS server.
Credit:
Nick Indge
Once you’ve updated the display to the proper firmware and pointed its connections at your server, you can write and design your own display templates. If starting from scratch isn’t your thing, TRMNL’s own plugins repo and a community-maintained catalog are available. A new Extensions Gallery in the Terminus web UI lets you import certain plugins for local hosting.
The options are almost overwhelming, and I imagine it will take some time to get everything dialed in exactly as I want it. I still plan to stick with the BYOS route, but the process isn’t as straightforward as I had hoped. For example, the setting for pointing the display at your local server is hidden under the “advanced” settings page during the web portal login.
Terminus Gallery options.
Terminus Gallery options.
Real-world impressions
Once I deployed the display in my kitchen, I could get a better sense of how it would fit into my day-to-day life. The 7.5-inch e-paper display is large enough to read from across the room, and all the plugins I had running looked crisp and legible. My son was enamored with the lunar cycles display and commented that “now I’ll always know what moon we have.”
That’s where the kit shines: showing little rotating bursts of useful information that you might never have thought to look up before.
Moon cycles on my kitchen cutting board.
Credit:
Nick Indge
Moon cycles on my kitchen cutting board.
Credit:
Nick Indge
Seeed Studio says the display can run for three months on battery power. I haven’t had the device long enough to verify that claim, but I’m not sure I need the battery for much more than backup. The device powers via USB just fine, so I’ll probably leave it connected to a nearby hub on the counter. The three-month estimate assumes that the display will update once every six hours. I prefer refreshes closer to once an hour, which would cut battery life significantly. Either way, the battery becomes largely irrelevant if you use a USB power source.
Final thoughts
The official TRMNL route is starting to look mighty tempting if it means getting the type of headache-free, set-it-and-forget-it Ron Popeil experience I was expecting from this setup. I’ll keep tinkering with the BYOS solutions, but since those still run on the official TRMNL firmware, I may switch back and use the rest of my 14-day trial to see what best suits my needs. The $50 license fee would push my total project cost over $100. That’s not a huge deal, but it’s double what I was expecting.
There’s a stocks plugin called “Stonks.”
Credit:
Nick Indge
There’s a stocks plugin called “Stonks.”
Credit:
Nick Indge
The TRMNL/Seeed Studio collaboration has produced a true DIY device. It will never compete with a home assistant device from Amazon or Apple, but it’s not meant to, and that’s a good thing. Not everyone wants a digital butler waiting for their next command. Sometimes you just want information that’s relevant to you and your life, displayed in a central place in your home.
Nick Indge is a Senior Technology Reporter at Ars Technica covering hardware, embedded systems, and self-hosted infrastructure. A former security investigator turned tech writer, he writes to help readers escape subscription traps and regain ownership of their digital lives. He lives in Chicagoland with his family and a goofball husky.
I use mine jointly with a Bloomin8 color e-ink frame : the Bloomin8 shows a painting of my liking, and the Seeed displays a description of it. Home Assistant is used to change the painting every couple days.
The painting of the day:
Quick tip for anyone without a 3D printer handy, it fits pretty well into those cheap photo frames like IKEA and a lot of supermarkets have. It was maybe a cm short for the one I had to hand, so little strip of black duck tape around the glass of the frame made an ideal bezel.
I've had ARS bookedmarked in my browser forever. Can't believe something I made just popped up on the homepage today!

articles.title: La cyberattaque des frigos change d’échelle et frappe désormais des supermarchés dans toute l’Europe
articles.text:
Bis repetita, mais cette fois à une échelle continentale.
Ce lundi 2 novembre, plusieurs enseignes de la grande distribution ont signalé en Belgique, au Luxembourg et en Suède des hausses soudaines de température dans leurs installations frigorifiques, ce qui a obligé des commerçants à jeter leurs produits frais et surgelés.
Une vague qui n’est pas sans rappeler ce qui s’est passé en France le mois dernier, lorsque des pirates ont visé les systèmes de réfrigération de centaines de supermarchés dans la nuit du 11 au 12 octobre.
Des frigos passés en mode dégivrage
La Belgique est pour l’instant le pays où l’attaque est la mieux documentée. Les installations auraient commencé à dérailler autour de minuit, entre dimanche et lundi.
Interrogé par l’agence Belga, Stephan Moelans, qui dirige le frigoriste Sabcobel, décrit la technique déjà employée en France, les pirates ayant déclenché à distance le cycle de dégivrage des évaporateurs, qui sert d’ordinaire à faire fondre le givre accumulé.
Selon RTL Info, le décompte atteint une quarantaine de points de vente chez Delhaize, quinze chez Carrefour, à peu près autant chez Intermarché et cinq chez Spar. S’y ajoutent l’Ikea de Mons et les boucheries De Laet et Van Haver, et le chocolatier Galler figurerait aussi parmi les victimes. À l’échelle du groupe, Ahold Delhaize fait état de plusieurs dizaines de supermarchés perturbés, Luxembourg compris.
Selon Reuters, l’enseigne suédois ICA a également admis qu’une part limitée de son réseau a été touchée, et Coop fait part de difficultés comparables.
Un bilan encore provisoire
Le décompte reste partiel, et aucun bilan financier global n’a été communiqué. Delhaize s’en tient pour l’instant à la formule d’« incident informatique » et mène l’enquête, tandis que Carrefour dit chercher à comprendre ce qui s’est passé.
D’autres pays sont touchés. En Estonie, la chaîne Selver a confirmé à l’audiovisuel public ERR qu’un de ses magasins avait été visé. Son fournisseur Kitman Coldtech explique que les attaquants ont réglé un congélateur à 50 °C, mais que l’intervention rapide des équipes a permis d’éviter toute perte, la température n’ayant gagné que deux ou trois degrés.
En Irlande, le groupe Musgrave reconnaît un incident limité à un « modèle spécifique » de frigo dans ses supermarchés SuperValu. D’après The Irish Times, 13 magasins ont dû retirer leurs produits frais et surgelés des rayons, sans pour autant fermer. Des perturbations sont également évoquées aux Pays-Bas, sans plus de précisions à ce stade.

articles.title: How Canada can build tech careers worth staying for | BetaKit
articles.text:
When Damjan Pelemis interviews engineers for positions at Capital One Canada, there’s a question he likes to ask once the conversation turns to what the company can offer them.
“Do they like to learn?” Pelemis said. “Because this is a place where they’re going to truly test that.”
“Canada has tremendous potential as a country to lead innovation globally. Stimulating and creating space for that is critical.”
Damjan Pelemis,
Capital One
As Chief Technology Officer for Canada, Pelemis leads Capital One’s tech strategy and engineering teams located in the GTA. In this role, he leads the development of financial products while managing local engineering operations.
His experience recruiting engineers offers a window into a wider issue facing Canada’s technology sector: how to turn a strong pipeline of skilled talent into a workforce that stays, grows, and contributes to innovation at home.
He believes Canada has a strong foundation to build on. Six Canadian cities ranked among the top 15 North American tech talent markets this year, and Pelemis pointed to Canada’s post-secondary institutions and quality of life as advantages in attracting skilled workers.
At the same time, today’s engineers have access to an increasingly global employment market, and some of Canada’s most highly trained graduates appear particularly mobile. Even with these strong foundations, Pelemis notes that employers must stay proactive to retain top talent as career opportunities expand worldwide.
He believes developing talented engineers is only one part of building a strong domestic technology sector. Canadian employers also need to offer careers that give those engineers reasons to stay here.
Work that opens doors
Engineers evaluating a new job are also thinking about what comes after it. Pelemis said candidates are wary of spending years working with systems so specialized that their experience becomes difficult to apply elsewhere.
Pelemis said prospective technologists want to know, “Am I just stepping into a niche? Am I stepping into something that’s going to take me sideways, and I’ll have to requalify when I decide I want to take on something new?”
Not long ago, engineers at large companies could spend years mastering technology that existed almost nowhere else. An employee could become an expert in one organization’s technology and still face a steep learning curve at their next job.
Cloud computing has made technical expertise far more transferable. Engineers working with widely adopted platforms can carry their expertise between employers and build on their experience without having to learn entirely new systems.
“An engineer going from one to the other is actually much better prepared and positioned to continue growing their career, as opposed to restarting it from scratch,” Pelemis added.
Capital One, for its part, operates entirely in the cloud, which Pelemis said appeals to candidates looking to develop skills they can use throughout their careers.
Today’s engineers also want a meaningful role in what they build. At Capital One, Canadian engineers developed products and features like Quick Check, which allows consumers to see which credit card offers they qualify for before applying. Capital One guarantees the offers presented, which required its engineers to work through software, data, and reliability challenges before launching the product.
“Software is just one component of it, but end-to-end ownership across the entire product lifecycle—from data architecture to system reliability—is a big part of the value that an engineer joining would realize,” he added.
Quick Check serves Canadian customers, and the technology components developed in the process are available to Capital One engineers worldwide. Pelemis believes that is just one example of Canadian teams developing products for the local market while contributing to Capital One’s global technology operations.
Investing in skills that last
A software engineer entering the workforce in 2026 faces a different set of expectations than one who graduated just a few years ago. AI is taking on more routine coding work, which means employers are prioritizing judgment, technical design, collaboration, and the ability to define problems.
“We do it because it makes business sense, makes sense for people’s growth, and supports the wider tech ecosystem.”
Pelemis believes employers need to adapt how they develop engineers as the skills required for the job continue to evolve. At Capital One Canada, employees have access to mentorship, online learning, and professional certifications in areas including cloud computing, cybersecurity, and architecture. The company also encourages employees to pursue training outside of their immediate specialties.
“Whether it’s our Tech College, or Tech Leadership Development Program for a software engineer, or a cyber course for a business analyst, we do it because it makes business sense, makes sense for people’s growth, and supports the wider tech ecosystem,” he said.
Capital One’s international footprint also gives engineers room to pursue different kinds of work as their careers evolve.
“What junior engineers get is immersion in a large, broadly scaled ecosystem,” Pelemis added. “What mid-career folks get is experimentation and continuation. What senior people get is actually pushing the envelope.”
He sees continued education as a responsibility shared across Canada’s technology ecosystem. Universities provide the foundation, but Pelemis argued employers have an equally important role in helping technologists develop the skills they will need throughout their working lives.
Turning talent into economic strength
Canada has invested heavily in developing technical talent, but some of its most sought-after graduates appear likely to pursue opportunities in other countries.
A 2025 Statistics Canada study found that 23 percent of Canadian computer and information science graduates from highly ranked universities were no longer filing Canadian tax returns three years after graduation, compared with just 10 percent of graduates from other institutions. The findings suggest that Canada might be losing some of its most highly trained technology alumni.
When skilled graduates leave Canada, their expertise goes with them, whereas keeping that talent in Canada allows knowledge to circulate between Canadian companies as engineers move through their careers.
Pelemis has seen that knowledge transfer himself. He stays in touch with former Capital One employees who have applied their experience throughout the Canadian tech ecosystem. He believes their career paths show why continued investment in professional education and ambitious engineering work can have an impact far beyond a single employer.
“Canada has tremendous potential as a country to lead innovation globally,” he said. “Stimulating and creating space for that is critical.”
