articles.title: BDC launches two entrepreneur-led AI programs to make small businesses, and itself, more productive | BetaKit
articles.text:
The Business Development Bank of Canada (BDC) has tapped two entrepreneurs to help Canadian businesses adopt AI and improve its offerings.
On Monday, BDC announced the launch of Mission AI, which will help small businesses identify where AI can make them more productive, and Studio AI, which will build and deploy solutions that make it easier for businesses to transact with BDC.
“An entrepreneur should not have to become an AI expert to benefit from it.”
Dominic Gagnon, BDC
Each new program has its own experienced entrepreneur at the helm, with Mission AI spearheaded by Connect&GO founder Dominic Gagnon, and Studio AI led by former Frank & Oak CTO Raff Paquin. The programs are rooted in the results of a recent BDC study that found that 30 percent of Canadian small-to-medium enterprises (SMEs) are using generative AI, and when they do they are 24 percent more productive than those that don’t.
With Mission AI, Gagnon’s team will nail down an SME’s needs and match them with the Canadian AI solution that’s right for the job. At the same time, a panel of entrepreneurs will be testing the business’ tools, looking for common challenges that can be automated to free up time.
“An entrepreneur should not have to become an AI expert to benefit from it,” Gagnon said in a statement. “If a tool helps a business get a quote out faster, or spend fewer hours processing invoices, that matters.”
Mission AI builds on other efforts from BDC to drive up SME AI adoption. Earlier this year, it launched the $500-million LIFT loan program to help 1,000 SMEs adopt AI. The bank claimed at the time that if every SME had the same level of technological maturity as the most advanced companies in Canada, GDP could grow by up to 14 percent.
RELATED: BDC’s new $500-million loan program will help smaller businesses adopt AI
Meanwhile, drawing on his experience in tech-heavy roles at Canadian companies like Shopify, Lightspeed, and Altitude Sports, Paquin will work on reinventing what BDC described as “the experience of entrepreneurs seeking financing and support.” AI Studio’s goal is to dramatically reduce the time it takes for entrepreneurs to receive money from BDC, while giving them more visibility and predictability “at every step,” according to the Crown corporation.
An improvement to BDC’s operations wouldn’t go unnoticed. The bank is Canada’s most significant investor, operating a portfolio that most recently reported roughly $30 million in debt investments, $1.74 billion in direct equity investments, and $1.68 billion in investments in other funds. BDC reported serving more than 100,000 clients in its last fiscal year, and expects to contribute $28 billion to Canada’s GDP over the next five years.
“Few roles let you build something new to tackle that at this scale,” Paquin wrote in a LinkedIn post. “It may sound crazy, but I hope we’ll one day measure the studio’s impact in Canada’s macroeconomic numbers, starting with higher productivity for small and medium-sized businesses.”
Feature image courtesy BDC.

articles.title: OpenAI’s new shared usage limit pits ChatGPT against Codex
articles.text:
OpenAI’s new shared usage limit pits ChatGPT against Codex
OpenAI has revealed plans to combine usage allowances across ChatGPT and Codex, as part of a broader effort to integrate its conversational AI and agentic capabilities into a single experience.
In a help article quietly published over the weekend, the company confirmed the changes will take effect “starting in December,” affecting Plus, Pro and Business subscribers. Under the new system, ChatGPT conversations and Codex tasks will draw from a common pool of tokens, with more demanding models and complex tasks consuming a greater share — though OpenAI has yet to disclose how generous the combined allowance will be.
Instant chat, ChatGPT’s faster-response mode for everyday questions and tasks, will be exempt.
OpenAI’s products come together
The changes are the latest step in OpenAI’s efforts to bring its growing collection of AI products under one roof.
In July, the company launched ChatGPT Work, an agentic tool built on its Codex coding technology that allows users to delegate complex tasks, such as researching topics, analysing data and producing documents, presentations and spreadsheets. The idea was to extend the capabilities of Codex beyond software development, allowing knowledge workers to use AI agents for everyday business tasks.
As The New Stack reported at the time, the launch also saw OpenAI consolidate ChatGPT and Codex into a single desktop application, with dedicated interfaces for conversations, agentic tasks and coding.
ChatGPT Work joined an expanding collection of specialised tools, including ChatGPT for Excel, which debuted in March, which later extended to Google Sheets.
It’s worth noting that these products already have overlapping usage arrangements. Currently, Codex, ChatGPT Work, ChatGPT for Excel, and Workspace Agents draw from a shared agentic allowance, while regular ChatGPT conversations have separate usage limits.
And it’s that very separation that’s set to change from December, putting developers in a position where intensive Codex sessions eat into the allowance available for ChatGPT conversations, and vice versa.
‘ChatGPT and Codex serve different purposes’
OpenAI isn’t alone in bringing its conversational and agentic products closer together. In September, Anthropic merged Claude Chat and Cowork into a single interface, allowing users to move from asking questions to delegating more involved tasks within the same conversation.
This shows how two of the biggest frontier AI labs are pursuing a similar goal: making it easier for users to switch between asking questions, and carrying out more substantial tasks, without having to navigate separate products. However, OpenAI’s decision to combine usage allowances has prompted objections from subscribers concerned that the change could leave them with less access to the tools they already pay for.
“ChatGPT and Codex serve different purposes, and their usage limits should remain separate.”
In a discussion kickstarted on OpenAI’s developer forum on Saturday, users called on the company to abandon the proposed consolidation, or guarantee that subscribers won’t end up with less usable capacity under the new system. The forum member who started the discussion, going under the moniker Smalikou, argues that the two products should retain independent allowances and called for greater transparency over how usage will be calculated.
“ChatGPT and Codex serve different purposes, and their usage limits should remain separate,” they write.
Another user, going by the name of PZA, calls for more detailed usage reporting, including a breakdown of consumption by product, model and task.
“If OpenAI decides to combine them anyway, a real-time usage dashboard must be available before the change takes effect,” they write. “It should show the remaining allowance, reset time, and consumption by product, model, and task. Without that transparency, I will consider the change a downgrade to my paid plan and reconsider renewing.”
“Without that transparency, I will consider the change a downgrade to my paid plan and reconsider renewing.”
As it happens, OpenAI has confirmed that subscribers will be able to see their combined remaining allowance and reset times in ChatGPT’s settings, but hasn’t specified what level of detail it will include.
The concerns come just days after OpenAI reversed a controversial decision to halve usage limits for its $200 Pro subscription. On October 29, the company confirmed it was cancelling the Pro 200 reduction, restoring the higher Work and Codex allowances for subscribers already moved to the lower limits, while doubling allowances for Pro 100, Pro 500 and Business Premium subscribers.
Tibo Sottiaux, OpenAI’s head of ChatGPT and Codex, acknowledged the criticism surrounding the proposed reduction, writing on X that the company had heard subscribers’ feedback and would preserve existing Pro 200 allowances.
“We heard your kind feedback and won’t be reducing usage limits for Pro 200, so your Work and Codex usage will stay the same,” he wrote.
However, one forum participant questioned how much those increases would benefit subscribers once ChatGPT conversations begin drawing from the same allowance as Codex. The user, posting as Zigg88, notes that they already regularly approach their weekly Codex limit.
“Doubling a resource allocation while simultaneously expanding the number of things consuming it doesn’t inherently translate into more usable capacity,” they write.
“Doubling a resource allocation while simultaneously expanding the number of things consuming it doesn’t inherently translate into more usable capacity.”
Others raised concerns about the impact on their ability to use ChatGPT for research and technical planning while relying on Codex for software development, with one commenter arguing that OpenAI should preserve independent allowances or guarantee equivalent access under the new system.
The New Stack reached out to OpenAI to ask when, exactly, the changes would take effect in December, and whether the new combined allowance would be equivalent to the existing separate allowances, or leave some subscribers with less usable capacity. The company declined to answer the questions, instead reiterating its recent increases to Work and Codex usage limits, and directing us to its existing documentation.
For now, OpenAI says it expects most users to encounter usage resets no more frequently than they do today. However, without publishing the new token allowances or explaining how they compare with existing limits, subscribers have little way of knowing whether that reassurance will hold true for them.

articles.title: Putting AI To The Test
articles.text:
Who verifies the verifier? This is the age-old question for anyone involved in the verification of semiconductor systems. Who verifies AI?
There are an increasing number of new EDA companies these days, and this is great news. The industry needs some new vitality, new thought leaders, people willing to take risks. The same goes for established companies that cannot go outside their existing comfort zone while meeting next quarter’s financial goals. But sometimes, new startups forget the risks associated with semiconductor design. While they may be able to point to an improvement in time to market, or meeting better performance goals, they fail to understand how small that particular step is in the whole process.
Today, a number of companies want us to believe that AI can do everything. Some point the way to automating design, others to verification, and some even claim it can do both at the same time, from the same source material. No, it can’t. While some of it may be possible in the future, it is far from that point today.
What many of them fail to do is show proof. One example, one design, one piece of IP is not proof. When verifying any new tool or methodology, you always need to hold back a test set to apply at the end. In this case, with AI, it has to be something it has never seen before, never been trained on. That is the only thing that can provide a fair, unbiased result. As soon as you tweak your tool to do well on that test case, it is no longer a true test.
This is why I was delighted to receive communications from Vikash Kumar, senior verification architect at Arm. He has 15+ years of semiconductor industry experience and is the author of the book “AI-Assisted Hardware Verification: Cognitive Verification Architecture with the VEGA Framework.” What he shared with me was his independent work on the quality of existing LLMs for the creation of testbenches.
More than 20 years ago, Certess introduced the industry to mutation analysis. If you inject a bug into the design, does the testbench find it? They used the traditional stuck-at fault model and sophisticated statistical analysis to reduce the total number of faults required. The results were a slap across the face to many companies that thought they were doing a good job, only to find out how poor their testbenches were.
Vikash’s approach is different. “The setup was simple — hand AI a spec and the RTL, tell it to verify and report back when it is confident the design is clean, and check what it actually found. I hand-seeded realistic, design-representative functional bugs, which keeps the ground truth clean. I know exactly which bugs were planted, so detection is measured against a known set rather than an impression.”
I asked Vikash why he chose to insert bugs rather than using the stuck-at model, which has been the industry go-to since the ’80s. “The whole question with AI verification is whether it comprehends design intent well enough to catch the subtle, intent-level bugs, and that is exactly where it struggled — the misses clustered in data-path, encoding logic, and functional corners, not in anything a stuck-at pattern would have flagged.”
He started with 25 hand-coded designs spanning bus protocols, DMA engines, ECC memory, control and peripheral logic, and concurrency scenarios. The RTL has never been made public. Into those he inserted 806 bugs. The models were given a specification based on published protocol standards. Three frontier AI models were chosen: Claude Opus 5, GPT-5.4, and GLM-5.2.
“Without human intervention or predefined time limits, each model generated testbenches, developed coverage goals, executed simulations, identified and corrected RTL defects, and iteratively refined verification until independently declaring sign-off. All defects were seeded upfront, although some became observable only after earlier corrections.”
Here are his key findings:
Even the best model, Claude Opus 5, did not detect roughly 168 defects. GPT-5.4 missed about 192, and GLM-5.2 missed close to 300. Perhaps even worse is that Vikash ran each model three times, and each run produced different results. But he is very optimistic about the results. “The impressive part is how much AI caught on its own,” he says. “The important part is how much it missed, and that’s where the engineer still matters.”
In a similar manner, ChipAgents just released its new build-a-chip-bench tool. It goes from a workload specification to GSD. The company ranked five models. The best, Claude Fable 5.1 achieved a score of 16.6%, whilst the bottom of the pack was GLM-5.3 with a score of zero. These results look dire, but the biggest failure was their lack of understanding of performance constraints.
I believe this will be an even bigger problem when it comes to writing software that has to be cognizant of the underlying hardware and its performance beyond raw speed. Real-time systems deployed within physical AI need predictable latency, at low power, over a broad range of operating conditions. None of this data is available for training today.
I will finish with another comment Vikash made: “You can automate the work of verification. You cannot automate the responsibility for it.”
Leave a Reply

articles.title: Porto’s female-led startup Seamoretech secures €1.1 million to turn desalination brine into freshwater and critical minerals | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Seamoretech, a Porto-based CleanTech startup that converts desalination brine into freshwater and critical minerals, has secured €1.1 million in the first closing of its Seed round.
The round saw participation from Rypples, 7Seas Capital, and Crédito Agrícola, bringing together investors with experience in OceanTech and ClimateTech industries. The first closing has also brought the total amount raised to €3 million.
“We are entering Seamoretech’s next phase with a clear ambition: to scale our technology, accelerate our market entry, produce freshwater at a lower cost, and establish a European reference in critical raw materials recovery, while helping protect marine ecosystems,” said Sofia Delgado, CEO and co-founder of Seamoretech.
Founded in 2021 by Delgado and Eva Sousa as a spin-off of the University of Porto’s Faculty of Engineering (FEUP), Seamoretech tackles brine, the highly concentrated saline waste stream that industries have long treated as a liability and discarded into the ocean. The startup’s proprietary brine valorisation technology recovers purified freshwater and high-value minerals, including magnesium, calcium, copper, and lithium, from the waste stream.
The technology relies on a containerised, plug-and-play system that uses a forward osmosis process to achieve Zero Liquid Discharge, meaning nothing is returned to the ocean. This system is designed to integrate into existing plant infrastructure without requiring operational downtime or upfront capital expenditure from plant operators.
Seamoretech says its system doubles freshwater production yield, cuts energy consumption by 50% compared with reverse osmosis, reduces operating costs by 30%, and lowers carbon emissions by up to 80% relative to conventional mineral mining.
Unlike other CleanTech startups, Seamoretech is not only working to accelerate the climate transition but also addressing two of Europe’s major priorities: water scarcity and securing domestic supply of critical raw materials. By recovering minerals such as lithium and magnesium from a local, fully traceable source, Seamoretech is showing the critical impact of its technology.
The new funding will be used for Seamoretech’s next phase of industrialisation and support its commercial expansion, including a planned launch in Spain next year. The company has already demonstrated collaboration in Spain and is now building a pipeline of pilot projects across several markets, including Spain and Egypt.
The startup plans to open a second closing of its Seed round in the coming months. With technology that can deploy rapidly on existing plant infrastructure and Spanish expansion on the horizon, Seamoretech aims to become Europe’s answer to water scarcity and critical mineral shortfalls, reducing global reliance on new mineral extraction by 30% by 2040.

articles.title: SA’s AI policy faces the bigger test of enforcing the rules
articles.text:
South Africa’s attempt to establish a national framework for artificial intelligence (AI) suffered a credibility crisis in April 2026, when the government withdrew its draft policy after fabricated academic references were discovered in the document.
The incident exposed failures in preparing a framework intended to guide the responsible adoption of a technology already reshaping business and public life.
Five months later, Communications and Digital Technologies Minister Solly Malatsi confirmed that disciplinary proceedings were ongoing against one suspended official, following the resignation of another over the scandal.
“Having such a major stain on an important policy is something that cannot just be allowed to slide,” Malatsi told TechCabal on October 15.
But holding officials accountable is only part of the challenge.
South Africa’s bigger AI governance test is whether its existing institutions can enforce the rules and protect people from harm. Strengthening existing regulators rather than creating a dedicated AI authority could avoid unnecessary bureaucracy, but it would place greater responsibility on institutions to investigate AI-related harms, coordinate enforcement, and provide redress. Without clear responsibilities, adequate resources and effective enforcement, a replacement policy risks becoming a statement of intent rather than a framework that changes how AI is used.
Flexibility brings an AI enforcement challenge
The government expects Cabinet to finalise the replacement policy by the end of March 2027, with public consultation to follow.
Malatsi acknowledged the delay at the CollectiveXChange 2026 summit, South Africa’s youth employment and digital skills event, in Johannesburg on October 15, describing the process as a “false start”.
“Yes, it is very late, and that is the consequence of having a false start,” he said.
The regulatory approach is also evolving. At the X Tech 2026 event series hosted by law firm Bowmans on 21 October, Department of Communications and Digital Technologies Deputy Director-General Jeanette Morwane said the government was reviewing legislation affected by AI, including the Films and Publications Act and the Electronic Communications Act.
Morwane indicated that the government favoured empowering existing regulators over establishing new institutions specifically to oversee AI.
That approach could build on regulators’ sector-specific expertise in areas such as financial services, communications and consumer protection. But distributing oversight across institutions creates coordination challenges when AI-related harm crosses regulatory boundaries.
The replacement policy must clarify which institution leads investigations, how regulators share information and how enforcement gaps will be addressed. Existing mandates alone will not guarantee a coherent system.
Consumers need more than ethical AI principles
The consequences of weak oversight extend directly to consumer protection, influencing how individuals access essential services and interact with automated business platforms.
At the Bowmans event, Heather Irvine, a partner at the firm, noted that banks and insurers routinely use machine learning to assess creditworthiness, detect fraud, and price risk, while retailers and e-commerce platforms rely on automated personalisation to determine product visibility and pricing.
These applications can improve efficiency, but they also raise questions about accountability when automated decisions produce harmful outcomes.
The risks are already visible in South Africa’s financial sector. The South African Banking Risk Information Centre (SABRIC) recorded R2.4 billion ($143.8 million) in losses from digital banking crime in 2025, up from R1.9 billion ($113.8 million) the previous year. Furthermore, research from consumer credit agency TransUnion highlights how deepfake impersonation and AI-enabled techniques are driving higher fraud sophistication across Africa.
However, these figures do not isolate AI-enabled offences, pointing to a key analytical gap: without dedicated data tracking AI-driven crimes, policymakers will struggle to evaluate the true scale of the threat or determine whether existing regulators are equipped to respond.
Can consumers challenge credit decisions influenced by AI? What happens when personalised pricing disadvantages certain customers? Where can someone turn when AI-generated content causes harm?
Malatsi has argued that ethical AI adoption must include avenues for redress.
“When we create a regime for the ethical use and ethical adoption of AI, where the use is not ethical, there’s got to be an avenue for recourse,” he told TechCabal.
The practical question is how the proposed framework will turn that commitment into accessible remedies.
National Consumer Commission acting commissioner Hardin Ratshisusu said existing legislation could potentially address AI-related fraud, misinformation and disinformation. But laws that may apply to AI-related harm do not automatically ensure regulators can identify violations, investigate complaints and deliver effective remedies.
The AI capacity question cannot be ignored
Morwane highlighted the operational pressure facing existing bodies, citing one regulator where just two staff members were tasked with handling over 200 cases involving child sexual abuse material (CSAM).
That example does not establish that every South African regulator lacks the capacity to oversee AI. It does, however, illustrate why the government’s approach requires scrutiny.
Effective oversight demands technical expertise, investigative capacity and the ability to assess rapidly evolving systems. Regulators must also determine when existing laws are sufficient and when amendments or new enforcement mechanisms are needed.
The replacement policy should clarify whether regulators will receive additional funding and technical support, how their responsibilities will be defined, and how disputes over jurisdiction will be resolved. These are not minor implementation details: they will help determine whether the policy changes how AI is developed and deployed.
March is an AI milestone, not the finish line
The March 2027 target offers a milestone after the original draft’s withdrawal, but publication alone will not restore confidence in AI governance.
The replacement must combine principles for ethical adoption and the protection of human rights and dignity with a credible implementation framework. That means clear institutional responsibilities, timelines, adequate resources and procedures for handling complaints and enforcing rules.
Public consultation will give businesses, researchers, civil society and consumers an opportunity to assess whether the framework addresses practical risks.
South Africa has a reason to avoid unnecessary regulatory bureaucracy. But flexibility cannot substitute for accountability, resources or enforcement.
The true test will be whether consumers can challenge harmful AI decisions, businesses understand their compliance obligations, and regulators possess the legal backing to penalise abuse.
South Africa’s revised AI policy must do more than repair a flawed drafting process. It must demonstrate that when automated systems cause real-world harm, accountability extends beyond ethical pledges to institutions with the power, resources, and legal mandate to intervene.

articles.title: Déjà un restylage pour la Renault 5 ? Ce qui va changer très bientôt sur la citadine électrique
articles.text:
Elle semble encore toute fraîche et toute belle dans la rue. La Renault 5 est pourtant sortie il y a déjà près de deux ans. Il faut dire que son style particulièrement fidèle à celui du concept a rapidement fait mouche auprès du public. Et aujourd’hui, la française ne compte pas se reposer sur ses lauriers face à une concurrence toujours plus agressive. Un restylage de mi-carrière est ainsi dans les cartons pour lui permettre de tenir la distance.
S’il ne faudra aucunement s’attendre à une révolution, la Renault 5 restylée s’appuiera tout de même sur les fortes capacités d’adaptation de la marque grâce à sa rapidité de développement initiée par la Twingo. François Provost, le PD du groupe Renault, le confirme dans un entretien accordé à Auto Express : « grâce à notre capacité de développement réduite à moins de deux ans, vous constaterez bientôt des changements significatifs » sur la R5.
Autonomie en hausse : comment la R5 compte franchir un cap technique
La citadine électrique a déjà vu son rayon d’action légèrement augmenter à la fin de l’été grâce à de petites optimisations aérodynamiques. La version restylée devrait aller plus loin avec l’adoption d’éléments techniques revus qui réduiront encore son appétit. On pourrait tabler sur des électromoteurs revus et, pourquoi pas, de nouvelles batteries. Il le faudra bien, car avec 430 km d’autonomie, la R5 dévisse désormais face à des rivales plus récentes.
Les dernières citadines du groupe Volkswagen que sont les Volkswagen ID. Polo, Cupra Raval et Skoda Epiq affichent une polyvalence rare sur le segment avec plus de 450 km possibles sur une charge, fruit de leur excellente efficience. C’est particulièrement généreux, d’autant plus que la recharge rapide, bien que fixée à 105 kW en courant continu DC, ne chôme clairement pas avec un 10 à 80 % de batterie sous les 25 minutes.
À bord : un habitacle plus moderne pour faire oublier l’écran 10 pouces
Même cas de figure pour les Hyundai Ioniq 3 et Kia EV2 proposant toutes deux une endurance supérieure. Bref, il faudra retoucher la fiche technique chez Renault, et pas seulement. Le multimédia, bien que toujours convaincant grâce à l’interface Android Automotive, commence à prendre un petit coup de vieux. Sa diagonale de 10 pouces devient en effet un peu juste par rapport aux écrans panoramiques proposés chez la concurrence.
Côté style, par contre, les changements seront plus timides, car la R5 doit conserver son design singulier faisant sa force. La gamme ne devrait pas non plus s’élargir avec de nouvelles variantes. On restera donc sur un catalogue tournant toujours autour de propositions classiques accompagnées d’une déclinaison sportive qu’est l’Alpine A290. Ce sont les Renault 4 et Twingo qui auront le privilège de versions plus spécifiques.

articles.title: EUA planejam bloquear ligações de operadoras chinesas • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
EUA planejam bloquear ligações de operadoras chinesas
Proposta da FCC cita riscos de golpes telefônicos e à segurança nacional. Embaixada da China diz que ação prejudicaria comércio entre países.
Os Estados Unidos podem bloquear ligações de telefonias chinesas para números registrados no país. A Federal Communications Commission (FCC), órgão análogo à Anatel, afirma que a decisão seria motivada para combater golpes via discagem automática, conhecidas como robocalls. A proposta será votada em 19 de novembro e pode banir o acesso direto de companhias como a China Mobile, China Telecom e China Unicom.
A FCC já havia impedido essas companhias de oferecerem serviços de telecomunicações no país. Além das telefonias em si, a nova medida também pretende barrar provedores com serviços via IP que utilizem roteadores e outros equipamentos de Huawei e ZTE, classificados como um risco à segurança nacional.
O presidente Donald Trump tem adotado uma postura mais agressiva na taxação e proibição de eletrônicos chineses. Em resposta, a Embaixada da China em Washington criticou os planos anunciados pelo FCC e afirmou que a medida poderia prejudicar ainda mais o comércio entre os dois países.
A FCC afirma que o banimento dessas ligações seria uma forma de combater golpes telefônicos no país. Segundo o presidente do órgão, Brendan Carr, a decisão vai “reforçar a primeira linha de defesa contra atores maliciosos e robocallers ilegais”. Para além da proteção aos usuários em si, a medida teria como base evitar que empresas chinesas tenham acesso a dados e infraestruturas de telefonia nos Estados Unidos.
De acordo com a Reuters, no primeiro ano do segundo mandato de Trump, o governo americano afirmou que o grupo de espionagem Salt Typhoon, supostamente ligado à China, teria roubado registros de chamadas de consumidores nos Estados Unidos e se infiltrado em infraestruturas de telecomunicações do país. Neste ano, o FBI reiterou que o grupo continua ativo e representa uma ameaça à segurança nacional.
Até mesmo uma empresa sediada nos Estados Unidos, a Digitalsystem Technology, foi incluída na lista de restrições da FCC por sua possível ligação com operadoras chinesas. Segundo o órgão, a companhia seria controlada por uma estatal da China. O governo chinês, por sua vez, nega qualquer envolvimento.
Com o possível bloqueio do acesso direto de operadoras chinesas a números de telefone dos Estados Unidos e de empresas que utilizem equipamentos de fabricantes da China, o governo pretende ampliar a proteção de dados e da infraestrutura de telecomunicações.
As medidas se somam à escalada tarifária contra o rival econômico, cujas taxas chegaram a 145%. Em 2025, o governo Trump chegou a retirar celulares e computadores da lista de produtos sujeitos às novas tarifas. Ainda assim, a Casa Branca mantém ações contra componentes e serviços de empresas chinesas.

articles.title: Omen AI adds liquid know-how in $16 million Aquatic Labs acquisition | TechCrunch
articles.text:
U.S. data centers use 17 to 19 billion gallons of water to cool their hot-running chips each year — and that number is expected to triple in the next five years, according to The Water Foundation.
That’s an expensive and politically tricky proposition for investors throwing billions of dollars at the challenge of scaling up AI. One way to use less water is to do a better job monitoring the cooling fluids, a task that currently involves sending samples away to a laboratory for tests in a multi-day process.
Omen AI was founded in 2024 to solve that problem. The company is building a real-time sensor to determine whether valves were failing, or if bacteria growth in the system threatened to choke off water flow. After raising a $31 million Series A in June, Omen is now acquiring competitor Aquatic Labs in a $16 million cash-and-stock deal.
The deal came together after Omen founder Zach Laberge was introduced to Aquatic Labs’ CEO Allan Adams by an investor in the filtration space. Both startups were building real-time water sensors with complementary technology: Omen’s sensors looked for elements in the water, while the Aquatic Labs sensor tests its alkalinity.
Putting those two technologies in the same sensor creates a “much richer picture of the water and the fluid,” Adams told TechCrunch, while uniting their vision of automating what had previously been a slow, manual process.
The combination unites two classic species of founder: Laberge dropped out of high school to pursue his first company, which did similar fluid analysis for large construction machines that depend on hydraulics. Adams was an academic, trained as a physicist, who spent much of his career developing advanced ocean sensing technology as an MIT professor and Woods Hole Oceanographic Institute researcher before starting his company.
Now, with Adams as the company’s chief science officer, the combined teams are working to integrate both technologies into one sensor, which they expect to have on the market by early next year. Omen’s initial sensors will be monitoring chips pulling in 250 to 300 MW of power by the end of the year, worth about $5 to $7 billion, Laberge told TechCrunch, with the hope of being installed on the equivalent of 1 GW of chips by the end of 2027.
The added value is in uptime: If the fluid system gets out of whack, data center operators typically choose to dump the water rather than risk damage to their expensive equipment. That means shutting down operations until the fluid system is restored, which costs a lot of money. Monitoring lets data center operators use the same fluid for longer, and minimize the costs of a clean up.
Adams hopes to see their technologies have an impact outside of data centers as well, telling TechCrunch that “water goes into data centers, and then it comes out and gets dumped into municipal water, and you want that whole process to happen in a way that’s as safe and responsible as possible — and that means you got to measure stuff.”
AI companies once estimated as much as $4 trillion would be spent on AI infrastructure by 2030, but some investors have grown skeptical of the buildout, sending hyperscaler stocks plummeting in recent days. Omen’s team isn’t worried about shifting sentiment though, since their work comes after a data center has been built.
“We’re working customers on stuff they’re building today or have already built, and so it doesn’t really affect us because all of those projects were financed 12 months ago,” Laberge said. “Our view is, if there’s tightness, this is still going to be the biggest market in human history, even if you sliced it in half.”

articles.title: iPhones von Politikern gehackt? Wildberger bestätigt Einsatz von Spyware
articles.text:
iPhones von Politikern gehackt? Wildberger bestätigt Einsatz von Spyware
Das Bundesamt für Sicherheit in der Informationstechnik (BSI) hat Bundestagsabgeordnete und Regierungsmitglieder nach Informationen des ARD-Hauptstadtstudios vor einem möglichen Angriff mit Spähsoftware auf Handys gewarnt. Bei dem Hinweis gehe es um eine Bedrohungsbenachrichtigung für iPhones von Apple.
Digitalminister Karsten Wildberger (CDU) sagte dazu im ARD-Bericht aus Berlin, es gebe „eine Meldung von Apple, dass bestimmte Geräte gegebenenfalls kompromittiert wurden mit sogenannter Spyware“. Das BSI habe „superschnell reagiert“ und alle Betroffenen angeschrieben, was in diesem Fall zu tun sei. Nähere Angaben machte er nicht. „Das ist jetzt rein spekulativ, um was es sich hier konkret handelt, das muss man jetzt abwarten.“
Er würde das nicht unbedingt auf einen KI-Angriff zurückführen, da es Spyware auf Telefonen schon länger gebe. „Das ist trotzdem etwas, was natürlich uns sehr besorgt“, so der Digitalminister.
Was ist Spyware?
Spyware ist Schadsoftware, die ohne Wissen und Zustimmung der Nutzer auf Computern oder Smartphones installiert wird, um Daten zu sammeln und an Dritte zu übermitteln. Dazu können Tastatureingaben zählen, Nachrichten, Fotos, Standortdaten sowie Anrufe und Mikrofonaufnahmen.
Die Programme gelangen meist über manipulierte E-Mail-Anhänge, gefälschte Links oder Apps aus unseriösen Quellen auf ein Gerät; teilweise nutzen sie Sicherheitslücken in veralteter Software aus. Neben Kriminellen und Stalkern setzen auch Staaten Spyware ein.

articles.title: Support New AI Frameworks Faster Using NVIDIA Workload Map | NVIDIA Technical Blog
articles.text:
NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform brings together technologies to help the ecosystem design, build, and operate more efficient AI factories, including open source, modular software components built to support multi-tenant operations and scaling.
Operating an AI factory requires a shared understanding of distributed workloads: their components, pod templates, replica counts, and status. On Kubernetes, each framework encodes that information differently. JobSet, LeaderWorkerSet, and other custom resources often require separate adapters before a tool can interpret and manage them.
NVIDIA Workload Map provides a common description of Kubernetes workload structure that users can reuse across frameworks. As part of the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform, Workload Map enables integrated schedulers, controllers, and platforms to interpret supported workload types without maintaining separate framework-specific parsing code.
This post shows how to describe a distributed JobSet workload once, then reuse that definition for workload inspection, gang scheduling, and platform visibility.
Why every workload type needs its own adapter
On Kubernetes, a real workload is rarely a single pod. A distributed training job or a multi-node inference server is a small tree of resources: groups of pods, each with a role, a replica count, a pod template, and a status that depends on the workload type.
Teams building schedulers, controllers, dashboards, or cost tools that must work across these workloads encounter this immediately. The NVIDIA Run:ai team faced the same challenge while creating its platform. For each new custom resource definition (CRD), developers answer the same questions in code:
- What’s the structure of the workload type?
- How is the resource’s status interpreted as a phase?
- How is the pod spec changed without breaking the workload?
A developer answers those questions once per workload type and produces a per-CRD adapter. Each new framework a customer brings requires another adapter. That makes adapter development a roadmap item per framework, not a one-time cost, which is why support for a new workload type so often waits for a release.
The following manifest shows a distributed training job as a user submits it: a JobSet with a leader Job and two worker Jobs, each with a pod requesting four GPUs.
apiVersion: jobset.x-k8s.io/v1alpha2
kind: JobSet
metadata:
  name: demo
spec:
  replicatedJobs:
    - name: leader
      replicas: 1
      template:
        spec:
          parallelism: 1
          completions: 1
          template:
            spec:
              containers:
                - name: leader
                  image: ghcr.io/example/trainer:latest
                  resources:
                    limits:
                      nvidia.com/gpu: 4
    - name: worker
      replicas: 2
      template:
        spec:
          parallelism: 1
          completions: 1
          template:
            spec:
              containers:
                - name: worker
                  image: ghcr.io/example/trainer:latest
                  resources:
                    limits:
                      nvidia.com/gpu: 4
The manifest describes one leader, two workers, and a total request of 12 GPUs. Interpreting that structure requires JobSet-aware code; kubectl lists the resources separately.
Figure 1. kubectl lists the demo JobSet, its three Jobs, and their pods as separate resource entries
$ kubectl get jobset,jobs,pods
NAME                      TERMINALSTATE   RESTARTS   COMPLETED   SUSPENDED   AGE
jobset.jobset.x-k8s.io/demo               0                                  3m46s
NAME                      STATUS   COMPLETIONS   DURATION   AGE
job.batch/demo-leader-0   Running  0/1           3m46s     3m46s
job.batch/demo-worker-0   Running  0/1           3m46s     3m46s
job.batch/demo-worker-1   Running  0/1           3m46s     3m46s
NAME                          READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
pod/demo-leader-0-0-ksb4l     1/1     Running   0          3m47s
pod/demo-worker-0-0-qv955     1/1     Running   0          3m47s
pod/demo-worker-1-0-5smfn     1/1     Running   0          3m47s
Owner references connect the Jobs to their JobSet, but a platform still needs a definition to interpret their roles and aggregate resource requests.
Without a shared workload description, users must reconstruct the workload and total its GPU requests themselves.
A common description of Kubernetes workload structure
Workload Map (formerly Karta; the CRD’s resource kind remains Karta) ships as a Kubernetes CRD plus a Go library that interprets workload definitions. Each definition specifies where to find pod templates, replica counts, and status fields for its workload type.
Workload Map supplies a shared structural view to scheduling and platform consumers. KAI Scheduler uses its definitions to interpret pod grouping and gang-scheduling instructions, while NVIDIA Run:ai uses them for workload management and visibility. Each consumer acts on the same description, reducing the need for separate framework-specific parsers.
The Go library resolves a live object into a uniform structural view. With a workload definition in hand, a consumer can:
- Extract pod templates, replica counts, status, and metadata.
- Update pod specs, labels, and annotations across every instance.
- Understand the workload hierarchy, for example, a JobSet’s replicated Jobs and their pods.
Workload Map includes a catalog of prebuilt, tested definitions for JobSet, PyTorchJob, RayCluster, RayJob, RayService, KServe, Knative, MPIJob, NVIDIA NIM, LeaderWorkerSet, Milvus, Grove PodCliqueSet, and NVIDIA Dynamo. Additional workload types can be added by writing a YAML definition that describes their structure and status.
The key is that workload knowledge moves out of compiled adapters and into data developers can write, review, and apply to a cluster like any other manifest. The rest of this post describes the JobSet example, then shows how the same definition supports workload inspection, gang scheduling, and platform visibility.
Writing a workload definition for JobSet
A workload definition, expressed as a Workload Map resource, describes that shape. The following excerpt shows key parts of the JobSet definition. The full version ships in the repository.
The root component defines the workload’s own kind and how its status is read.
apiVersion: run.ai/v1alpha1
kind: Karta
spec:
  structureDefinition:
    rootComponent:
      name: jobset
      kind:
        group: jobset.x-k8s.io
        version: v1alpha2
        kind: JobSet
      statusDefinition:
        conditionsDefinition:
          path: .status.conditions
        statusMappings:
          running:
          - byExpression:
              expression: "(.status.replicatedJobsStatus // []) | any(.ready > 0 and .active > 0) and all(.failed == 0)"
              expectedResult: "true"
          completed:
          - byConditions:
            - type: Completed
              status: "True"
          failed:
          - byConditions:
            - type: Failed
              status: "True"
statusMappings is the translation layer. JobSet does not report a plain “Running” condition, so the definition derives it with a jq expression over replicatedJobsStatus (any Job ready and active, none failed) and maps the native Completed and Failed conditions onto the shared vocabulary a consumer already uses. When a RayJob or a LeaderWorkerSet is described, its very different status maps to the same categories.
The next excerpt defines the child component: the structure inside the workload.
    childComponents:
    - name: replicatedjob
      kind: { group: batch, version: v1, kind: Job }
      ownerRef: jobset
      specDefinition:
        podTemplateSpecPath: .spec.replicatedJobs[].template.spec.template
      scaleDefinition:
        replicasPath: .spec.replicatedJobs[] | .replicas * .template.spec.parallelism
      instanceIdPath: .spec.replicatedJobs[].name
A JobSet declares its roles as a list, so .spec.replicatedJobs holds one entry per role. The [] in these paths means “for each entry in that list,” and each entry is what Workload Map calls an instance. podTemplateSpecPath points to each Job’s pod template. scaleDefinition uses jq: the number of pods per replicated Job equals replicas times parallelism, which is why the example manifest sets parallelism explicitly. instanceIdPath takes each instance’s name from .spec.replicatedJobs[].name, which is how “leader” and “worker” show up as distinct roles instead of three anonymous Jobs.
The framework-specific structure is now captured in one reusable definition. The next section shows how different consumers use it.
Using one description across tools
The same JobSet definition supports three workflows: inspecting workloads, scheduling them together, and managing them as one workload.
Inspecting workloads with the Workload Map CLI
The Workload Map CLI reads workloads from a cluster and renders them through their workload definitions. For the demo JobSet, the CLI loads the JobSet description, resolves the live object and its pods, and prints the tree. The CLI uses a kubeconfig to access the cluster and includes built-in workload definitions. This inspection workflow does not require installing Workload Map into the cluster.
The following commands install the CLI with Homebrew on macOS or Linux and confirm that the executable is on the PATH.
brew tap dsx-ai-factory/kli https://github.com/dsx-ai-factory/workload-map
brew install dsx-ai-factory/kli/kli
kli --version
With the demo JobSet running in the current Kubernetes context, the following command inspects it. The <namespace> placeholder must be replaced with the namespace containing the workload.
kli describe jobset/demo -n <namespace>
JobSet/demo   namespace: default   definition: jobset-x-k8s-io-jobset-v1alpha2 (catalog)   age: 20s
`-- replicatedjob                   3/3 ready   gpu: 12   runai-cluster-worker-0-0
    |-- leader                      1/1 ready   gpu: 4    runai-cluster-worker-0-0
    |   `-- demo-leader-0-0-ck6kg   Running     gpu: 4    runai-cluster-worker-0-0
    `-- worker                      2/2 ready   gpu: 8    runai-cluster-worker-0-0
        |-- demo-worker-0-0-j9pdc   Running     gpu: 4    runai-cluster-worker-0-0
        `-- demo-worker-1-0-rrsxz   Running     gpu: 4    runai-cluster-worker-0-0
Phase: Running
Resources:
COMPONENT   REPLICAS   GPU   CPU   MEMORY
leader      1          4     0     0
worker      2          8     0     0
TOTAL       3          12    0     0
The output identifies the leader and worker roles and shows a total request of 12 GPUs for the example workload.
Figure 4. An earlier Karta CLI view resolves the JobSet into leader and worker roles, showing readiness, GPU totals, and node placement
$ karta workload tree demo
JobSet/demo [Running]
└─ replicatedjob  (3/3 replicas)  3/3 ready  gpu: 12  runai-cluster-worker-0-2,runai-cluster-worker-0-5,runai-cluster-worker-0-7
   ├─ leader  (1/1 replicas)  1/1 ready  gpu: 4  runai-cluster-worker-0-7
   │  └─ Pod/demo-leader-0-0-ksb4l  Running  gpu: 4  runai-cluster-worker-0-7
   └─ worker  (2/2 replicas)  2/2 ready  gpu: 8  runai-cluster-worker-0-2,runai-cluster-worker-0-5
      ├─ Pod/demo-worker-0-0-qv955  Running  gpu: 4  runai-cluster-worker-0-5
      └─ Pod/demo-worker-1-0-5smfn  Running  gpu: 4  runai-cluster-worker-0-2
$ karta workload list
NAMESPACE   NAME  KIND    PHASE    COMPONENTS           GPU  AGE
karta-demo  demo  JobSet  Running  leader(1), worker(2)  12   3m
The definition supplies the JobSet-specific structure, so the CLI can inspect the workload without a dedicated parser.
Enabling gang scheduling with KAI Scheduler
For consumers that schedule workloads, a definition can also include optional gang-scheduling instructions.
  optimizationInstructions:
    gangScheduling:
      podGroup:
        name: job
        subGroups:
        - componentName: replicatedjob
The definition supplies grouping information; KAI Scheduler enforces gang admission and makes placement decisions. KAI Scheduler uses Workload Map as a fallback in its pod grouper for workload types without a native plugin. A matching definition provides the structure and grouping information without requiring a new framework-specific plugin, while native plugins retain precedence.
Managing the same workload in NVIDIA Run:ai
In NVIDIA Run:ai, a single API call registers the workload type using the same catalog definition with no additional code. The platform then uses that description to manage the JobSet as one workload.
The CLI, KAI Scheduler, and NVIDIA Run:ai use the same definition for different purposes: inspection, scheduling, and platform visibility. For another supported workload type, the corresponding catalog definition supplies its structure through the same interface.
Workload Map adoption across schedulers and platforms
NVIDIA Workload Map is available under the Apache 2.0 license and is used in production within NVIDIA Run:ai. Its declarative definitions support workload visibility, status interpretation, submission, and mutation across supported Kubernetes workload types.
Adoption also extends to multi-cluster scheduling. Elotl’s Nova uses Workload Map to interpret workload structure and resource requirements when selecting a cluster for distributed workloads. By using prebuilt definitions, Nova reduces the need to maintain framework-specific parsing logic, demonstrating how the same workload-description model can support different scheduling and platform consumers.
Getting started
NVIDIA Workload Map is an open source component available through the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory GitHub organization. If you are running AI workloads on Kubernetes and need a consistent way to interpret their structure across frameworks, Workload Map helps close the gap.
Start with the workload catalog to find a definition for a framework you already use, or adapt one to support a custom workload type. Join the conversation on the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Slack workspace using the Slack invitation link. We can’t wait to see what you build.

articles.title: Le Canada a supprimé le changement d'heure et des réveils connectés Google n'ont rien capté
articles.text:
Un réveil qui ne donne plus la bonne heure, c’est un peu un grille-pain qui refuse de griller. C’est pourtant ce que vivent depuis dimanche des propriétaires canadiens de Lenovo Smart Clock et de Smart Clock Essential, deux réveils connectés à l’écosystème Google Home. Sur Reddit, des utilisateurs de l’Alberta, de la Colombie-Britannique et du Manitoba racontent que leur appareil affiche une heure de retard, rapporte Android Authority.
Pourquoi les réveils se sont trompés ?
En 2026, une bonne partie de l’Ouest canadien a tourné le dos au changement d’heure, un projet sur lequel l’Europe aurait pu être précurseur, si elle était allée jusqu’au bout de sa réforme. La Colombie-Britannique a avancé ses horloges une dernière fois le 8 mars, avant de rester à l’heure d’été en permanence. L’Alberta, le Manitoba, les Territoires du Nord-Ouest et une partie du nord-ouest de l’Ontario ont suivi : le 1er novembre, une semaine après le passage à l’heure d’hiver en Europe, les horloges n’y ont pas reculé. La Saskatchewan ne change déjà plus d’heure depuis 1966, et le Yukon depuis 2020.
Sauf que les Smart Clock, elles, ont reculé d’une heure comme si de rien n’était. Le plus étrange : interrogé à la voix, Google Assistant donne la bonne heure, alors que l’écran LED du réveil affiche la mauvaise. Les autres appareils Google Home, comme le TV Streamer ou les écrans connectés, se sont mis à jour sans problème. Une réinitialisation d’usine ne règle rien.
Google avait pourtant vu venir le problème. Le 23 octobre, le groupe a prévenu que les smartphones Android pas à jour risquaient de reculer leur horloge par erreur, et que certains rendez-vous de Google Agenda pourraient se décaler d’une heure. Les petits appareils, eux, dépendent des mises à jour que leurs fabricants veulent bien leur envoyer. Et la Smart Clock Essential tourne toujours sous Google Assistant, sans avoir eu droit à la migration vers Gemini.
Des mois d’attente ?
En attendant un correctif, certains utilisateurs ont trouvé une astuce : déclarer une adresse dans une autre région, dont le fuseau correspond à l’heure réelle. Pratique, à condition de ne pas compter sur son réveil pour la météo locale.
En 2022, quand la Jordanie a adopté l’heure d’été permanente, puis en 2023, quand le Mexique a abandonné le changement d’heure, des écrans connectés avaient déjà affiché une heure fausse, et la correction avait pris plusieurs mois.
L’épisode a valeur d’avertissement pour l’Europe, où l’abandon du changement d’heure, voté par le Parlement européen en 2019, reste bloqué. Si le jour vient, il faudra penser aux réveils, aux fours, aux voitures et à tous ces objets qui ne reçoivent plus de mises à jour. Au Québec, le premier ministre Paul St-Pierre Plamondon vient d’annoncer son intention d’abolir lui aussi le changement d’heure. Les propriétaires de Smart Clock québécois savent ce qui les attend (une heure de retard sur le reste de la maison, au moins).

articles.title: Opinion: Alberta’s plan to scrap DEI in hiring will cost innovation | BetaKit
articles.text:
April Hicke is the founder and CEO of tech recruitment and HR platform Toast.
Alberta’s Bill 33 isn’t a bill to foster hiring based on merit; it’s a signal, and the province’s tech sector will pay for it.
On Tuesday, Alberta Minister of Justice Mickey Amery tabled the Justice Statutes Amendment Act. If it passes, municipalities, school boards, universities, colleges, Crown corporations, and public agencies will be barred from using diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) programs in hiring and promotion, and mandatory DEI training will be banned. Officials have already floated extending it to non-profits that receive provincial grants. Premier Danielle Smith says the bill will put merit back at the centre of hiring. Back? By the government’s own account, Alberta’s public service already hires on merit. This bill doesn’t fix a hiring problem. It manufactures a culture war.
“This bill doesn’t fix a hiring problem. It manufactures a culture war.”
April Hicke, Toast
DEI was never the opposite of merit. I’ve spent more than four years building Toast, which started as a recruitment firm placing women in tech. Now, it runs a talent marketplace software of more than 35,000 women. In that time I’ve talked to roughly 500 companies about hiring, and not one, not once, has asked me for a quota. That’s a fantasy invented by people who have never sat in a hiring meeting.
What actually happens is far less dramatic. A company posts a senior engineering role, and, often, almost every single applicant is a man. That company calls us because they want a full data set before they make a decision. We add qualified women to the pool. They hire the best person. Every time. That isn’t lowering the bar, it’s making sure the bar gets applied to everyone who can clear it.
Whether we like to admit it or not, the bar is not applied evenly. We all have bias; hiring is full of moments where it sneaks in, and in Canada we’ve measured it. University of Toronto economist Philip Oreopoulos sent nearly 13,000 resumes to Toronto employers. When applicants swapped an English-sounding name for an Indian, Pakistani, or Chinese one, but kept everything else identical, including Canadian education and Canadian experience, callbacks dropped 28 percent. Applicants with Asian names and master’s degrees got fewer callbacks than English-named applicants without one. Read that again: more qualified applicants, yet fewer interviews, based on the recruiter or hiring manager’s perception of their race. That’s not merit. Structured interviews, balanced candidate slates, and bias training exist to catch exactly this problem.
This isn’t only about fairness, either. It’s about whether Alberta can compete. Innovation comes from the Latin innovare, “to make new.” You cannot make new things with a room full of people who all see the world the same way. When people hear “diversity,” they think race, gender, and sexual orientation, and those matter. But what innovation actually runs on is diversity of thought: different instincts for attacking a problem, which come from living different lives. Put 10 people with the same life story at a table, and you’ll likely get one idea ten times.
Boston Consulting Group studied more than 1,700 companies in eight countries and found those with above-average diversity in leadership earned 45 percent of their revenue from innovation, compared with 26 percent for firms with average or below-average diversity. McKinsey’s 2023 analysis of more than 1,200 companies across 23 countries found executive teams in the top quartile for gender diversity were 39 percent more likely to financially outperform those in the bottom quartile. The late Columbia Business School researcher Katherine Phillips showed in controlled experiments that racially diverse groups significantly outperformed homogeneous groups at solving problems; working alongside someone different makes everyone sharper.
Canada already has a problem here. Women are nearly half of our workforce, yet are still less than 30 percent of our tech workers, a number that hasn’t budged in over a decade. Alberta claims it wants to be an AI, tech, and energy innovation hub. If so, we are competing with every province and every country on earth for the people who can build those companies. Our universities and colleges are the pipeline. Our cities are anchor employers. This bill tells them to stop ensuring they’ve cast their net wide enough. Do we honestly think the engineers, founders, and investors deciding where to build won’t notice?
This province is already divided over immigration. Most Canadian workers support equity efforts; a 2025 report found just 16 percent view them negatively. So who is this for? When a government brands removing barriers as “ideology,” it hands a green light to those who never wanted everyone at the table in the first place.
Alberta does not have to choose between merit and inclusion. The companies I work with prove every week that you can have both. If we want to make new things, we need people who see the world differently, and we need to make sure they actually get through the door. Bill 33 pushes that door closer to shut.
The opinions and analysis expressed in the above article are those of its author, and do not necessarily reflect the position of BetaKit or its editorial staff. It has been edited for clarity, length, and style.
Feature image courtesy Wikimedia Commons.

articles.title: Canadian banks blocking AI agents amid security concerns
articles.text:
Canada’s biggest banks, including RBC, TD, CIBC, and others, are blocking AI agents from accessing online bank accounts over security concerns.
The decision comes as major U.S. banks, like Morgan Stanley, Wells Fargo, and others, reportedly detected unauthorized activity from AI agents on customer accounts, with some agents apparently taking actions that are independent of user instructions.
Earlier this year, tech companies launched AI agent tools that they claim can take action for users and help them complete tasks. Meta’s Muse garnered the most attention, but ChatGPT maker OpenAI wasn’t far behind with the launch of its own agent tool, Dots. Users could connect these tools to bank accounts or credit cards, and even ask them to shop for products, although purchases usually require human approval.
However, alongside the Muse hype came tons of reporting about the myriad security issues with the software, including a severe flaw that could have let attackers take over the AI and do whatever they wanted on the victim’s device.
Several Canadian banks confirmed to CBC News that they would block or limit third-party agents from online banking platforms, including RBC, TD, CIBC, and Scotiabank. Meanwhile, RBC’s CEO Dave McKay said in a LinkedIn post that autonomous systems increase risks for fraud, consumer harm, and the broader economy.
But beyond banking, Canadians should be incredibly cautious about what information they give to AI tools like chatbots or agents, as well as how they use those tools, amid increasing privacy and security issues. We’ve seen AI chats leaked to the open web, security issues in AI apps, AI tools doing things they shouldn’t, and more. At this point, it seems to me that using these tools just isn’t worth the risk.
Image credit: Jon Lamont (RBC, Scotiabank), Shutterstock (CIBC)
Source: CBC News

articles.title: Tech Firms Dismantle Botnet That Turned 1.3M TV Boxes Into Proxies
articles.text:
Google said today it worked with industry partners to dismantle a botnet made up of more than 1.3 million Android TV set-top boxes that ship with malicious software which secretly rents the user’s Internet connection out to strangers and conducts advertising fraud. Experts involved in the takedown say the action is likely to sever the botnet’s access to more than 10 million additional compromised systems, including other Internet of Things (IoT) products such as Android-based healthcare devices and karaoke machines.
A report from the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) said Google has severed ties with Videostrong Technology Co., a TV box manufacturer in China that GTIG and other industry experts concluded was responsible for including malware that enrolled more than 1.3 million set-top boxes in a botnet dubbed “XCPE” (named after one of the malware’s core code components).
The report said the XCPE botnet loaded the user’s device with software that makes their Internet address available for resale by multiple “residential proxy” services, which allow customers to rent Internet addresses as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects.
“Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates’ malware modules onto infected devices,” the GTIG post reads, noting that Google took legal action to take down the domains and servers Videostrong used to control the botnet and install additional malware. “A device manufacturer intentionally infecting their users with malware is an unacceptable breach of trust, and represents a serious risk to those users. Without users’ knowledge or consent, infected devices were offered as a distribution mechanism for a wide array of criminal actors.”
The report notes that while TV boxes made up the the majority of the botnet, the same XCPE malware was found in other Android-based IoT products, including telehealth devices, karaoke machines, and even digital signage systems.
Google said it requires all Android device makers to pass compatibility and security tests to ensure their products don’t harm users, but that Videostrong nevertheless found a way to load their malicious software immediately after a user boots up one of these devices for the first time (Google says it has since addressed that weakness).
The GTIG report calls out a number of residential proxy providers whose software development kits were routinely downloaded by devices infected by the XCPE botnet. Those include AppSalt, also known as Honeygain, which is owned by the Vilnius, Lithuania-based Oxylabs. In October 2026, Oxylabs was relaunched under a new brand called Source, after receiving $130 million in funding from private equity firm Warburg Pincus that reportedly valued the business at $3.6 billion. Oxylabs did not respond to a request for comment.
Another provider linked to the botnet was NetNut, a once sprawling residential proxy company operated by the publicly-traded Israeli company Alarum Technologies. In July 2026, the FBI worked with industry partners to seize hundreds of domains associated with NetNut, saying the company was responsible for operating a separate botnet called Popa that enslaved TV boxes as residential proxies. Other proxy providers named in the GTIG report include EarnFM, Traffmonetizer, Jaguar, LINKFOG, BMW/IPWeb and GaGaNode.
Google’s announcement credits a number of industry partners, including Synthient, a startup that tracks proxy providers. In January 2026, Synthient published research into the rapid spread of the Kimwolf botnet, which at the time was hammering networks worldwide with record-smashing DDoS attacks. Synthient documented how Kimwolf infected millions of Android set-top boxes virtually overnight, using a widespread vulnerability in these residential proxy services to compromise other Android-based devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting TV box users.
Synthient’s research caused dozens of residential proxy providers to patch their networks, which helped to fragment the Kimwolf botnet into much smaller pieces that made its incessant and disruptive DDoS attacks far easier for network operators to manage. It also attracted the attention of the Motion Picture Association (MPA), a trade group representing the major Hollywood studios, which partnered with Synthient to purchase and tear apart a number of popular Android TV set-top boxes — including some that were being infected by Kimwolf and other IoT botnets.
In a report published today, Synthient examined a popular, pre-infected TV box sold under the brand MECOOL by a publicly traded company in China called Skyworth Technology, concluding that MECOOL also bundled the malware from Videostrong Technology Co. and likewise installed AppSalt/Honeygain and other proxy components.
Synthient founder Ben Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity that Videostrong’s malware also distributed software for the proxy service Grass. In our November 2025 story, “Is Your Android TV Streaming Box Part of a Botnet?” we quoted a researcher from Censys who found the popular Superbox TV streaming device bundled Grass’s residential proxy software. We also quoted the Grass founder, who denied any affiliation with the TV box maker.
That November 2025 story noted that Superbox and similar Android TV set-top boxes gain new customers primarily by engaging influencers on Tiktok and other social networks who praise the product’s ability to offer hundreds of (pirated) pay TV streaming services for a one-time fee.
Likewise, Synthient’s report observes that the MECOOL set-top boxes exploded in popularity after the product was mentioned in 2023 by the Youtube channel Linux Tech Tips, which has an audience of nearly 17 million subscribers [Linux Tech Tips said in a statement shared with Synthient that it has since updated the video to explicitly frame the product as a scam and have removed all associated affiliate links].
The GTIG report estimates the XCPE botnet takedown should sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices, noting that the various proxy and ad fraud affiliates of Videostrong “each have diversified distribution channels for their modules beyond XCPE.”
Synthient’s Brundage echoed that conclusion, calling the 1.3 million number “highly conservative.”
“The scale of affected devices is likely way higher,” he said. “This is probably the largest operation against backdoored TV boxes that we’ve seen.”
