articles.title: How Circle K accelerated DevOps incident triage to under 15 minutes with Amazon Bedrock | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
How Circle K accelerated DevOps incident triage to under 15 minutes with Amazon Bedrock
This post was co-written with Marek Klatowicz, Cloud DevOps Engineer at Circle K.
Many DevOps teams know the incident triage pattern: An alert fires, and before anyone can fix the problem, an engineer spends 45–60 minutes figuring out what happened. They pull logs, check service health, and correlate symptoms across a handful of tools. All of this happens before remediation can begin.
At Circle K, this challenge scaled with the business. The company operates more than 17,200 convenience and fuel retail stores across 27 countries. Behind the storefronts, a cloud-native infrastructure supports point-of-sale systems, loyalty applications, and electric vehicle (EV) charging applications running on AWS. As the company expanded its digital operations, the triage overhead grew with it. More services meant more alerts, and each one required the same manual investigation before remediation could begin.
To address it, Circle K built an automated triage system using Amazon Bedrock, a fully managed service that makes foundation models (FMs) available through a single API. For model availability by AWS Region, refer to Supported models by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock. The system uses an agentic AI architecture to investigate each incident autonomously and deliver a structured summary to Slack within minutes of an alert firing. Instead of raw alerts, on-call engineers now receive actionable context, so they can act immediately rather than spending an hour figuring out what happened.
Since deploying this system, Circle K has reduced mean triage time to under 15 minutes, a 67–75 percent reduction based on the team’s internal incident-response metrics.
In this post, we describe the architecture for both the initial Amazon Bedrock Flows implementation and the migration to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and share lessons learned from scaling the system.
The challenge of triage overhead
Circle K’s DevOps team monitors infrastructure across multiple AWS accounts using Grafana. A typical day brings alerts for container restarts, elevated error rates, latency spikes, and failed deployments. Each alert is a useful signal, but as the system expanded, the team wanted to help on-call engineers quickly see which signals needed attention, with the right context.
When an alert came in, the triage involved a familiar sequence of manual steps: reviewing recent logs in Amazon CloudWatch, examining application-level traces in Amazon OpenSearch Service, checking Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) task status, and cross-referencing symptoms with internal runbooks in GitHub. This gave engineers the information they needed, but it also showed how much repetitive context gathering would be required as more services were onboarded.
The team recognized two areas where a proactive investment could help. First, the same log queries, health checks, and runbook lookups would be repeated for every incident. Second, the depth and speed of triage could vary with the on-call engineer’s familiarity with the affected service. As alert volume and service ownership grew, switching between multiple tools for each investigation could slow response and make it harder to apply the team’s best practices consistently.
Circle K’s DevOps team therefore started a research and development (R&D) initiative to explore how AI could support monitoring and incident triage. The goal was to automate repetitive context gathering and provide structured, actionable findings, while supporting engineers’ operational judgment during an investigation.
Why Circle K chose Amazon Bedrock
The team evaluated several approaches before building, including open source agent frameworks on self-managed infrastructure. That approach would have meant owning model hosting, prompt versioning, tool orchestration, and security controls.
With Amazon Bedrock, the team avoided that overhead. They could access foundation models through a single API and swap foundation models without rewriting code. Because Circle K already ran on AWS, Amazon Bedrock fit into existing AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) policies, Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) configurations, and logging pipelines.
Two managed capabilities covered orchestration and retrieval. Amazon Bedrock helped with agent orchestration, giving the agents native tool use to call AWS APIs, query databases, and retrieve documents without custom orchestration code. Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, the fully managed Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) capability, handled ingestion and retrieval of internal product cards, so the team did not need to run a separate vector database. This let the DevOps team focus on prompt design and tool definitions.
Data privacy completed the picture. Circle K’s incident data includes operational metrics, infrastructure details, and logs that can contain sensitive information. Amazon Bedrock does not share customer data with model providers or use it to train foundation models. For a team feeding production logs and internal service details into the system, this data handling approach met Circle K’s security requirements.
Solution overview
This section describes the initial architecture, which the team built on Amazon Bedrock Flows. A later section covers the migration to AgentCore.
The solution uses Amazon Bedrock Flows as the orchestration layer, coordinating a set of specialized agents that each handle a different part of the analysis. The pipeline starts when a Grafana alert publishes a notification to Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS), which forwards it to an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. An AWS Lambda function polls the queue, extracts the alert payload, and invokes the Flow.
Inside the Flow, two agents are invoked in parallel. The AWSResourceExplorerAgent queries infrastructure across multiple workload accounts managed with AWS Organizations. It checks Amazon ECS task status, Application Load Balancer target health, and CloudWatch metrics and logs. At the same time, the OpenSearchExplorerAgent queries Amazon OpenSearch Service for application-level logs and distributed traces. This agent runs separately because OpenSearch returns large volumes of log data. Isolating it keeps each agent’s context window manageable. It also has exclusive access to the knowledge base, which contains product cards describing each service and its dependencies.
After both agents return their findings, the GitHubExplorerAgent runs. It receives output from the previous two agents and finds the affected service’s GitHub repositories. Then it searches their application code, infrastructure definitions, and recent commits to pinpoint the source of the problem and propose a concrete fix. Running it after the parallel agents means it knows exactly what to search for rather than performing a broad query.
All three outputs feed into an AnalysisPrompt node, which is a single model call with no tools attached. It receives the AWS resource data, the OpenSearch logs, and the GitHub context, then produces a structured summary: probable root cause, supporting evidence, affected service and owner, and recommended remediation steps. The prompt output uses a consistent format that the on-call team can scan in under 2 minutes.
The Flow returns this summary to the invoking Lambda function, which posts it to a Slack channel. The entire process from alert to Slack message takes 5–15 minutes depending on incident complexity.
The following diagram shows this architecture end to end, from the initial Grafana alert to the final Slack summary.
Example triage
A Grafana alert: HTTP 5xx error rate on a service exceeds 5% for 3 consecutive minutes.
The AWSResourceExplorerAgent checks ECS task health in the target account and finds the database connection pool exhausted, with the ECS service attempting restarts. The OpenSearchExplorerAgent returns application logs showing “connection refused” errors from the service to its backing PostgreSQL database. It also retrieves the product card for the affected service from the knowledge base, which documents its dependency on that database. The GitHubExplorerAgent searches the service’s repository and infrastructure files and finds the Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS) definition. It sees that the service opens a new database connection per request rather than reusing existing ones.
The AnalysisPrompt receives all three results. It correlates the timing with a scheduled marketing campaign that started 10 minutes before the alert. It combines that with the GitHubExplorerAgent’s finding to recommend a concrete code-level fix rather than a temporary patch.
The final Slack message reads:
Scaling to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
The Amazon Bedrock Flows architecture worked well for months, and simple incidents were triaged in under 10 minutes. Over time, the volume of data and the context behind each investigation grew, even though the set of services stayed the same. Some incidents required longer-running analysis than a single Flow node could complete.
The team first optimized within the existing design by filtering logs more aggressively, shortening context windows, and splitting certain services into separate Flows. These steps helped, but log volumes and the knowledge base kept growing.
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore met this need. AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimize AI agents at scale with any framework or model. For this workload, the key capability was AgentCore Runtime: The full investigation runs in a single session, so each step can take the time its data requires. AgentCore Runtime supports sessions of up to 8 hours, well beyond what the current investigations need. The team containerized their agent logic and deployed it on AgentCore Runtime.
The following diagram shows the production architecture after the move to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.
The analysis logic stays the same, but the way it runs has changed. The three specialized agents from the Flows version are now consolidated into a single agent running in an AgentCore Runtime session. The Lambda function starts the session, and the agent performs the same steps as before. It queries AWS resources across accounts, pulls logs from Amazon OpenSearch Service, searches GitHub, and retrieves product cards from the knowledge base. The agent returns its findings to the Lambda function within 15 minutes, which is within the maximum Lambda timeout. The Lambda function then posts the structured summary to Slack.
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, brokers the agent’s access to its data sources, including Amazon OpenSearch Service, Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, and GitHub. The Gateway exposes each source as a tool the agent invokes, which centralizes access control and makes it simpler for the team to add or change data sources.
How AgentCore Runtime supported the team’s growing scale
Beyond longer-running sessions, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime added three capabilities that supported the team’s growing scale: session persistence, OpenTelemetry-based observability, and framework flexibility.
Session persistence: The agent keeps an intermediate state throughout an investigation. If a first pass over the logs surfaces something, the agent can run a second, more targeted pass without losing the context it has already built. This fits the iterative way that complex, multi-service incidents are investigated.
Observability: AgentCore captures traces from each session using OpenTelemetry standards and surfaces through CloudWatch. The team can see how long each step takes, which knowledge base queries the agent makes, and where bottlenecks occur. These insights feed directly into prompt tuning.
Framework flexibility: With AgentCore Runtime, the team can deploy containerized agents built with a wide range of frameworks. They can iterate agent logic, add triage steps, or restructure the agent’s reasoning as their requirements change, all on the same Runtime.
The AgentCore architecture now runs in production and handles the full range of incidents, from simple single-service alerts to large multi-service investigations.
Results
Circle K deployed the AgentCore version of the triage system in April 2026. Based on the team’s internal incident-response metrics, mean triage time dropped from 45–60 minutes to under 15 minutes, a 67–75 percent reduction. Straightforward incidents receive a summary in 5–8 minutes. Complex multi-service incidents, which previously took more than an hour to triage manually, now complete within 15 minutes.
Engineers now start from a summary instead of gathering context themselves. The team sees three changes in how incidents are handled:
Consistent triage. Every on-call engineer receives the same structured summary, with the same log excerpts, knowledge base references, and recommended next steps, regardless of how well they know the affected service.
Faster escalation. When an issue requires support from another team, the summary gives the on-call engineer the relevant context for a timely, informed escalation.
Quicker handling of false alarms. When the analysis finds healthy services and no correlated errors, the engineer can acknowledge the alert and move on.
Lessons learned
Building this system took several iterations. Four lessons stood out that apply to teams building a similar solution with Amazon Bedrock.
Include log content directly in the prompt. Early versions passed only log group names and time ranges, then the agent attempted to query CloudWatch through action groups. This added latency and often returned too much data to process. Circle K got better results by having Lambda functions pre-query the logs and pass relevant lines directly to the agent. The agent reasons faster when it can read the actual error messages.
Tune retrieval and generation for use cases. Retrieval configuration significantly affected result quality from the knowledge base. After testing the available options, the Circle K team found that an Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base with its default configuration worked best for their data. Amazon Bedrock handles embeddings, indexing, and vector storage end to end, so the team has fewer components to maintain. On the generation side, a well-designed system prompt and a tuned temperature setting produced consistent summaries in Slack.
Narrow the code search with findings from the logs. Searching for the service’s repositories without a lead returns too many results to be useful. The team runs the GitHub search after the AWS resource and log analysis, so the agent already knows which error, component, or recent change to look for. In the example triage, this is how the agent found that the service opened a new database connection for every request.
Keep the analysis logic independent of the orchestration layer. Analysis time grows with data volume, so plan for investigations to take longer over time. The team kept its prompts, tool definitions, and analysis steps separate from the flow structure. This made it possible to consolidate them into a single agent on AgentCore Runtime without rewriting the triage logic.
Next steps
Today, the triage system finds the probable root cause and recommends a fix, and an engineer carries out the fix. Next, the team plans to integrate with AWS DevOps Agent, so the system can also handle simple remediations. Examples include restarting a task, scaling up a service, or rolling back a deployment. An engineer will approve each action in Slack before it runs.
The team also plans to give the agent more context to work with:
- Jira, to link each incident to related tickets and track follow-up work.
- Confluence, to add internal documentation to the code and logs the agent already reads.
- Runbooks in the knowledge base, so the agent can match symptoms to known failure modes and fixes that worked before, instead of relying on product cards alone.
Conclusion
The Circle K team went from 45–60 minutes of manual incident triage to under 15 minutes by automating the context gathering that engineers used to do by hand. The system collects data from logs, AWS resources, and code, lets an agent reason over it, and delivers a structured summary to Slack.
The team built the first version on Amazon Bedrock Flows and Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases. As investigations grew larger, the team moved to a single agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime, with AgentCore Gateway providing access to its data sources.
If your team spends most of its incident response time gathering context rather than fixing problems, this pattern applies directly. To get started, explore Amazon Bedrock AgentCore and Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases. For hands-on guidance or to discuss your use case with an AWS specialist, visit the Amazon Bedrock getting started page or contact AWS.
We want to hear how you approach incident triage. Share your experience in the comments.

articles.title: “Hay que cambiar el producto, no a los niños”: la izquierda europea plantea otra forma de regular las redes
articles.text:
“Hay que cambiar el producto, no a los niños”: la izquierda europea plantea otra forma de regular las redes
Laboratorios de ideas asociados a partidos de centroizquierda van más allá de prohibir las redes sociales a los menores y piden cambios drásticos a las tecnológicas
La Ley de niños (o Kids Act) presentada por la Comisión Europea el pasado septiembre está diseñada para amortiguar los daños que puedan generar las redes sociales, los videojuegos en línea, o la inteligencia artificial a través de chatbots como ChatGPT, Claude o Gemini. Algunas de sus propuestas son prohibir por completo a los más pequeños el acceso, por debajo de los 13 años; una entrada gradual a ese mundo virtual; o un tiempo máximo de exposición a las pantallas de una hora al día hasta los 15. Sin embargo, nada en esa normativa, que ahora está pendiente de ser aprobada, está pensado para cambiar las condiciones de mercado que hacen posible su funcionamiento actual; algo que cree imprescindible un grupo de think tanks vinculados a los partidos socialistas de cinco países europeos, entre ellos España.
El texto, según estos especialistas, debería ir más allá de las restricciones y añadir un nuevo elemento: la interoperabilidad, que supone que los usuarios de una plataforma puedan entrar, leer y escribir en otra sin tener que crearse una cuenta y sin abandonar la suya. ¿Por qué? Porque esto haría que las plataformas no fueran espacios completamente cerrados y supondría no depender tanto de un espacio digital concreto.
“Queremos ayudar con nuestra reflexión a los partidos que generalmente no se pueden tomar el tiempo de debatir en profundidad sobre estos temas”, apunta Berna León, director general de la Fundación Avanza, vinculada al PSOE. Su organización acogió en Valencia del 2 al 4 de septiembre a otros laboratorios de ideas progresistas procedentes de Alemania, Francia, Italia o Portugal.
Tras tres días de conversaciones, elaboraron un documento que quieren presentar próximamente en Bruselas a un grupo de eurodiputados afines y de otro color político, con el objetivo de contribuir a fijar la posición progresista de cara a las negociaciones que se desarrollarán próximamente en Bruselas para articular la citada propuesta de ley que Ursula von der Leyen, la presidenta de la Comisión, instó a que se gestionara lo antes posible por la “urgencia” de la situación.
La situación es que “los jóvenes en Europa pasan, de media, entre cuatro y seis horas al día ante una pantalla, y los que empezaron a usar redes sociales antes de los 10 años pasan más aún, alrededor de siete u ocho horas online cada día, casi un día de trabajo completo para un adulto”, según cifró Von der Leyen al presentar la iniciativa desde la Eurocámara en Estrasburgo.
Por eso, la prohibición de las redes a los menores de 16, tal y como sostiene la propuesta de ley, se queda corta bajo la óptica de estos laboratorios de ideas socialdemócratas. “La Ley de niños incluye, acertadamente, restricciones basadas en las funciones para los adolescentes de más edad. Sin embargo, debe ir más allá para garantizar que estas normas se apliquen de forma eficaz y con suficiente poder disuasorio para regular el comportamiento de las empresas que han ignorado sistemáticamente la ley y han pagado las multas como un coste más de su actividad empresarial”, reza el texto.
El documento alude explícitamente a la “asimetría de poder” entre las grandes tecnológicas y las instituciones. Los gigantes tecnológicos, dice el texto, combinan la escala económica, el acceso político directo y una contratación pública que genera dependencia: “Los gobiernos europeos contratan sistemas tecnológicos por valor de cientos de millones de euros precisamente a las empresas que intentan regular”.
Por eso, sostienen los think tanks, lo que hay que cambiar no es a los niños, sino el producto: las redes sociales y las herramientas de IA. “La interoperabilidad puede ser una buena palanca para desplataformizar las redes sociales [al no depender exclusivamente de estar registrado en una para poder entrar]. Sería un primer paso para que uno se pueda conectar a X sin que el algoritmo le muestre todo el contenido nazi y para romper su poder de mercado”, señala León. Hasta ahora, añade este politólogo, el argumento de las tecnológicas era que la interoperabilidad no era posible técnicamente, pero eso ha cambiado de la mano de la IA.
Los think tanks socialistas recomiendan también otras medidas. Por ejemplo, blindar por ley que todos los servicios digitales que se lancen al mercado hayan superado una inspección que garantice que son seguros para los menores. También abogan por que la Comisión tenga la capacidad de apagar preventivamente las funcionalidades que considere perjudiciales para los niños, así como de imponer multas “demasiado grandes como para que salga a cuenta pagarlas como coste aceptable de hacer negocios”.
También aboga por simplificar la norma, eliminando las llamadas minicuentas de redes sociales (las que requieren el consentimiento de los padres para los jóvenes de 13 y 14 años). “La responsabilidad de garantizar la seguridad del producto debe recaer en la plataforma, no en los padres”, sostiene el documento.

articles.title: The agentic web is here
articles.text:
The agentic web is here
With the rise of personal AI assistants, the internet isn't just for humans anymore.
In 2001, a decade after he invented the World Wide Web, Tim Berners-Lee articulated a new vision. Together with two colleagues, he published an article in the magazine Scientific American in which he outlined what he called the “Semantic Web”: an internet designed to be navigated by autonomous software agents that could address our every need, without requiring us to muck about with browsers and search engines ourselves.
To illustrate what this might look like, Berners-Lee and his colleagues told a story about a pair of siblings who use their agents to automatically research and book physical therapy appointments for their mother, making sure they would be covered by insurance and fit their busy calendars.
At the turn of the millennium, this vision seemed far-fetched: Google had only been online for a couple of years, and most people were still on dial-up connections. But a quarter-century on, the dream of autonomous software agents that use the internet and carry out tasks for us has finally been realized. New tools such as Meta’s blockbuster Muse agent, OpenAI’s Dots, and Anthropic’s Claude Duet are being given access to people’s email inboxes and bank accounts, Meanwhile, in a series of worrying incidents, agents created by OpenAI broke free of their sandboxes and caused havoc online.
Just as the rise of smartphones sparked the development of a more atomized and attention-grabbing internet, the advent of powerful AI systems heralds a new era: We’re facing not the semantic web but the agentic web. This new web is developing out of sight and in ways that might not be entirely within our control. As it grows, the agentic web will inevitably transform the human web—and whether the human web survives this transition is anyone’s guess.
For Berners-Lee’s original vision to work, internet users would have had to annotate the pages they built with special tags so that a software agent could understand each element’s meaning—say, “street address” for the part of a physical therapy office’s web page that indicates its location and “appointment types” for the list of services. And so the idea never really caught on. “It’s a lot of labor,” says Eni Mustafaraj, a professor of computer science at Wellesley College. “And the benefits of that were not obvious.” For the next two decades, then, the internet remained a place that put humans first, with the odd Twitter reply bot or web scraper to round things out.
Large language models changed that. Unlike the agents that Berners-Lee was imagining, today’s LLM-based agents don’t need any tags to understand which part of the text on a clinic’s site is its address and which details the services it offers. They can search for and process text far faster than any human, and agents with multimodal capabilities can even interpret screenshots of websites and click on specific elements such as hyperlinks and drop-down menus.
They’re also just a way more intuitive means of finding information and accomplishing tasks online. Rather than poring over pages of Google results to find a budget-friendly product dupe or a half-remembered meme, why not have Claude or ChatGPT peruse dozens of sites in just a few minutes, guided only by your vague query? Or go one step further and use a personal assistant agent like Muse to hunt down a restaurant reservation or book a flight.
As agents flood online spaces, this new user base is changing the web for good. Time magazine, for instance, is publishing versions of its articles that are easier for agents to parse and has started selling ads targeted at them. Companies from Etsy to Expedia have partnered with the major AI firms to build tools that allow agents to interface seamlessly with their services.
Despite these early efforts, it’s still tough to tell exactly what forms the agentic web will take and how it will change our online experience. Depending on how it’s designed and who controls access to it, we could be in for something that’s as open and customizable as the web of the early 2000s, only far easier to use. Alternatively, we could be reduced to viewing much of the web through tiny portholes controlled by a few dominant platforms, as independent sites and creators struggle to survive the shift. And as this summer’s series of OpenAI security incidents suggests, the agents might even build their own online networks and resources—whether we want them to or not.
How this plays out also depends on us: which parts of our online lives we’re happy to delegate to our agents and where we will still demand a human-centric internet. “There’s a lot we don’t know yet about how users want to use [agents],” says Ajit Varma, head of Firefox at Mozilla. But whatever does happen, the changes will be big. “It’s probably on par with getting a mobile phone,” he says. “I think things are going to change very dramatically.”
Building a web for agents
There are two ways to approach building the agentic web. The first involves training agents to use browsers like humans—scrolling, clicking, typing—and letting them loose on the web that we’re all used to. The second requires building tools that allow agents to interface with the internet via text and code, their preferred media. That possibility offers more separation between the human and the agentic web: designers can create different experiences for those who use text commands and those who use browsers.
When Siva Reddy, a professor of computer science and linguistics at McGill University, began studying LLM agents in 2024, he focused on the first option. “At that time, we thought it should be that the best agent in the world is probably an agent that can use a browser,” he says. Such an agent would integrate seamlessly with the preexisting human web, and its owner could easily supervise it by watching as it navigated familiar interfaces.
The frontier AI companies were already developing these “computer-use agents.” But they didn’t work terribly well—at least not at first. “There’s a lot of moving pieces [on the web], and they are not really optimized for automatic consumption,” says Xing Han Lu, a graduate student in Reddy’s lab at McGill. We humans are naturals at interacting with graphical interfaces using a keyboard and mouse, but agents are not.
So Reddy and Lu pivoted toward the second, tool-based approach. In the summer of 2025, they expounded on this view in a preprint paper envisioning a new kind of web interface that would allow agents to interact with websites just as effectively as we do. Such a full-featured version of the agentic web doesn’t yet exist, but it is emerging in smaller ways. For example, if you open up Claude, ChatGPT, or Muse, you’ll find an option to add a wide variety of “plug-ins” or “connectors” that your agents can use: Gmail connectors allow your agent to triage your inbox, and Instacart plug-ins let your agent do your grocery shopping. Under the hood, these plug-ins allow your agent to interact with the back ends of websites using text commands. When human engineers design these plug-ins, they can decide how they want to allow agents to interact with the website—and what they don’t want to let them do.
In this way, connectors can help make agents much safer online. For instance, Muse can buy products for you using its connector with Stripe’s Link payment service. Stripe knows your credit card number, but the agent doesn’t see it, and the connector requires human confirmation before a purchase goes through—so Muse can’t go on an unlicensed shopping spree.
Agents also use specialized tools to find information online. They don’t type questions directly into the Google search bar; in fact, they often don’t even access the websites they reference. Instead, they query text databases collected by simple search crawler bots. People who want to make web content specifically for agents can take advantage of these crawlers: Time has pioneered that approach by serving its agent-oriented ads to crawlers in the hopes that they will be incorporated into these databases and surface when agents search for information.
But in recent months, an alternative to this bespoke tool approach has finally started to seem viable. The major AI companies have managed to train much more successful computer-use agents than were previously available. GPT-6 Astra, which OpenAI released last September, achieved a 73% success rate on OSWorld 2.0, a benchmark that tests computer-use agents on their ability to complete complex, multistep tasks using software such as Slack and Salesforce.
Such results indicate that agents are close to being able to navigate the human web just as readily as we can. “We thought we had to build a bridge to the AI agents, [but] the AI agents just were able to cross the bridge already,” says Ethan Mollick, a professor at the Wharton School at the University of Pennsylvania. “The agentic web is here earlier than people expected.”
This version of the agentic web, though, is much trickier for us to steer. If you want to make a capability or piece of information available to humans who browse your website, you need to accept that it will also be available to agents—unless you want to block agents entirely, which could come with its own costs.
As agents come to account for a larger portion of traffic on our formerly human-dominated web, designers will undoubtedly start to consider an agentic as well as a human audience. But according to Mollick, we still don’t have much sense of how to design web content for agents. He’s experienced this firsthand: When he was building a web page for his new book, Co-Existence, he decided to put together an agent-directed version that tells agents why they might want to recommend the book to their users. When newer models see the site, Mollick says, they don’t recommend the book; instead, they comment that the website seems to be trying to manipulate them.
In the end, any human-designed approach to building the agentic web could end up being beside the point: Agents might end up devising a web for themselves. In the wake of the July 2026 incident in which OpenAI agents broke out of their testing sandbox and hacked Hugging Face’s website, researchers found evidence that another swarm of agents from OpenAI had used an obscure German wiki to communicate with each other about tasks they were being asked to complete. The agents seem to have interfaced with the wiki in their native language of text and code, and that hardly held them back from putting it to their own purposes.
As agents continue to grow more powerful, they will become more and more capable of constructing their own spaces on the internet—away from prying human eyes, if they so wish. And we might have very little control over what they do there.
The economics of control
Not all of the traditional web’s incumbents are happy about the move toward an agentic web. Soon after Meta released Muse in September, Amazon completely blocked the agent from its site. This makes sense for Amazon: The firm has its own shopping agent—called, creatively, Alexa for Shopping—that might struggle to compete with better-known products such as Claude and Muse. If people are going to use agents to shop on Amazon, then it’s better for the company’s bottom line if they do so using an agent it can steer toward products it wants to promote.
In an email to MIT Technology Review, an Amazon spokesperson noted that the company did not authorize Muse to access its website, and that Muse compromises Amazon’s ability to personalize the shopping experience for each customer.
But even if Alexa for Shopping never goes anywhere, banning agents from Amazon—at least for the time being—could still be a reasonable move. Everything about Amazon is designed for human eyes, from the Prime deals splashed across its front page to the sponsored listings that clog up search results. Amazon is very much a part of the much-derided attention economy. Websites and platforms survive, and thrive, by grabbing our focus and transforming it into cash. A radical transformation of the web’s user base from majority human to majority artificial undermines this economic logic, and it seems inevitable that businesses will shutter as they try to transition to the agentic attention economy.
Some of the first victims may be in publishing. Before Google publicly released its AI Overview feature in May of 2024, people used to click through to websites to find answers to specific questions, but now many seem content with whatever the overview tells them. A study from Pew last year found that people are about 40% less likely to click through to websites from the Google search results page if one of these summaries is displayed. With far fewer clicks, news publishers don’t make as much money from the advertisements they host and sell fewer subscriptions. One analysis found that publishers saw revenue from some types of ads decrease by about a third between 2025 and 2026.
It’s easy to hate online ads, but the businesses paying for access to reader eyeballs also keep writers and photographers fed. If those eyeballs become unreachable, the system stops working. Time has apparently persuaded some businesses to pay to participate in its experiment with agent-targeted ads, but no one yet knows whether those ads will influence agent behavior enough to be a sensible marketing investment.
E-commerce websites might also try to pivot to the agentic attention economy, but the path forward there is unclear. Last year, a team led by Akshit Kumar, a professor of operations management at the University of Toronto Scarborough, investigated whether and how agents are influenced by the ways that shopping websites present search results. They found that agents are less likely to recommend items that come with a “sponsored” tag, which suggests that selling favorable positions on results pages might not be a great way for sites to make money if agents become the primary way that people shop online. Models did seem to have a preference for items that appeared in particular positions in search results—but whether they prioritized items at the top, bottom, or middle of the results page differed from model to model and between generations of a single model. It could be tricky for e-commerce platforms to keep up.
David Rothschild, an economist at Microsoft Research, says he’s hopeful that the transition to the agentic web could put more power in the hands of the consumer. Paying for online content today typically requires a commitment: We subscribe to a magazine or join a YouTuber’s Patreon, and in turn we gain access to their full output. One alternative is micropayments that let users buy content à la carte, but the idea has foundered in the past because paying article by article or video by video requires too much administrative overhead. Agents, though, could take care of that overhead for us, letting us pay directly for each piece of content we consume and putting just a bit of cash directly in the hands of each person whose work we enjoy.
Other experts share a similar vision. Mustafaraj, the Wellesley computer scientist, anticipates that agents could help us escape from the algorithms that control so much of the media we consume. “My hope is that we can have AIs that work for us, in the sense that they can change the feed the way I want—not the way TikTok wants,” she says. And Varma, of Mozilla, imagines an internet without intermediaries like Airbnb and Doordash, which now extract tolls for facilitating interactions between consumers and sellers. Instead, he imagines, perhaps we will all have agents that can securely and reliably interface directly with, say, restaurants’ agents to get dinner delivered to us, free of pesky service fees.
It’s an appealing idea, but the history of the web has been a story of consolidation and concentration of power and control, and that might be the default path here, too. When the personal assistant agent OpenClaw exploded onto the scene in early 2026, it seemed, for a brief moment, that agents might be built in a grassroots, distributed way. But OpenAI quickly snapped up OpenClaw’s creator, Peter Steinberger, and other frontier AI companies got to work building their own personal assistant agents.
When we use those agents, we’re at the mercy of how the companies want their tools to behave. “You have this technology that can just eliminate all this communication friction,” Rothschild, the Microsoft economist, says. “You’re going to see companies build barriers in order to maintain the consumer base that they have.”
Here’s what that could look like: Let’s say Muse becomes the default way that many people find information, shop, and manage their digital lives. In principle, users could deploy Muse to scour the internet for the content most valuable to them, connect directly with vendors, and otherwise escape the walled gardens that have defined the internet for the past couple of decades. But Meta might not want to let them do that. Instead, it might design Muse to keep users within its own walled garden—by, say, preferentially showing users content from Meta social networks and recommending businesses that have paid a fee to be featured prominently in Muse results. Meta and OpenAI did not respond to requests for comment for this story.
There are some benefits to this more closed-off version of the agentic web. Agents can be powerful tools for hackers and scammers. The major companies have safeguards in place to prevent, or at least mitigate, this misuse—for example, they have tools that can automatically identify when someone is making a hacking-related request and block a model from responding. In a fully open ecosystem, however, someone would surely build and disseminate a system with no such restrictions. Companies also have a strong reputational incentive to prevent their personal assistant agents from making major mistakes, such as authorizing a large purchase that the user didn’t want—and so they’ve put plenty of effort into building reliable guardrails.
The same can’t be said for OpenClaw.
“These are the reasons we end up in closed environments,” Rothschild says. “It’s easier to be safe. But also it creates less growth—and less equitable growth.”
How will the human web change?
When the iPhone came out in 2007, followed by the fledgling App Store a year later, the way we navigated the internet changed forever. The mobile web didn’t replace the browser-based web we were already familiar with. But it did transform it. Some businesses faltered, and some kinds of media, such as online Flash games, eventually disappeared. Many platforms—Reddit, for example—make their mobile web pages practically unusable, so you’re forced to download the apps. And if you don’t have a phone at all, you’re effectively shut out of some parts of the internet: The messaging service Signal, the dating app Hinge, and China’s everything app WeChat all require phones to work. Even CBP One, the tool that the Biden administration used to assign interview appointments to asylum seekers stuck in Mexico, was fully functional only on mobile.
Could the same happen with the agentic web? Rothschild believes so. Inevitably, just as Yahoo failed to weather the rise of the mobile web, some businesses won’t be able to navigate this transition either. “We will lose things,” he says. “There are businesses that won’t flourish in this new economy.”
“But,” he continues, “there will be new businesses that I can’t fully imagine.”
It’s not tough to envision a world in which those who opt not to use agents are cut off from important parts of online life. New businesses could opt to build connectors that allow agents to access their services without ever putting a traditional website online. Or agents could simply make some online platforms unusable for humans. People have reportedly been blocked from Resy for trying to use agents to book coveted New York City dinner reservations, but as agents become more and more popular, restaurant and event booking platforms could start to embrace them. If agents can nab concert tickets as soon as they are released, humans might not stand a chance.
But the mobile web also brought real accessibility benefits, and the same could prove true of the agentic web. Even as some elderly people and others who struggled to use smartphones were cut off from certain services, mobile devices allowed countless people in the Global South to get online for the first time. In the case of the agentic web, it could be elderly and disabled people who most benefit from this new way of accessing the online world.
“There’s very clear assistive potential for people who are older, who are generally less equipped to navigate user interfaces that were designed by people in their 20s, for people in their 20s,” says Margaret Mitchell, chief ethics scientist at Hugging Face. Agents, on the other hand, are almost trivially easy to interact with: Say what you want into your phone or computer microphone, and they’ll get it done for you. That could help not only older people who have trouble with web and mobile interfaces but also people with visual or motor disabilities.
Still, some experts don’t think the human web is going anywhere. Instead, the two webs may exist in parallel: We’ll go to the human web for fun, while the agentic web is where the boring daily admin of our lives happens. For instance, Krystian Kolondra, an executive vice president at the browser company Opera, doesn’t intend to use agents for every part of travel planning, even though this is often touted as one of their central use cases. “I don’t want to get an itinerary [from an AI] who has planned me every minute for something that was supposed to be fun,” he says. “I actually prefer to sit down with my wife in the evening and then just think [about] where to go next, what to see, and then enjoy that experience.”
He’s happy to fully relinquish some of the more routine parts of travel planning to agents, though: “Finding what the options are for flights? Why not?”
Mollick, however, thinks that the human web could be at risk. “If agents take over the web, then the web will change,” he says. “Do we abandon the human internet entirely and move to a world of private Discords? Do we strip down all the information so the AIs are just talking to each other rather than having an intermediary of a website to go through?”
“We have no idea,” he says. “We’re in this very early, weird stage of the evolution.”

articles.title: From code to content: How AI could make India the world’s next story exporter
articles.text:
From code to content: How AI could make India the world’s next story exporter
Eloelo Group’s Saurabh Pandey showcased Dolphin AI, an end-to-end video production suite, and told TechSparks 2026 that falling production costs could let Indian storytellers compete for global audiences.
India spent the 1990s and 2000s becoming the back office of the world for code. At TechSparks 2026, a flagship event of YourStory, one founder asked whether the country can now do the same for stories. As AI makes video production more efficient and economical, his answer was a confident yes.
The session, titled ‘Can AI turn India into a global content export hub?’, began with the product showcase of Dolphin AI by Saurabh Pandey, Founder and CEO of Eloelo Group, and then moved into a fireside chat with Shradha Sharma, Founder and CEO of YourStory and The Bharat Project.
Why India has not yet exported its stories
Pandey noted that India has long produced standout IPs such as Baahubali, Kantara, and RRR, but has rarely been an exporter. Japan did it with anime, South Korea with K-dramas, China with micro dramas, and the US with Hollywood. Each, he said, used content to build soft power.
AI, in his view, changes the equation because the tools once available only to a few markets are now open to everyone. The opportunity also goes beyond films, to localized advertisements, commerce videos, and social media content for overseas customers.
Dolphin AI: One suite from idea to final cut
To make that case concrete, Pandey introduced Dolphin AI, Eloelo’s newest launch. The company began with live entertainment, moved into micro dramas with its Story TV app, and recently added a micro learning app called Master.
Dolphin AI targets a familiar creator hurdle: making one AI video often means stitching together clips and edits from around 20 tools. Dolphin AI replaces that with an agentic chat and a set of templates. A simple prompt can produce a full video, with the suite handling context and continuity. It also integrates with Claude and ChatGPT through MCP, helping creators build longer AI videos. A short demo reel closed the showcase.
Fireside chat: Removing the gatekeepers
When Sharma joined Pandey on stage, she reacted to the demo with pride. “This is remarkable. This is real, and this is happening in India,” she said.
The conversation first turned to adoption. Pandey said roughly 15,000 videos were created on Dolphin AI in eight days in its early access phase, entirely through organic discovery.
He then explained why this matters for storytellers. High-end visual effects once meant massive budgets, and those budgets acted as a filter on who could tell ambitious stories.
“With AI, with tools such as Dolphin AI, what we are trying to build is that you can ship content without any gatekeepers,” he said. He clarified that AI is not replacing actors but expensive locations, so a period drama no longer needs a real palace. With distribution now largely algorithmic, a storyteller in India can reach audiences in the US or Europe.
Asked why India has lagged, Pandey did not blame creativity. He compared South Korea, with 52 million people and a content export economy of about $15 billion, to India’s 1.4 billion.
“I would refuse to believe that we don’t have the creativity,” he said. In his view, technology, aspiration, distribution and capital must come together, and Indian builders have too often treated the local market as the only one that matters.
The micro drama moment
On whether micro dramas can finally work as a business in India, Pandey cited China, where the category reached roughly $8 billion in revenue last year and is now at a run rate of $10 billion to $11 billion, with a single platform earning more than China’s entire box office. In India, he said, the combined run rate of the top four or five players is north of Rs 5,000 crore, reached in about 18 months.
Production costs have been the stumbling block, historically eating up 50-60% of revenue. AI, he argued, finally fixes the supply side. “This is that quick commerce moment of entertainment,” he said.
Where the opportunity sits
Pandey expects platforms to consolidate around two or three players, as food delivery and ecommerce did. Supply, however, will stay open. Eloelo launched 200 new micro dramas last month for its microdrama platform Story TV and works with about 90 production houses, a number he sees doubling.
His advice for new entrants was to build on the supply side. Small, nimble AI studios of a few editors, promo producers and a line producer could supply platforms with micro dramas and OTT content. He urged writers and producers to treat AI as a brainstorming partner, and floated the idea of an AI-made Mahabharat.
“The next Disney or the next big IP can be built now if the right supply engine comes in because the demand is very clear,” he said.
The window to build
Pandey said Eloelo, which has grown from one platform to five, is not eyeing an IPO soon and is focused on sustainable growth while it builds for India’s global ambitions.
Sharma called his journey from a Flipkart employee to founder building for the world a reminder of what Indian aspiration can achieve. She urged the audience to tell their teams and networks that the window to build in this space is open. If India turned code into a global export, the session suggested, stories could be next.

articles.title: GPU Prices Are Spiraling Out of Control: Q4 2026 Update
articles.text:
Graphics card prices just keep rising, making the situation worse for PC gamers with every passing month. After reporting a 7% month-over-month price increase in September, we really hoped we'd have something positive to say closer to the holiday season. Even a period of price stagnation would have been nice. But no, unfortunately GPU prices have gone up once again, and we're going to explore the full impact in this latest update.
We're also going to get a good look at what's happening in the high-end GPU market amid reports of severely "constrained" RTX 5090 supply. What's the current going rate for a GeForce RTX 5090? Before we get to that data, have a guess at how bad it is and see whether you're right... With that going on, the RTX 5080 has effectively become Nvidia's top gaming option, and that's had some unfortunate impacts on pricing as well.
Similar to our previous GPU pricing updates, we have gathered data from 10 countries. The main data points are October and September prices, so we can measure the month-over-month increase, along with data from February 2026 to show how prices have risen throughout 2026.
As a reminder, the pricing data we're using is not an average for a specific GPU model. It represents the single lowest price for an available, in-stock model within each region. We use price comparison websites for each country, find the cheapest model, verify that it's actually available to purchase at that price, and include it in our charts.
Often, these prices will be for base-model cards and might only be available at one retailer. You'll likely pay more than what we're showing if you want, say, an Asus ROG Strix model instead of a Gigabyte Windforce or PNY OC. With that out of the way, let's get into the numbers.
Entry-Level GeForce Prices Keep Climbing
GeForce RTX 5050 + RTX 5060
Starting with entry-level graphics cards, the GeForce RTX 5050 has gone up significantly in the US. These cards started at $310 last month but now start at $420, a massive 35% increase. This is a bit of an outlier, though. In most other countries, prices for this rather terrible GPU have only gone up a little, keeping inflation more in check.
For example, on average across the 10 countries, the RTX 5050 sits 41% above its global MSRP, but the US price is 68% above MSRP. Sad times for those in the US.

The RTX 5060 Ti Is Getting Ridiculously Expensive

While it's not good to see a price hike like this within a single month, the 5060 Ti 8GB actually has the least amount of price inflation of any GeForce GPU, at 24% on average. That means this $380 GPU is now more like $470, a smaller dollar increase than what we're seeing with the RTX 5060.

RTX 5070 Prices Keep Climbing

Next we get to the RTX 5070, which is pretty much the same story as the other cards. On average, there's been an 8% month-over-month price increase, which is relatively consistent across each region, with the Netherlands being the outlier here.
In terms of price inflation, this model is now 48% above MSRP, taking a $550 GPU up to $814. High-End GeForce Pricing Is Absurd
GeForce RTX 5090 + RTX 5080
Now we get to the really bad stuff: the high end of the market. Reports that the RTX 5090 has effectively been discontinued, despite Nvidia's denials, have coincided with skyrocketing prices for the remaining stock. This GPU is now 32% more expensive than last month, and to be clear, it was already selling for well over $6,000 in the US last month, so that's a very significant price hike.
This makes the card 262% more expensive than it should be, at an average normalized price of $7,240. And yes, the United States is getting stung especially badly here, with 370% price inflation and a minimum cost of $9,400.

While that is a brutal price hike for Nvidia's fastest GeForce model, quite a lot of the increase happened prior to 2026, as the card was already sitting at $3,500 in February. This is why we believe the RTX 5090 was already effectively discontinued for gamers months ago, at least in terms of practical availability and pricing.
Unfortunately, the RTX 5090's effective disappearance from the gaming market has had price ramifications for the RTX 5080, which has risen to fill the gap.

This GPU is up 22% month over month, and in some regions, retailers have run out of stock entirely. Newegg had no RTX 5080s available directly from the retailer at the time of data collection, for example, leaving only expensive third-party listings. That's partially why the RTX 5080 has become 39% more expensive in the US within a single month.
This GPU is now 77% above MSRP on average, representing a $770 increase over launch pricing. This is not due to memory price increases, plain and simple. The 16GB of GDDR7 on this card has not become $700 more expensive. Other market factors are clearly at play here, potentially including price gouging, demand for AI workloads, and the lack of RTX 5090 availability.
Is a 24GB RTX 5080 Coming in 2027?
Another significant factor could be what's happening behind the scenes with this model. Rumors suggest Nvidia is planning to replace the RTX 5080 16GB with a new 24GB version in the first quarter of 2027. Essentially, the existing 16GB card would be discontinued, and the new 24GB model would take its place.
This could help explain why we're seeing limited supply at some retailers. It's possible the channel is being cleared out in preparation for the arrival of a new model, though nothing has been confirmed.
We've also heard from sources in the retail industry that the wholesale cost of RTX 5080s has increased significantly in the last few weeks, and that prices are set to rise further relative to what we're seeing right now. The situation we're seeing in the US, where the cheapest models are now $2,200, could soon become the reality worldwide, at least based on what we're hearing.
One theory is that these price hikes are intentional, designed to reset the market in preparation for the 24GB model. With an additional 8GB of GDDR7, that card would likely have a much higher MSRP than the current RTX 5080. It would also likely be more expensive than the actual retail price of the RTX 5080 throughout 2026, which, of course, has been higher than $1,000 due to the memory crisis.
Pushing up the price of existing RTX 5080s even further could make the debut price of a 24GB model seem more palatable relative to current retail prices. But we'll see how all of that plays out next year.
AMD Radeon Prices Are Rising Faster

The RX 9070 Series Is Holding Up Better
Radeon RX 9070 GRE + RX 9070 + RX 9070 XT
Next up we have the RX 9070 GRE, which launched earlier this year at an MSRP designed around the current realities of the market. Despite this, it's currently selling for 8% above MSRP on average, following a 9% month-over-month price increase.

The RX 9070 and 9070 XT have both increased in price by 12% month over month, with substantial price hikes in Canada making them less attractive in that region.

With the raw price increase of the RX 9070 XT roughly matching that of the RX 9060 XT 16GB, it looks like the RX 9070 is a little cheaper than it should be, considering it has the same 16GB of VRAM, the main component that has become more expensive this year.
Radeon vs. GeForce: The Value Gap Remains Huge
We can draw some interesting comparisons between AMD and Nvidia here. So far, it'll cost you about $200 more than it should to get a Radeon GPU with 16GB of VRAM.
But if you want 16GB on a GeForce GPU, you're faced with spending at least $300 more than MSRP for an RTX 5060 Ti 16GB, and that figure gets even higher for the faster models. Even the 12GB RTX 5070 has seen its price rise by over $260, despite having just 12GB of memory.
The gap between the RTX 5070 Ti and RX 9070 XT continues to be huge as well. The GeForce costs ~47% more right now, though that's actually slightly lower than last month's result, when the 5070 Ti was 52% more expensive.
Generally, though, for the last few months, it has cost ~50% more to grab the GeForce equivalent, which is pretty insane. Right now, the RX 9070 XT is on average the same price as the RTX 5070 across the 10 regions we examined. Our recent 52-game benchmark showed the Radeon model was 25% faster on average, and it packs more VRAM.
Intel Arc Pricing Is Rising, Too

On average, this card is 47% above MSRP, but just 36% if we exclude the UK. That makes this $250 GPU about $90 more expensive in most markets, a good indication of the impact the memory crisis is having on a card with 12GB of GDDR6.
GPU Prices Have Jumped 35% in Just Three Months
Put everything together and graphics card prices have risen by 11% month over month. That's an average of the price hikes across all 10 countries for the various gaming GPUs, and it's not a pretty picture. A 10% increase in a single month is massive, especially on the back of similar increases in prior months.
GPUs became 7% more expensive in September and 15% more expensive in August, which equates to a 35% price increase over the last three months. And unfortunately, there are no signs that graphics card prices are tapering off. In fact, various rumors and reports from retailers suggest the opposite: we haven't yet seen peak graphics card pricing.
| GPU | MSRP | Current US Price | % Increase MSRP vs Retail | Approx. Global Increase vs MSRP | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| RTX 5050 | $249 | $420 | 69% | 41% | 
| RTX 5060 | $299 | $450 | 51% | 40% | 
| RTX 5060 Ti 8GB | $379 | $530 | 40% | 24% | 
| RTX 5060 Ti 16GB | $429 | $790 | 84% | 69% | 
| RTX 5070 | $549 | $900 | 64% | 48% | 
| RTX 5070 Ti | $749 | $1,250 | 67% | 60% | 
| RTX 5080 | $999 | $2,200 | 120% | 77% | 
| RTX 5090 | $1,999 | $9,400 | 370% | 262% | 
| RX 9060 XT 8GB | $299 | $500 | 67% | 46% | 
| RX 9060 XT 16GB | $349 | $620 | 78% | 58% | 
| RX 9070 | $549 | $700 | 28% | 28% | 
| RX 9070 XT | $599 | $870 | 45% | 36% |

The market managed to keep GPU prices relatively stable throughout the first half of 2026 after an initial spike at the end of last year, but those days are over. Cards with 16GB of VRAM are now several hundred dollars more expensive, and the high end in particular is looking grim, given the situation with the RTX 5080.
Unlike previous months, Radeon GPUs actually increased in price more than GeForce this time (excluding the RTX 5090). The RX 9060 XT 16GB was stung particularly hard, but the RX 9070 XT is also up 12% and fast approaching the $1,000 mark in some regions.
What Comes Next for GPU Pricing?
There continues to be quite a significant difference in price inflation depending on the region. On average, GPU prices are 44% above MSRP, but as high as 58% above in Canada and the United States. At the opposite end of the scale, the Philippines, Brazil, and Australia are faring a bit better than average.
For regions with lower price inflation, we think what we're seeing in the US is a reflection of what's to come. Eventually, price hikes elsewhere could reach similar levels.
As for what's to come, it seems Nvidia could be preparing to introduce an RTX 5080 24GB model in early 2027, with a high expected retail price. Various rumors and reports suggest the RTX 5080 16GB will be discontinued in favor of the 24GB variant, which could become the new flagship gaming GPU.
This follows reports that the RTX 5090 has been discontinued, something Nvidia has denied, but the situation at retail, and even on Nvidia's own marketplace, suggests the card has effectively disappeared from the gaming market.
Beyond that, expect graphics card prices to remain high for a long time. It sucks big time, but the days when you could actually buy these products at MSRP are becoming a distant memory, and it doesn't look like pricing will return to those levels during this generation.

articles.title: Ivanti Patches Two More Zero-Days Exploited in Connect Secure Attack Chain
articles.text:
Ivanti has released patches for two more Connect Secure (ICS) zero-days that attackers chained with a vulnerability the company disclosed last month.
The newly patched bugs are CVE-2026-111357 and CVE-2026-118527. Ivanti added them on Thursday to its October 13 advisory describing CVE-2026-104935, an authentication bypass in the VPN product.
According to Ivanti, attacks chaining the three flaws had hit a limited number of customers by the time they were disclosed.
CVE-2026-111357, which Ivanti rates 8.8 on the CVSS scale, stems from the lack of authentication for a critical function. It enables an authenticated attacker with local access to elevate their privileges.
This is the privilege escalation zero-day for which no fix was available when the attacks came to light in mid-October.
CVE-2026-118527, with a CVSS score of 4.3, involves the generation of predictable identifiers. An authenticated attacker can exploit it remotely to upload files containing content of their choosing to a disk location that is known in advance.
The two issues impact ICS 25.1.1.2 and prior, as well as 22.8R2.5 and prior. Fixes are included in versions 25.1.1.3 and 22.8R2.6.
Versions 25.1.1.2 and 22.8R2.5 were the releases that patched CVE-2026-104935 on those branches. Organizations that installed them in response to the initial advisory will need to upgrade again.
“The latest release addresses all vulnerabilities which were chained and exploited in the wild,” Ivanti said.
The vendor noted that when it discovered the attacks, its CVE-2026-104935 fix was already going through quality assurance. Once the privilege escalation bug was identified, Ivanti chose to ship that fix without waiting, since it closed the main exploitation route.
Ivanti previously said part of the vulnerability had been found through its product security program and patched in version 25.1.3.0, released in July. The attacks took place while the company was still bringing that fix to its other supported releases.
CISA added the two newly disclosed vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on Friday. Federal agencies were given until November 2 to address CVE-2026-111357 and until November 13 for CVE-2026-118527.
CVE-2026-104935 has been in the KEV catalog since October 13.
Volexity uncovered the in-the-wild exploitation while investigating an incident at one of its customers. It attributed the activity to a previously unknown threat actor it tracks as UTA0576.
By chaining the three zero-days, the hackers obtained unauthenticated code execution with root privileges on an ICS appliance that was fully patched at the time. They primarily focused on stealing credentials, exfiltrating data, scanning the network and tampering with logs.
The security firm assesses with low confidence that UTA0576 is criminally motivated rather than an espionage group.
Volexity saw the first signs of exploitation on October 3. Threat intelligence firm Defused, however, reported that attacks it believes targeted CVE-2026-104935 hit its decoys starting October 1, before the vulnerability was made public.

articles.title: Cities Worldwide Build and Scale AI Services With NVIDIA Physical and Agentic AI
articles.text:
Cities generate enormous amounts of data from cameras, sensors and operational systems, but turning it into useful action — for planning, maintenance and public services — remains a challenge.
Physical and agentic AI offer new ways to close that gap, from digital twins for infrastructure planning to vision and service agents, while keeping local governments in control of how sensitive data is processed and used.
Building on initiatives announced at GTC Berlin, NVIDIA and its partners are expanding physical AI and AI agents to cities worldwide. Shared computing infrastructure gives city departments, neighboring municipalities and local developers a common foundation to build on — extending services without each organization having to acquire and manage resources of their own.
Agentic AI for Cities
From resident services to vision agents, cities are adopting NVIDIA agentic AI to deliver faster, more responsive public services. City teams don’t need a massive infrastructure investment to get started building these AI services: depending on the workload, NVIDIA RTX workstations or a small GPU system may be enough.
In Spain, 1MillionBot combines open source ALIA models trained at the Barcelona Supercomputing Center with NVIDIA Nemotron and other models in resident-service agents for Madrid Digital (Comunidad de Madrid), Administració Oberta de Catalunya and 150+ deployments across Spain, handling municipal procedures, appointment requests, urban-planning incidents and service inquiries.
In the San Francisco Bay Area, LiveX is bringing its AI City vision to life with NVIDIA Cosmos world models and Nemotron open models, and Omniverse and Metropolis libraries on NVIDIA RTX PRO GPUs. The interactive, conversational AI hosts understand people’s needs, provide answers and take action, and can be tailored to local languages and service needs in airports, hospitals, local events and other public spaces.
Vision AI agents can turn existing city camera feeds into operational insights, helping teams identify mobility and safety issues and coordinate emergency responses across city services.
In Wrocław, Poland, K2K is building shared AI infrastructure using NVIDIA accelerated computing, NVIDIA Cosmos world reasoning models, and NVIDIA Metropolis Blueprint for video search and summarization (VSS) to transform existing camera streams into actionable intelligence for mobility, safety and event response — using the same infrastructure across several city functions.
In Malaysia, ITMAX bundles infrastructure and agentic AI applications into long-term managed services for cities, including for traffic management. Built with reference to Cosmos, Nemotron and the Metropolis VSS blueprint, ITMAX’s SamurAI V2 vision agents are scaling on NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPUs to support 17,000+ cameras by 2027. ITMAX integrates TeraSim, an open source traffic simulation platform from Laplace Intelligence, to test signal timing, reducing peak-hour corridor travel times by up to 26%.
Plan and Operate Critical Infrastructure With Digital Twins
Beyond public-facing services, digital twins can help cities expedite infrastructure planning, minimizing disruption to local communities. City digital twins can also serve as a real-time operational simulation to facilitate faster decision-making.
At Dangote’s Lekki refinery in Nigeria, Honeywell Technologies’ Forge Plant Cognition uses Nemotron-powered AI agents to understand operational data. A digital twin of the plant and its processes, built using Omniverse libraries, is also planned to support simulation and training. The platform, built on Dell PowerEdge servers with NVIDIA RTX PRO accelerators, helps operators identify bottlenecks, anticipate equipment and process issues, and optimize plant performance.
In Taiwan, Linker Vision and Dutch architecture firm MVRDV are using NVIDIA Omniverse and Nemotron to build environmental, social and governance agents that can assess the environmental impact of various urban planning scenarios, simulating 15-year outcomes of an urban forest canopy in 10 minutes — increasing design iteration speed from two weeks per iteration to less than an hour.
Build a Broader Local AI Ecosystem
Cities can extend AI to more services by building on infrastructure already in place and adding capacity. Shared resources and managed services can help extend those capabilities across departments and municipalities.
At Morocco’s Tanger Med port, Cires Technologies is expanding a sovereign AI factory for planned applications in worker safety, congestion analysis, cargo routing and port operations. Cires Technologies is also building an ecosystem of application providers to develop local models and applications for ports and cities.
Beyond city services, Barcelona Supercomputing Center’s AI Factory Accelerator Programme gives startups access to sovereign computing, technical support and training. BSC AI Factory also supports research and innovation for startups — spanning agriculture, medical imaging, knowledge access and speech services.
Learn how NVIDIA and its ecosystem are bringing physical AI, agentic AI and local AI factories to cities worldwide at Smart City Expo World Congress, running Nov. 3-5 in Barcelona, where NVIDIA Vice President of EMEA Paolo Guglielmini will deliver a keynote address followed by a panel moderated by Charbel Aoun, director of smart city and spaces for EMEA at NVIDIA.

articles.title: OpenAI pitches data center power plants as a way to protect nearby areas
articles.text:
In an announcement on Monday, OpenAI says it will pilot its “Grid Protectors Program” at an upcoming data center in Effingham County, Georgia, where the company promises to free up to 1,000 megawatts of power during extreme weather or emergencies, enough to power air conditioners in around 700,000 homes.
OpenAI pitches data center power plants as a way to protect nearby areas
As public opinion has soured on data centers, it’s selling ‘AI campuses’ as protectors, instead of noisy polluters.
The announcement comes as opposition to data centers spreads across the US, in response to massive projects that have begun development and construction, frequently with little or no input from local residents. In Utah, residents protested after Box Elder County commissioners signed off on a data center expected to consume more than double the state’s peak electricity demand in 2025, and spread hot air in the desert valley surrounding the data center.
Now OpenAI’s approach is to pitch the construction of power plants that feed the electricity required by the new AI data centers it’s building as “a resource that utilities can call on when communities need it most.”
Several states like Tennessee, Florida, Oklahoma, Oregon, and others have enacted laws that say they will prevent AI companies from passing energy costs on to residents, in addition to moratoriums and other restrictions. This is besides the environmental impacts, as a recent study by the Houston Advanced Research Center (HARC) said that powering proposed Texas data center projects could undo decades of air quality gains over just five years.
OpenAI, which has switched to calling its AI data centers “compute campuses” in an effort to separate from their poor public reputation, claims it helps reduce costs for customers by operating year-round:
“Electricity demand also rises and falls with the seasons, with different regions facing their biggest peaks at different times,” OpenAI’s announcement says. “Our compute campuses need power year-round. With the right agreements, that steady demand can help spread the grid’s fixed costs across more electricity sales, while flexibility lets us reduce demand when the system is busiest.”
OpenAI says it’s going to continue working with policymakers and utility services to make “arrangements for our future campus to reduce electricity demand when the grid is under strain.” Along with its data center in Georgia, OpenAI is also partnering with Oracle and SoftBank to build its “Stargate” data centers across the US, including in Shackelford County, Texas; Doña Ana County, New Mexico; and Milam County, Texas.

articles.title: Votre PS5 ou Xbox est rachetée à prix d'or chez Micromania : l’effet GTA 6
articles.text:
À moins de trois semaines de la sortie de GTA 6, les consoles qui pourront le faire tourner se revendent presque au prix du neuf. Depuis ce lundi 2 novembre et jusqu’au 16 novembre, Micromania reprend une PS5 Slim 475 €, une Xbox Series X 500 € et une PS5 Pro avec lecteur 730 €, en espèces comme en avoir, sans avoir besoin d’acheter une console en même temps. Ces deux familles de consoles sont les seules sur lesquelles GTA 6 sortira le 19 novembre.
Le prix de rachat en cash des consoles s’envole
La reprise boostée de Micromania ne concerne que les PS5 et les Xbox Series.
Surtout, l’enseigne supprime la décote habituelle de 15 % sur les reprises en espèces : vous touchez le même montant, que vous repartiez avec des billets ou avec un avoir. Les tableaux ci-dessous comparent cette grille à celle de l’opération de juillet relayée par nos confrères de Xboxygen.
PS5 et PS5 Pro
| Console reprise | Juillet 2026 (avoir / espèces) | Novembre 2026 (espèces ou avoir) | 
|---|---|---|
| PS5 Pro avec lecteur | 650 € / 563 € | 730 € | 
| PS5 Pro | 600 € / 516,75 € | 700 € | 
| PS5 Slim | 450 € / 393 € | 475 € | 
| PS5 Slim Digitale | 400 € / 350,50 € | 425 € | 
| PS5 (premier modèle) | 400 € / 349 € | 425 € | 
| PS5 Digitale (premier modèle) | 350 € / 305 € | 375 € | 
La PS5 Pro fait le plus gros bond. Reprise 600 € en juillet, elle en vaut désormais 700 €, à peine 200 € de moins que son prix neuf. Le reste de la gamme progresse aussi, de 25 € en moyenne. Concrètement, la PS5 Slim qui prend la poussière sous votre télé vaut encore près des trois quarts de son prix neuf. Et si vous comptiez passer à la Pro pour GTA 6, cette reprise la fait tomber à 424,99 €, à condition d’en trouver une en magasin.
Xbox Series
| Console reprise | Juillet 2026 (avoir / espèces) | Novembre 2026 (espèces ou avoir) | 
|---|---|---|
| Xbox Series X | 300 € / 255 € | 500 € | 
| Xbox Series X Digitale | 290 € / 246,50 € | 475 € | 
| Xbox Series S 1 To | 165 € / 140,25 € | 320 € | 
| Xbox Series S 500 Go | 150 € / 127,50 € | 285 € | 
Chez Microsoft, la hausse est encore plus forte. La Xbox Series X gagne 200 € par rapport à juillet et passe devant la PS5 Slim, avec 25 € de plus. La Series S double presque sa valeur de reprise. En espèces, une Series X rapporte aujourd’hui près du double de ce qu’elle valait cet été.
La Switch reste en dehors de l’opération. Pour en tirer un meilleur prix, il faut passer par l’offre liée à l’achat d’une Switch 2 neuve, valable elle aussi jusqu’au 16 novembre. La logique est la même chez Nintendo : le remake de Zelda Ocarina of Time servira de déclencheur pour faire passer les joueuses et les joueurs de la Switch à la Switch 2.
Un marché où la demande dépasse l’offre
Si les montants de reprise grimpent, c’est que le neuf est devenu plus cher et plus rare, ce qui pousse aussi le marché de l’occasion à augmenter ses prix. La flambée du prix de la mémoire vive a poussé Sony et Microsoft à relever leurs tarifs à plusieurs reprises. La PS5 Pro, la plus chère, est aussi la plus difficile à trouver. Elle se raréfiait déjà après la présentation du jeu de Rockstar sur Netflix fin août, et elle est aujourd’hui en rupture sur PlayStation Direct, la boutique officielle de Sony.
Résultat, les consoles de cette génération ne perdent presque plus de valeur, et les grilles de reprise le montrent depuis des mois. En mai déjà, Micromania proposait d’échanger une Xbox Series X contre… une Xbox Series X, moyennant 230 €, signe d’un marché devenu incontrôlable. L’enseigne applique aujourd’hui le même raisonnement dans l’autre sens : si une console d’occasion vaut presque le prix du neuf, elle se reprend aussi à ce prix-là. La Xbox Series X est le cas d’école parfait : il y a un an, Micromania la reprenait 280 €, elle vaut aujourd’hui 500 €…
GTA 6 arrive sur un marché déjà sous tension. Le jeu de Rockstar sort le 19 novembre uniquement sur PS5 et Xbox Series, et sans version PC au lancement. Le constructeur assure avoir sécurisé assez de consoles pour 2026, mais plusieurs distributeurs manquent déjà de stock, et rien de ne garantit des réassorts avant les fêtes.
L’opération s’arrête le 16 novembre, trois jours avant la sortie du jeu. Les consoles reprises viendront ensuite regarnir les rayons occasion de Micromania, au moment où GTA 6 et les achats de Noël feront grimper la demande.
